editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: PROLOGUE. One might say of me, aptly enough and in mockery, that for me the by-work is greater than the work itself. For in truth I ought long ago, having let go of public affairs and withdrawn from their turmoil, having departed from the midst of the world and chosen to live by myself, and having sentenced myself to a perpetual exile—since He who is above us has so arranged our circumstances, when He broke the bonds that held me and deprived me of those most dear, by reasons known to Himself, painful indeed to me but in every way for my benefit—I ought, I say, to have pursued nothing else but those things that set the soul in order and cleanse it of the defilements that have sunk into it through the baseness of its deeds, the things by which the Divine is reconciled, against whom I have provoked anger by transgressing His commandments and ordinances, and to have sought in this way pardon for my faults. Yet I, disposed toward the work negligently out of my sluggishness toward what is good, have strained my zeal upon the by-work instead.

But, that I may also say something in my own defense, it was not of my own impulse that I set out upon the undertaking; rather, friends spurred me to it, seeing me at leisure and saying, "Use your leisure for a work of common benefit, and from this too a recompense shall be laid up for you with God." For they pressed upon me the example of those who labored over histories and recorded events of long ago. Some of these wrote out at greater length the various deeds of the men of old and their stratagems, narrating battle-lines and the clashes of armies, encampments and palisades and whatever follows upon these; and besides this, descriptions of regions and the difficult passages of roads, steep and impassable mountains, the narrows of ravines, the strength of cities, and the lofty—one might almost say ethereal—heights of towers. Others composed their writings for display, showing off what power they had in writing, and for this reason inserting public speeches and using language in a more digressive or more rhetorical manner. In some, ambition ended even in dialogues, so that whenever they wrote against certain men who held false opinions and erred concerning correct doctrines, they would compose discourses against them as though they were present, and refute their wrong belief, drawing their proofs from Holy Scripture; or again they would argue against the Jews and show them to be willfully obstinate in not receiving our mystery, and would make use of prophetic testimonies; and again they would set themselves against the Greeks, bringing their nonsense into the open, mocking the myths they tell, and producing their own writings as a refutation of their false belief; and in some places they would offer maxims and moral reflection. "But these things," they said, "the greater part of those who read the writings of those histories—not to say all—consider burdensome and superfluous, both because they require more leisure, and because, even if some who take up the histories should obtain that leisure, their labor over them turns out to be in vain, since the long narratives about battle-lines and wars and the array of armies and the rest of such matters slip from the memory, while the public speeches and discourses come to nothing useful for those who take up the history. For what profit," they said, "will anyone have from knowing what this popular leader said to the people, what this general said to his soldiers, or what that emperor said to the envoys from the Persians, or another to those from the Celts or Scythians, or to those from Egypt perhaps, or to those from the Dacians and Triballians, or what someone else said in addressing the Senate or the common multitude?" They said, then, that some had published their historical writings of this kind—expanded, that is, and inclining toward the more ambitious manner—while others had set themselves to the writing of histories in the opposite way, using such brevity that they thereby did harm in the essential matters to those who had labored over their own works, since they passed over the very weightiest of the deeds of the men whose history they told—some of whom even deserved to be celebrated—and said only the briefest things about them, things that revealed neither their character nor their nature and purpose, nor how each of the kings came to hold his kingship, nor who reigned before him, nor from whom he was descended. They added, too, that some of these writings had been published in a style far too plain, and were set forth in vulgar or sometimes even barbarous expressions, and composed with too many solecisms, so that those acquainted with eloquence found them distasteful. Saying such things, and faulting the historical writings in the way described, they often urged me to take the books in hand, and—passing over the greater part of them, of which some, owing to their bulk, are by nature unfit to settle in the memory, while others end in nothing profitable—to cut down the expanded narrative and publish a concise history, teaching in a summary fashion those who take up the work the more essential of the things done, or otherwise come to pass, by those of whom the writing treats.
These men, then, urged me to gird myself for such a labor and to lay hold of such a work;

THE BEGINNING OF THE FIRST BOOK, STARTING FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE CREATION OF THE WORLD. God is a Nature that lacks nothing, sufficient unto Himself for glory and for knowledge, neither needing glory from others nor comprehensible by another—unless one were to say that what is comprehensible about Him is His infinity and His incomprehensibility. And when I say God I mean Father and Son and Holy Spirit, which is the Godhead, according to the great father and theologian Gregory. The Divine, being thus, first gives substance to the angelic powers and the heavenly ministers and singers of the splendor above—not as needing them, but so that He might not be moved by the contemplation of Himself alone, but that the good might be poured out and make its way, and the benefaction extend to more; for this was the mark of the highest goodness. Then He also brings into being this material and visible world. And in the beginning He made the heaven and the earth. And while the earth was hidden in invisibility, since there was also darkness, and water lay upon its surface, God brought forth the light. And He separated the light and the darkness, and the light He called day, and the darkness He named night; to the beginning of the latter He gave the name evening, and to the first shining of the day the name morning. And there was evening, and there was morning, one day. Now I know that it is written in the Lesser Genesis that on the first day the heavenly powers too were given substance before the rest by the Maker of all things; but since this Lesser Genesis is not numbered among the books of Hebrew wisdom approved by the divine fathers, I reckon nothing of what is written in it to be certain, nor do I assent to its account. Then He established the firmament, stretching it out in the midst of the waters, so that the waters above it were held off, while those below were poured around the earth. It was called the firmament because its body is solid and does not have a thin or rarefied nature like the waters out of which it took its composition; and this was also named heaven. These things came to pass on the second day. On the third, God commanded the water that covered the whole face of the earth to be gathered together, and the dry land to appear. And the word became deed, and deep hollows came to be and received the waters. And the dry land He named earth, and the gatherings of the waters He named seas. On this same day plants and seeds were sent up from the earth; for it was needful that the earth, being unadorned, should be adorned with grasses and the countless growing things and the flowers and fruits of every kind and the graces of the trees. The fourth day had the coming-to-be of the luminaries, the sun and the moon and the rest of the stars. With these the Maker made the heaven resplendent, and He placed in these luminaries the light that had been brought forth on the first day, ordaining for them their motions and risings and courses and settings, so that through them the region of the earth might be lit and time might be numbered by their risings and settings, and so that they might furnish signs through these to those who attend most rightly to their shinings—and not to those who scrutinize them too curiously, or who, as one might say (to put it exactly), foolishly imagine that all our affairs are carried along together with the motion of the heavenly bodies. On the fifth of the days, again, when God commanded, the waters sent up the creeping things of living souls and the birds; of which some dwell in the waters and swim in them, while the birds cleave the air, creeping, as it were, aloft through it. On the sixth, the earth was commanded to bring forth the living soul—four-footed beasts and creeping things and wild animals—and according to the divine command all of these were brought forth. Now Scripture states that the earth was commanded to make the bringing-forth of the living soul, so that in this way it might show the difference of the soul of man from it. For the soul of the other living creatures grew up from the earth according to the command, and being earthy might reasonably be reckoned also perishable, since elsewhere too the Scripture says, "the soul of every beast is its

David had just returned from the slaughter of the foreigners when a man came to him bringing word of the defeat of the Israelites and the death of Saul and Jonathan. When David questioned him as to whether his report was true, the man said that Saul had been mortally wounded and, being too weak to take his own life, had begged him to lay the blow upon him as he fell upon his own sword, so that he might not be taken alive by the enemy; and that he had done as he was commanded and dispatched the king. To confirm his words he held out the royal crown from Saul's head and the gold from his arms, and offered them to David. David, then, and those with him mourned for Saul and Jonathan, but the man who had killed Saul he punished, because he had laid his hand upon the Lord's anointed. After this, at God's command, he went up to Hebron, a city of Judah, together with both his wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, and the men with him with all their households; and there he was chosen king by the tribe of Judah. David blessed the men of Jabesh for having buried the bodies of Saul and Jonathan.

But Abner, Saul's commander-in-chief, took the surviving son of his lord, Ishbosheth, and proclaimed him king over all Israel, apart from Judah. Ishbosheth was forty years old when he became king, and he held the kingship for two years. Abner was angry with the tribe of Judah for having made David king, and he marched against it. Joab, who was David's commander-in-chief, met him with a force. First twelve men from each army fought in single combat; and when all of these had fallen, the two armies engaged each other, and Abner's men were defeated. Abishai and Asahel were brothers of Joab. Asahel, who prided himself on the swiftness of his feet, pursued Abner from behind. Abner urged him to turn back, but when he could not persuade him, he struck him from behind and killed him with a mortal blow. The dead man's kinsmen, enraged at the slaying of their brother, pursued Abner. But he, standing on the top of one of the hills, cried out to Joab, saying, "Do not goad men of one nation into battle; for Asahel too was at fault in not heeding my advice to turn back, and from this he has been wounded and has died." Joab, taking these words as an appeal, ordered the trumpet to sound the recall and halted the pursuit. From that time civil war took its beginning among the Hebrews, and it continued for a very long while, with David's side growing stronger and Saul's side growing weaker.

To David, while he was in Hebron, there were born from different wives six sons, of whom the firstborn was Amnon. When Abner had lain with a concubine of Saul, Ishbosheth was indignant with him on account of his father's concubine. This became the cause of Abner's going over to David. David, sending to Ishbosheth, demanded his own wife Michal. Ishbosheth tore her away from the husband to whom Saul, after David's flight, had given her in marriage, and sent her to David. Then Abner, after conferring with the elders of the multitude of the Israelites and with the captains, persuaded them to go over to David, this being also the eager wish of all. Having done this, he came to David to receive sworn pledges. And when he had been gladly received, he departed to gather the multitude together, so that David might be proclaimed by all. But Joab, coming to Hebron and learning what concerned Abner, and fearing that he would surpass him, spoke much against the man to David; and when he could not persuade him, he sent secretly the man who should summon Abner as if from David, and Abner turned back. Joab, meeting him and pretending to confer with him on some more private matter, led him away from his own men and killed him, striking him with a sword beneath the flank. When David learned of this he grieved greatly, and cursed the man who had killed him, and mourned the dead and buried him with all honour. Ishbosheth, a little later, was treacherously slain while he slept. And those who killed him, being two men, took his head and brought it to David. But he not only judged that the men had done him no favour, but ordered that they be put to death, exacting the penalty for the murder. Then all Israel went to David, and they anointed him king over all the tribes. David was thirty years old when he became king over Judah, and he ruled in Hebron over the tribe of Judah alone for seven years, and over all Israel for thirty-three.

Nebuzaradan, having razed Jerusalem, conveyed to Babylon the people and the high priest Saraeas and the sacred vessels. Nabuchodonosor dedicated the vessels of God to his own gods, and settled the captives in his own country. Those who during the siege had deserted to the Babylonians, and the poor, Nebuzaradan left behind in Judaea, and set over them as governor Godolias, a man of good family, fair and just, and charged them to work the land and ordered them to pay tribute to Nabuchodonosor. The prophet Jeremiah he urged to go off to Babylon; but he wished to remain among the ruins of his homeland. And he left him there, charging Godolias to take all care of him. He released to him also his disciple Baruch, who was exceptionally learned in the ancestral tongue. As many as had fled from Jerusalem on account of the siege came to Godolias. And he counselled them to farm the land and to dwell in whatever city each one wished, and to rebuild the ruins. Recognizing Godolias to be a worthy man, they loved him greatly.

There returned with the others also one named Ishmael, who was of the royal line, who had fled to the Ammonites at the time of the siege. When he came to Godolias, certain men said that he was plotting against him; and if he would allow them to kill the man, he would escape the plot. But Godolias would not believe it, and said he counted it better to die himself than to kill a man who had trusted himself to him. After a time this Ishmael came with others to Godolias, and being entertained as a guest he killed both Godolias and those feasting with him. Then, falling upon by night the Babylonians left in the city, he killed both them and all the Jews there. On the next day, when eighty men from the country came to Godolias with gifts, Ishmael killed these too, save a few who promised to show him household goods and clothing and grain hidden in the fields. And taking many captives with him, he went off to the Ammonites. Learning this, certain leaders of the Jews, having spurred on those with them, pursued him; and they recovered the captives, but Ishmael with eight men escaped.

The survivors, fearing the Babylonians, deliberated about going off to Egypt. Though Jeremiah counselled them to remain—for if they remained, the deity would provide that they suffer no harm, but if they departed, would not be with them—they did not believe him, but disobeying they set out for Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them. When the prophet had gone there, the deity revealed to him what was to come. And he foretold to his countrymen that the Babylonian would march against the Egyptians and master Egypt, and that he would kill some of them and lead the rest off as spear-won captives. For this he was stoned by his fellow-countrymen and died. But the things he had foretold came to pass; for the fifth year after the sack of Jerusalem was being completed when Nabuchodonosor set out against Coele-Syria, and having taken it he came against the Ammonites and Moabites, and from there marched against Egypt, and subduing it killed the king and set up another in his place, and removed the Jews there to Babylon. When Jeremiah had been buried in Egypt, it is said that king Alexander, having become master of Egypt, since the Egyptians sang the prophet's praises, removed his bones, along with other things, to the city founded by him, Alexandria.

The prophet, then, foretold, as I have said, the things that were to come; and the race of the Hebrews found such an end, removed beyond the Euphrates. For the ten tribes, while Hoshea reigned in Samaria, were taken captive by the Assyrians, and the two tribes afterward were taken spear-won by Nabuchodonosor, and all who were left after the capture of Jerusalem. And Shalmaneser removed the nation of the Cuthaeans from Persia to Samaria, while Nabuchodonosor left Judaea desolate, and it remained thus for seventy years. The time between the captivity of the ten tribes from Samaria and that of the two from Jerusalem came to a hundred and thirty years, six months, and ten days.

but I, being relaxed in my disposition—for the truth shall be told—and living at my ease, and also seeing that the matter required leisure free from other concerns and many books, hesitated and shrank back from the undertaking. Yet those who prodded me did not let up, and at last, by the persistence of their proddings, they roused me to the work. For if the steady dripping of a drop can hollow out the hardness and obduracy of a rock, much more can a steady word, knocking at the ears, rouse the ease of a relaxed disposition and a slackened purpose. Then, too, it came into my mind that the labor and the occupation of writing would not be without gain even for the benefit of the soul. For upon a mind at rest the breath of wickedness is more apt to blow, stirring up surges now of base notions and now of shifting thoughts, and to overwhelm it by the continual succession of assaults, and either to make it slip toward sin—if not in deeds, then at least in consents—or, for the time being, to swell up against it a great storm and turmoil. But if the mind is occupied with something, it for the most part escapes the towering waves that come from the multitude of thoughts and from wicked notions. So then, both because of the spurring on from my friends and for the warding off of foul or vain thoughts, I applied myself to the task.

In this way, then, it came about that I set my hand to the present work. But if I do not make the account of each of the things recorded a precise one, I ask those who come upon it to grant me pardon. For perhaps I shall not have at hand as many books as are needful to me for the work, since I am now passing my time in this remote place; nor have all the writers of histories recorded the same things about the same matters, but they disagree in many points, if not indeed in most. And if I should wish to be precise about each of the things related, and to set out what this writer says about this matter and what another says about the same, I too would make my treatment of each thing run to many lines. For these reasons I have resolved to pass over the points on which those who wrote about the same matters contradict one another, unless some matter be of the very greatest importance and such that, if it were left out, it would do harm to the essential parts of the writing. And if the character of the style varies and is not throughout consistent with itself, let no one wonder, nor blame the work or me, its father. For having gathered the histories from many books, in many places I shall use the compositions and expressions of those writers, while in whatever places I myself paraphrase or recast, I shall adapt the form of my own style to their character, so that the writing may not seem out of tune with itself.

blood," and blood is in every way perishable. But the soul of man the earth did not send up; rather, the Divine put it into Adam as an in-breathing; and for this reason it is believed to be something divine and immortal.

The sixth of the days had also the man, fashioned by the hand of God. For the supreme Artist, having first established all things and brought forth the world in order and rhythm—wherefore it is also named "cosmos"—and having prepared it beforehand as a palace for the reception of a king, then brings forth the man himself, as a kind of king over the things on earth, ruled from above; and Him He did not establish by a mere command, but fashioned with His hands, making his creation not like that of the others, but distinct and incomparable. For all the rest were brought forth by a word, but man was deemed worthy of God's own handiwork. For "having taken dust from the earth," the book of Genesis says, "God formed the man, and breathed into him a living soul," through which man is also said to have come to be in the image of God. For certain of the things that belong essentially to the divine Nature are imaged in the soul of man—not present in it by nature, but by grace. For by nature the Divine is invisible and immortal, incomprehensible and incorruptible; and these belong to the soul too by grace, not by nature, for neither is its nature and substance comprehensible nor indeed visible, and it is incorruptible and immortal. And other distinguishing marks of the divine Nature have been observed in the soul by grace. The one fashioned He named Adam, which in the Hebrew tongue means "red," as Josephus says, because he had been fashioned out of red earth; for such is the virgin earth. Having thus brought forth the world in six days, on the seventh He rested; wherefore among the Hebrews the seventh of the days is held to be a day without work, whence it is also called the Sabbath; and "Sabbath" in the tongue of the Hebrews means "rest."

And God placed Adam in the paradise that He Himself had planted, where there was the tree of life and the tree of knowledge—or, according to Josephus, of understanding. And He commanded him to enjoy the rest, but to abstain from the tree of knowledge, and He foretold that death would be the penalty of transgression. The paradise is watered by a river, and from there this river goes forth, divided into four. The name of the one is Pishon, which means "multitude"; among the Greeks this is named the Ganges, which traverses India and empties into the sea. The second is called Gihon; the name signifies the one that empties from the east, which Josephus says the Greeks call the Nile. After this is the Tigris, which the same writer says is also called Diglath, the name conveying what is sharp together with narrowness. The remaining one is the Euphrates, that is, Phora—either "flower" or "dispersion." And both of these flow into the Red Sea. And God presented all the animals to Adam, who set a name upon each kind of them. And God created the woman, taking one of the ribs of Adam while he slept, and brought her to him. And he recognized her as having come from himself, and named her woman; for among the Hebrews woman is called "Eve," and she had been named Eve. There was, then, a blessed way of life for the two of them in paradise, since they were naked in their simplicity and lived an artless life. But they are envied by the serpent, or rather by the intelligible dragon. And the serpent approaches the woman and counsels her to taste of the plant of understanding. (Josephus says that at that time all the animals spoke the same language.) And she is persuaded, and being pleased with the eating, she persuades her husband too to share in the fruit. And they knew themselves to be naked, and out of fig leaves they made themselves girdles, and Adam and the woman hid themselves from God because of their nakedness. And God asked the reason, and Adam put forward his nakedness and fastened the blame upon the woman; and she said she had been deceived by the serpent. And God, having first cursed the serpent and deprived it of feet and taken away its voice (according to Josephus), and commanded it to crawl upon the ground, and declared it an enemy to the seed of those who had been deceived, turns to the woman, and makes her subject to her husband, and lays upon her the pangs of childbearing. Then He brings Adam too under a penalty; and this was his being turned back toward the earth from which he was taken, and the eating of his bread in sweat, and the earth's sending up thorns and thistles for him. And He removes them from paradise, clothing them in garments of skin—perhaps the coarser, mortal, and resistant flesh. From this comes our wretched and painful life, and our proneness to slip into evil.

He set out from Hebron, he and those with him, and came to Jerusalem. At that time the city and that land were inhabited by the Jebusites, from whom the city was called Jebus; and they were related by descent to the Canaanites. They, setting the blind and the lame and others maimed upon the battlements by way of mockery, said that even these would not yield to David the entrance into the city. Angered at this, David took the city by siege, and having driven out the Jebusites from it and rebuilt it, he named it after himself the City of David, though in the time of Abraham it had been called Salem. And he dwelt in it, having built himself a palace. Still more children were born to him from many wives and concubines. The foreigners marched against David, but he, with God's assent, went out against them with his own army and conquered. Then they gathered in far greater numbers and came on again. When David again inquired of God, God commanded him to encamp with his army in the groves of the Place of Weeping, and not to attack the enemy until the groves should begin to shake. Doing so, he routed the enemy, and pursuing them to their own borders, slaughtered them. After this David summoned the priests and Levites and all the people to Kiriath-jearim. And the priests set the ark of the Lord upon a new cart, bringing it down to Jerusalem. The people and the king went singing before it as they marched. When the ark was in danger of overturning, Uzzah the son of Abinadab stretched out his hand and held it fast and steadied it so that it should not fall. He died at once, God being angered because he had touched the ark, since he was not a consecrated priest; and from this that place was called the Breach. David was afraid to bring the ark into the city, and set it in the house of Obed-edom, a man of the Levites; and it remained there three months, and the house of that man profited from much good. When David heard of this he brought the ark from there into his own city, seven choirs going before. He himself played upon the harp and danced in his rejoicing. But his wife Michal, seeing him dancing and leaping, reproached him as behaving unbecomingly; but he said that he felt no shame, since these acts, being done before God, were no unseemliness. They brought in the ark and set it in the tent that David had pitched for it. Then he wished to build a house for the ark. But God commanded the prophet Nathan to say to David, "You shall not build me a house, but your son, who after your death will succeed to your kingdom." When the prophet had reported this to David, he turned to giving thanks. After this he struck the foreigners and overcame them and their allies, and made Syria tributary, setting a garrison in Damascus. And on his return he struck Idumaea, and all the Idumaeans became servants to David. Remembering his covenant with Jonathan the son of Saul, David sought whether anyone of Saul's family was left; and learning that there survived a son of Jonathan, lamed in his feet, called Mephibosheth, he summoned him and gave the man all his grandfather's property, and commanded that he should always share his table, and assigned him his ancestral servants. To one of these, called Ziba, he entrusted the management of what had been given to his master, and the bringing in of the profit from it. And Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem and dined with the king.

The Babylonian made eunuchs of the more nobly born of the captive children, both those related to king Zedekiah and the more vigorous and comely of the rest, and handing them over to tutors he had them taught both the letters of the Chaldaeans and the native lore, assigning them their diet from his own table. Four of the children were of the royal stock, fair in appearance and good in their natures; of whom the Babylonian renamed the one called Daniel Baltasar, the one named Ananias he called Shadrach, the other called Mishael Meshach, and the remaining one, Azarias, Abednego. These he held in greater honour than the rest, since through their natural gifts they advanced in wisdom. These youths, then, begged the eunuch who had charge of them not to feed them on what was provided from the royal table, but on pulse and dates and other such things. He said he feared that, fed on such fare, their bodies might grow thin, and that on this account he himself might be ill-treated by the king. But they begged him to feed them thus for ten days, and if their bodily condition was not changed, to feed them so for the future too, but if he saw their bodies wasting, to keep to the former diet. The one in charge of the children was persuaded by this, and having done so, when he saw that they suffered nothing from such food—but rather had become more flourishing than the rest—he gave them lifeless foods. And they, with their minds made keen, mastered all Chaldaean and Assyrian learning. And Daniel devoted his zeal also to the interpretation of dreams.

Then Nabuchodonosor, having beheld an extraordinary dream, and having learned its interpretation in his sleep, forgot both the dream and its interpretation. At dawn, therefore, summoning the Chaldaeans and the seers and magi, he demanded of them that they tell him both the dream and its meaning. But they wished him first to tell the dream, and so to ask from them its significance. The king was angered at this and condemned them all to death, when they said they could not discover the dream. With these, as being wise men, Daniel and the three children were both summoned and condemned. Daniel therefore went to the commander of the king's bodyguard, and asked that the execution of those condemned be put off for one night; "for perhaps," he said, "during it we shall beg of God and learn the dream." The king yielded to the request. And Daniel, taking with him his three kinsmen children, supplicated God through the night. There was therefore revealed to him from God both the dream and what it signified. And after a day he went off to the king and said that both the dream and its interpretation had been made known to him from God, who had pitied those in danger of dying unjustly for it; "and no less you too, who wished without cause to kill so many for demanding what is impossible, things knowable to the divine nature alone. What you saw is this. You seemed to see a great statue standing, whose head was of gold, but whose shoulders and arms were of silver, while the belly with the thighs was of bronze, and the shins and the feet were partly of iron and partly of clay. Then a stone, broken off from a mountain, seemed to fall upon the statue and shatter it, and to grind the gold and the silver and the bronze and the iron and the clay so fine that they were winnowed away by the wind and scattered. And the stone seemed to grow and to come to so great a size that the whole earth was filled by it. This, then, is your dream; and what is revealed to you by it, as you take thought concerning the kingdom and who will rule after you, is this. The golden head is both you and the remaining kings of the Babylonians, and the gold indicates the great prosperity of your rule; the two hands and the shoulders represent two kingdoms by which your dominion will be destroyed; the bronze belly and the like thighs indicate a king clad in bronze, who will overthrow those who destroyed you; and his kingdom in turn another, more powerful, will bring to an end; for iron is stronger than gold and silver and bronze." For gold, and especially the purest, is softer than silver; and silver is denser than gold, but softer than bronze; and iron again is firmer than bronze. The kingdom of the Assyrians, then, is likened to the head, as being earlier than the others and leading in time. The second he called the kingdom of the Medes and Persians, who destroyed the rule of the Assyrians. For Cyrus, as will be related, was a Persian on his father's side, but related to the Medes through his mother; he, taking both nations together and making war on the Assyrians, overthrew their kingdom. By the pair of the hands the pair of these two nations is represented. The third kingdom he calls that of the Macedonians. This he likened to bronze as being stronger, inasmuch as it overthrew the Persian rule. And by the belly the monarchy of Alexander is figured, and by the thighs the division of the kingdom after his death and its parceling out. The fourth kingdom he called that of the Romans, to which he assigned iron because of its hardness. He figured it by the shins because it was later in time; for the kingdom of the Romans was later than the other great kingdoms, and the shins and the feet are the last parts of the body. The clay mixed with the iron hints that the kingdom is strong, but has in itself something brittle and weak; for such is the nature of clay, composed of mud.

But before the history let it be said, in a more summary way, what the things to be related are, so that those who come upon the work may know that they will gain knowledge of many histories, and those the most necessary. This epitome comprises, then, the Octateuch and all that is recorded in it; the books of Kingdoms are included along with it, and besides these the Chronicles, and whatever the Hebrew Josephus said in his antiquarian work beyond the older writers, or whatever he related in a more digressive way or otherwise differently from them; and the matters concerning Ezra, and the captivities of the Hebrews—the earlier one, that of the ten tribes, which came about through the Assyrian Shalmaneser, who took Samaria by siege, led the nation captive, brought it across the Euphrates and settled it there, and removed into Samaria certain nations who were called Cuthaeans—then the captivity brought upon Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, and how the city became desolate and the temple was burned and the whole nation was enslaved, and how, after seventy years, according to the predictions of the prophets, it was granted to the people by Cyrus, who had overthrown the kingdom of the Assyrians, to return to Jerusalem, to raise up the city and to restore the temple; and who Cyrus was, and how he overthrew the kingdom of the Assyrians, and who reigned after him; and how, and by whom, the building of the city was hindered, and by whom in turn its raising up was permitted; and concerning the prophet Daniel, and how he interpreted the dreams of Nebuchadnezzar and the vision of Belshazzar, when that barbarian saw the joint of a hand writing upon the wall, and concerning certain of the prophet's visions, all of which are recorded with a concise interpretation; and concerning the three youths and the extraordinary things done by God to them or through them; and concerning Esther, and how she delivered the race of the Hebrews from utter destruction; and concerning Judith, who by her cunning slew Holofernes and gave over his army to ruin; and concerning Tobit, and how, smitten with blindness and driven from prosperity into bitter poverty, he again, on account of his good deeds, by the providence of God obtained the power to see and came to have abundance of wealth. But the affairs of Alexander the Macedonian are also abridged here, the history being obliged to make mention of him as well, both for other reasons and because, after Darius's first defeat at Issus, he came to Jerusalem and honored the high priest exceedingly, and how he overthrew the kingdom of the Persians and made it subject to himself, and how long he reigned, and how, when he died, his kingdom was divided into four governments; and all that came upon the Jews from Antiochus Epiphanes, who happened to be a descendant of one of Alexander's successors; and how the Hasmoneans resisted him and rescued their countrymen from his tyranny, and who these men were, and how, and for how long, they presided over their own people; and how, after the return to Jerusalem from the captivity under the Assyrians, the nation of the Jews was not ruled by a king but governed by the high priests, and how the descendants of the aforesaid Hasmoneans, while invested with the high-priestly office and directing the affairs of the nation, also set a diadem upon themselves; and how, when the brothers Hyrcanus and Aristobulus were at variance over the kingdom of Judaea, Pompey the Great, then commanding the Romans, having been summoned to arbitrate between the kinsmen, took the city of Jerusalem and subjected the nation to the Romans; and how Herod, the son of Antipater, afterward came to hold the kingdom of the Jews, and who this man was and from where he was descended, and all that befell him in his household, and for how long those descended from him held the kingdom; and in what manner and from what time governors were sent from Rome to Judaea; and all that Josephus wrote concerning our Savior Jesus Christ, and indeed concerning John the Baptist also; and for what reasons the Jews revolted from submission to the Romans, and how their nation was warred upon by the Romans, and by whom and how Jerusalem was sacked—that last sacking from which it found no recall.

Children, then, are born to them, of whom Cain was the first—the name means "possession," because they had gained possession of a man—and Abel was the second; the name signifies "mourning," for through him mourning was to come upon them. And Abel was a herdsman of a flock and gave heed to virtue, while Cain tilled the earth and was utterly wicked. When it seemed good to them to bring firstfruits from their own labors to God, Abel offered the better of the firstborn of his beasts, while Cain offered whatever came to hand of the fruits of the earth. And God gave heed to the gifts of Abel, but to the offering of Cain He did not give heed. And he, envying because of the preference, kills his brother, and becomes accursed before God, and is condemned to groan and to tremble. And being cast out from the presence of God, he dwelt in the land of Nod, where he also begot children. This man devised measures and weights and was the first to fix boundaries of land, having proved himself a guide to wickedness. And he built a city after the name of his firstborn son, Enoch. The son of Enoch was Gaidad, and his child was Maviael, whose son was Methuselah, whose son was Lamech. This man, having taken to himself two wives, who were named Adah and Zillah, had from both of them seventy-seven children; of whom Jabal was a herdsman of cattle and loved the keeping of sheep, while Jubal devised music and contrived the lyre and the psaltery, and Tubal, born of Zillah, was a smith, that is, a worker of iron and bronze. And to Adam, after the death of Abel, when he was two hundred and thirty years old, another son was born, whom he called Seth. And Adam died, having lived nine hundred and thirty years. And Seth, when he was two hundred and five years old, begot Enos, who first hoped to call upon the name of the Lord God—that is, to address the Lord as God. And Seth, having lived in all nine hundred and twelve years, and having left sons and daughters, departed. He pursued virtue and left behind his descendants as imitators of it; and they understood the wisdom concerning the heavenly bodies, and they inscribed their discoveries upon two pillars, the one made of stones and the other of brick, so that they might be preserved for those who came after; for Adam had foretold that there would be a destruction of all things by fire and by water. And from Enos was born Kenan, and other sons and daughters, and he died, having lived nine hundred and five years. And from Kenan there sprang Mahalalel and other children, and he died, having lived a count of nine hundred and ten years. The son of Mahalalel was Jared, and others, who ended his life at eight hundred and ninety-five years. Jared was the father of Enoch and of other children after him, and he died, having lived nine hundred and sixty-two years. The son of Enoch was Methuselah, and others. And Enoch pleased the Lord and was translated and was not found, having been three hundred and sixty-five years old. The son of Methuselah was Lamech, and others, and he dies, having lived nine hundred and sixty-nine years. And Noah was born to Lamech, and Lamech died, having lived seven hundred and

About that time the king of the Ammonites died, who had been a friend to David, leaving his son Hanun, who succeeded to his father's rule. David therefore sent to Hanun men to comfort his grief for his father and to announce that David maintained their friendship with him. But Hanun, supposing those sent to be spies, shaved off half of their beards and cut away the lower halves of their cloaks, and sent the men away. When David saw them so disposed, he gave the choicest part of the army to his commander Joab and sent him against the Ammonites. Joab, engaging them, defeated both them and their allies the Syrians, and they turned to flight. But once more, taking on allies, they came to battle. David, engaging them with all his army, killed many; and Shobach, who led the army of the enemy, mortally wounded in the battle, died of his wound. The allies of the Ammonites, who were Syrians from Mesopotamia, surrendered themselves to David. Again he sent out Joab against the Ammonites, who shut them up in the mother-city of their land and laid siege to it.

David, passing his time in Jerusalem and seeing from the palace a woman bathing in her house, called Bathsheba, fell in love with her. He sent for the woman and lay with her. She conceived, and made the matter known to the king. He summoned her husband from the siege, a man named Uriah, and after asking about the army, and giving him a meal, bade him go off to his house. But Uriah did not go, saying that it was not right that the general and his fellow-soldiers should suffer hardship in the camp while he lay with his wife. When the king again urged him to go home, and received him with toasts, so that he was brought almost to drunkenness, Uriah slept before the gates of the palace. The king then sent Uriah back to the camp, putting into his hand a letter to Joab commanding him to set Uriah where the enemy was hardest to fight, and to draw back those with him, leaving him there alone, so that he might be killed. It happened according to the king's order, and Uriah died. His wife mourned for her husband, and when she had ceased from her mourning, David took her to wife; and she bore him a son. But God was angered, and sent Nathan to David. He came to the king and said, "There were two men, the one having flocks and herds, the other possessing a single ewe-lamb. When a stranger was a guest to the rich man, he did not sacrifice from his own, but taking the single ewe-lamb of the poor man slaughtered it and feasted his friend." And David condemned the man who had done this to repay the lamb fourfold, and to die himself. But Nathan said, "You have passed sentence against yourself, O king; for you are the man who has wrought this lawless deed." And he recounted to him the adultery and the murder, and the wrath of God on their account, and foretold what he would suffer, and that the son born to him of the adultery would die. But David cried out in deep feeling, "I have sinned against the Lord," and Nathan answered that the sin had been put aside for him by God. Afterward the child born of Bathsheba fell ill. And David grieved greatly, and for seven days he fasted and clothed himself in black, and lying upon sackcloth he begged God for the life of the child. On the seventh day the child died, but he, learning of it, rose up, and having washed and changed his clothes he gave thanks to God and ordered a table to be prepared for him. When the king's attendants marvelled at what had happened, he said, "While the child was still living I humbled myself and made supplication, hoping that God might be moved; but now that he is dead, grief and prayer for him are in vain." Bathsheba bore David yet another son, and he called him Solomon.

Joab, besieging the Ammonites, had the capture of the city very near at hand, and made this known to the king. He went there and took the city and gave it over to the army for plunder; and he took its king's crown for himself and wore it, a crown that drew a talent of gold and held a precious stone; and he destroyed the multitude of the city. So too he did with the other cities of the Ammonites, and returned to Jerusalem.

If one were minded to refer the vision to the earlier constitution of the Roman dominion, when the senate and the dictators and the consuls and the tribunes and the people held the management of public affairs, he will find in many places the people at variance with the senate and factions arising, the senate enacting some things and the multitude introducing others, so that from this they fought one another and their affairs through this discord sometimes inclined to the worse and weaker. One might figure the senate by iron, on account of the firmness of its judgement, but the multitude might be likened to clay, being mingled with the magistrates and the council, both because of its rabble-like and grovelling quality—for such is the mud from which clay is made—and because of the fickleness and weakness of its disposition. For the multitude is wont to be unstable and easily led and easily changed of mind; and one will find these things often happened to the Roman state, going through the ancient writings about it.

If, then, one were to refer the difference of the materials and their mixture to the earlier constitution of the Roman state, he would perhaps reckon thus; but if to the later, when affairs were brought by the Romans from aristocracy to monarchy, and to the subsequent establishment of the empire, then too he would find that the discord of the Romans with one another brought the greatest harm to the state. For Caesar, reaching after monarchy, set on foot civil wars against Magnus Pompey and the others who claimed the ancient liberty; and against those who had killed him, in turn, Caesar Augustus and Antony got up the like battles; then again these two, at variance with one another over sole rule, set in motion grievous wars, kindred being destroyed on both sides in all the battles, and from this the Roman power being diminished. Nor would one see the factions abating in later times either. And if one compares the nature of the iron and the clay with the later empire, he will find the Roman rule in one respect strong, in another weak, and having cast away the most of its old dominion, and now circumscribed within a small fraction of that ancient sway.

Such, then, are the matters of the four kingdoms. But the remaining and indestructible kingdom, which the stone figured—the stone that was cut without hands and ground fine the materials of which the image was composed, and filled the whole earth, which the prophet said would not be destroyed unto the ages—this would be the future manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ, which will appear when the iron kingdom has become weaker through the admixture of the clay; when all things will be subjected to him, and he will deem worthy of an unending and incorruptible kingdom those who have made themselves worthy of it. For Scripture is wont to call Christ a stone. For David said, "The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner," and Isaiah, in the person of God, says, "Behold, I lay in Zion a cornerstone." And the great Paul calls Christ a cornerstone, upon whom he wrote that believers are built. And again he says, "No one can lay another foundation than the one laid, which is Jesus Christ." And again elsewhere, "They drank of a spiritual following rock, and the rock was Christ." And he is called a rock of offence and a stone of stumbling, and in many places the Lord would be found called stone and rock. The being cut without hands prefigured his birth above nature, without seed, apart from marital union. For the tribe of Judah, from which David sprang, may be reckoned the mountain; and Christ is the stone, cut from it in respect of his humanity; and without hands, because he came forth not according to the natural laws, but from an unwedded and holy womb. He at first seemed small because of the nature of his humanity, but advancing he filled the whole world with his own glory, and will fill it yet more at his future manifestation.

The prophet, then, reported the dream to Nabuchodonosor and disclosed its interpretation; and he, marveling, fell upon his face and worshipped Daniel and ordered sacrifice to be made to him—not that boastful and haughty man rendering all the honour to Daniel, but to the God worshipped by him. For he said, "In truth your God is the God of gods and the Lord of kings and the revealer of mysteries." He gave him many gifts, and set him as ruler over all Babylon, and named him Baltasar, giving him the appellation of his own god.

Since, then, the history makes mention of the Romans and of Rome, it seemed necessary to me to write about these matters as well, and to hand down from where and from whom the nation of the Romans took its beginning, and by whom the land of Italy was inhabited in former times; whence Romulus was brought into the light, who became the founder of Rome, and how Remus his brother was slain, and how he himself afterward vanished from sight; and how this city was first ruled by kings, and what customs and laws it observed; and how Tarquin the Proud, having turned the kingship into a tyranny, was deposed, and how many and what kind of wars Rome bore on account of his overthrow; and how the Roman state was changed into an aristocracy, and then into a democracy, with consuls and dictators, and afterward tribunes, conducting the administration of public affairs; and what the consulship was in old times, what the dictatorship was, what the work of the censors was, and what term was fixed for each of these offices; and what manner of thing the triumph was among them, and whence this name was derived; and all that came to pass in the times of the consulships, even if not everything, for want of the books that relate these things; and how afterward, out of these, the rule passed over to monarchy among the Romans; and how Gaius Julius Caesar first laid claim to this, though not in a pure form, and then, when he had been slain upon the rostra by those who clung to liberty, how Augustus Octavius Caesar, being the nephew of the slain Caesar and adopted by him, pursued the murderers of his adoptive father—having Antony as his partner in the work, but afterward falling out with him as well, and conquering him in a sea battle near Actium, and then, when he had fled with Cleopatra to Alexandria, overtaking him and reducing the man to such straits that he laid hands upon himself; and how great a destruction of the Romans there was in these civil wars—first when Octavius and Antony were set against Brutus and Cassius and the other slayers of Caesar, and then when they fought against one another; and how Cleopatra, the queen of Egypt, a descendant of the Ptolemies, was taken alive, and how she too made an end of herself, as was conjectured, by the bite of an asp; and how Octavius, having thus returned to Rome with splendid triumphs, laid claim to sole rule and transferred the dominion of the Romans into a strict monarchy; and who reigned after him as monarchs, and how each came to the rule, and how and for how long he ruled, and with what end of life he met; and who, under these emperors, after the venerable apostles, adorned the thrones of the four great churches—I mean those of Rome and Alexandria and Antioch and Jerusalem—and how many of them were deemed worthy of a martyr's end; and how Diocletian and Maximian Herculius raged against the Christians more than the others, and how, having laid down the rule, they appointed others as Caesars in their place, one of whom was Constantius Chlorus, the father of Constantine the Great, the government of the Gauls and of Britain having been allotted to him; and how, as he was dying, he made his firstborn son—this very Constantine, the equal of the apostles—the successor to his own rule; and how this man became sole ruler, having overcome the rest, when the sign of the cross appeared to him through stars in the heaven; and how he came over to Christ and extended the faith, granting freedom to its preaching, and how in Byzantium he built a city named after himself, calling it New Rome, and transferred the empire from elder Rome to this city; and who reigned in it after him, and what each was in his character, and indeed in his piety, and how long he held the rule and how he departed this life; and who presided over the church in Constantinople, and for how long each, and which of them held to the correct doctrine, and which became heterodox, and how each of them departed from here; and under what emperors and patriarchs, and against whom, the councils were convened. And thus the account, descending as far as the emperors of our own time, brings the writing to its end, having made mention along the way of many other histories, including obscure ones. But I must make the beginning of this writing the first beginning, the cause of all things, the one without beginning and without time, and must speak of the bringing-forth and the coming-to-be of the things produced by that cause out of non-being into existence and substance.

seven and fifty-three years. And to Noah three sons were born: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. And when the sons of God saw the daughters of men, they took to themselves wives. By "sons of God" Scripture means the descendants of Seth, as pursuing virtue, just as it also calls the virtuous "sons of the Most High"; and by "daughters of men" it means those descended from the offspring of Cain. But Josephus says that angels took the daughters of men, having so named them, I suppose, as those well pleasing to God and following their manner of life. But men, being multiplied, inclined toward evil; and to them were born children, insolent and reckless through their confidence in their strength. With these the Divine was angered, and cut short their length of life, limiting the life of men to a hundred and twenty years.

But Noah found grace before God. Therefore, when the dry land was changed into sea through a rainfall of many days and great violence, all the human race perished, but Noah alone was saved by the providence of God in a wooden chest, which he had built four-square, with a length of three hundred cubits, a breadth of fifty, and a depth of thirty. Into it he himself and his sons embarked, and the mother and their wives, having placed within it seeds of every kind and animals of every kind for the preservation of their species—two of the unclean, but seven of each kind of the clean. Now Noah was the tenth counting from Adam, and after one thousand six hundred and fifty-six years the flood was brought upon the earth, for forty days a violent rain pouring down upon the earth, so that the water rose fifteen cubits above the highest of the mountains. And when the rain had ceased and the water was diminishing, after a hundred and fifty days the chest ran aground on a certain mountain of Armenia in the seventh month. At that time Noah, having opened it, sends forth a raven; and it did not return. And after some days he let go a dove, which again came back. And when seven days had passed, he let it go again, and it came back bearing a sprig of olive. And from this he knew that the water had failed from the earth. And Noah went out, and his wife and his sons with their wives, and the animals that were with them in the ark, and he sacrificed to God. Josephus says that the place in Armenia is called Apobaterion ("the place of disembarking"), and that remains of the chest are shown there. And he says that many of those who wrote the histories of the barbarian peoples make mention of the flood and of the ark—Berosus the Chaldaean, and Hieronymus the Egyptian, who wrote the antiquities of Phoenicia, and Mnaseas of Damascus. And God promised no longer to bring such a calamity upon the earth. And He commanded them to use the animals for food, save only that they should not eat flesh with the blood of the soul in it, and that they should keep from the murder of men. And as a sign that He would no longer flood the earth with rain He set the bow in the cloud, signifying the rainbow by "the bow." And Noah, having lived three hundred and fifty years after the flood, dies, having been nine hundred and fifty years old. These things have been said by Josephus concerning the long life of those men of that time. Let no one, then, judging by present life and the brevity of years, suppose the things recorded about the ancients to be false. For being dear to God and made by God Himself, and because their nourishment was better suited for a longer span, they reasonably lived so great a number of years; and then, too, on account of the usefulness of the things they devised, astronomy and geometry, which they could not have understood and stated with certainty had they not lived six hundred years; for it is in so many years that the Great Year is fulfilled.

David had a daughter named Tamar, sister of Absalom by the same mother. Amnon, the firstborn son of David, was in love with her, and his love was so great that the lover fell sick. When his father came to visit him, he asked that Tamar might come to serve him; and his father consented. Tamar therefore came and prepared cakes for him. But he sent everyone away, and asked that his sister alone should serve him. When the girl was left alone, he forced her; and having violated her he straightway conceived a hatred opposite to his former love, and ordered her to leave at once, and commanded his servant to put her out. She, in great pain at the violence and the outrage, tore her tunic, and scattering ashes upon her head, went away weeping. Her brother Absalom counselled her to keep silent, but he was enraged against Amnon on his sister's account. When the king learned what had happened, he was grieved, but he was unwilling to pain Amnon, because he was his firstborn. After two years had passed, Absalom was about to shear his own flocks, and called his brothers to a feast. He commanded those who served him, as the feast went on, to strike Amnon and kill him. And the servants of Absalom did so. The rest of the king's sons, seeing what had happened, fled. When a report went abroad that Absalom had killed all the king's sons, David tore his garment and fell upon the ground, weeping. Meanwhile the king's sons came and announced the death of Amnon, mourning. Absalom fled to his grandfather on his mother's side, the king of Geshur, and spent three years there. When in time his anger had subsided, Joab devised a way to reconcile the king with Absalom. For he prepared a certain woman to come to the king in mourning and to lament that, having two sons, and one of them having killed the other, the kinsmen were seeking to destroy the survivor for the murder of his brother; and to beg the king to grant her the saving of her son's life. So she came to the king and said this with deep feeling, and the king promised to grant her the life of the son. The woman acknowledged her thanks to him, and said, "That I may have a pledge of what you have promised, first be reconciled yourself with your own son, and do not add a second, deliberate killing to the death of the son who died against your will." The king understood that the woman's words were a pretext, and that they had been devised by Joab, and gave him leave to bring back Absalom; and Joab went and brought him to Jerusalem, though it was not granted him to come into his father's sight.

After this the king was reconciled with Absalom, and calling him he forgave him when he asked pardon, and promised forgetfulness of his offence. Absalom acquired horses and chariots and many followers, and every day went up to the palace, and by conversing graciously with the multitudes he disposed many to favour him. Now when four years had slipped by since his return, he pretended to go off to Hebron for the sake of a sacrifice, as having made this a vow while in flight; and he was given leave by his father. Going there he sent to many, and very many flocked to him, and among the rest also Ahithophel, his father's counsellor. And he was proclaimed king by all. Learning this, David set out from Jerusalem with those about him; and the six hundred men who had been with him in Saul's time again set out with him. It was reported that Ahithophel too had gone over to Absalom, which made his fear the greater and his grief the more. He called upon God, and committed to him the judgement of all. Hushai, being a companion of David, by David's own design pretended to desert to Absalom. As David departed, Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, came to him, leading a pair of asses laden with provisions, and accusing his master of having remained in Jerusalem and of expecting that the kingdom would come round to him, since the multitude would choose him. David was indignant at this, and gave to Ziba all that he had formerly given to Mephibosheth. Then on the road Shimei came upon him, a man of Saul's kindred, and threw stones at the king and cursed him and called him a man of blood and a transgressor. When those with David rushed to kill Shimei, the king would not allow it, saying, "The Lord has told him to do this; let him alone." And coming to the Jordan, he there refreshed those with him who had grown weary.

Then, having set up a golden statue sixty cubits in height and six in breadth, he summoned the chief men from all his realm, ordering that, whenever they heard the trumpet, they should then fall and worship the statue, and that those who disobeyed should be cast into the furnace of fire, which he had kindled there great and fierce. When all worshipped, the three youths, whom the history has handed down as kinsmen of Daniel, unwilling to transgress their ancestral law, did not worship. And they were at once cast into the furnace; but the fire did not touch them, and standing in the midst of that irresistible flame they sent up a hymn to God. And there stood with the three a fourth; it was an angel, who had come down with them and was turning that fiery air into a dewy breeze. These things astounded the brutish and unfeeling soul of that king, and, laying aside his pride, he came forward and called the youths by name and blessed their God, and deemed those men worthy of honour and appointed them governors over all the Jews in Babylon.

A little later that Assyrian saw another dream. He saw a tree great and reaching to the ends of the earth, adorned with leaves and laden with fruit. Beneath it the wild beasts sheltered, and the birds dwelt in its branches. Then he saw a Watcher coming from heaven and crying out with strength, "Cut down the tree, and pluck off its branches, and shake off its leaves, and scatter its fruit; only leave the stock of its roots; and in an iron band, and in the grass of the earth, and in the dew of heaven let it lodge, and let its portion be with the beasts, and let its heart be changed from that of men, and let a beast's heart be given to it, and let seven seasons be changed over it." Having seen this vision, he again summoned the magi and the wise men of Babylon and sought to learn what was signified by it. But they were at a loss and could not tell the interpretation of the dream. Then again he took refuge with Daniel and related to him the dream, and asked him to tell its interpretation; "for you are able," he said, "because the holy spirit of God is in you." And he said, "My lord the king, may this dream be for those who hate you." Then he expounded its meaning to him and said, "The great tree which you saw is you, O king, because you have been magnified and grown strong, and your greatness has reached to heaven, and your dominion to the ends of the earth"—he called greatness the exaltation of the mind and the swelling of pride. "And as for your seeing a Watcher coming down from heaven"—that is, a divine angel; for the word Ir, translated into Greek, signifies the one who is awake, by which he hints at the incorporeal; for he who is clothed in a body is enslaved to sleep, but he who is not enslaved to it has an incorporeal nature—"since, then, you saw that Watcher crying that the tree be cut down, but its root-stock be left, and the rest, expect that you will fall from the kingdom and be driven out from the fellowship of men, and lodge with beasts and eat grass; yet not to be utterly deprived of the kingdom, but that it will again be restored to you; for of this the leaving of the root-stock of the tree is a sign." Such was the interpretation of the vision that Daniel gave to Nabuchodonosor. And all came to pass according to the divine oracle, and the king, falling sick with madness because of his boastfulness and pride and spending seven years in the wilderness, no one assailing his kingdom, received it again, having appeased God. Having reigned forty-three years, he died. Josephus says that many of the ancient historians mention him, Berossus and Megasthenes and Diocles and Philostratus.

When he had died, his elder son Evil-merodach succeeded to the rule. He at once freed from his bonds the king Jehoiachin, also called Jechonias, whom Nabuchodonosor had kept imprisoned, and deemed him worthy of honour, and gave him gifts and had him as his table-companion continually.

So Cyrus brought to an end the empire of the Assyrians. In the first year of his reign, which was the seventieth since the Hebrews had been carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon, he permitted the Jews in Babylon to depart to Jerusalem and to rebuild both the city and the temple, just as the prophet Jeremiah had foretold, and before him Isaiah had spoken of it. For Jeremiah lived at the time when the city was taken and the temple razed, while Isaiah lived a hundred and forty years before the city was captured and the temple destroyed. And Cyrus not only granted the captives their return and the raising up again of the city and the temple, but also sent back with them the vessels of the temple which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off to Babylon, handing them over to Mithridates his treasurer and to Zerubbabel to convey. He wrote also to the satraps in Syria to help them in the building of the works and to supply the whole cost from the royal funds. When Cyrus had so decreed, the leaders of the two tribes, of Judah and of Benjamin, together with the Levites and the priests, set out; but many remained in Babylon, unwilling to abandon their possessions. When they reached Jerusalem, all of Cyrus's officials assisted them in the building and worked together with them. Those who returned were forty-two thousand six hundred in number.

While they were already pressing forward with the building of the city and the temple, the surrounding nations, and above all the Cuthaeans, whom Shalmaneser had settled in Samaria when he carried the Israelites into captivity, out of envy first won over the satraps not to assist the Jews in the building. Then, when Cyrus had ended his life and Cambyses his son had succeeded to the kingdom, they wrote to Cambyses, slandering the Hebrews as a rebellious and ungovernable nation, and saying that, if they completed the city and the temple, they would neither pay tribute nor be subject. By writing these things and many more of the kind they persuaded him to forbid the rebuilding of the city and the temple; and the works were halted until the second year of the reign of Darius the son of Hystaspes, for nine years. For Cambyses, having reigned seven years and in that time having subdued Egypt, died at Damascus on his return, while the Magi made themselves masters of the kingdom. It is well to recount these matters too in summary.

Cambyses had a brother named, according to Xenophon, Tanaoxares, but according to Herodotus, Smerdis. While Cambyses was in Egypt, it seemed to him in his sleep that someone stood over him and said that Smerdis had sat upon the royal throne and touched the vault of heaven with his head. Fearing then for his kingdom, he at once sent Prexaspes to Susa to kill his brother secretly. And so Smerdis was destroyed; but Cambyses did not escape his destiny. For there were two Median brothers, called Magi, of whom one was named Cataziethes and the other Smerdis. This Smerdis shared with Smerdis the son of Cyrus not only his name but also his appearance. One of these two Cambyses had taken as the steward of his affairs. While Cambyses lingered in Egypt, Cataziethes, learning of the murder of Smerdis the son of Cyrus and that his death was known to few, planned to seize the kingdom; and he set his brother, who bore the name of Smerdis and had a great resemblance to him, upon the royal throne, not as his own blood-brother, but as the son of Cyrus and the brother of Cambyses. And he sent heralds everywhere to proclaim Smerdis the son of Cyrus as king. When Cambyses learned of this, he examined Prexaspes as one who had not carried out his command. But Prexaspes maintained that it was not his brother who had risen against him: "For I," he said, "as you commanded, killed and buried him." Cambyses therefore ordered the man who in the army was proclaiming that Smerdis the son of Cyrus reigned over the Persians to be arrested. When he was arrested, he was asked whether he himself had seen Smerdis, and whether Smerdis had ordered him to say what he was saying. He answered that he had not seen Smerdis, but that he had been ordered to say these things by the Magus who governed the palace. Learning the truth from this, Cambyses lamented that he had killed his brother in vain, and at once set out to march against the Magi. But as he leaped upon his horse, the cap fell from the scabbard of his sword, and the bared blade struck his thigh a mortal blow. He asked then what the city was called, and learning that it was Ecbatana, he said, "Here it is fated for me to die." For it had been prophesied to him that he would die at Ecbatana; and he had supposed that his end would overtake him at the Median Ecbatana, but the oracle meant not that place, but the Syrian Ecbatana. So a few days later he died childless,

having reigned seven years and five months. And the Magus, when Cambyses was dead, reigned without fear, ascribing to himself the name of Smerdis the son of Cyrus. He sent word to every nation he ruled and proclaimed remission of taxes for all for three years. But when he had reigned seven months, it became known who he was, and it became known in this way. Otanes was a man who rivalled the foremost of the Persians in birth and wealth. Cambyses had married his daughter, who was called Phaedymia; and the Magus made use of her, as of the other women whom he found in the palace. Her father, therefore, secretly sent and asked her whether she lay with Smerdis the son of Cyrus or with some other man. She answered that she had never seen Smerdis the son of Cyrus, and did not know with whom she shared a bed. Again he sent to her, charging her, if need be, to take the risk, in order to fulfil her father's command, and instructing her that, when she should lie with the king and find him asleep, she should feel for his ears; and if she found that he had ears, she should know that she lay with Smerdis the son of Cyrus, but if he had none, she should consider him to be the Magus Smerdis. Phaedymia obeyed her father, and finding that the man who lay with her had no ears, she made it known to her father. He had no ears because Cyrus had once cut them off for some offence. Then Otanes shared the secret with Aspathines and Gobryas, the foremost of the Persians and his friends. They, already suspecting the matter, at once accepted his words. They resolved to take in others as well. And Otanes brought in Intaphernes, Gobryas brought in Megabyzus, and Aspathines brought in Hydarnes; and to Darius the son of Hystaspes, who had just come to Susa from Persis, they communicated the secret. He too accepted the proposal, and advised them to set about the deed at once, saying that if the present day passed in vain, he himself would become the informer of the plot to the Magus. The others were persuaded by Darius's advice and held to the work.

Something else also occurred which spurred them to hasten the attempt. For the Magi, knowing that Prexaspes had with his own hand wrought the murder of Smerdis the son of Cyrus, and that for this reason he stood accused among the Persians, summoned him, made him their friend, and bound him beforehand with oaths and brilliant promises not to reveal their device to anyone. When he had agreed to do this, they went further and proposed that they would gather the multitude beneath the wall of the palace, and that he should climb upon a tower and cry out within hearing of all that they were ruled by Smerdis the son of Cyrus and by no other; for they had spared him, and had not killed him as Cambyses had commanded. When he had agreed to do this too, the multitude was gathered, and Prexaspes went up upon the tower and told of all the good that the Persians had received from Cyrus. But he added that he himself had killed Cyrus's son Smerdis, compelled by Cambyses, and declared plainly that it was the Magi who held the kingdom, and called down curses on the Persians if they did not avenge themselves on them. Having said this, he threw himself down and died.

The seven men, learning on the road what Prexaspes had done, hastened at once to the palace and entered it, unhindered by the guards, who stood in awe of the eminence of the men. Passing into the court, they met the eunuch messengers, who asked them on what errand they had come and tried to prevent them going further. They cut down the eunuchs on the spot and ran on inside. The Magi, who were within, learning of the tumult from the eunuchs, turned to defend themselves: one took up a spear, the other a bow. The one with the spear struck Aspathines in the thigh and Intaphernes in the face, whereby his eye was injured; but the bow proved useless to those who fought hand to hand at close quarters. The one who held it slipped into a chamber, and Darius and Gobryas burst in after him. Gobryas grappled with the Magus, while Darius, at a loss because of the darkness and afraid of striking his comrade, stood idle. Gobryas asked why he stood inactive; and he told the cause. "Then thrust your sword through both of us," said Gobryas. Darius drove in his dagger, and struck the Magus. So they killed both, and cut off the heads of both. The two wounded men they left in the citadel, both because of their wounds and to guard the acropolis; the rest, carrying the heads of the Magi, ran out and showed them to the Persians and explained what had happened. The Persians, learning of the deception, killed every Magus they met.

When the tumult had subsided and some days had passed, they took counsel about the management of affairs. Otanes urged them to choose a democracy, Megabyzus an aristocracy, but Darius advised that they choose a kingdom once again. The other four agreed with his opinion; and they resolved to mount their horses, and that whoever's horse, when they had come into the suburb, should neigh first at sunrise, he should hold the kingdom. Darius explained the plan to his groom. The man was clever, and "Take courage, master," he said, "for the kingdom shall be yours." When night came, he took a mare which Darius's horse loved, and tying it in the suburb he led the horse there and walked it close to the mare, and at last let it cover her. At dawn, when the seven had come into the suburb and were riding through it, as soon as they reached the place where the mare had been tied, Darius's horse, remembering her, went forward and neighed; and thereby the kingdom fell to Darius. Some say that it was Oebares — for that was the name of Darius's groom — who contrived this; but others say that his contrivance was different: that he touched with his hand the parts of the mare which Darius's horse loved, and kept his hand hidden in his trousers; and when the sun was rising and the seven men were mounting their horses, he brought his hand to the nostrils of Darius's horse, and the horse, at once catching the scent, snorted and neighed. Whether it happened in the one way or the other, Darius obtained the kingdom.

This man, while still a private person, had vowed to God that, if he became king, he would send to the temple in Jerusalem all the vessels of God that were still in Babylon. He had also long had a friendship with Zerubbabel, on account of which Zerubbabel, having lately come to him from Jerusalem, had been thought worthy to serve among his bodyguards together with two others. In the first year of his reign Darius prepared a banquet for his nobles; and when they had feasted and departed, he himself fell asleep beside his couch. Having slept a little, he woke and conversed with his bodyguards. He set each of them a contest of speech: to the first, whether wine prevails over all things; to the second, whether kings do; and to the remaining one — this was Zerubbabel — whether women, and above them truth, prevail. And he promised to give the victor as a prize to wear purple, and a turban of fine linen, and a golden collar, and to drink from golden cups, and to sleep upon gold, and to have a chariot with a golden bridle, and to sit next after himself, and to be called his kinsman. At dawn, then, summoning the nobles, he bade each of the bodyguards declare his opinion on the question.
