When the surrounding nations destroyed many of the Jews, lying in wait through envy, Judas defended them with wars and held the enemy off.

Antiochus, learning that there was a city in Persis rich in wealth, named Elymais, with a temple of Artemis in it full of costly offerings, set out against it and besieged it. But being repulsed by those in the city, who came out against him, he fled to Babylon, and lost most of his army. While Antiochus was grieving over this, the defeat of his generals by the Jews was announced to him. The grief being added, he fell sick; and knowing that he would die, he gathered those under him, and said that he suffered thus because he had afflicted the nation of the Jews and plundered the temple. Saying this, he expired, leaving Philip, one of his friends, as steward of the kingdom, and giving him the diadem and the ring, that he might convey these to his son Antiochus. But Lysias, learning that Antiochus was dead, proclaimed his son king, calling him Eupator.

The Macedonians in the citadel of Jerusalem harassed the Jews who went up into the temple to sacrifice. Therefore Judas was eager to remove the garrison and besieged it vigorously. The young Antiochus, learning this, was angered, and with a great force set out against Judaea and Jerusalem. Judas, meeting him, killed about six hundred of his advance guard. And Eleazar, the brother of Judas, also called Auran, seeing the tallest of the elephants armed with royal trappings, and supposing the king to be riding on it, attacked it with a violent rush, and getting beneath the beast's belly, struck and killed it. But the elephant, sinking down upon Eleazar and crushing him with the weight of its body, destroyed him. Seeing the strength of the enemy, Judas returned to Jerusalem and prepared for a siege. Antiochus, coming to Jerusalem, besieged the temple, while those within defended it vigorously; but as their food ran out, many slipped away. Since Philip, whom Antiochus had left as steward of the kingdom when he died, was usurping the kingdom, Lysias the general and Antiochus, learning this, made terms with the besieged, that they should use their ancestral laws. So Antiochus was received into the city; but seeing the temple very strong, he broke his oaths and razed the wall; and so he returned, taking with him the high priest Onias, who was also called Menelaus, on the charge of having persuaded his father to compel the Jews to transgress the ancestral customs and of being the cause of many evils. And sending him to Beroea in Syria, he destroyed him, after he had held the high priesthood for ten years and had been impious. Alcimus, who was also called Joacim, became high priest. Antiochus, having made war on Philip and overcome him, killed him. But Onias, the son of the high priest Simon, whom his father at his death had left an infant, as has been said, seeing that Antiochus had given the high priesthood to Alcimus, who was not of the family of the high priests, fled to Ptolemy in Egypt; and being honoured, he received a place in the Heliopolitan district, and built there a temple resembling the one in Jerusalem.

Demetrius the son of Seleucus, fleeing from Rome and coming to Tripolis in Syria, seized both Antiochus and Lysias and destroyed them both, Antiochus having reigned two years. To this Demetrius the high priest Alcimus came, and many of the Jews, fugitives and wicked men, accused Judas Maccabaeus and the whole nation of having killed his friends. Provoked, he sent Bacchides, a very close associate of his, with a very great force, charging him to kill both Judas and those with him. Coming into Judaea, he sent to Judas and his brothers, calling them to peace. But they did not trust him. Some of the people, however, having received oaths from Bacchides, came over to him; but he, despising the oaths, killed sixty of these, and so checked the impulse of the rest to come over to him. He ordered all in the country to obey the high priest Alcimus. And having done these things, he returned to Antioch. Alcimus, dealing with each man in a way to please him, and winning all over, quickly gathered a large force, the greater part of whom were from among the fugitives and the impious, through whom he killed those who held with Judas; and Judas on the other side destroyed the partisans of Alcimus. Alcimus incited Demetrius against Judas. The king therefore sent Nicanor again with a very great force, charging him not to spare the nation. He, going forth, tried to seize Judas by guile and invited him to peace; and Judas, having given and received pledges, received Nicanor with his force. But Nicanor, greeting him and conversing with him, gave a signal to his men to seize Judas. The man, perceiving the plot, sprang out toward the Jews and escaped. When the ambush became known, Nicanor joined open battle, and conquered. From this Judas fled to the citadel of Jerusalem. Nicanor threatened the people that, if they did not hand Judas over to him, he would pull down the temple. But Judas, conversing with the thousand who were with him, roused them to valour, and engaging the enemy he conquered, many falling, including Nicanor himself; and the rest fled, and were all destroyed as they were overtaken. And so for a little while the Jews
had rest from wars.

When the high priest Alcimus, also called Joacim, was struck with a heaven-sent stroke and so ended his life, four years after he had become high priest, the people assigned the high priesthood to Judas. Judas, hearing that the Romans were very powerful, and had subdued the Galatians and Iberians and Carthaginians and Libyans and all Greece and the kings Perseus and Philip and Antiochus, sent asking for friendship, and asked them to write to Demetrius not to make war on the Jews. The senate both agreed to friendship and consented to be allies of the Jews. Demetrius, learning of the death of Nicanor and the destruction of the army, again sent Bacchides. He hastened against Judas, who had encamped in a certain village with a thousand men. They, fearing the army with Bacchides, advised him to withdraw and save himself. But when he said, "May the sun never see this happen, that I turn my back to the enemy," many of those with him fled. Engaging Bacchides, he fought for a long time on equal terms; but toward sunset, pressing forward with the bravest on the right wing, where Bacchides himself was, he broke the phalanx and turned it to flight. But those on the left wing, advancing, surrounded Judas. He, standing firm, fought with those about him, and after killing many, at last fell himself; and when he had fallen, those with him fled. Having distinguished himself in the high priesthood for three years, and having been a noble man, and ready to do and suffer everything for the freedom of the nation, he died.

When he was dead, Bacchides committed the charge of the country to those of the Jews who were impious and had transgressed the ancestral customs. They afflicted their countrymen in every way, and seizing those who held with Judas, brought them to Bacchides, who, after tormenting them, then destroyed them. The remaining companions of Judas, having persuaded Jonathan his brother, appointed him general of the Jews. Bacchides sought to kill Jonathan by guile; but he, with his brother Simon and his companions, fled to the wilderness. Bacchides set out against them; and Jonathan sent his brother John to the Nabataean Arabs, for they were friends, to deposit with them the baggage. As John was departing, the sons of Amaraeus, lying in wait, killed him with his followers and plundered what was being conveyed. Bacchides attacked Jonathan on the sabbath, supposing he would not fight because of the law. But Jonathan, saying that the danger was for their lives, drew up against him, and after killing many and rushing at Bacchides as if to strike him, but missing, he leaped into the river with his companions and swam across. Bacchides returned to the citadel in Jerusalem, and taking as hostages the sons of the chief men of Judaea, shut them up in the citadel. Jonathan made it his care to avenge the murder of his brother John. When the sons of Amaraeus were celebrating a wedding, and were conducting the bridegroom and the bride from one city to another with a costly procession, he lay in ambush in a mountain with his men and fell upon those in the procession, and destroyed them all, and plundered all that they carried. Jonathan and Simon, with their followers, retired to the marshes of the river. Bacchides, leaving a garrison in Judaea, returned to Demetrius. The nation being thereafter at peace for two years, Jonathan and his men dwelt in the country in safety. The impious Jews therefore sent to king Demetrius, declaring that Jonathan could be taken without difficulty if someone were sent against him. And the king sent Bacchides. He, coming into Judaea and striving to seize Jonathan, was not able; and when fifty of Jonathan's men had made the report to the king, he killed the chief of them as having lied. Jonathan and Simon and their followers withdrew into the wilderness, where, having built towers, he awaited the event. Bacchides came and besieged him. But Jonathan, leaving his brother Simon there, himself went out secretly and, gathering many from the country, by night attacked Bacchides and his army. He himself killed many, and Simon killed many also, having come out from the strongholds, and they burned the siege-engines. Dispirited by this, Bacchides wished to break camp, but sought a respectable pretext for the withdrawal. Jonathan, learning this, sent an embassy concerning friendship, that each side might restore to the other the captives they held. Bacchides accepted the embassy and made terms. And they swore no longer to make war on each other, and exchanged the captives. So Bacchides, returning, no more came against Judaea; and Jonathan, having obtained security, directed the affairs of his countrymen and punished those who had transgressed.

Alexander the son of Antiochus Epiphanes, having received Ptolemais by treachery, so disturbed Demetrius that he gathered his forces and sent to Jonathan concerning goodwill and alliance. He permitted him to raise an army, and granted that he should take back the sons whom Bacchides had shut up in the citadel as hostages. Receiving the king's letter, Jonathan came to Jerusalem, and read it in the hearing of the people and the garrison, and taking the sons from the citadel, gave each one back to his own parents; and he himself stayed in Jerusalem, renewing the city and rebuilding its walls. Alexander too wrote to Jonathan, calling him to alliance and making him his friend and granting him the high priesthood and sending him gifts. Receiving the letter, he put on the high-priestly robe at the feast of Tabernacles, four years having been measured out since his brother Judas died, and gathered a force and prepared arms. Joining battle with Demetrius, Alexander conquered, Demetrius having fallen with his horse into a deep and hard-to-escape mire, where, the enemy standing around him, he was wounded and fell, having himself killed many. He had reigned eleven years.

Alexander, having received the kingdom of Syria, betrothed to himself as wife the daughter of Ptolemy Philometor. As the marriage was being celebrated, he wrote to Jonathan to come to Ptolemais. Arriving, he was honoured both by Ptolemy and by Alexander. When Demetrius, the son of the deceased Demetrius, sailed from Crete to Cilicia with a heavy force, Alexander was in distress, and hastened to Antioch to secure things there, leaving Apollonius the Daus as governor of Syria. He, sending to Jonathan, said it was unjust that he alone should not submit to the king, and challenged him to battle, and reproached the nation for cowardice. Provoked by this, the high priest joined battle with Apollonius, and conquered, and killed many of the enemy, and took cities of Syria, and with much spoil returned to Jerusalem. King Alexander, learning this, sent to Jonathan, rejoicing at the defeat of Apollonius, as one who had fought against him, his friend and ally, contrary to his wishes. But Ptolemy Philometor, going to the aid of Alexander with a naval and land force, and coming to Ptolemais, was nearly endangered, Alexander having plotted against him through one of his friends, Ammonius. Escaping the plot, he demanded Ammonius for punishment; but Alexander would not give him up. Whence Ptolemy, perceiving Alexander to be privy to the plot, both withdrew from the alliance and dissolved the marriage-connection. For taking his daughter from him, he sent her to Demetrius, promising to be his ally and to join his daughter to him and to establish him in his ancestral kingdom. And Demetrius gladly accepted the marriage and the alliance. Ptolemy was eager to persuade the people of Antioch to receive Demetrius. And he easily accomplished what he sought, the people of Antioch hating Alexander both because of his father's transgressions against them and because of Ammonius; and they quickly drove him out of Antioch. He, being cast out thence, came to Cilicia, and the people of Antioch proclaimed Ptolemy king, and compelled him to wear two diadems, as ruling both Syria and Egypt. But he, being able through prudence to reckon the future, lest he should seem envied by the Romans, who were now very powerful, persuaded the people of Antioch to receive Demetrius. When Alexander came against Syria with a large army and ravaged the territory of the people of Antioch, Ptolemy, together with Demetrius, to whom he had now joined his daughter in marriage, marched against him; and Alexander, defeated, fled to Arabia, while Ptolemy, fallen from his horse, which was startled by the cry of an elephant and threw him off, received many wounds on his head as the enemy stood around him, and was with difficulty snatched away by his bodyguards, and lay for four days, neither understanding nor speaking. Recovering on the fifth of the days, and receiving the head of Alexander sent to him by the ruler of the Arabs, and pleased at his destruction, he himself died a little after.

Demetrius the son of Nicanor, having received the kingdom of Asia after Alexander, who had reigned five years, began to destroy Ptolemy's soldiery, forgetting both the kinship and the alliance. The soldiers, fending off his attempt, withdrew to Alexandria; but he gained control of the elephants. Jonathan the high priest besieged the citadel of Jerusalem, which had within it Macedonian guards and some of the impious Jews. Some of these, going out by night, reported the siege to Demetrius. He came with a force to Jonathan, and being at Ptolemais wrote to him to come to him. But he did not cease the siege; instead, taking the priests and the elders of the people and bringing much money, he came to Demetrius. Having gratified him with these things, he was honoured by him and confirmed in the high priesthood.

When, since no war was pressing, Demetrius reduced the soldiers' pay, and from this was hated by them, a certain general of Alexander, surnamed Tryphon, perceiving the hatred toward him, went to Malchus the Arab, and asked for the son of Alexander, Antiochus, who was being reared with him, saying that he would restore to him his ancestral rule; and Malchus gave him up. Demetrius, sending to Jonathan, asked for an alliance, promising him many favours. Jonathan therefore sent him three thousand men, through whom he routed the people of Antioch, who had risen against Demetrius out of the enmity they nursed because they were ill-treated by him; and he burned the city and killed many of them, until they were forced to lay down their arms and surrender themselves to him. So the revolt was ended; and Demetrius sent the Jews back to Jonathan, presenting them with gifts and acknowledging his gratitude to him. But later he broke his promises and threatened him with war. And he would have carried out his threats, had not Tryphon, returning from Arabia into Syria, set a diadem upon Antiochus, who was then a stripling, and stirred up war against Demetrius, the soldiers who had abandoned Demetrius because of the reduction of pay coming over to him. Tryphon, having gained the upper hand in the battle, took Antioch and the elephants. Demetrius went off to Cilicia; and the boy Antiochus summoned Jonathan to an alliance. He agreed to be his friend and ally, and undertook to make war on Demetrius, and at once set about the work. First he made many cities go over to Antiochus, having revolted from Demetrius; then, leaving his brother Simon in Judaea, he advanced against the generals of Demetrius. Simon besieged Bethsura, a place in Judaea held by Demetrius's men, who, hard pressed by the siege, on receiving pledges abandoned the place; and Simon set his own garrison in it. Jonathan, engaging the generals of Demetrius, both turned them to flight and, after killing about two thousand, returned to Jerusalem. And he sent an embassy to Rome, to renew the former friendship which they had with the nation. The members of the senate ratified again what had before been decreed. The envoys, on returning, came also to Sparta, having this too charged upon them by Jonathan. And the Spartans received the envoys kindly, and passed a decree concerning friendship and alliance with the Jews. But the generals of Demetrius, eager to retrieve their defeat, came against Jonathan with a larger force. He met them swiftly. Afraid to stand against him in open battle, they fled by night. By day, learning of their flight, Jonathan pursued, but did not overtake them; instead, coming into Arabia and falling upon the Nabataeans, and driving off much spoil from there and taking captives, he returned. Gathering the people, he advised them to renew the walls of Jerusalem and to set up again as much of the circuit of the temple as had been pulled down. The counsel pleasing all, he himself set to the work, and sent his brother Simon to secure the country.

Demetrius came into Mesopotamia, intending to take over Babylon and the upper satrapies. For the Greeks and Macedonians who dwelt there promised to surrender themselves to him and to help him make war on Arsaces the king of the Parthians; and so they received him. But joining battle with Arsaces, he lost his whole army and was himself captured. Tryphon, learning what had befallen Demetrius, plotted against Antiochus, contriving to kill him and usurp the rule. But he feared Jonathan, who was a friend of Antiochus. And he was eager first to take him by deceit, and so to attempt what concerned Antiochus. Therefore he went to Scythopolis, where Jonathan met him with forty thousand fighting men. Tryphon, dealing with him deceitfully, received him with gifts and honours, wishing to remove all suspicion, that he might take him off his guard. He advised him to dismiss his army, and himself to come with him to Ptolemais with a few men, to take over the city and all the strongholds there. Jonathan, suspecting nothing, sent back his army, and went off keeping only a thousand men. But being shut up in Ptolemais, he himself was taken alive, and those with him were destroyed. When those in Jerusalem learned this, they fell into fear because of the surrounding nations, which, learning of the seizure of Jonathan, had been stirred against the Jews. But Simon, conversing with the multitude and encouraging it, was chosen by it as leader, and gathering the fighting men of the people, he attended to the walls of the city, and took thought for all that concerned the security of affairs. Tryphon came into Judaea, leading Jonathan a prisoner. Simon met him with a force; and Tryphon sent to him, declaring that he would give a hundred talents of silver and two of Jonathan's sons as hostages, if he wished his brother to be released. Simon understood the villainy of Tryphon, but, that he might not be blamed for being unwilling to save his brother, sent both the money and the sons. Receiving these, Tryphon did not keep the agreement, but went up with his army toward Jerusalem. Simon followed alongside, always encamping opposite. But a heavy snowfall hindered his arrival at Jerusalem; and he turned aside into Syria, and as he departed killed Jonathan.

Simon, when his brother Jonathan was dead, after a high priesthood of four years, was himself put forward as high priest by the multitude, and no longer paid tribute to the Macedonians. The nation prospered greatly under him, and they mastered the surrounding nations, and subdued many of the cities, that they might not be bases for the enemy. And the mountain on which the citadel was built, being very high, by labouring continuously for three years they moved into a plain, so that the temple might stand above it.

The sons of Noah—Shem, Ham, and Japheth—settled from the mountains into the plains. And Noah, having planted a vineyard, drank of the wine and became drunk and lay uncovered. And Ham, seeing the nakedness of his father, told his brothers, as though in mockery of his father. But they, putting the garment upon their backs, covered their father's nakedness, going backwards and not looking upon their father. Therefore, when Noah had come to himself, he requited the others with blessings, but cursed Ham. And the plain in which the sons of Noah dwelt was called Shinar. And as many children were born to each and went forward into generations, their descendants were multiplied. Now a certain Nimrod, a grandson of Ham, who first appeared as a giant upon the earth, bold and mighty of hand, taking the lead over the rest, turned affairs toward tyranny, and proposed to them to build a tower, made of baked brick and bitumen. And God, seeing them thus gone mad, made them of different tongues and unable to understand one another's speech, through the division of languages. And the place in which they were building the tower is now called Babylon, because of the confusion concerning speech; for the Hebrews call confusion "Babel." And thereafter they are scattered by the diversity of tongues, so that every continent and island was filled with them.

When the descendants of Noah had been scattered, the nations were formed and named from them. Japheth, then, begot seven sons, who went forth from the mountains Taurus and Amanus—in Asia as far as the river Tanais, and in Europe as far as Gadeira; and from their names nations too were called: the Gomarites from Gomer, who are now called Galatians; Magog named those descended from him Magogites, and they are now called Scythians. From Javan the Ionians and all the Greeks were named, and from Madai the Madaeans, who are now called Medes. Tubal named those from him Thobelians; these are the Iberians. Meshech founded the race of the Meschenians; these are reckoned to be the Cappadocians. Tiras called those from him Tirasians, who were later renamed Thracians. And of the descendants of Japheth, those called Rheginians were brought forth from Ashkenaz, while the Riphathaeans—so they formerly called the Paphlagonians—are believed to draw their descent from Riphath; and the Thorgamaeans inscribe Thorgama as their ancestor, who were later renamed Phrygians. Elisha became the founder of the Elisaeans, who are the Aeolians. And Tarshish was the ancestor of the Tarshishaeans; for in old times the Cilicians were called Tarshishaeans, whence the most notable of the cities among them is called Tarsus, the theta having been changed into tau; for so it is written by Josephus concerning Tarsus. But others say that Perseus, having come to the country of the Cilicians and wishing to found a city, in showing the builders the site of the city struck the ground with the sole of his foot, and from this the city was named Tarsus. And Kittim settled the island Chettima; this is Cyprus, so called by the Greeks because of the goddess among them, Aphrodite, whom they call Cypris. The sons of Ham held the land from Syria and the mountains Amanus and Lebanon, and they seized whatever of it faced the sea, as far as the ocean. And from Cush came the Cushites; these are the Ethiopians. Mizraim became the forefather of the Mestraeans; so the Egyptians are called, and the country of Egypt is named Mestren. Phut settled Libya, and called the people of the country Phutians, and the country itself Phute. But its name was afterward changed to Libya, from Libyos a son of Mizraim. Canaan, settling the land later called Judaea, named it Canaanitis and those from it Canaanites. The sons of Mizraim held the land from Gaza to Egypt. Only the portion of Philistim preserved its name, which the Greeks have named Palestine. Sidonios, the firstborn son of Canaan, raised up a city in Phoenicia, calling it Sidon. Amathi founded the city Amathe, which the Macedonians renamed Epiphaneia after one of the Ptolemies called Epiphanes. To Shem the son of Noah five children are born, who dwell in Asia as far as the ocean toward India, beginning from the Euphrates. Elam, then, left the Elamites, who are the founders of the Persians; Asshur settles the city Nineveh and named those under him Assyrians; and Arphaxad was the forefather of the Chaldaeans; Aram named those later called Syrians Aramaeans after himself; and Lud brought forth the Ludians, who were afterward called Lydians. And of the sons of Aram, who were four, one settles Trachonitis and Damascus, which lies between Palestine and Coele-Syria, another settles Armenia, and the other the Bactrians. The son of Arphaxad was Kenan, and the son of Kenan was Salah. He was the father of Eber. And Eber begot Peleg, so called because of the division of the earth; for when the division of the men of that time took place, then too came the division of the earth; for the Hebrews name division "phalek." And the nation of the Hebrews was called from Eber in the beginning. The son of Peleg was Reu, and Reu was the father of Serug, who begot Nahor, and from Nahor came Terah, and from Terah Abraham.

When Absalom had come to Jerusalem, he said to Hushai, who came to him, "Why, being a companion of my father, have you come to me, leaving him?" And he said, "I will be with him whom God has chosen, and I will follow him who has been chosen by all the people." Absalom asked Ahithophel what he should do. And he counselled him to lie with his father's concubines, so that thus all might know that the enmity between him and his father was irreconcilable. And Absalom did according to this counsel. When Ahithophel asked for ten thousand men, that he might at once pursue after King David and those with him, who were exhausted from their toil, and might strike David down and turn the rest back, Absalom asked Hushai concerning the counsel. He declared it not good, saying, "You are not ignorant of the valour and experience of your father and those with him. I think it necessary that you gather an army from the whole country, and so yourself march against your father and command the war in person, and you will certainly conquer, joining battle with few by means of many." And Absalom and those with him said, "The counsel of Hushai is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." Hushai charged Zadok and Abiathar the priests to make all this known to David. They sent to David men to inform him of what had happened. It was reported to Absalom about these men, and he pursued them. Knowing this, they took refuge in a certain house, and going down into a well they hid themselves and were not discovered, and coming out from there they reported to David what had been disclosed. He by night crossed the Jordan with those with him. Ahithophel, however, finding himself outdone, and knowing that ill would befall Absalom, went off to his house and hanged himself.

When David numbered those with him he found four thousand. And he divided the army into three parts, and set over each a general; but he himself was not permitted by his friends to march out with them, since they said that if they were routed with him present, they would fall from all hope, but if he were preserved, hope would still be left to them. He therefore sent his people out to fight, and exhorted them to spare Absalom if they should conquer. When the battle was joined, David's men prevailed, and they pursued Absalom as he fled. Carried upon a mule, and entering a thicket, his hair was caught in a great oak—for he wore his hair very long—and he was left hanging from the oak, while the mule went on. Someone, seeing Absalom hanging thus, informed Joab. He, striking him with three arrows in the heart, put him to death, and sent the man to announce the victory to the king. When the victory was reported to him, he asked whether his son was alive; and hearing that he was dead, he wept aloud. Joab, coming to the king, persuaded him by what he said to cease his mourning; and he ceased, and showing himself to the soldiers, praised them. And all submitted to him as before. He went off to Jerusalem; and as he went, Shimei met him, asking pardon for the wrongs he had committed. The king swore to remit the offence both to him and to all who had transgressed against him. Mephibosheth too met him. And the king asked why he had not shared in his flight. He said that Ziba was most to blame, in not having prepared for him what was needed for the departure; and that he himself, being lamed in his feet, was unable to follow; and that Ziba had also maliciously slandered him and lied against him. To this David granted him pardon and ordered that half of his estate be restored to him.

When he too had passed away, the kingdom passed to his brother, called Baltasar, against whom Cyrus marched with the Persians and Medes. Now this man, holding a banquet for his nobles, and reclining with his concubines and growing drunk, ordered the sacred vessels to be brought which Nabuchodonosor had plundered from Jerusalem and dedicated to his own gods; and when they were brought, those which his father had not used, he himself used, and while drinking he blasphemed against God. He saw, then, the joints of a man's hand coming forth from the wall and writing upon the plaster of the wall; and he was beside himself, and his form was changed. And calling the Chaldaeans and the magi he demanded the interpretation of the letters, and proclaimed that he would give great rewards to whoever should make clear their meaning; but the writing was unknown to all. While the king was in despondency and confusion, his grandmother, seeing him, said, "If Baltasar the Jew be sent for, who explained to Nabuchodonosor many things which no one else could declare, he will signify to you the secret of these syllables; for the holy spirit of God is in him." At once, therefore, calling Baltasar, that is Daniel, the ruler asked him to make plain to him about the writing, and not to hold back, even though its meaning were grievous; and he promised to give him as reward to be clothed in purple and a golden necklace, and the third part of the rule. But Daniel refused the gifts, and said that the writing announced to him the end of his life, because he had not been chastened by those things for which his father had been punished for his impiety, but had used the vessels of God with his concubines for service. He read the letters thus, "Mane Thekel Phares," and interpreting their meaning he said, "God has numbered the time of your life and of your rule, and it has come down to very little"—for the word, translated into Greek, would be "number." Thus he interpreted the "mane"; and "thekel," he said, signifies a weight; "having set, then, the measure of your kingdom, God shows that it is brought low and broken"; and "thekel" signifies a fragment in the Greek tongue. And "phares," the prophet interpreting as "division"—for this is what the word, rendered into Greek, signifies—he said that his kingdom would be divided by God among the Persians and Medes. Thus, then, Daniel read what was written on the wall and made such an interpretation of those syllables. And grief seized the king. A little later the prophet's prediction came to pass, when Cyrus the king of the Persians marched against him, by whom both Babylon was taken and Baltasar killed in the capture. There are some who say that on that very night, on which he saw the hand writing, both the city was taken and he was slain.

After the capture of Babylon the prophet Daniel was removed to Media by Darius the Mede, who was also named Cyaxares and was Cyrus's maternal uncle, being the son of Astyages who had reigned over the Medes, and he was deemed worthy of all honour. Being thus, he was envied by the leading men among the Medes, and they contrived a way by which they hoped to destroy him. For seeing him pray to God thrice a day, they came to Cyaxares, that is Darius, asking him to make a law that for thirty days no one should pray to the gods, nor make request of any one save the king himself, and that whoever did not keep the law should be cast into the den of lions. He, ignorant of the plot being brewed against Daniel by them, set forth a decree ordaining what was said. The others, then, kept quiet according to the decree, but Daniel, according to his custom, prayed to God. And the satraps accused him to the king, and according to the law demanded that he be cast into the den of lions. When the prophet had been cast there, the king sealed the stone upon the mouth and withdrew. In anguish and grief he passed the night sleepless; for he hoped that Daniel would not be harmed by the beasts, knowing that the holy spirit of God was in him, but nevertheless in his fear he was anxious lest some ill befall him, not fully knowing, as a barbarian, the power of God. As soon as day dawned he stood by the den and called Daniel; and he answered. And the king ordered the prophet to be drawn up at once, and seeing him untouched and unharmed he was amazed. When his accusers said that the lions were sated with food and for this reason did not touch Daniel, the king, hating them for their wickedness and understanding the device and guile against the prophet, ordered abundant food to be set before the beasts, and when they were sated he ordered the accusers of the prophet to be cast into the den of beasts, "that we may know," he said, "whether the lions refrain from touching them through being sated." When those wicked men were at once torn apart, it became clear to all that some divine power had preserved Daniel, muzzling the beasts. Therefore the king magnified the God of the prophet, and held him in greater honour.

Now Tryphon destroyed Antiochus, who was also called the God, after he had reigned four years, having been his guardian. He gave out that the boy had died of disease, and promised the soldiers money if they would make him king. They, hoping to gain much, chose him as their ruler. Having received the kingdom, Tryphon laid aside his pretence; and the army, hating him, went over to Cleopatra the wife of Demetrius, who was shut up in Seleucia. While Antiochus, who was called Soter and was the brother of Demetrius, was wandering and shut in on every side because of Tryphon, Cleopatra sent for him, inviting him to marriage and to the kingdom; for she feared lest the people of Seleucia should give the city to Tryphon. So Antiochus, coming to Seleucia, set out against Tryphon, and defeating him drove him out of upper Syria, and besieged him when he had fled to a certain fortress, and invited the high priest Simon to friendship. Simon accepted the invitation, and supplied provisions to those besieging Tryphon. Fleeing thence and coming to Apamea, Tryphon was besieged, taken, and destroyed, after he had reigned three years.

But Antiochus, forgetting the services done him by Simon, sent Cendebaeus, charging him to ravage Judaea and to seize Simon. Simon, standing against him, conquered. And he passed the rest of his life in peace, having ruled Judaea for eight years. He died, plotted against by Ptolemy his son-in-law. The wife of Simon and his two sons were seized and bound, but the third, John, who was also called Hyrcanus, escaped, and was received by the people of Jerusalem on account of his father's benefactions, when Ptolemy came they thrust him away. Having recovered his ancestral priesthood, Hyrcanus marched against Ptolemy, who was in a fortress called Dagon. He prevailed in the siege, but was overcome by pity for his mother and brothers; for Ptolemy, bringing them up onto the wall, tortured them within his sight. But his mother begged him not to be softened on her account. While the siege thus dragged on, the seventh year came, in which it is the custom of the Jews to rest; and on account of this Ptolemy, released from the war, killed the mother of Hyrcanus and his brothers, and fled to Zeno, called Cotylas, the ruler of Philadelphia. Antiochus, angry with Simon for what he had suffered, came against Judaea, and overrunning the land besieged Hyrcanus; and raising very high towers on the northern side of the city, from them he assaulted the wall. But he accomplished nothing, both because of the courage of those within and because of the strength of the walls and the abundance of water from a recent rainfall. Hyrcanus, fearing lest necessities should fail them, chose out only the fighting men of the multitude and thrust the rest out of the city; but Antiochus would not let them depart, and so, remaining outside the walls, they were dying. Those within, pitying them, received them back again. When the feast of Tabernacles came, Hyrcanus, sending to Antiochus, asked for a truce of seven days on account of the feast. Antiochus both gave the truce and sent a costly sacrifice with offerings; whom, for his piety toward the divine, they called the Pious. Knowing the reverence of Antiochus toward God, Hyrcanus sent an embassy, asking that their ancestral form of government be restored to them. Antiochus said that, if they would surrender their arms, and agree to pay tribute on behalf of the other cities except Judaea, and receive a garrison, he would refrain from war and do the other things they asked. The Jews accepted the other terms, but did not consent to the garrison; instead they gave hostages and five hundred talents of silver. When Antiochus yielded on these terms, the siege was raised. Hyrcanus, opening the tomb of David, took from it three thousand talents of silver. Making friendship with Antiochus, he received him into the city, and joined his expedition against the Parthians; where Antiochus, fighting against Arsaces, perished together with the greater part of his army.

His brother Demetrius became successor to the kingdom of Syria, Arsaces having released him when Antiochus marched against the Parthians. When Antiochus died, Hyrcanus took many cities of Syria and others of Idumaea. And having subdued the Idumaeans, he permitted them to remain in the country if they would be circumcised and follow Jewish customs. For the sake of their homelands they submitted to circumcision and the rest. Demetrius, resolving to march against Hyrcanus, was checked, the Syrians and the soldiers hating him for his wickedness, and sending an embassy to Ptolemy Physcon to give them one of the kindred of Seleucus to take over the kingdom. He sent Alexander, called Zebinas. When a battle was joined between him and Demetrius, Demetrius was routed and fled to Ptolemais, and not being received by his wife Cleopatra, escaped to Tyre, where he was captured and, after suffering much, was destroyed. Alexander, having taken over the kingdom, made friendship with Hyrcanus. But when Antiochus Grypus, the son of Demetrius, rose against him, he was defeated in battle and perished.

This Antiochus, having become king of Syria, fought for many years over the kingdom with his brother Antiochus, surnamed Cyzicenus because he was reared in Cyzicus. This Cyzicenus was the son of Antiochus who died among the Parthians, the brother of Demetrius, so that he was a half-brother of Antiochus Grypus; for Cleopatra had lived with the two brothers, first with Demetrius and then with Antiochus, as has been written before, and by Demetrius she bore Antiochus Grypus, and by Antiochus Soter, the brother of Demetrius, she bore Antiochus Cyzicenus. While these were fighting one another, Hyrcanus remained at peace, and despising the two Antiochi, he revolted, no longer paying them anything; and at his leisure he reaped the fruit of Judaea, so that he gathered an immeasurable quantity of treasure. Marching also against Samaria, he besieged it through his sons Aristobulus and Antigonus. When famine pressed the city, the Samaritans summoned Antiochus Cyzicenus to their aid. He, joining battle with the forces of Aristobulus, was defeated; then again, gathering a multitude, he ravaged the country of Hyrcanus, that he might thus compel him to raise the siege. But losing many of his men, he departed to Tripolis. Hyrcanus took Samaria and utterly destroyed it. It is said that on the very day on which his sons were fighting Antiochus, he himself, as high priest, burning incense alone in the temple, heard a voice saying that his sons had just then conquered Antiochus; and going out he announced to the multitude what he had heard. And so it was.

Hyrcanus, having prospered, was envied by the Jews, and was especially hated by the Pharisees. These are one of the sects among the Jews, of which there are three. Now the Pharisees hold the doctrine of fate, but also that it falls to us that some things happen and others do not. The Essenes hold that fate is mistress of all things, and that all things befall men from it. The Sadducees reject fate, and place all things in our power, teaching that we are ourselves the causes of our good things, and that we choose the worse from our own want of counsel. Now the Pharisees had formerly been on friendly terms with Hyrcanus, for he had been a disciple of theirs; but it happened, from a certain cause, that he came to have enmity with them. And these men had great power with the multitude. Hyrcanus joined himself to the party of the Sadducees, breaking off from the Pharisees, and resolved to abolish the ordinances handed down by them. For the Sadducees said that those things ought to be held lawful which were written, but not to observe the things from tradition. For these reasons Hyrcanus was hated by the Pharisees. Having lived prosperously for thirty-one years, he died, leaving five sons. It is said that he was thought worthy of prophecy, and foretold concerning his two elder sons that they would not remain masters of affairs.

When Hyrcanus died, Aristobulus succeeded to the rule; and resolving to change it into a kingdom, he set a diadem upon himself, four hundred and eighty-one years after the people returned from Babylon to Jerusalem. He imprisoned the rest of his brothers and his mother, who had quarrelled with him over the rule, but loved Antigonus, who was next to him, and thought him worthy of equal honour. His mother he destroyed by starvation; and he made away with his brother Antigonus also, trusting in slanders. For when Antigonus had returned brilliantly from a campaign, Aristobulus was sick; and as the feast of Tabernacles was being kept, Antigonus went up to the temple with his men-at-arms about him splendidly adorned. Those who slandered him to his brother said that he had come to the feast not as a private man, but in royal splendour, and that, going up with so great a guard of soldiers, he was plotting against him.

Aristobulus, taking thought both for his own safety and for his brother, set bodyguards in a certain dark underground passage, charging them to spare his brother if he came unarmed, but to kill him if he came with weapons; and he sent to Antigonus, bidding him come unarmed. But the wife of Aristobulus and those who agreed with her against Antigonus persuaded the messenger to tell Antigonus, "Your brother, hearing that you have had new arms made, asks you to come armed, that he may see them." Antigonus, suspecting nothing, went, clad in his full armour; and when he came to the tower of Strato, where the place was without light, he was killed by the bodyguards. A certain Judas, an Essene by sect, who foretold many things and spoke truly, seeing Antigonus then passing by the temple, cried out and prayed to die, as one proved false while Antigonus still lived; for he had foretold that Antigonus would die on that day at the tower of Strato; and that place was six hundred stades distant, so that it was impossible for Antigonus to be there, the day being already on the wane. While Judas was saying this, it was announced that Antigonus had been killed in the underground passage, which itself was named the tower of Strato, with the same name as the coastal Caesarea.

Such was the end of Antigonus; and justice for the fratricide at once overtook Aristobulus. For when his bowels were destroyed and he began to bring up blood, one of those who served him, carrying it out, slipped at the very spot where Antigonus had been slain, which still bore stains of his blood, and poured it out, so that the blood of both was mingled. When a cry arose from those who saw it, Aristobulus, learning what had happened, groaned and was moved to tears, and said, "So I was not, after all, to escape the notice of God in such impious deeds." And adding some other words, he died, having reigned a year.

Salome his wife, who was also called Alexandra, having released her husband's brothers — for Aristobulus had held them in bonds — set up as king Jannaeus, also called Alexander, who excelled in age and was most moderate. Having received the kingdom, he killed one of his brothers, who was making revolution, but honoured the other, who lived without meddling in affairs. Having made certain wars against certain peoples, and in part prevailing and in part being defeated, at last he took up arms also against his own countrymen, who rose against him. For when there was a feast and he had gone up to the altar to sacrifice, the multitude pelted him with citrons — it being the custom at the feast of Tabernacles to hold in the hands wands of palm and citron — and heaped insults upon him. Provoked by this, Alexander killed about six thousand of them. Then, joining battle with the Arabs and being defeated, he fled to Jerusalem; and when the nation attacked him in his misfortune, fighting against it for six years — for he kept Pisidians and Cilicians — he destroyed no fewer than fifty thousand. For these things he was hated still more, so that, when he asked what should be done that their enmity might cease, the multitude cried out that he should die. And after this too the Jews fought against Alexander, and very many were destroyed. Having shut up the most powerful of them in a certain city, he besieged it, and mastering them led them away to Jerusalem. And feasting with his women in a conspicuous place, he committed a most savage deed, crucifying eight hundred of them, and slaughtering their children and wives before the eyes of the men while they still lived. This cruel deed persuaded those of the opposite party, who were about eight thousand, to flee. And Alexander from then enjoyed quiet.

Then Antiochus, called Dionysius, marched against Judaea. And when a fierce battle had taken place against the Jews, Antiochus died in the war, while conquering and going to the aid of the part that was hard pressed. When he was dead, his army fled and was destroyed by famine. After Antiochus, Aretas reigned over Coele Syria, and marching against Judaea, and conquering Alexander in battle, withdrew on terms.

Alexander, however, afterward took many cities of the Idumaeans and Cilicians and Phoenicians and Syrians, and having spent a third year on campaign, returned, the Jews receiving him eagerly because of his good fortune. Then, falling sick from drunkenness, and wrestling for three years with a quartan fever, he did not refrain from his campaigns. The queen, seeing him now given up, lamented for herself and her children. But he advised her to hide his death from the soldiers, until she should take the place — for he happened to be besieging one — and then, coming to Jerusalem as from a victory, to grant some authority to the Pharisees. For they could make the nation well disposed toward her; and he said that he himself had given offence to the nation because of these men, who had been insulted by him. "So you," he said, "summoning their rulers, allow them to use my corpse as they wish, as one who had grievously outraged them, and promise to do nothing against their judgment. If you speak thus, I shall be buried lavishly, and you will rule securely." Having given his wife this counsel, he died, after ruling twenty-seven years, having lived forty-nine. And Alexandra, having ordered all things according to her husband's advice, made the Pharisees well disposed toward herself and secured the kingdom, and gave her husband a burial more splendid than those of the kings before him.

Two sons had been born to Alexander, Hyrcanus and Aristobulus. Hyrcanus was sluggish in character and unfitted for the management of affairs, but the younger was energetic. Their mother appointed Hyrcanus high priest because of his lack of ambition, and committed everything to the Pharisees, and ordered the multitude to obey them; and she herself held the name of the kingdom, but the Pharisees held the power. The country was at peace, only the Pharisees stirring up trouble and persuading her to kill those who had advised Alexander to the destruction of the eight hundred. They slew one of them for the time, and after him others one upon another, until the powerful men, coming into the palace, and Aristobulus with them — for he was not pleased with what was being done — by speaking much and bewailing those already destroyed, moved those present to pity for those in danger and to tears. And Aristobulus on this account blamed his mother; but she had nothing she could do.

At this time it was announced that Tigranes had invaded Syria with a great army and would come against Judaea. This frightened both the nation and the queen, and they sent him many and very valuable gifts and envoys while he was besieging Ptolemais. He both received these and made fair promises. But just as he had sacked Ptolemais, it was announced to him that Acelaus had set out for Armenia, and on this account he withdrew to his own land. When the queen fell grievously sick, Aristobulus secretly slipped away and went to the fortresses where his father's friends were stationed, only his wife being privy to the deed, and was received by them. When his mother learned of his flight and that he had won over all the fortresses, she and the nation were in great disorder; and they placed his wife and children in the fortress above the temple. Hyrcanus and the elders of the Jews, learning that in fifteen days Aristobulus had mastered twenty-two strongholds and gathered much money and assembled an army, begged the queen to give her counsel concerning Aristobulus. But she said that affairs no longer concerned her, since she was already failing, and left them to do what they should judge expedient. And not long after she died, having reigned nine years and lived seventy-three.

When Alexandra was dead, Aristobulus at once took up war against his brother, and many of Hyrcanus's soldiers deserted to Aristobulus. Hyrcanus fled to the citadel, where the wife and children of Aristobulus had earlier been shut up. Coming to terms, the brothers dissolved their enmity, so that Aristobulus should reign, and Hyrcanus should live without meddling in affairs. Having confirmed the agreement with oaths, the one withdrew to the palace, and Hyrcanus to the house of Aristobulus.

A certain Antipater, an Idumaean, a friend of Hyrcanus, factious and energetic and abounding in much money, conversing secretly with the powerful among the Jews, and slandering Aristobulus to Hyrcanus as plotting to kill him, persuaded him to flee to Aretas the king of the Arabs. Hyrcanus sent Antipater to Aretas to receive pledges that he would not surrender him to his enemies if he came to him. Having received the pledges, Antipater returned, and taking Hyrcanus with him by night, brought him to the place called Petra, to Aretas. Hyrcanus begged him to bring him down into Judaea and restore him to the kingdom, promising, if this were done, to give him the territory and the twelve cities which his father Alexander had taken from the Arabs. And Aretas marched against Aristobulus and prevailed in the battle. When many deserted to Hyrcanus, Aristobulus fled to Jerusalem. And the Arab, assaulting the temple, besieged Aristobulus, the people also joining Hyrcanus, only the priests remaining with Aristobulus. A certain Onias, a just man and dear to God, who, when there was once a drought, had by prayer entreated God and broken the lack of rain, the Jews asked to pray against Aristobulus and those with him; but he would not. When he was compelled, he said, "O God, king of all, since both those who stand with me are yours, and the besieged priests are yours, I beg you neither to grant these men's prayers against those, nor those against these." At once they surrounded the man and stoned him. But not long after, the divine power exacted justice on them for their impiety, a violent wind blowing and destroying the fruit of the land.

Scaurus, sent into Syria by Pompey, who was warring against Tigranes in Armenia, received envoys from both Aristobulus and Hyrcanus, each asking for an alliance. Receiving four hundred talents from Aristobulus, he joined himself to him. And ordering Aretas to withdraw or be judged an enemy of the Romans, he raised the siege. When it was raised, Aristobulus marched against Aretas and Hyrcanus, and joining battle conquered. Not long after, when Pompey had come to Damascus, envoys came from many places and from Judaea, bringing a great gift from Aristobulus, a golden vine of five hundred talents. Josephus says he saw this at Rome, dedicated to Zeus in the Capitol. And again there came to him Antipater on behalf of Hyrcanus and Nicodemus on behalf of Aristobulus. He ordered the disputants themselves to come. When the Jews and their leaders had come to Damascus, some asked that they not be ruled by a king; for it was their ancestral custom to be ruled by the high priests, but these men, being of that family, had changed the rule into a kingdom. Hyrcanus accused his brother, that, when the rule had been allotted to him because of his greater age, it had been taken from him by Aristobulus, and he strung together many other charges against him. More than a thousand of the most respected Jews joined him in saying these things, Antipater having arranged it. Aristobulus, as the cause of Hyrcanus's losing the rule, brought forward his nature, which was inactive and on that account contemptible; and said that he himself had taken it up of necessity, for fear lest it pass to others; and that he was named what his father too had been. Pompey condemned the violence of Aristobulus, but speaking gently with them then, ordered them to keep quiet for a time, and promised that, coming into the country, he would arrange everything. Aristobulus, however, did not wait, but departed for Judaea. Angered, Pompey marched against him. When he had fled together to a stronghold called Alexandrium, Pompey ordered him to come to him. He, his friends asking him not to make war on the Romans, came down, and after pleading his case returned to the place from which he had come. When Pompey ordered him to hand over the strongholds and to write with his own hand to the garrison commanders — for they had been forbidden otherwise to abandon them — he obeyed, but, in vexation, withdrew to Jerusalem and prepared for war. While Pompey was marching against him, the death of Mithridates was announced to him, brought about by his son Pharnaces. When Pompey was near Jericho, where balsam is grown, the choicest of perfumes, which, when the bushes are cut with a sharp stone, oozes forth like sap, Aristobulus came to him and begged him to cease from war, giving money and receiving him into Jerusalem, so that he might do as he wished. Pompey, granting him pardon, sent Gabinius for the money and the city. But the soldiers of Aristobulus not allowing the agreement to be fulfilled, Gabinius returned without success. Pompey therefore came against the city, having imprisoned Aristobulus. Those within were not of one mind. For some thought to receive Pompey, but the partisans of Aristobulus thought the contrary; and they, having seized the temple, prepared for a siege. The others handed over the city and the palace to Pompey. He, encamping within, besieged the temple. When it was taken about the third month, the enemy rushed in and slaughtered those in it; but they no less continued to perform the sacred rites and to sacrifice. Everything was filled with slaughter; for some of the Jews were slain by the Romans, others by one another, or even threw themselves down from the heights. Pompey passed into the inner, untrodden part of the temple, and some of those about him, and they saw what was unseen to all but the high priests. He touched none of the offerings or the treasures in it, out of piety. The next day, ordering the temple to be purified and sacrifice to be made according to the law, he handed over the high priesthood to Hyrcanus, putting to death by the axe those responsible for the war, and making Jerusalem tributary to the Romans. Pompey, departing for Rome, took with him Aristobulus in bonds and his children. He had two daughters and as many sons, of whom the elder, Alexander, escaped and later overran Judaea, Hyrcanus being unable to withstand him.

When Gabinius came to Syria, he sent Marcus Antonius with an army against Alexander. A battle taking place, the Romans killed about three thousand of the enemy and took no fewer alive. When Alexander fled to a stronghold called Alexandrium, Gabinius besieged it. Alexander therefore sent an embassy to Gabinius asking pardon, and handed over the strongholds he held. The high priest Hyrcanus was brought down to Jerusalem by Gabinius. But Aristobulus, escaping from Rome and coming into Judaea, tried to fortify Alexandrium, which had just been demolished. Gabinius sent men to prevent him or even to seize him. Many of the Jews flocked to Aristobulus, of whom the greater part happened to be unarmed. These Aristobulus dismissed, but the armed ones, about eight thousand, he kept with him. When a battle was joined between them and the Romans, the Jews were defeated and fled, and some were killed, while the rest were scattered. Aristobulus fled to Machaerus with his son Antigonus, who had escaped from Rome with him. After two days, being wounded, he was captured, and with his son Antigonus was led as a prisoner to Gabinius, and sent back again to Rome, where he was kept in bonds, after reigning and serving as high priest three years. Gabinius departed for Egypt. Returning thence, he found Alexander the son of Aristobulus invading the country with a great army and killing all the Romans he met. Engaging him near Mount Itabyrium, where he was leading thirty thousand Jews, Gabinius killed about ten thousand. Having settled affairs in Jerusalem as Antipater wished, and having performed other great deeds of generalship, he departed for Rome, handing over the command to Crassus. This Crassus, coming into Judaea, took all the treasures in the temple, which Pompey had not touched, amounting to two thousand talents, and stripping the temple of all its adornment, plundered it, reckoned at eight thousand talents of gold. He took also a beam of hammered gold made of three hundred minas. The mina among the Jews weighs two pounds and a half. Taking these, he set out against the Parthians, and was destroyed together with his army. Cassius, fleeing thence into Syria, went up into Judaea. Antipater had great power with him, and among the Idumaeans, among whom he married a wife from Arabia, named Cypros, by whom he had four sons — Phasael and Herod, Joseph and Pheroras — and a daughter, Salome. Some time later Julius Gaius Caesar, having mastered Rome after Pompey and the greater part of the senate had fled from it, released Aristobulus and sent him into Syria with an army. But those who favoured Pompey, getting in first, destroyed Aristobulus with poison. Scipio, at Pompey's instruction, beheaded Aristobulus's son Alexander. After Pompey's death, Antipater made himself useful in many ways to Caesar, who was warring in Egypt, so that Caesar employed him throughout the whole war; in which it happened that he too was wounded. Antigonus the son of Aristobulus came at that time to Caesar and begged him to take pity on himself, who had been driven from his rule, and reminded him of his father, and how he died on Caesar's account. Antipater, who was present, made his defence. His words being judged the stronger, Caesar confirmed the high priesthood to Hyrcanus, and appointed Antipater procurator of Judaea. When Caesar departed for Rome, Antipater set in order the affairs of Judaea. Seeing Hyrcanus slow and sluggish, he appointed Phasael, the eldest of his sons, general of Jerusalem and the surrounding parts, and set Herod, who was next to him and very young, over Galilee.

Herod, being noble in spirit, made his command an occasion for displaying his valour, and seizing the chief brigand Ezekias, who was plundering the parts of Syria near at hand with a great band, he killed him and very many of those with him; whence he was loved by the Syrians. On this account he also became known to Sextus Caesar, who was a kinsman of the great Caesar and governor of Syria. Phasael too emulated his brother. They did these things that Antipater might obtain royal honour from the nation. But the rulers of the Jews on this account envied Antipater and his sons, and feared, seeing Herod violent and bold and enamoured of tyranny, and they accused Antipater to Hyrcanus, and incited him against him and his sons, saying that they were not procurators of the affairs of the kingdom, but masters. For Herod, they said, had killed Ezekias and many of those with him, though the law forbade a man to be put to death, even were he wicked, unless he had first been condemned by the council. Hyrcanus was stirred by this to anger. And the mothers of those murdered by Herod further kindled his anger, asking that he be brought to justice for what he had done. Hyrcanus, being moved, summoned Herod to be tried. He came with a band sufficient to keep him from going to trial defenceless and unguarded. Entering the council with his band, he struck terror into all, and no one dared to accuse him, but there was perplexity as to what should be done. But a certain man named Samaeas, a just man and confident as a lion, said, "Men, I know of no one summoned to trial who has stood thus, nor, I think, do you; but everyone who is to be judged stands in the posture of one afraid. But this excellent Herod, fleeing a charge of murder, stands with men-at-arms around him, ready, if he is condemned according to the law, to kill us. Yet I do not blame Herod, but you, who have granted him such license. Know, then, that God is just, and that this man, whom you now wish to release for Hyrcanus's sake, will one day punish you and Hyrcanus himself." That this came to pass the account will show as it proceeds. Hyrcanus postponed the trial to another day, and secretly advised Herod to slip away from the city. So Herod departed, and the members of the council were indignant. When Sextus sold to Herod for money the command of Coele Syria, not much time passed before Herod came with an army, angry against Hyrcanus because he had been called to trial at all. But his father and brother prevented him from attacking Jerusalem.

Such was the state of affairs in Judaea; but in Syria there was disorder, from a cause of this kind. Caecilius Bassus, one of those who favoured Pompey, killed Sextus Caesar by treachery, and himself mastered affairs. When the generals of Julius Caesar set out against Bassus, Antipater, through his sons, fought as their ally, remembering the benefits he had received from Caesar. While the war dragged on, Marcus came from Rome to the command of Sextus. Caesar, however, was killed at Rome by Brutus and Cassius and their party. When war broke out over the death of Caesar, and those in authority were scattered here and there for the gathering of armies, Cassius came into Syria, and going around it gathered arms and soldiers, and levied very heavy tribute, and exacted from Judaea seven hundred talents of silver, the collection of which Antipater divided between his two sons. So Herod, being the first to bring in what was assigned to him to Cassius, was especially his friend. Malichus would have been killed by Cassius, had not Hyrcanus checked his impulse, mollifying him with a hundred talents through Antipater. But when Cassius had now departed from Judaea, Malichus plotted against Antipater, since, if he were destroyed, there would be security for Hyrcanus in his rule. This did not escape Antipater, but he guarded himself; and Malichus denied it with oaths. Marcus, who was general in Syria, would nearly have killed Malichus, had not Antipater, by entreating him, saved him. Cassius and Marcus, gathering an army, committed the care of it to Herod, making him general of Coele Syria, and promising to declare him king of Judaea after the war, which had then been joined against Antony and the young Caesar. Then Malichus, having corrupted Hyrcanus's cup-bearer with money, killed Antipater with poison; for both were feasting with Hyrcanus. When the sons of Antipater learned of the plot, Malichus denied it. To Herod it at once seemed right to avenge his father's murder, but Phasael wished rather to deal with Malichus by guile, that they might not become the cause of civil war. They therefore pretended to believe Malichus's denial. When a feast came at Jerusalem, Herod came with an army to the city; but Hyrcanus, persuaded by Malichus, prevented his entrance into the city, on the pretext that a foreign crowd ought not to mix with the multitude keeping itself pure. But Herod, paying no heed to the words, entered the city by night. Malichus still held to his pretence, weeping for Antipater and calling him a friend, but secretly took measures for his own safety. When Cassius took Laodicea, both went off to him. And Herod was waiting there to exact justice from Malichus; but he, suspecting the matter, since his son was a hostage in Tyre, planned to steal him away and to escape into Judaea and seize the rule. But Herod, suspecting Malichus's intention, sent secretly beforehand to Tyre and persuaded the tribunes to go out against Malichus and destroy him. For it had already been determined for them by Cassius to assist Herod in a just deed. They, meeting him near the city, stabbed him to death. Hyrcanus from fear was speechless. Recovering, he asked how Malichus had been slain; and learning that it was by Cassius's order, he praised the deed, saying that Malichus was a wicked man and a plotter against his country.

When Cassius departed from Syria to Antony, Herod distinguished himself in various ways, and meeting in battle Aristobulus's son Antigonus, who had just set foot on the borders of the land of the Jews, he conquered and drove him from its borders. Whence, when he came to Jerusalem, both the people and Hyrcanus crowned him. He betrothed the granddaughter of Hyrcanus, the daughter of Alexander the son of Aristobulus. He had had earlier another wife, a commoner, called Doris, by whom a son Antipater was born to him, the eldest of the rest.

When Antony and Caesar had defeated Cassius and Brutus near Philippi, the one went off to Gaul, and Antony to Asia. When he was in Bithynia, embassies came to him from everywhere. There were present also Jews accusing Phasael and Herod. But when Herod came to make his defence, Antony treated him with honour, and the accusers were not even thought worthy of a word, Herod having bought this from Antony with money. When Antony came to Ephesus, Hyrcanus sent him a golden crown, and asked that the Jews whom Cassius had enslaved, contrary to the law of war, be set free, and that the land which Cassius had taken from them be restored. Judging the request just, Antony ordered it to be carried into effect. After this, when Antony came into Syria and was mastered by his love for Cleopatra, a hundred of the most powerful Jews came to him and accused Herod and his party, Hyrcanus also being present. Antony asked Hyrcanus which party governed the nation better; and he said that of Herod, being his kinsman. So Antony, being well disposed toward them because of the hospitality of their father, named both tetrarchs and committed to them the affairs of the Jews; and binding ten of the accusers, he would have killed them, had not the brothers interceded. Again a thousand met Antony near Tyre. He, prepossessed by gifts, ordered the local governor to punish the Jews as making revolution. But Herod advised them to depart quickly, that they might not suffer some great evil. When they did not obey, the Romans, rushing out, killed some and wounded many; and the rest, escaping, kept quiet. When the people cried out against Herod, Antony, provoked, killed those whom he had bound.

Antigonus promised Pacorus the king of the Parthians to give a thousand talents and five hundred women, if they would take the rule from Hyrcanus and hand it over to him, and destroy Herod and his party. For these things the Parthians marched against Judaea, bringing back Antigonus; and Herod's party, joining battle with them often, prevailed. But the general of the Parthians came into the city with a few horsemen, supposedly to quell the strife, but in truth to cooperate with Antigonus. When Phasael had entertained him, he persuaded Phasael to go on an embassy to Barzapharnes. And Hyrcanus and Phasael went as envoys, Herod not consenting; and the general escorted them. Barzapharnes at first received them genuinely, then plotted against them. Phasael's party were in suspicion of the barbarians, and learned that they were being watched secretly even by night. It was disclosed to them that they would have been seized, had not the barbarians put it off until Herod should be taken by the Parthians there, lest, learning what concerned them, he should escape. Some advised Phasael to ride off at once, and Ophellius even promised boats for flight, for the sea was near. But he would not abandon Hyrcanus. So they were seized and bound. When Herod learned this, taking the men-at-arms he had by night, and his mother and sister and the girl betrothed to him, the daughter of Hyrcanus's daughter, and the mother of this betrothed, and all the household, he went off toward Idumaea, unnoticed by the enemy. When the carriage overturned on the road, and his mother was in danger of death, he nearly killed himself. Having recovered his mother and provided care for her as the occasion pressed, he marched more vigorously toward the stronghold of Masada. On the way he both fought the pursuing Parthians and the Jews who again attacked him, and conquered and prevailed. But since the multitude following him was large, and the fortress of Masada, toward which they hastened, was not sufficient to receive all, he dismissed the greater part, giving them provisions, and taking with him those who were nimble and the most necessary, he came to the stronghold. And leaving there the women and the household with sufficient provisions, he himself set out for Petra in Arabia. At dawn the Parthians plundered the rest of Jerusalem, even the palace, but kept their hands only from Hyrcanus's treasures, amounting to about eighty talents; and the Parthians afflicted the country.

So Antigonus, having thus been brought into Judaea, received Hyrcanus and Phasael as prisoners. Fearing lest the multitude should restore the kingdom to Hyrcanus, he cut off his ears, the law ordering that those who are to be priests be whole. Phasael, knowing that he was to be slaughtered, since his hands were bound, dashed his head against a rock and so took himself out of life, and deprived the enemy of the pleasure of killing him. But before he entirely expired, hearing that his brother Herod had escaped the enemy, he died with good cheer, leaving an avenger and a punisher of his enemies. Herod hastened to Malchus the king of the Arabs, who had earlier been benefited by him, to receive from him money as ransom for his brother; for he had not yet learned what had befallen him. But when Malchus, through certain men, sent word to him to withdraw, since the Parthians had charged him not to receive him, he answered that he came to give no trouble, but to confer about the most pressing matters. And saying this, he went off to Egypt, and on the way heard what had befallen his brother. Malchus repented, and sent men to turn Herod back; but he was far away. Brought down to Egypt and coming thence to Rome, he told Antony what had befallen him and Phasael, and how Antigonus had been brought into the kingdom by the Parthians for the promise of money and women, and all that he had done and suffered. Pity for Herod's change of fortune came upon Antony. And Caesar too, both for other reasons and to gratify Antony, who grieved greatly for Herod, was the more ready to help. So they presented Herod to the senate, and recounted the benefits of his father and told of his goodwill toward the Romans; and they accused Antigonus, and called him an enemy, both on other grounds and because he had received the rule from the Parthians, slighting the Romans. Antony added that it was also expedient for Herod to be king for the war against the Parthians. This being approved by all, they decreed it.

So Herod received the kingdom, but Antigonus continued to besiege Masada. Those within it were in want of water, so that even Herod's brother Joseph planned to escape with two hundred men to the Arabs; but he was prevented, a rain falling by night. Ventidius, the Roman general sent from Syria to drive back the Parthians, made his way into Judaea, supposedly to aid the besieged, but in fact to extort money from Antigonus. Having fulfilled his purpose, he withdrew, and left Silo with part of the army, so that the bribe might not become evident. Herod, having sailed from Italy to Ptolemais, marched against Antigonus, having gathered a force. Taking Joppa on the way, that the enemy might have no stronghold, he hastened to Masada to rescue his household; and taking them up, he marched toward Jerusalem; and the army with Silo was with him. He encamped outside; but those within, fighting from the wall, drove them back from the towers. And Silo had some of his own soldiers cry out against Herod because of the scarcity of necessities, and began to move the camp as if to withdraw. He did this out of regard for Antigonus, because of the bribe. But Herod begged him to stay, and setting out, brought back a quantity of provisions, so as no longer to leave Silo a pretext for withdrawal. So they were in abundance; and Herod, coming to Samaria, deposited there his mother and the rest of his household, while he himself went off to Galilee. And he won over all of it except those dwelling in the caves. The caves were enclosed in mountains everywhere broken and rugged, surrounded by sharp rocks. These too he mastered, with difficulty but nevertheless. Having settled affairs there, the king set out for Samaria, intending to decide matters by battle with Antigonus. Meanwhile, Pacorus having fallen in war, and the Parthians having been routed by the Romans, Ventidius sent Machaeras with an army as a help to Herod. With him Herod left his brother Joseph, charging him not to take risks nor to quarrel with Machaeras, while he himself hastened to Antony, who was besieging Samosata, a city on the Euphrates. As Herod drew near, Antony sent the army to meet him, and when he came, greeted him, and charged him to assist Sossius; and Herod fulfilled the command. But Joseph the brother of Herod, hastening to Jericho, fell among the forces of Antigonus, and being cut off in difficult ground, died fighting nobly, and lost his whole army. Antigonus, cutting off his head, sold it to his brother Pheroras for fifty talents.

The Galileans, revolting, drowned in the lake those who favoured Herod, and there were many uprisings in Judaea. These things were announced to Herod, together with the death of his brother at Daphne near Antioch. As he hastened on, when he came into Galilee, the enemy met him. Being defeated, they shut themselves up in a certain place; but he hurried to Jericho, wishing to avenge himself on them for his brother. Antigonus sent to Samaria a general named Pappus with a force, giving the enemy the impression of one warring from a position of strength. Herod came against Pappus, and joining battle with the enemy, prevailed, and followed the fugitives into the village, killing whomever he overtook. When the houses were filled with men-at-arms, and many fled up onto the roofs, by pulling down the roofs of the houses he mastered them. As the roofs were pulled down, the lower parts were seen full of soldiers, whom they killed by throwing stones from above. This broke the spirit of the enemy; and Herod would have come at once to Jerusalem with his army and accomplished everything, had not a heavy winter prevented him. Then, it being evening, king Herod entered a certain small room to bathe, and stripping bathed, with one servant attending him. But in the inner chamber some of the enemy had fled together, armed, and were hiding there for fear. And while the king was bathing, one came out with a drawn sword, and after him another, and again another likewise armed, striking no one out of fear, but content if they themselves were saved. Such a danger did Herod escape. The next day, cutting off the head of Pappus, who had already been slain, he sent it to his brother Pheroras in payment for Joseph; for this Pappus had been Joseph's slayer with his own hand.

When the winter ended, he came to Jerusalem and encamped very near the city; and leaving there those who should prepare for the siege, he himself went to Samaria to be wed to the daughter of Alexander, already betrothed to him, as has been recorded. After the marriage he came from Samaria; and Sossius too came with an army. They gathered before the wall of Jerusalem, and raising mounds and bringing up siege-engines, they shook the wall. Those within, generaled with desperation rather than prudence, withstood them. There mounted the wall first twenty chosen men, then centurions of Sossius. For the first wall was taken in forty days, the second in fifteen. When the outer temple and the lower city were taken, the Jews fled together into the inner temple and the upper city. These too were taken, and everything was filled with slaughter. Antigonus, mindful neither of his present fortune nor of his former, came down from the citadel and fell at Sossius's feet. But Sossius, taking no pity on him for his change, mocked him and called him Antigone, and binding him kept him under guard. When the allies rushed to behold the temple and the holy things in the sanctuary, king Herod, exhorting some, threatening others, and even checking some with arms, restrained them, and prevented also the plundering in the city, promising himself to distribute their wages to each from his own funds.
