And so, having preserved the rest of the city, he fulfilled his promises. To Sossius himself he gave most royal gifts. Sossius left Jerusalem, leading Antigonus in bonds to Antony. Herod, fearing lest Antigonus, brought to Rome, should plead his case before the senate, showing himself to be of royal stock and Herod a private man, and that, even if he himself had offended against the Romans, the kingdom belonged to his children, persuaded Antony with much money to kill Antigonus. So he was killed, and the rule was taken from the family of the Asamonaeans, which had lasted a hundred and twenty years, and passed to Herod the son of Antipater, who was of private stock and a commoner's house.

So Herod, having taken up the rule of all Judaea, drew to himself those who favoured him, and punished those who opposed him. He honoured especially Pollio the Pharisee and Samaeas his disciple; for when the siege was being formed, these advised that Herod be received. This Samaeas, as has already been said before, had foretold to Hyrcanus and the judges that Herod, if preserved, would punish them all. He killed forty of the chief men of Antigonus's party and took their property, and there was no end of evil. Hyrcanus, however, who was a prisoner among the Parthians, found the Parthian king Phraates gracious, and being loosed from his bonds, was permitted to dwell in Babylon, where there was a multitude of Jews, who honoured Hyrcanus as high priest and king. When he learned that Herod had taken over the kingdom, he resolved to go over to him, both because of the marriage-connection and supposing that Herod would remember that he had saved him from danger when on trial for murder. The Jews in Babylon asked him to stay, since he was honoured by them as high priest and king, and because, even if he went, he could not obtain the high priesthood, having been maimed in body by Antigonus. So they tried to prevent him, but he would not be persuaded, both longing to return himself and being invited by Herod. Herod sent an embassy to Phraates and sent gifts, asking him not to hinder the kindnesses he wished to show his benefactor. But his zeal was not for Hyrcanus's sake; rather, since he did not rule worthily, fearing reasonable changes, he was eager either to put Hyrcanus out of the way or to keep him for the present in his hands. The Parthian permitting his departure, Hyrcanus went and was treated by Herod with all honour, being called father and given precedence at banquets, and deceived in every way, that he might not perceive that he was being plotted against.

Herod, being cautious about appointing one of the distinguished men as high priest, sent for from Babylon a priest of the more obscure, named Ananel, and assigned to him the high priesthood. But Alexandra, the mother-in-law of Herod, who had a son by Alexander the son of Aristobulus, most beautiful in his prime, called Aristobulus, took the slighting of her son hard; and she wrote to Cleopatra to ask the high priesthood for the boy from Antony. When Antony was rather sluggish about the request, Dellius, coming into Judaea and seeing Aristobulus, admired him, and no less Mariamme, who lived with the king; and he persuaded Alexandra to send Antony portraits of both children; for, he said, when Antony saw them, he would fail of nothing he asked. So she sent the portraits to Antony, but he was ashamed to send for the girl, who was married to Herod, and at the same time he avoided the slanders concerning Cleopatra. He wrote to Herod to send the boy, adding, "if it does not seem burdensome." Herod, judging it not to his advantage that Aristobulus, who was very handsome and superior in birth, should come to Antony, who was powerful as a Roman and prone to loves and easily inclined to pleasures, wrote back that, if the youth left the country, everything would be filled with disorder. And so he excused himself to Antony; but gathering his friends, he blamed Alexandra as plotting that he be deprived of the rule. "But I," he said, "shall not on this account be unjust; instead I now give the priesthood to the youth; for it was because he was altogether a child that I formerly made another high priest." When he had said this, joy and fear together possessed Alexandra — joy because of her son's honour, fear because of Herod's suspicion. And she defended herself in tears, saying that she had been zealous for the priesthood, but had not attempted the kingdom; and that she now accepted the honour for her son, and would be obedient in everything.

Having so conversed, they parted, as if all suspicion were removed. When the high priesthood had been given to the boy Aristobulus, it seemed good that the affairs of the household should be tended. But Alexandra was suspect to Herod, and he required that she stay in the palace and do nothing on her own authority, and certain men carefully guarded her. She grew savage, preferring to endure anything rather than to live in slavery and fear; and she begged Cleopatra to aid her, making known the state she was in. Cleopatra bade her flee to her with her son. So preparing two coffins as if for the carrying out of dead bodies, she meant to put herself and her son in them, having charged those of the household who were privy to it to carry them out by night and bring them to the sea, where a boat had been made ready for them to sail to Egypt. Herod, learning this from one of her household, and letting it go forward as far as the attempt, seized her in the very act of the flight. He passed over the offence from fear of Cleopatra, not from clemency. But it had been resolved by him to put the youth out of the way. So when Aristobulus was seventeen years old, he went up to the altar to sacrifice at the feast of Tabernacles, robed as high priest. And an impulse of goodwill arose in the multitude toward him, because of his beauty and the size of his body and the dignity of his birth; they rejoiced and were moved together, and uttered auspicious cries mingled with prayers. Stirred by this, Herod fixed the more upon his design against the youth. And when the feast had passed, after a banquet, treating the youth kindly, he sported with him and played with him in friendly fashion. And they swam in the pools; and Herod's friends, swimming with him as in play, who were privy to the secret, did not let up but kept pressing Aristobulus down and dipping him until they drowned him. So he perished, not yet having completed his eighteenth year, and the calamity was felt by all as a private misfortune. And Alexandra, understanding also the cause of his destruction, was the more gripped by grief, but endured for fear of further evils. Herod did everything to put away the suspicion, weeping and showing distress and providing a costly funeral. But Alexandra was softened by none of these things, and wrote to Cleopatra of her son's destruction by Herod's plotting. Cleopatra urged Antony to avenge the boy's murder. So Antony sent, ordering Herod to come to Laodicea and make his defence. He, fearing the charge and Cleopatra's hostility, on departing left Joseph his uncle as procurator of affairs there, charging him secretly that, if he himself should suffer anything from Antony, he should at once kill Mariamme, that she might not, after his death, belong to another because of her beauty. So Herod departed; and Joseph, managing the affairs of the rule and continually meeting with Mariamme and Alexandra, told them of the king's disposition toward Mariamme. When they spoke ironically about his words, he was led to reveal the secret of the charge. But this drove the women into greater despair. There was also a report, spread by those who hated Herod, that Antony had killed him. Meanwhile letters came from Herod recounting Antony's honour toward him, and how he sat with him in his deliberations and feasted with him, and that he enjoyed these things even though Cleopatra was hard upon him with her slander. When these letters were brought, the false report ceased.

When king Herod, having escorted Antony against the Parthians, returned into Judaea, at once his sister Salome and their mother accused Alexandra and Mariamme. Salome even brought a charge against her own husband, that he had consorted with Mariamme; this was Joseph, the procurator of the affairs of the kingdom. She said these things out of long-standing resentment, because he reproached her with her low birth. Herod was at once disturbed, and out of jealousy questioned Mariamme privately. When she swore her innocence, he relaxed his anger, and was mastered by his love, and assured her of his affection toward her. But she said, "It was no sign of love to charge that I too be destroyed if anything harsh should befall you from Antony." This word troubled Herod, and he cried out that by this Joseph's love for her was clearly detected. For he would not, he said, have revealed the secret, unless a great intimacy had joined them. And he would have killed his wife at once, had he not been enslaved by his love for her. But Joseph, without even bringing him into his sight, he ordered to be put to death, and bound and guarded Alexandra as the cause of all.

Antony, corrupted by his love for Cleopatra, or rather by her sorceries, was enslaved to her wishes. She destroyed by poison her brother, to whom the kingdom belonged, and through Antony killed her sister Arsinoe; and she pressed Antony to assign Judaea and Arabia to her. He, ashamed of so manifest an injustice, yet compelled to gratify her because of his loves and her enchantments, cut off parts of both lands and with these appeased her insatiable greed. So Antony marched against Armenia, and Cleopatra, returning, came into Judaea, Herod meeting her. When familiarity arose between her and Herod, she invited him to her bed, being unrestrained in her appetite for intercourse, and perhaps too feeling something amorous toward him; though, what is more likely, she was contriving the beginning of an ambush against her husband by means of this intimacy. Herod rejected her words, but treating her with gifts, escorted her to Egypt.

When the seventh year of Herod's reign had now come, the land of the Jews was shaken as never before, and there was great destruction of cattle, and of men about thirty thousand were buried in the fallen houses. When Herod had farmed the tribute of the lands assigned to Cleopatra out of Arabia and Judaea, the Arab was negligent about the payment of the tax. The king therefore resolved to go against the Arab, and being permitted this by Antony, and joining battle often, at last conquered, and was chosen by the Arabs to be protector of their nation. And he returned home, having won a great name by his exploits and being full of spirit.

Just as Caesar had defeated Antony in the battle at Actium, Herod's affairs were thrown into confusion or wholly despaired of. For there was no hope, so great a friendship having been formed between him and Antony, that he should not be harmed by Caesar. Whence, planning to put Hyrcanus out of the way, he thought then more than ever that the attempt was to his advantage, that no man might survive worthier than himself to obtain the kingdom. So Herod had resolved; and a certain occurrence further spurred him to the deed. For Alexandra, being a contentious woman, did not cease urging her father to go over to Malchus, who held Arabia. He at first rejected the words, but when she pressed him, at last he wrote a letter to Malchus about receiving them, and gave it to a certain Dositheus, one of his friends. He delivered the letter to Herod; and Herod asked Dositheus to give the writing to Malchus and to bring back his reply. When Dositheus had done this, the Arab wrote back that he would receive Hyrcanus himself and all who were with him. So Herod, receiving this letter, sent for Hyrcanus and questioned him about the agreement with Malchus; and when he denied it, Herod showed the letters to the council and put the man to death. Many say that the affair of Hyrcanus was a pretext of Herod's, who wished to put him out of the way, and they make the man's mildness or simplicity a proof of it, and the fact that he had shown no boldness or rashness even in his youth; and at that time he was eighty-one years old.

Herod, hastening to Caesar, settled his mother and sister and all his family at Masada, but brought his wife Mariamme together with her mother Alexandra to Alexandrium, setting over them, on the pretext of honour, as guards Joseph the steward and the Ituraean Soemus, the most faithful to him, charging them that, if they should learn anything harsh concerning him, they should at once kill both women, and keep the kingdom for his children and his brother Pheroras. Having given such instructions, he hastened to Rhodes to Caesar. When he landed, he took off the diadem, but yielded nothing of his other dignity; rather, conversing with Caesar, he displayed the greatness of his spirit, neither turning to supplications nor giving an account of his deeds with any concealment. So he won Caesar over in no small measure, and Caesar restored the diadem to him and treated him with honour. Having thus, beyond hope, secured his kingdom more firmly, he escorted Caesar to Egypt, presenting both him and his friends most generously; and he returned to Judaea with greater honour and freedom, but found his household in disorder. For Mariamme and Alexandra, supposing — what was the truth — that they had been shut up as in a prison at Alexandrium, that they might not even have power over themselves, took it hard, and won over the guards by attentions, and especially Soemus, courting him with words and gifts. He yielded little by little, and revealed to them the king's instructions. They were grieved at these, and especially Mariamme. For when Herod, as was fitting, told his wife first the good news about himself and greeted her before the rest, she groaned at his greetings and seemed vexed at his good fortune, so that the king was disturbed and distressed by the strangeness of her hatred, and was often impelled to avenge himself for her contempt, but was checked because he was held captive by love. Above all he feared lest, in punishing her, he should unwittingly do himself the greater harm, his beloved being no more. His mother and sister provoked Herod with slanders that put jealousy and hatred into him. And he was always worse disposed toward her, she not concealing her feeling toward him, and his love always changing to anger. And had he not been hastening to Caesar, who had now prevailed, Antony and Cleopatra being dead, into Egypt, perhaps the dreadful deed would at once have been done. But as it was, he left the affairs of his household as they were, and coming to Egypt was thought worthy of the greatest honours by Caesar, and returned more brilliant. But he loved Mariamme, and that very ardently. She, though in other respects chaste and faithful to him, presuming upon her husband, who was enslaved by his love, often insulted him, and mocked his mother and sister for their low birth. The hatred broke out into the open from such an occasion. At midday the king entered his chamber to rest, and called for Mariamme; but she, coming in, reproached him as the murderer of her grandfather and her brother. The king was vexed at this. And Salome, seizing the moment, having already corrupted the cup-bearer to accuse Mariamme, persuaded him to go then to the king and tell him what he had been taught by her. He said that he had been bribed by Mariamme, who urged him to give the king a love-potion; and that it was a certain drug whose power, he insisted, he did not know. Hearing this, the king was moved still more to anger, and tortured the woman's cup-bearer, who was most faithful to her. But he neither knew nor said anything about what he was tortured for, but said that the woman's hatred had arisen because of the words which Soemus had told her. Scarcely had he brought his words to an end when Herod, crying out loudly, said, "Indeed, Soemus would not have made light of my instructions, unless some intimacy had arisen between him and the woman." So he ordered Soemus to be killed at once, but accused the woman, gathering his most intimate friends, concerning love-potions and drugs, and was disposed angrily against her. Those present, seeing him so disposed, voted her death. And she was led off to die, but her mother Alexandra, now fearing also for herself, and pretending ignorance of the charges against Mariamme, leaped out and called her daughter wicked and ungrateful toward her husband, and said that she suffered justly. But Mariamme, neither disturbed at this nor giving a word, went off to her death with calm bearing and noble spirit, showing her nobility even in her last moments.

So she died, Salome having hastened her death; but Herod was then the more inflamed with love for her, and there were often callings of her name and unseemly lamentations. And his grief so mastered him that he even ordered his servants to summon Mariamme. And at last giving himself over to solitude, and brooding in it, he fell into a dreadful disease; and there was inflammation, and pain in the back of the head, and derangement of mind. While he was thus sick, Alexandra in Jerusalem, learning of the king's illnesses, tried to seize two fortresses near the city. When Herod learned this, he ordered her to be killed at once. He himself, scarcely escaping the danger from his sickness, was harsh and ill-tempered and ready for punishments and murders; and there were murders not only of many ordinary men, but even of his most intimate friends. He transgressed the ancestral customs too, and corrupted the ancient order with foreign practices. At these things the multitude was disturbed and aggrieved. Ten men of the citizens, conspiring together and hiding daggers in their garments, went to the theatre by a signal, either to kill Herod himself or at least many of those about him. Being detected, and not even denying their plan, but even displaying their swords, they endured every torment and were destroyed. The one who informed against them was a little later seized by some men and torn limb from limb and thrown to the dogs. Herod, finding them out, punished them with their whole households. But the anger of the multitude remained.

There befell at that time most grievous calamities throughout the country, both famine and diseases of the body arising from the unaccustomed diet caused by lack of food, and on top of all these a plague. Herod, eager to help in the crisis, neither had abundance of money, having spent it beforehand on the rebuilding of cities for display, nor did the neighboring lands have grain, the same scarcity prevailing in them too. But resolving to help as best he could, he cut up into coin the adornment that was in the palace, and sent to Egypt and bought grain from there. When it was brought, to those who were able by their own efforts to prepare their food he distributed grain; but for those who, through age or other weakness, were not able to prepare food for themselves, he took thought, appointing bakers and providing them with ready food. These things not only changed the minds of those who had formerly been hostile to him, but even turned them to goodwill. And so, having recovered his rule, which had been harmed, he no less relieved also the neighboring peoples who were suffering equally in the calamity, so that the measures of grain given outside his realm came to ten thousand, and those within his kingdom to about eighty thousand. The measure, according to Josephus, equals ten Attic medimni. This generosity and the timeliness of the favour turned even the Jews from enmity to love, and won him good repute among those outside.

He brought about for himself also a marriage from amorous desire. For a certain priest, Simon, in Jerusalem, had a most beautiful daughter; with her Herod fell in love. But since Simon was unfit for the marriage-connection because of his obscurity, Herod took the priesthood from the one who then held it, Jesus the son of Phabes, and made Simon high priest, and married his daughter. When all things went well for him, he surrounded himself with security from without, conversing skillfully with the cities and courting the rulers, so that everything increased for him in every way. But by his ambition in this and his courting of Caesar and the most powerful Romans, he both transgressed the customs and corrupted the laws, founding cities and raising temples, not in the land of the Jews but in the country outside, defending himself to the Jews that he did these things by command and not of himself, but rendering favours to Caesar and the Romans by departing from the ancestral customs for their honour. For he set up statues and molded images and built cities and broad and sheltered harbours and costly palaces and splendid dwellings.

While he was thus engaged, he sent his sons Alexander and Aristobulus to Rome to meet with Caesar. Caesar received them kindly, and granted Herod to assign the kingdom to whichever of his offspring he wished, and added more territory, and joined him also to the governors of Syria, charging them to do everything with his consent. Having prospered so greatly, he asked Caesar for a tetrarchy for his brother Pheroras, and remitted a third part of the taxes to those in his kingdom — as he said, that they might recover from the dearth, but as it seemed to others, that he might cure the ill-will of the multitude toward himself; for, their customs being changed, they took it hard. Therefore too he took away their liberties, always giving them orders and forbidding assemblies and watching their walks and ways of life and most severely punishing those caught; and both in the city and on the roads there were men who watched those who gathered together. Some say that he himself, taking the guise of a private man, sometimes by night mingled with the crowds and tested their mind toward his rule. Those who were defiant he pursued in every way, but the multitude he required to confirm their loyalty to him with oaths. So most yielded; but those who were displeased he made away with in every manner. He tried to persuade Pollio the Pharisee and Samaeas and most of those who studied with them to swear. But these neither were persuaded nor were punished, the king sparing them out of respect for Pollio. From this necessity the so-called Essenes too were exempted; this is a sect that follows a Pythagorean way of life. He honoured them because of Manaem. This Manaem was one of them, a man good in other respects and one who foresaw the future, who, when Herod was still a boy going to school, saw him and addressed him as king of the Jews. Herod said he was a private man. But Manaem, smiling and striking him gently, said, "Nevertheless you will be king, and will conduct the rule most happily, and remember these blows of mine. You will be best if you love justice and piety toward God and clemency toward the citizens. But I know you will not be such." When Herod became king, he summoned Manaem and asked about the length of his rule. When Manaem was silent, Herod himself asked whether the years of his reign would be ten or twenty or thirty; but Manaem set no limit to the term of his life. Herod, content even with this, dismissed Manaem with honour, and for his sake honoured all the Essenes.

When he was now completing the eighteenth year of his reign, he resolved to rebuild the temple, and to raise it to a greater height and to finish it more worthily. But the multitude hesitated at the undertaking. He said that he would not pull down the temple until he had prepared everything needed for the work. When all had been prepared, pulling it down and laying other foundations, he raised the temple to a length of a hundred cubits, and a height of twenty more. It was built of white and strong stones, each of them about twenty-five cubits in length, and eight in height, and about twelve in breadth. On the northern side a well-fenced corner-citadel was built into the wall, remarkable for its strength, which the kings of the family of the Asamonaeans, who were at once kings and high priests, had built and called the Baris, so that the high-priestly robe was stored in it. This Baris, then, Herod rebuilt more strongly for the security of the temple, and named it Antonia in memory of Antony. The temple itself and all that pertained to it were built in eight years. It is recorded that during that time when the temple itself was being raised — for in one year and six months it was built — it did not rain by day, but the showers came in the nights, that the works might not be hindered.

Trying to check wrongdoing, Herod made a law that house-breakers be sold for export from the country; this was both burdensome as a punishment for those who suffered it, and not least a dissolution of the laws. For to serve foreigners and to be forced to live according to their customs was, so far as it lay with them, a dissolution of their religion. For the laws ordered thieves to be sold, if they had not the means to repay fourfold what they had stolen, but not to foreigners — rather to their countrymen, that they might neither fall away from their religion nor serve through their whole life, but obtain release after six years. These things were part of the slanders against him and of the ill-will of the multitude toward him.

Coming into Italy at that time, that he might confer with Caesar and see his sons staying at Rome, Herod was kindly received by Caesar, and took his sons, as now perfected in their studies, to lead them home. When they returned, they became conspicuous both for their spirit and for the beauty of their forms, and were objects of envy to Salome the king's sister and to those who had wrought their mother's destruction by slanders. And these now made ready their weapons against the young men also, with which they had overcome the one who bore them, spreading the report that the youths bore themselves resentfully toward their father because of their mother's murder, and from this they contrived, as far as they could, that hatred should grow in the father toward his sons. For a time, however, the father, still affectionately disposed toward them, both shared honour with them and, when they had come of age, joined them in marriage — to Aristobulus the daughter of Salome, Berenice, and to Alexander the daughter of Archelaus the king of Cappadocia, Glaphyra. But these things rather fostered Salome's ill-will toward the young men, since she made an ally of everyone who had helped accomplish Mariamme's murder. And the young men too gave some handles, by their memory of their mother and their desire for power; for there were slanders from them against Salome and Pheroras, and the ill-will of these against them grew, and malicious slanders against them advanced, taking their occasions from the young men themselves. For when the abominable Salome spoke evil of them and their mother, and drew them into speech, they would represent their mother's end as pitiable, and call themselves wretched at being forced to live with her murderers. These things happened while the king was abroad. When he returned, at once Pheroras and Salome brought their words to him, saying that great danger hung over them, the young men openly threatening to avenge their mother's murder. Herod, with others too reporting these things, was disturbed. So disposed, he resolved, for the bringing down of the young men, to make a close ally of another son named Antipater, born to him while he was still a private man; and he resolved to honour him, that he might check the boldness of Mariamme's sons, making them know that the succession of the kingdom was owed neither to them alone nor of necessity. So he brought in Antipater as a kind of rival. He, being a clever man, when he obtained free speech, had one single design — to cling to his father and to estrange his brothers by slanders. And they still gave occasions, weeping as though dishonoured, and calling on their mother, and openly saying their father was not just. These things the party of Antipater maliciously reported to Herod with additions, and produced greater enmity toward them. The father, wishing to humble Mariamme's sons, gave Antipater greater honour; and at last he brought in his mother too. And he commended him to Caesar, writing on his behalf, and sent him to Rome with many gifts, so that now everything seemed to rest on him, but the youths were wholly thrust aside from the rule. Antipater, fearing lest, during his absence, his father should become more lenient toward Mariamme's sons, even while abroad did not cease continually writing to his father against his brothers and inciting him to enmity, until he brought him to this — to sail to Rome and there accuse the young men before Caesar. Going off to Rome with his sons, he presented them to Caesar, and accused them of madness, as hating their own father and plotting to make away with him and so take the kingdom. While the father was still speaking, the young men were in tears and at last in lamentation, fearing that, if they kept silent, they would seem from a guilty conscience to be without means of defence. When they perceived goodwill on Caesar's part, and that of the rest some wept with them and all grieved with them, Alexander undertook to dissolve the charges, making a speech to his father. When he had spoken rather persuasively, Caesar, who even before had not believed the slanders against them, was the more moved, and kept looking at Herod, seeing him too somewhat confounded. And the assembly was in suspense. But Caesar said that the young men, even if they seemed far from the slanders, had erred in this very thing — that they had not shown themselves to their father such that there should be no charge against them; and he urged Herod to be reconciled to his sons, putting away all suspicion; for he judged it not just to hold these charges against the sons credible. Giving such counsel, he nodded to the young men to fall at their father's feet. As they rushed forward, the father, anticipating them, embraced them weeping and clasped each one. So then, having given thanks to Caesar, they departed together, and Antipater with them, pretending to be pleased at the reconciliation. The next day Caesar granted Herod the authority to appoint whichever of his sons he wished as successor, or even to divide the kingdom among them all — but after his death; for during his life he did not permit the division, but wished him to be master both of his sons and of the kingdom. As he returned, near Cilicia, Archelaus the father-in-law of Alexander met Herod, rejoicing with him over the reconciliation of his sons. Thence Herod, coming into Judaea and gathering an assembly, recounted what he had done abroad, and ended his speech with an admonition to his sons, and announced to them that he would leave the kingdom first to Antipater, and then to Mariamme's sons. Having said this, he dissolved the gathering.

He was in disposition, toward others, most ambitious and most beneficent, but toward his subjects oppressive and most unjust, and toward his own household and friends an inexorable chastiser. The causes of these things were love of glory and love of rule. For out of love of glory, if he was likely to obtain remembrance or good repute hereafter or in the present, he did not spare expense; but being of great expenditure, he pressed his subjects with heavy exactions and was harsh toward them. And out of love of rule, if he had any suspicion that someone aimed at the rule or sought to disturb anything about it, he treated him like an enemy, and on this account punished kinsmen and friends without sparing, wishing to be honoured alone. A proof of his wishing to get money from every quarter because of his great expenditure is this: having heard that Hyrcanus, who had reigned before him, opening the tomb of David, had taken three thousand talents of silver, he opened the tomb by night and entered, taking with him the most faithful of his friends, that the deed might not be made known. And he found no money — silver, that is — but much adornment of golden treasures, which he took all of. He was eager to advance further into the inner chambers, in which the bodies of the kings David and Solomon had been laid up. But as he was forcing his way in, two of his bodyguards were destroyed by a flame that met them from within, as the report goes; and he himself came out in terror. And on account of this attempt his household affairs seemed to fare worse; for what concerned the royal court resembled a civil war. Antipater always plotted against his brothers, being clever, involving them in charges through others, but himself often pleading on their behalf, that, seeming well disposed toward them, he might be unsuspected by his father in his designs and might seem alone to care for his father's safety. And he was everything to his father, while Mariamme's sons were ever more harshly treated, and could not bear the dishonour because of their nobility, being thrust aside and holding a more dishonourable rank. And the wives — Glaphyra, who lived with Alexander, the daughter of Archelaus, hated Salome both because of her disposition toward her husband and because of Salome's daughter, who lived with Aristobulus, toward whom Glaphyra bore herself haughtily, and resented her equality of honour. There arose also a certain occasion that brought the king's brother Pheroras into suspicion and hatred with his brother. For the king's daughter had been betrothed to him; but he, mastered by a slave-woman with whom he was, and madly in love with the woman, paid no heed to his brother's daughter, but clung to the slave. Herod was vexed at this, and married the girl to the son of Phasael; but when time had passed, he both blamed his brother for the former matters and asked him to take the second daughter, supposing that his love for the slave had now passed its peak. But Pheroras sent away the slave, by whom he had a child, and undertook to take the king's daughter after thirty days. But when the appointed time had passed, he was so maddened with love for the slave that he set at naught what had been agreed, and went back to the former woman. These things drove Herod to fury; and always some new thing falling out did not allow him to be at rest. And Salome, being harsh toward Mariamme's sons, persuaded her own daughter, who lived with Aristobulus, not to be well disposed toward her husband, but to report to her if he should say anything in private. She said that the young men remembered their mother and hated their father, and threatened, when they obtained the rule, to make the sons of Herod's other wives village clerks, and to shut up the wives so that they should not even see the sun. These things were reported to the king through the wicked Salome. He heard them with grief, but tried to set things right; and when the sons defended themselves, he became calmer.

Pheroras again threw affairs into confusion, telling Alexander that he had heard Salome saying that Herod was in love with Glaphyra. Alexander was disturbed at the word from jealousy, and not bearing the pain, reported to his father what had been said by Pheroras. Herod, deeply distressed, and not enduring the falsehood of the slander, and being thrown into confusion, sent for Pheroras, and said, "Most wicked man, in saying such things against us, do you think you have put a word into your son's soul or a sword into his right hand?" Pheroras said that Salome had persuaded him to it, and that the words were hers. She denied it, and clutched at her hair and beat her breast, but because of the wickedness of her ways she was not believed. At last the king dismissed both his brother and his sister, but praised his son for his self-control and for referring the words to him.

Another thing fell out that again raised disturbances in the king's household. He had eunuchs prized for their beauty, of whom one was appointed to pour his wine, another to bring his dinner, and another to put him to bed. These, it was reported, had been corrupted by Alexander with money. And when the eunuchs were given over to torture, they confessed to intercourse with the young man, but knew nothing else against the father with Alexander. When the torturers intensified the scourgings, they said that Alexander had ill-will and hatred toward his father, and advised Herod to give up because of his age, and to attend to him, since the kingdom would come round to him, even if the father were unwilling, both because of his birth and because of the disposition of the commanders and friends. Hearing this, Herod was full of fear, and held suspicions and hatreds toward all, and forbade many of his friends access to the palace. The cause of all was Antipater. So Herod first examined under torture all whom he supposed faithful to Alexander, whether they knew of anything ventured against himself; but they died, having nothing to say. One man, not bearing the tortures, said that Alexander, when praised for the size of his body and his accuracy in shooting from a bow and the rest, used to say that, if anything good had been given him by nature or had come from training, it turned to misfortune, for his father was grieved at his good qualities. He added that Alexander had even plotted with Aristobulus to kill the father in a hunt and to flee to Rome to claim the kingdom. There were found also letters of Alexander to his brother, saying that their father did not act justly in preferring Antipater. On these grounds Herod seized and bound Alexander. But he was eager to get some greater proof against his son, that he might not seem to have bound him rashly. So he tortured many even of those in office and destroyed them, though they said nothing of the kind he expected. But when one of the younger men came under the tortures, he said that Alexander was writing to his friends in Rome, asking to be summoned by Caesar to inform that Mithridates the king of the Parthians had made friendship with his father against the Romans; and that he had a drug prepared at Ascalon. These things Herod reckoned as a consolation for his haste. The drug, however, when at once sought, was not found. But because of the excess of his evils Alexander, being contentious, and wishing to avenge himself on his enemies, that they might perish along with him, sent letters to his father saying that there was no need to torture; for the plot had been devised, and Pheroras and the most faithful of his friends shared in it; and that Salome had even come to him by night and lain with him against his will; but that all came to one thing — that, with him out of the way, they might be freed from the constant expectation of being destroyed.

Archelaus the king of the Cappadocians, learning this, and being anxious for his daughter and his son-in-law, came, and skillfully set about the correction of the troubles, condemning the young man and calling Herod reasonable, and saying he would dissolve the marriage. When Archelaus said such things, Herod gave way from his harshness and was moved to grief and tears, and begged him not to dissolve the marriage, but to relax his anger at the young man's errors. Archelaus, seeing Herod now softened, shifted the blame onto others, and especially onto Pheroras. Pheroras then turned to Archelaus, that he might be his reconciler with Herod. Archelaus advised him that it was better to go to his brother by himself and entreat him, confessing that he himself was the cause of all; for thus he would soften the harshness of his anger; and he promised that he himself would be present and help. Pheroras was persuaded. And Alexander was freed from the charges, and Archelaus reconciled Pheroras to Herod.

After some time the affairs of Herod's sons and household became much worse. For Eurycles, from Lacedaemon, not undistinguished among those there, but a most wicked man in his purpose, having come to Herod, gave him gifts, and receiving more, became one of the king's chief friends. His lodging was with Antipater; but he also approached Alexander, saying he was known to Archelaus too, whence he pretended also to honour Glaphyra. To this man, having become his familiar, Alexander bewailed his condition, and told him about his mother, and said that things did not seem bearable. He, in grief, made such speeches to Eurycles, who reported everything to Antipater. Antipater treated him with gifts and asked him to tell his father these things. He so disposed the king as to make his hatred irrevocable. So he departed, having got his pay; but Herod was so enraged against his sons that he no longer needed slanders, but himself busied himself with their affairs and watched everything.

Two of the king's bodyguards, who had been thrust away in his anger, rode about with Alexander's party and received gifts from him. Suspecting these, Herod at once tortured them. At first they held out, then reported that Alexander urged them to kill Herod while he was hunting. And the commander of the garrison of Alexandrium was examined, as having promised to receive the young men in the fortress. He confessed nothing, but his son testified that this had been done, and produced letters about it, which, as could be conjectured, were in Alexander's hand. So Herod was no longer in doubt about his sons' plot, but Alexander insisted that the little letter had been forged by Antipater. So then there was a guarding of the young men, and they had the disrepute and fear of the condemned. Aristobulus, supposing that his mother-in-law Salome shared his grief and hated the one who believed such things, said to her, "This same thing forebodes danger to you too, who are slandered in the hope of marriage with Syllaeus." She at once brought these words to her brother. He ordered both his sons to be bound and separated from each other, and that each write down what they had plotted against their father. They wrote that they had neither conceived nor contrived any plot against their father, but had planned flight, and that of necessity, since their life was suspect and full of fear. Then, when an envoy from Archelaus came, Herod brought out Alexander in bonds and questioned him about the flight, in the hearing of the envoy, where and how they had resolved to withdraw. He said he had agreed with Archelaus to be sent on from there to Rome, but had reckoned nothing else amiss or harsh against his father. When these things had been so spoken, the king, giving letters to Caesar to two of his men, ordered them, putting in at Cilicia on their voyage, to meet Archelaus and blame him for having taken part in the plot with his sons. Archelaus, however, defended himself, saying that he had agreed to receive the young men for the advantage both of them and of their father, but not to send them to Caesar. When the bearers of the letters had been conveyed to Rome, they gave them to Caesar. He wrote back that he grieved over the sons, but gave Herod full authority to act; and if they had done anything unholy, to proceed against them as parricides, but if they had only thought of flight, to admonish them otherwise and do nothing irremediable. He advised him to gather a council at Berytus, and taking the commanders and the king of the Cappadocians Archelaus and as many others as he knew distinguished in dignity, to consider with them what should be done.

Having received this letter, Herod called to the council those he wished, excluding Archelaus out of enmity, or because he thought he would oppose his opinion. When the commanders and the rest had gathered, the king accused his sons, and read out what they had themselves written; in which nothing else was written than that they had planned flight, and certain reproaches against him containing insults because of their ill-will. And at last, saying that authority had been given him both by nature and by Caesar, he added an ancestral law, which ordered that, if parents accusing someone laid their hands on his head, the bystanders should be obliged to stone him and so put him to death. He said that he himself could do this in his country and kingdom, but had awaited their judgment. When Herod had said this, those of the council confirmed the authority to him, the young men not even being brought into the council; and some condemned the sons of Herod, but not even to death, while the greater number declared that they should be punished even with death. And on this the council was dissolved. Herod came to Tyre, leading his sons. When they came to Caesarea, all were in suspense, awaiting what would come to pass concerning the young men; and they were displeased at what was happening, but it was not without danger either to say anything on their behalf or to listen to another speaking, but they bore the excess of their grief painfully but in silence.

A certain soldier named Tero, whose son, of the same age, was a friend of Alexander, said many things to the multitude, and speaking freely to the king himself, asked to meet him alone. When the king consented, he said, "Where, then, has that excellent mind of yours gone? What is this desolation of friends and kinsmen? Will you not consider what is being done, if you destroy two young men born to you of a royal wife and supreme in every virtue, leaving yourself in old age with one son and with kinsmen whom you yourself have so often condemned to death? Will you not bear in mind that the silence of the crowds too is because of the greatness of their grief, and that the whole army has pity for the unfortunate and hatred for those who bring these things to pass?" The king at first heard this not unfavourably. But Tero, using immoderate and soldierly frankness, disturbed Herod. And he was stirred to indignation at the soldiers, and ordered them to bind Tero and keep him in custody. The king's barber, Tryphon, seizing the occasion, attacked too, saying that he had often been urged by Tero to cut the king's throat with a razor; for, he said, he would be among the first with Alexander. Having said this, he too was seized. And Tero and his son and the barber himself were put to torture. When Tero held out under the tortures, his son, seeing his father in distress, said he would tell the king the truth, if he would rescue his father and himself from the tortures. Receiving pledges, he said there had been an agreement for Tero to attack the king with his own hand. Saying this, he delivered his father from the torment. But Herod, leaving no doubt in his soul about the killing of his children, at last carried out his purpose. And brought to Sebaste, Alexander and Aristobulus, at their father's order, were strangled with a cord. Bringing before the multitude the three hundred commanders who had come under accusation, and Tero with his son and the barber, he accused them; and the crowd, pelting them with whatever was at hand, killed them.

But for Antipater, who had wrought the destruction of his brothers, the attainment of the kingdom was the more troublesome, since hatred toward him sprang up in the nation, and especially in the army. For the time he ruled jointly with his father and was trusted by him. Herod sent Alexander's wife back to her father, but reared the children of the dead with great care. Alexander had two sons by Glaphyra, and Aristobulus three sons and two daughters by Berenice. The king also had a son Herod by the daughter of the high priest. For nine wives lived with the king, it being ancestral to live with several at the same time. There were the mother of Antipater and the daughter of the high priest, by whom, as has been said, a son was born to him of the same name. There was also a daughter of his brother married to him, and a cousin with her — that is, a second cousin; for the ancients called second cousins "cousins," as may be found in many places, both in Plutarch and in the books of law. There was also among Herod's wives one of the nation of the Samaritans, whose children were Antipas and Archelaus and a daughter Olympias. Cleopatra of Jerusalem too was numbered among his wives; and her children were Herod and Philip. And Pallas was among his consorts, having borne him a son Phasael. And besides the rest, Phaedra and Elpis lived with him. Herod had also two daughters by Mariamme; and by Phaedra and Elpis there were born to him daughters Roxane and Salome.

Such was the family of Herod; but affairs looked only to Antipater. And he was fearful to all, not so much by his power as by the wickedness of his ways. Pheroras especially courted him and was courted in return. But Salome opposed them, being always disposed contrary to the meaning of her name; for the name signified one peaceable and of peace, but she was very warlike, and stirred up others to fights and factions and the estrangement of kindred. She, spying out the intimacy of Antipater and Pheroras, told Herod that their goodwill was for his harm. So they, learning of Salome's slander, openly affected hatred and reproaches toward each other, but secretly kept their concord with each other. But they did not escape Salome, who tracked out everything and reported to the king their secret meetings and banquets and unspeakable councils. And he himself for the most part understood. The Pharisees, making the women's quarters their own — men who prided themselves on exactness in the ancestral law and opposed the king — when all had sworn to be loyal to Caesar and to king Herod, they themselves were not persuaded, being more than six thousand, and being well disposed toward Pheroras's wife, foretold to Herod that the end of his rule had been decreed against him by God, and that it would be assigned to Pheroras and his offspring. This did not escape Salome's malice, and it was at once reported to the king. So those of the Pharisees who were convicted of these things were killed, and the eunuch Bagoas, and a certain Carus, distinguished for the beauty of his body and a favourite of Herod, and others of those about the king, as accomplices. Then the king, convening a council, accused Pheroras's wife and enumerated many charges, and at last, turning his speech to Pheroras, said that he ought, even before being bidden, to have sent the woman away on account of these things. "Now then, if you lay claim to my kinship, give up your life with her." But he answered that he would rather die than be deprived of his wife while alive. From this Herod forbade Antipater and his mother to associate with Pheroras or to meet with the women. They agreed, but met one another and reveled together as occasion offered. Antipater, fearing his father's anger, wrote to his friends in Rome to write to Herod to send Antipater to Caesar. So Antipater was sent to Rome with gifts, bearing also a will of Herod giving him the rule, but, if he should die first, giving it to Herod the son of the high priest's daughter. And Herod ordered Pheroras, since he would not give up his wife, to withdraw. He departed to his tetrarchy, having sworn not to return until he should learn that his brother had died. So that even when the king fell sick and summoned him, he did not obey, that he might not break his oath. But Herod later, when Pheroras was sick, came to him uncalled, and when he died, honoured him.

The death of Pheroras became the beginning of evils for Antipater, his uncle exacting from him the penalty of his fratricide. For two freedmen, honoured by Pheroras, begged Herod not to leave his brother unavenged, who had been destroyed by poison. These things, seeming credible, moved the king to inquiry, and women both slave and free were tortured. The others held out in silence, but one of them said nothing else, but called upon God that Antipater's mother had fallen into such necessities, as the cause of evils. This moved Herod to further search; and the women, subjected to more severe tortures, made everything known — the revelries and the secret meetings, and the words Antipater had spoken to the women of Pheroras, his hatred toward his father, his lamentations to his mother that his father's life was prolonged to the utmost, so that he could not even taste the pleasures of the kingdom, if ever it should come to him, because of the old age already pressing upon him; and many other things, too, touching his father, the women said. On these grounds the king, now condemning Antipater, took from his mother Doris all the adornment about her, worth many talents, and sent her away. But what especially roused Herod against his son was Antipater's own procurator, who, among other things told under torture, said that Antipater had given a drug to Pheroras, charging him to give it to his father during his absence, that he might be unsuspected by not being present, and that Pheroras had kept it to give to his wife. The woman admitted it, and going out to fetch the drug, threw herself from the roof, yet did not die. When she had recovered, the king again questioned her; and she swore to tell everything as it had been done. She said she had received the drug from her husband, prepared against the father by Antipater. "But when Pheroras fell sick, since you yourself came and tended your brother, he, seeing your goodwill toward him, said, 'Bring the drug, woman, and burn it before my eyes.' And I at once did as he charged, giving the most of it to the fire, but keeping a little for myself, that I might use it on myself if any harm should come to me from you when Pheroras was gone." And she brought the box and the drug into the open. The king's wife too, the daughter of the high priest, was accused as privy to everything; her he at once cast out, and struck her son from the will, in which he was mentioned to reign. And he took the high priesthood from his father-in-law Simon the son of Boethus, and appointed another, Matthias the son of Theophilus.

Meanwhile a freedman of Antipater, Bathyllus, came from Rome bringing a drug to Antipater's mother and Pheroras; he, on examination, said it had been sent so that, if the former did not affect the father, by this at least he might be destroyed. He carried also letters from Herod's friends in Rome, containing an accusation against Archelaus and Philip, who were staying at Rome for their studies, as though they accused their father over the murder of their brothers and feared for themselves too. These things were done for Antipater at great cost. Herod, concealing his anger, ordered him not to delay; and bringing reproaches against his mother, he promised to lay these aside for her when he arrived. With these letters Antipater met near Cilicia. At Tarentum, learning of Pheroras's death, he took it hard, not out of goodwill, but because Pheroras had died before he had killed Herod, as he had promised. When he landed at the harbour called Sebastos, so named after Caesar, his evils were already plain, no one coming to him or greeting him. He came to Jerusalem, while Varus the governor of Syria was sitting in council with Herod, summoned for advice about present matters. And he entered the palace still wearing his purple robe. Those at the doors received Antipater, but kept out his friends. He was already troubled, perceiving where he had come, since his father too thrust him away as he came up to greet him, calling him fratricide and a plotter against his life, and saying that Varus on the morrow would be the hearer and judge of these things. So he went off amid such evils. His mother and his wife met him — this wife was a daughter of Antigonus, who had reigned before Herod — and from them, having learned everything, he prepared for the contest. The next day Herod and Varus sat in council; the friends of both came together, and the kinsmen of Herod, and the informers of what Antipater had plotted, and the slaves of Antipater's mother, bearing a letter from her that he should not return, since all had become known to his father, and that his only refuge was Caesar and not to fall into his father's hands. When Antipater fell at his father's feet and begged him to hear him and so to vote, Herod ordered him to be led into the midst, and himself bewailed the disposition of his sons and that his old age had come round to Antipater, and said he was astonished that Antipater should come to such a pass, who was written down as successor of the rule and during his father's life had power over everything, and in return for these things incited his kinsmen to his father's murder. Saying these things, he was moved to tears. And Nicolaus of Damascus, the king permitting, accused Antipater, recounting everything in order. Many others too spoke against Antipater of their own accord. When Nicolaus ended his words, Varus ordered Antipater to make his defence. But he lay prostrate on his face, calling upon God to witness for him that he did no wrong. When nothing was said by Antipater except the calling on God, Varus ordered the drug to be brought into the midst. When it was brought, one of those condemned to death was bidden to drink it; and drinking, he died at once. Varus, rising, departed from the council, and Herod at once bound Antipater, and sent letters about him to Caesar at Rome.

There was caught at that time also a little letter sent by Antiphilus to Antipater, saying, "I have sent you the letter from Acme, not sparing my own life. For you know that I am again in danger from two households, if I should be discovered. May you prosper in the matter." The king sought the other letter too. And the slave of Antiphilus insisted he had not received another. But someone, seeing the slave's inner tunic stitched up, guessed that the little letter was hidden there; and so it was. So they took the letter, which made plain: "Acme to Antipater. I have written to your father such a letter as you wished, and making a copy of one as though sent by Salome to my mistress, I have sent it, and I know that when he reads it he will punish Salome." The letter to Herod was as follows: "Making it my business that nothing be hidden from you of what is being done against you, I have found a letter of Salome to my mistress against you, and have sent you a copy of it, at risk to myself but to your benefit." Now Acme was a Jewess by birth, and was a slave of Julia the wife of Caesar, and did these things, having been bought with much money by Antipater. Herod set out at once to kill Antipater as a stirrer-up of great affairs, but Salome, beating her breast, roused him and asked to be killed herself, if any credible proof should be found against her. Restraining himself, he sent for his son, ordering him to make no answer that aroused suspicion. Antipater laid the cause of everything on Antiphilus. Herod again sent letters to Caesar accusing Antipater, making plain also what Acme had been found to have wrought together with him; and he sent also copies of her letters.

Meanwhile the king fell into a sickness and wrote a will, giving the kingdom to the youngest of his sons, out of hatred toward Archelaus and Philip because of Antipater's slanders. Despairing of living longer, being about seventy years old, he grew savage; the cause was that he seemed to be despised and that all rejoiced at his misfortunes. He was roused to this from such a thing. Many things had been done by Herod contrary to the law, one of which was the golden eagle set up over the great gate of the temple. But the law forbids the dedication of images or the making of likenesses of living things. This eagle Judas and Matthias, men most learned among the Jews and dear to the people because of their teaching of the young, resolved to pull down. For even if anyone should be in danger because of this, they said, that man is blessed who dies for the laws. Inciting the youth with such words, a report arose that the king had died. And at once, in the middle of the day, they pulled down the eagle and cut it to pieces with axes. So many of the young men were seized, and Judas and Matthias, the instigators and trainers of those who did this, and they were brought to Herod. He asked whether they had dared to pull down his offering. And the men said, "It is done; and there is no need to wonder if we prefer the laws which Moses, taught by God, left us, to your decrees." So he sent those who were bound to Jericho, and calling the chief men of the Jews, lying on a couch, he reminded them of his benefactions to them and of the building of the temple, and cried out that, even while he yet lived, they insulted him by pulling down his offerings, so as to seem to insult him but in truth to commit sacrilege. They, fearing his cruelty, said that those who had dared this deserved punishment. The king dealt more gently with the rest, but took the honour from Matthias the high priest and appointed another to officiate, Joazar the brother of his own wife; but Matthias, who had raised the sedition, and some of the rebels, he burned alive.

The disease, however, grew more bitter upon him, exacting the penalty of the things he had done unlawfully. For a slow fire afflicted his inward parts, and there were ulcerations of the intestines, and especially pains of the colon, and a watery and clear discharge about his feet, and an affliction of the abdomen and a putrefaction of the privy parts breeding worms, and besides these a difficulty of breathing, offensive both in its odour and in the constancy of its panting, and convulsions came over every limb of his. Yet even so afflicted, he was in hope of life, and did not refuse to use even desperate remedies. Crossing the Jordan, he used the warm springs at Callirrhoe, which, besides their other virtue, are also drinkable. There, lowered by the physicians into a tub full of oil, he seemed to expire. Recovering, he was brought to Jericho, where black bile seized him upon everything.

As he was dying, he devised an unholy deed. For by his command the most honourable of the whole nation came there, and shutting them all up in the hippodrome, he charged his sister Salome and her husband Alexas that, when he himself should give up his soul, they should kill all those imprisoned, that the people might not rejoice at his death, saying, "Nor let them applaud, but, with each one mourning his own, so I too shall seem to be mourned, and my departure will be honoured by the tears of many." He gave these charges weeping and entreating, and they promised not to transgress the command.

Meanwhile letters were brought, sent by those in Rome, making plain that Acme had been put to death, and referring the matter of Antipater to the father's judgment. Hearing this, Herod was glad and revived a little. But as his pains grew great, he abstained from food, and asking for an apple and a knife, he intended to kill himself. And he would have done the deed, had not someone, foreknowing it, restrained his right hand. When he cried out loudly, there was lamentation and great tumult, as though the king had gone. And Antipater, supposing him now dead, took heart, and begged the keeper of the prison to release him, promising great things. But the keeper made his intention known to the king. And he both cried out and sent some men to kill him at once. Then he altered his will again, giving Antipas the tetrarchy of Galilee and Peraea, and assigning to Archelaus the kingdom, but allotting to Philip his son, the true brother of Archelaus, the tetrarchy of Gaulanitis and Trachonitis and Batanaea and Paneas, and granting to his sister Salome Jamnia and Azotus and Phasaelis. Having done these things, and leaving gifts of many talents to Caesar and his wife Julia, he died on the fifth day after he had killed Antipater, having reigned, after he killed Antigonus, thirty-four years, and, after he had been declared king by the Romans, thirty-seven.

Salome and Alexas, before his death became known, sent away those shut up in the hippodrome, saying that the king ordered them to go off to their farms and tend their own affairs. And this was a very great benefaction from them to the nation. Then the king's death was made public, and the will was read, allotting the kingdom to his son Archelaus. But Ptolemy, who had been entrusted with the king's signet ring, said that the will could not be ratified otherwise than through Caesar. And at once there was a shout of those acclaiming Archelaus king. And after this the king's funeral was carried out lavishly.

The forefather of the race of the Hebrews and the patriarch of his line was this great Abraham, who was a Chaldaean by descent, the tenth from Noah, two hundred and ninety-two years having passed since God flooded the whole earth with rain. He, being of impious forebears, was the first to know one God, the Maker of all, having grasped the Maker from His works, and he said that to this God alone honor must be rendered. And when, on account of this, the Chaldaeans rose against him, he removed from there at the command of the God who had become known to him, and took possession of the land of Canaan. But when famine pressed upon Canaan, he migrates into Egypt. And being admired for his understanding, he hands down to the Egyptians, who were ignorant of these things, arithmetic and the matters concerning astronomy. And these are said to have passed from the Chaldaeans to Egypt and from there to the Greeks. When the Assyrians came against the Sodomites, among whom Lot also dwelt—being the nephew of Abraham and brother of Sarah—and many of the Sodomites had fallen and the rest had been taken captive, Lot too had been taken captive with the Sodomites. Learning this, Abraham, with three hundred and eighteen of his servants and three friends, pursued after the Assyrians, and saved both the Sodomites and Lot. And as he was returning from the pursuit, the king of the city Solyma received him, called Melchizedek—which, rendered into the language of the Greeks, means "righteous king"; for Solyma was then the name of the city Jerusalem; so ancient was the city, and by length of time it had obtained precedence over all. And God, having approved Abraham for his virtue, promised him a recompense for it; but when Abraham said that every benefaction seemed to him without grace, since he had no one to inherit it—for he was still without legitimate offspring, because Sarah's womb was barren—God promised to give him a child also, and that from him a great nation would come forth, equal in number to the stars; and He commanded that he himself and the males under him should be circumcised, so that his race might be unmixed with the other nations; and they were circumcised. There is born, then, to Abraham, when he was a hundred years old, a child from Sarah, whom God ordered to be named Isaac; the name means "laughter," either because it was a cause of smiling to Sarah that she should bear a child, when God had so declared, on account of the unlikelihood of the promise, since she was past the prime of age and did not expect to bear—for she happened to be ninety years old when she bore Isaac—or because the child became to its parents a cause of laughter, that is, of gladness and joy. And the father circumcised this child on the eighth day after his birth; whence it is the custom among the Jews too to be circumcised in this way. But the Arabs are accustomed to circumcise their children after the thirteenth year, because Ishmael their forefather was circumcised at this age; for he was thirteen years old when God commanded the circumcision to Abraham. And this name means "God-heard," since God hearkened to the supplication of Abraham and gave him a child. And he begot him from a maidservant whom Sarah laid beside him. For being herself at that time without offspring, she asked her husband to have intercourse with her own maidservant, named Hagar, an Egyptian by race; and when she had borne Ishmael, Sarah made the child her own. But when she had borne Isaac, she condemned Hagar with her son to flight, out of jealousy. When Isaac had come to manhood—according to the Hebrew Josephus, who says that Isaac was then twenty-five years old—God brings a test upon Abraham, and calling him He commands him to offer his son as a sacrifice, and to lead his only-begotten, his beloved, to one of the mountains and offer him as a whole burnt offering. And Abraham did not refuse, but taking his child and leading him up to the mountain appointed to him, he shares with him the divine oracle, and exhorts him to bear the consecration nobly, at God's command. And he is persuaded and willingly offers himself for the consecration, saying that it was not right to resist the will of God and his father. So these things are recorded by Josephus. Then Abraham is commanded to spare his son, and a ram is given in his stead of its own accord for the whole burnt offering. After this Sarah dies, being a hundred and twenty-seven years old, and Abraham took another wife, called Keturah, from whom six sons are born to him. And to Isaac, when he was about forty years old, his father betroths Rebekah from Mesopotamia, the daughter of Bethuel, the son of Nahor, Abraham's brother. Then Abraham dies, having lived a hundred and seventy-five years. And Isaac, having married Rebekah, begets twin children from her; of whom upon the elder thick hair grew over the whole body, whence he was called Esau, on account of the hairiness; while the younger held with his hand the heel of his brother, having sprung forth before him from the mother's womb, wherefore he was named Jacob; and the name means "supplanter" among the Hebrews.

When the king came to Gilgal, all the people of Israel gathered there, accusing the tribe of Judah of having gone secretly to him. But they said that they ought not to be reproached for this, being kindred by descent to the king. This word seemed harsh to the people. And a certain Benjamite, a seditious and wicked man called Sheba, cried out, "We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse," and sounding a horn he drew all away from David, only the tribe of Judah remaining with him. The king put forward Amasa as general and sent him to gather an army from the tribe of Judah, and to return within three days. But when Amasa delayed, Joab was ordered to take the force present there and march against Sheba, "so that," he said, "while we delay, the enemy may not the more prepare himself." And at once Joab went out to war. As he marched with a great force, Amasa met him; and Joab, as Amasa approached him, let the sword which he had girt on fall from its scabbard, and picked it up from the ground, and drawing near to greet Amasa thrust the blade into his belly and killed him. Taking over Amasa's people too, he pursued Sheba, who fled to a strong city. Joab besieged the city, and a wise woman from the wall cried out to him, "Why do you wish to overthrow a mother-city of Israel?" He answered, "Because of Sheba." She went to the citizens and persuaded them to cut off Sheba's head and throw it over the wall. When this had been done, Joab raised the siege and went off to Jerusalem, and was again appointed commander-in-chief of all the force.

After this there came a famine, and for three years it pressed upon the people. When the king inquired about this, God revealed that the famine came on account of the Gibeonites, and that they must receive satisfaction for those whom Saul had killed of them, in that he had not kept the oaths made to them by Joshua and the council of elders. The king therefore called the Gibeonites and asked what they would have done for them by way of atonement; and they asked that seven men be given them from the house of Saul. The king gave them the seven men as they asked, sparing Mephibosheth; and they, taking the men, killed them. And God brought rain down upon the land. After this, when there was a war against the foreigners, David with his own army pursued the enemy. And having become exhausted he was overcome with weakness; and one of the enemy, seeing him so disposed, rushed to strike him, but Abishai the brother of Joab, shielding the king, killed the foreigner. Because of this those about David swore that they would no longer allow him to go out to war. And again, when the foreigners marched out, the king sent an army against them and caused many to be slain, and the rest who were left to flee. After a short interval the foreigners came once more against the land of the Israelites. And there was among them a giant of a man, having six fingers on each hand and likewise on his feet; closing with him, Jonathan the nephew of David threw him down and stripped him, and gave the turn toward victory to his own people. From then on the foreigners no longer ventured to fight with the Hebrews.

These things, then, happened later; but in the first year of the reign of Baltasar the prophet saw a dream. The vision was of this kind. Four beasts seemed to come up out of the sea, of which the first had the form of a lioness and wings as of an eagle, which was also lifted up from the earth and stood on a man's feet, and a man's heart was given to it. The sea signified human life, full of waves and receiving very many and continual changes and reversals; and the beast, the lioness, figured the kingdom of the Assyrians; and its being lifted up from the earth indicated the cessation of that rule and the removal of its power. And its standing on a man's feet hinted that it would become equal to its subjects; and a man's heart being given to it, that it would be taught by experience to have human thoughts and not to imagine anything beyond human nature out of arrogance; for the wings, which had grown upon the beast contrary to nature, indicated the exaltation of those kings and the cloud-towering pride of their mind.

The second beast was likened to a bear, and stood up on one side, and had three ribs and wings in its mouth. And it was said to it, "Arise, eat much flesh." The bear was the figure of the kingdom of the Persians, because of the rawness and harshness of the nation; for of all barbarians the Persians were the harshest in punishing, devising the bitterest and most prolonged tortures by impalement-in-the-boats and by flaying.

It is likely that the punishment of the boats is unknown to some; it is well, then, to make this too plain to those who do not know it. They fasten two boats equal to one another together, and cut them out so that the head of the one being punished is left outside the boats, and the hands, and likewise the feet, and they lay the tortured man on his back inside, and so nail the boats to one another. Then mixing a compound of honey and milk they pour it into the mouth of that wretched man, until he becomes over-sated; and from such a compound they pour over his face and his feet and his hands, and setting him in the open they make him be heated by the sun, and so they do to him each day. Flies, then, and wasps and bees, gathering on account of the sweetness of what is poured over, settle upon his face and the other limbs that are left outside the boats, as has been said, troubling and even wounding the wretch. And his belly, filled with the honey and milk, sends forth liquid excrement, in which, as it rots, maggots and worms boil up; and he, his flesh too rotting with the moisture, and being himself consumed by the worms, thus dies a more pitiable and lingering death. This punishment is recorded to have been used by Parysatis too, the mother of Cyrus and Artaxerxes, against the man who boasted of having killed Cyrus when he fought his brother for the kingdom, the punishment of the boats being prolonged to the fourteenth day.

The punishment of the boats, then, is recorded to be of this kind. The "Arise, eat flesh" is not the word of one giving permission, but of one foretelling what is to come; for great destruction of the Assyrians and of those allied with them came about at the hands of the Persians and Medes. One might also say that the "eat much flesh" is significant of the rawness of the nation. The three ribs or wings which it held in its mouth prefigured the rule over the three divisions of the inhabited world. For Cyrus, who overthrew the kingdom of the Assyrians, subdued all the east as far as the Hellespont. His son Cambyses brought both Egypt and Ethiopia under him; and these are southern lands. Darius the son of Hystaspes subdued also the nomad Scythians; and these dwell in the northern clime. And Xerxes the son of Darius set out against Europe, attempting to master it too, but was driven back, defeated in a sea-battle by the Athenians, and withdrew in disgrace. The beast's standing on one side is significant of its not falling wholly from rule, but being circumscribed within a small part of it. For that kingdom, formerly mastering all Asia and the Ethiopians and Egyptians and Palestine and Phoenicia and Libya itself, fell from the rest, but there was left to it Media and Persia. Or otherwise the beast's standing on one side will be taken to mean that the kingdom of the Persians was for a time idle and inactive. For when Alexander had overthrown it, and then died, his monarchy was divided into four rules. And as his successors moved against one another and were weakened in their wars with one another, the Persians, again seizing the opportunity, took courage and recovered much of their own rule.

The third beast was like a leopard, and had four wings of a bird above it, and four heads grew on this beast, and it says that authority was given to it. This beast figured the Macedonian kingdom. For Alexander was likened to a leopard because of his swiftness and agility, which the wings also indicated. And their tetrad hinted at the four parts of the inhabited world, which he traversed in the manner of a bird and well-nigh mastered them all. And the four heads signified the division of the rule after his death. For his dominion was divided into four kingdoms, and Ptolemy son of Lagus mastered Egypt and his descendants down to Cleopatra; Seleucus took control of Syria and the lands adjoining it; Antigonus brought Asia under him; and Antipater ruled Macedonia, or, as some relate, Aridaeus, a half-brother of Alexander on his father's side. For Chaeron says that Perdiccas, being in greatest power after Alexander's death, at once dragged Aridaeus along like a prop of his kingship, a man born of an obscure and common woman, and imperfect in understanding, not brought to such a state by nature but because Olympias by drugs had corrupted his mind.

After these things Isaac grows old and is blinded in his eyes. And he summons Esau—for he was attached to him because of the rights of the firstborn—and bids him to hunt and to prepare a meal for him, "so that," he says, "having eaten, I may bless you before I die." And Esau went out to the hunt; but Rebekah, loving Jacob more, called him too and told him what his father had commanded Esau, and urged him to hasten to the flock and bring her two tender kids, that from these she might prepare for the old man the kind of dish she knew he loved, and that having eaten he might bless him. And he does according to his mother's commands. And when the dishes were already prepared, she wraps the arms of the boy with the skins of the kids, and gives him the meal to take to his father. But Isaac, perceiving by the voice that the one approaching was Jacob, summons him very near and feels his hands. And since God had in any case judged Esau unworthy of the blessing, it seemed to Isaac that his firstborn stood before him—he was perhaps deceived by the thickness of the hair—and having eaten he blessed Jacob.
