And Esau too returned and brought a meal to his father and asked for the blessing. But he understood the trick and said, "Your brother came and took your blessing." And when he lamented and demanded to be blessed—since there was not, he said, a single blessing left with him—Isaac, moved to compassion, set out to bless him; but because it did not seem to the divine Spirit that prompted him that Esau should obtain a blessing, since he was not worthy of it, the words of Isaac were shaped for him into a curse instead of a blessing. On account of these things Esau was hostile toward his brother. And Jacob, fearing his brother, departs into Mesopotamia by his mother's counsel. And as he was going, he is deemed worthy in his sleep of the famous vision of the ladder, of which the one end was set upon the earth and the other upon heaven, and he is initiated into things to come by the Higher Power, and the place in which he saw the vision he called Bethel; which means "divine hearth" among the Greeks. And having come to Haran, he was brought to Laban, the brother of his mother Rebekah, and obtained hospitality from him and is entrusted with the care of the flocks. Now Laban had two daughters, of whom the elder was called Leah and the other Rachel; and Jacob was stirred to love of the younger, who was comely in form beyond her sister, and he brings words to Laban concerning her. And he agrees to give Rachel in marriage to Jacob, if he will serve him for seven years. The lover consents to this; the time passes; the father-in-law prepares the marriage; but by night he lays the elder of his daughters beside Jacob. And learning by day that he had been deceived, he charges his father-in-law with wrongdoing. But he promised Rachel to him as well, after the service of another seven years. Jacob is persuaded again to serve, being enslaved by love, and after another seven years he is also wedded to Rachel. Now to Leah there were children by Jacob. And she calls the firstborn Reuben, because he came to her by the mercy of God; for she was grieved that her sister was beloved by her husband, and she expected rather to become more honored if she should conceive in her womb. And the second she names Simeon; this means that God became a hearer to her. And after him Levi is born; the name means "confirmer." After whom Judah is born to her; the name signifies "thanksgiving." But Rachel had no child, and fearing that on account of her childlessness she should be esteemed less, she asks her husband to go in to her maidservant. And he is persuaded and goes in to Bilhah, and Bilhah bears a child from Jacob, and the child was called Dan; the Greeks would say "God-judged." And from the same maid again is born Naphtali, "resourceful," as it were, because she contrived in rivalry against her sister's good fortune in children. At these things Leah is jealous, and she too lays her own maidservant Zilpah beside Jacob. And she too bore a son, Gad; one might call him "the chance-born." And after him she bears another, who was Asher; he might be called "the blessing-bringer," as having become a cause of good repute and felicitation to Leah on account of her many children. And when Reuben, the son of Leah, had brought mandrake apples, Rachel asked her to share some of them with her, and offered her sister in exchange the bed of Jacob on that night; for that night had been allotted to Rachel. And on account of this Jacob is wedded to Leah, and the woman bears yet two more children, Issachar—the name signifies "the one born from hire"—and Zebulun, which means "the one pledged by goodwill toward her"—and a daughter called Dinah. And to Rachel too a son, Joseph, is born; the name signifies the addition of someone to come.

Enjoying peace thereafter, David composed songs to God, and having fashioned instruments he taught the Levites to sing the hymns with them. The instruments were these: the harp had ten strings and was struck with a plectrum, while the lyre, having twelve notes, was plucked with the fingers; there were also cymbals of bronze, large and broad. About David too there was a company of noble men. The most distinguished of these were thirty-seven, who had often distinguished themselves in valour. Once, when the foreigners were encamped against Bethlehem, the king longed to drink water from the well in Bethlehem. And three of the brave men about him ran and passed through the middle of the enemy's camp and drew water from that well, and again passing through the enemy, who were astounded at their daring and stood still, brought the water to the king. But he said, "The Lord be merciful to me; I will not drink this, brought at the price of the men's blood and the peril of their lives." So he did not drink it, but poured it out as a libation to God.

Wishing to number all the people, he ordered Joab to make the counting. But when Joab did not approve the plan and said the act was not good, the king would not be persuaded. So Joab went and numbered the people, and the number of Israel was eight hundred thousand men of force drawing a sword, and five hundred thousand fighting men of the tribe of Judah. Then David repented and confessed that he had sinned. Gad the prophet, at God's command, went to David and said, "Choose one of these three, whichever is to your mind: whether you choose that there be famine in your land for seven years, or to be pursued by enemies for three months, or that death fall upon your people for three days." He said, "Things are narrow for me on every side, but it is better for me to fall into the hands of God." And death came upon the people from morning until the hour of the midday meal, and there died of all the people seventy thousand. And David supplicated God. The destroying angel stretched out his hand over Jerusalem. The king said therefore, "I have sinned, O Lord, I the shepherd; but the flock, the people, have not sinned. I am worthy of punishment, and not these." Moved by the king's contrition, God stayed the destruction, and through the prophet Gad commanded an altar to be set up on the threshing-floor of Ornan the Jebusite, and to sacrifice there. And David did so, having bought the threshing-floor from Ornan. As Josephus wrote, it is said that in that place Abraham brought Isaac to offer him as a whole burnt-offering. David also wished to build a temple to God there, but he was prevented by God.

When David had grown very old, he was sensitive to cold from his age. Therefore they chose a young girl—her name was Abishag—and the girl lay with the king and warmed him. But he did not know her, for through age he was unable for marital union. Adonijah, who was fourth among the king's sons and exceedingly handsome, seeing his father grown old, laid claim to the kingdom, with Joab the commander-in-chief and Abiathar the high priest supporting him. Once, having prepared a lavish sacrifice, he summoned his brothers and the leading men of the tribe of Judah and Abiathar and Joab; but Solomon and the prophet Nathan and Benaiah the commander of the bodyguard he did not call. Nathan therefore said to Bathsheba, "Have you heard that Adonijah has become king?" She went in to the king and said, "You swore, my lord the king, that Solomon your son should reign after you, and behold, Adonijah has become king, and you do not know it." While Bathsheba was still saying this, the prophet Nathan came in and asked the king whether Adonijah had become king with his consent. And the king swore by God that "this day Solomon shall be king." Calling the high priest Zadok and Benaiah, he ordered them to take with them the prophet and the men-at-arms of the royal court, and to set Solomon upon the king's mule, and leading him out beyond the city to the spring called Gihon, to anoint him with the holy oil, and to proclaim him king with trumpet-blasts upon the horns, and to escort him back through the middle of the city. And they at once did as they were ordered; and the proclamation of Solomon was noised abroad everywhere. When this became known to Adonijah and those feasting with him, the rest went off to their homes, but Adonijah, in great fear, took refuge at the altar and asked of Solomon pledges of his safety. Solomon forgave him his offence for the time, but said, "If hereafter he be found doing any evil, he shall be put to death."

Seeing his death drawing near, David summoned Solomon and charged him to keep the commandments of God and to govern according to his laws, "so that our seed," he said, "as the Lord promised me, may be upon my throne forever." And he added that he should not leave Joab unpunished, who had killed Abner and Amasa, nor indeed Shimei, who had cursed him as he fled. And after charging him with other things, and enjoining him to build a temple to the Lord, he gave him the plan of the temple's construction, and roused both him and the rulers and the tribe of Levi to the work with his words, saying that he was leaving much for the building of the temple—ten thousand talents of gold, a hundred thousand talents of silver, emerald and other precious stones, bronze and iron past counting, and other material in abundance; and that now he was adding to what had already been collected three thousand talents of pure gold for the inner sanctuary, and ten thousand staters, and ten thousand talents of silver. And if anyone had any precious stone, each brought it and gave it into the treasuries. A little later David died, having lived seventy years, having reigned in Hebron seven years and in Jerusalem thirty-three, a man who had achieved every virtue befitting a king. His son Solomon buried him royally in Jerusalem, and entombed abundant wealth with him.

The form of the fourth beast the prophet did not declare, but said that it was exceedingly fearful and astounding, having great teeth of iron, eating and grinding and trampling down what was left, and that it differed greatly from the beasts that went before. By this the kingdom of the Romans is signified. Therefore the prophet set neither form nor name to it. For the rule of the Romans is of many kinds, being directed at first by kings from Romulus to the Tarquins, and when their tyranny was destroyed governed as an aristocracy, the senate and consuls managing affairs, and sometimes too as a democracy, the people often rising in faction against the senate, and afterward falling again into monarchy, and from this returning to the name of kingdom. He said the beast was fearful and astounding because this kingdom became more powerful than the others, and all that the Macedonian kingdom did not subdue, this one brought under itself—all Greece, that is, Carthage with Libya, Sicily, Sardinia and other islands and various western nations besides, which Alexander did not rule; which things whoever wishes to know, let him read the books of the Roman Dio and the writings of Polybius. He said the beast was fearful and astounding and having iron teeth, since the rule of the Romans became more terrible than all the other kingdoms. For in the image seen in the dream by Nabuchodonosor he set the iron as the figure of the fourth kingdom. With its iron teeth, then, he said the beast ate and ground, and trampled the rest with its feet. The eating and grinding is taken to mean the levying of tributes, since heavier taxes were imposed on the subjects, which feed and fatten the rulers but make the payers themselves thin and poor. And those who would not pay tribute, claiming their freedom, these the beast trampled with its feet and destroyed; and by the feet the soldiery is hinted, since on this the kingdom is propped and stands and passes from one place to another. He says the beast had ten horns, indicating that at the last the kingdom would be divided into many dominions. And in the midst of the ten a little horn came up, and three of the horns were uprooted by it, and that horn had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and warred with the saints. This horn some have understood of the Antichrist. It was called little as being about to spring from a small tribe of the Hebrews. It will overthrow three of the ten kings. By the eyes is hinted his wickedness and craft, in that through these he will deceive many. By the mouth speaking great things is shown his boastfulness and the exaltation of his pride. The making war with the saints shows that he will display all zeal to make all men sharers in his own wickedness and blasphemy. And of his blasphemy against God this is expressive, that "he will speak words on high."

Upon this the prophet added, "I beheld until thrones were set and the Ancient of Days sat, and his garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head as pure wool, his throne a flame of fire, his wheels burning fire; a river of fire drew forth issuing before him; thousand thousands ministered to him and ten thousand times ten thousand stood beside him. The court sat, and books were opened." The horn, then, which was said to do these things, was shown to Daniel not to endure for long, but until the Eternal sat as judge—that is, set a time of judgement and unfolded the memory of what each had done. For by books he called the recollections, and by the Ancient of Days the Eternal. The whiteness of the hairs and the purity of the garment show his being clean on every side and without blemish. And that he might show that the deeds of the Antichrist will come to pass by God's permission, and not as though the divine nature were unable to stay them or to refuse to permit them to come about at all, he introduced the thousand thousands of ministers and the ten thousand times ten thousand standing by, and the fiery throne and the like wheels and the flaming river. "And I beheld until the beast was slain and its body given to the burning of fire." For on account of the madness of the Antichrist the whole kingdom will be taken away. And not the beast itself will be given to the burning, but its body. For since the beast hints at the kingdom, it is likely that in the kingdom there are many who worship God and pursue virtue. It is not these, then, that he says will be given to the burning, but the workers of wickedness and those given over continually to the desires of the body and minding nothing spiritual.

After the destruction of the beast the prophet says he saw as it were a son of man coming on the clouds and reaching to the Ancient of Days, to whom he says was given the rule and the honour and the kingdom, and that all peoples and tongues and tribes should serve him, and that his authority would be eternal and not pass away, and that his kingdom would not be destroyed. These things clearly foretell the second manifestation of our Saviour Jesus Christ. For he is called Son of Man because of our nature, which he assumed, and as coming on the clouds according to his own promise, when he said, "You will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven."

Now for twenty years Jacob shepherded for his father-in-law; then, wishing to withdraw, he was not permitted. Therefore he fled secretly with his wives, together with the maidservants and the children, taking along his possessions and the flocks that had been allotted to him as wages for shepherding. And Rachel also carried off the idols of her father—not as honoring them, but that she might have these as a refuge, if her father, pursuing them, should overtake them. And when Laban overtook them on the seventh day, God commanded him in a dream to make a treaty with Jacob. By day there are words between the two, and when Jacob had shown that he did no wrong, Laban charged him concerning the ancestral gods. But he, conscious of nothing concerning them, allowed him to search. And he searched. But Rachel had placed the idols in the saddle of the camel that bore her, and she sat upon it, saying that the flow of her monthly periods was troubling her. And Laban, thinking that his daughter would never approach his gods with such an affliction, passed her by. And he turned back; but Jacob, fearing his brother, sends ahead a message declaring to him his return, and dispatches gifts to him. And when night came on, meeting with a phantom he wrestled with it and seemed to prevail. And perceiving that it was an angel of God, he begged it to tell him what fortune he would have; and it said that the prevailing over a divine angel must be deemed a sign of great good things, and bade him be called Israel. This name some interpret as "a mind seeing God," but Josephus says it signifies "one who withstood a divine angel." And Jacob calls the place Peniel, that is, "the face of God." And since a pain arose in him during the wrestling with the angel, about the broad sinew, he renounced the eating of it, and on his account it is forbidden also to all his race. When Esau met his brother, they came together and embraced. Then Esau departed, and Jacob came to Shechem. And while the Shechemites were keeping a festival, his daughter Dinah went into the city to see the festival. So Shechem, the son of the king of the city, beholding her, defiled her by violence. Then his father begged Jacob to give Dinah in marriage to Shechem; but he would not consent. And Simeon and Levi, the brothers of the girl by the same mother, while those in the city were feasting on account of the festival and were heavy-headed, going in by night, slew every male of full age, and the king and his son. So Josephus says. But the book of Genesis records these things more credibly. For it says that, when Hamor the father of Shechem asked that Dinah be married to his son, Simeon and Levi said, "If all the males in the city should be circumcised, we will give our sister to your son," and that they accepted the proposal and were all circumcised. And on the third day after the circumcision, while those who had been circumcised were in a bad state and in pain from the inflammation, they fell upon them and slew them all, without Jacob's knowledge. And when he was angry at these things, God bade him take courage. And Jacob, having come to Bethel, where he had seen the dream, sacrificed. And going on, he buries Rachel, who had died in childbirth, at Ephratha. And the child born from her he called Benjamin, on account of the pain that befell its mother at his birth. And coming to Hebron, a city of the Canaanites, he found his father Isaac still living, but Rebekah had died beforehand. And after a little while Isaac too dies, and is buried with his wife in the ancestral tomb, having lived a hundred and eighty-five years. Now Esau ruled over Idumaea, having called the country after himself. For he was called Edom, because, returning once from the hunt famished, and finding his brother having prepared lentils for himself as food, he asked him to give him some; but Jacob compelled him to sell him his birthright in exchange for the lentils. And Esau yields it to him with oaths on account of the famine; whence he was called Edom, on account of the yellowness of the lentils; for they were exceedingly of such a color. And among the Hebrews "Edom" means "red."

When Solomon took over the kingdom he was very young, being in the twelfth year of his age. Now Adonijah went to Bathsheba the mother of Solomon and said, "You know that the kingdom belonged to me both by seniority of birth and by the choice of the people, but it passed to my brother Solomon, and I must love what has happened as having happened by the will of God. One request I ask: that the girl who lay with my father, Abishag, be given me in marriage, since my father, through age, never knew her, but she is still a virgin." Bathsheba undertook to convey his words to her son and to bring about the marriage for him most zealously. And going to her son she begged him to give Abishag to his brother Adonijah. But he, angered at the word, said he wondered whether she would not also think it right that he yield the kingdom to Adonijah as the elder. And at once he ordered Benaiah, the commander of the bodyguard, to kill Adonijah. He ordered Abiathar to go to his native place and to live in the fields, "for," he said, "all that you toiled together with my father saves you from death." So, as God had foretold to Eli, the honour of the priesthood was taken from the house of Ithamar and passed to Zadok, who was of the line of Phinehas. The general Joab, learning this and having become greatly afraid, took refuge at the altar, and when summoned said that he would never come out, but would die there and nowhere else. When this was reported to the king it persuaded him to send and kill Joab even there. From then on Benaiah was put forward as general of all the force, and Zadok was deemed worthy of the high priesthood. Shimei the king confined within Jerusalem, so as not to go out of it; otherwise he set death as the penalty for him. But after three years, when his servants had fled, he went out in search of them; and learning this, Solomon ordered the man to be put to death.

Solomon took to wife a daughter of Pharaoh, and raised the walls of Jerusalem higher and made them stronger. When God appeared to him in a dream, he told him to ask whatever he wished; and he asked that understanding and prudence be given to him. And God, accepting him for his request, promised to give him wisdom and a great mind such as no other before him nor any after him should have, and to add even what he had not asked—wealth and victory and renown—if he kept his commandments and his ordinances.

After this two women came to him; of whom the one said, "O king, we two dwelt together and no one was with us. We both bore a male child at the same time. And a little later this woman, lying upon her own son, found him dead when she awoke. And she put the dead child, while I slept, into my arms, and taking the living one from me made it her own. And when I perceived the deed I seek my child; but she does not give him to me." The other firmly maintained that the living child was her own, and the dead one her adversary's; and she swore she had not gone so far in wrongdoing. When those standing by were at a loss how the truth might be discerned, the king ordered the living child to be cut in two with a sword and a part given to each of the women. This the true mother of the infant took grievously, and refused the sentence, and begged that the child be given living to her adversary; but the false one, calling herself the mother of the child, both praised the judgement and urged on the division. And the king ordered the living child to be given to the woman who refused its division, saying, "This is its mother, who was in deep anguish when the child was about to be slaughtered." The whole people took this as a sure proof of the king's prudence.

He surpassed all who were before him in wisdom and prudence. He composed three thousand parables and five thousand songs, and he wrote on all things from the cedar to the hyssop, and he examined and philosophized concerning the nature of living creatures, the land-dwellers, the creatures of the air, and the swimmers, and their properties; and against demons he devised incantations for the cure of men, and left forms of exorcism by which the demons were driven out. And this remedy, Josephus says, was still in force down to his own day; and he relates a thing of this sort to confirm the account. One Eleazar of his own nation, he says, possessed a ring having beneath its seal a root such as Solomon had pointed out, and would bring it to the nostrils of the demoniac, and through the smelling, by the man's nostrils, the demon would be drawn out. Then, recalling Solomon, he would recite incantations such as Solomon had composed, and adjure the demon never to return into the man. He says that Eleazar did this in the presence of Vespasian and his sons; and to give proof of his power over the demons he would set a cup full of water and command the demon, as it went out of the sufferer, to overturn it; and the cup was overturned, none seeing him who overturned it.

These things, then, Daniel was instructed in in the first year of the reign of Baltasar; and in the third year he saw another vision. "For being in Susa," he says, "I lifted up my eyes, and behold, a ram standing by the Ubal, and it had high horns, and the one higher than the other, and the higher came up last. And it was butting toward the sea and the north and the south, and all the beasts could not stand before it, and it did according to its will, and was magnified." Again here the prophet is taught about the kingdoms. And the rule of the Persians was likened to a ram on account of the wealth surrounding it, and the ram was standing by the Ubal, that is, by the gate of Susa; for this was the city, the mother-city of the Persians, and there the kings had their palace, and the prophet, dwelling in this city, saw the vision. And the two horns that directed this kingdom figured two lines. For the lesser horn figured Cyrus and his son Cambyses—for up to him the rule of the kingdom stood, and the line of Cyrus did not advance further—while the greater horn hinted at the line of Darius, which advanced to the last Darius, whom Alexander conquered in war. For when Cambyses the son of Cyrus had died, the magi by guile usurped the kingdom; and when they had ruled for a short time and it became known who they were, the seven houses of the Persians overthrew them. From these reigned Darius the son of Hystaspes, whose line endured to the end of the kingdom. For this the prophet shows by adding that the higher came up last, signifying that one of the horns endured for long and to the end of the Persian kingdom. The ram butted toward the south and north and sea; for it subdued both the southern and the northern clime, and the most of the islands—for these he hinted at by the sea—it brought under servitude; and the dwellers in the islands were allies of Xerxes when he marched against Greece; therefore the prophet saw the ram butting toward the sea also. And none of the beasts could stand before it. By beasts he called the lesser kingdoms, as being fearful to their subjects. These would be the kingdom of the Syrians, of the Cilicians, of the Arabs, of the Egyptians, of the Jews, and others; none of these, then, was able to withstand the rule of the Persians to the end, but he subdued all whom he assailed. "And it was magnified," either because the rule became great, mastering many nations and lands, or because, swollen with prosperity, it imagined great things beyond human nature.

While the prophet was perplexed about what he saw, he sees a he-goat coming from the southwest over all the earth, and it had one notable horn between its eyes. And reaching to the ram it grew fierce against it and smote it and broke its horns and threw it to the ground and trampled it, and there was none to deliver the ram from its hand. The he-goat figured the Macedonian kingdom; for it is swifter than the ram and more agile. It came from the southwest, because Alexander, having first brought Egypt under him, so set out a second time against Darius, and routing him overthrew the kingdom of the Persians. For at Issus in Cilicia he engaged him formerly and defeated him, and took his wife and daughters and his chariot and his bow and plundered the Persian camp; and Darius fled from there, and again gathering forces fought with Alexander when he had set out from Egypt against him, and was defeated again at Arbela and perished as he fled. He says the horn was notable, that is, conspicuous and renowned; and by this too he hints at the kingdom of Alexander. And he says the horn grew between its eyes, on account of the shrewdness and understanding and noble spirit of Alexander. And "the he-goat came," he says, "to the ram with the horns, and I saw it reaching to the ram, and it grew fierce against it and smote the ram and broke both its horns, and the ram had no strength to stand before it, and it threw it to the ground and trampled it." And both the horns of the ram were broken, he says, when the he-goat dashed against it—that is, both its powers, in which it had trusted, the Persian and the Median. For the kings of the Persians ruled over Persians and Medes, since Cyrus, as has been said, sprang from both and held the kingdom of both under him, and both these lines overthrew the kingdom of the Assyrians. "And the he-goat was magnified exceedingly." For he not only brought under him those subject to the Assyrian rule, but subdued many others as well. For he assailed India and conquered Porus and won over Taxiles and held other parts of India. Then, the prophet showing that this one too, having prospered for a little while, would pass away, added, "And when it grew strong its great horn was broken, and four horns grew up from beneath it." For when Alexander, after that prosperity, had died suddenly, his rule was divided into four, as has already been said in the case of the third beast, which seemed to Daniel in his sleep to come up out of the sea, having four heads.

"And out of one of the horns came a fearful horn, and it was magnified exceedingly toward the south and toward the east and toward the southwest and toward the host. And it was magnified to the host of heaven, and there fell to the earth some of the host and of the stars, and it trampled them." The things concerning Antiochus Epiphanes Daniel is taught beforehand by these words; he was the son of Antiochus the Great, and growing stronger than the kings before him—those from Seleucus, that is—and mastering Egypt and other lands, he marched also against the Jews and gained control of the city of Jerusalem, and indeed of the whole nation, and plundered the temple and defiled it, sacrificing swine in it, and setting up an altar to Zeus he forced the whole nation to follow Greek ways, preventing them from circumcising their males. For his madness against God the "it was magnified to the host of heaven" hints. The "there fell from the host and from the stars to the earth, and it trampled them" indicates those of the Jewish people who became impious because of the compulsion laid on them by him, who fell away from their lawful and divine manner of life, yielding to the tyrant and being trampled by him. They were called stars because of the purity and surpassing brightness of their piety, or because God promised Abraham to multiply his seed as the stars of heaven. "And it was established as far as the prince of the host." For he raged even against God himself, the prince of the powers above. "And the sacrifice was troubled by a falling, and it came to be and prospered, and sin was given upon the sacrifice, and righteousness was cast to the ground." For sacrificing things forbidden, he troubled the sacrifice—that is, confounded and defiled it. By "fallings" he means the swine, and by "sin upon the sacrifice" the lawlessness committed at it. By the "righteousness was cast to the ground" the abolition of the divine ordinances and the unjust murders of those who would not consent to be impious are shown. But even doing these things and being so impious, Antiochus prospered, he says.

Upon this Daniel adds, "And one holy one said to the Phelmuni, How long shall the vision stand, and the sacrifice taken away, and the sin of desolation given? And he said to him, Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days, and the holy place shall be cleansed." To the prophet, anxious because of what he saw, angels are sent showing him that the hardships will have an end, and teaching the time of their passing. And one asked the other; for the word "phelmuni," translated into Greek, signifies "a certain one." He asked not as one ignorant, but that Daniel might learn. And the one questioned answered, "Two thousand days, and until evening and morning, and the holy place shall be cleansed." By evening he called the beginning of the woes, or also their whole duration—for things grievous are like night and darkness—and by morning the peaceful state after the calamities. This, then, he signifies by what he says, that from the beginning of the evils to their end so great a time would pass. The days, reckoned against years, make up six years and an equal number of years according to the reckoning of the Hebrews; for over so long a time the calamity brought upon the Jews under Antiochus prevailed. These things were imparted to the prophet by the archangel Gabriel, as he sought understanding.

Now Jacob loved Joseph, the son of Rachel, more than the other children, both for the goodliness of his body and for the virtue of his soul. And indeed his father's affection, and the dreams that he saw, stirred his brothers to envy of him. Of the dreams the one was of this kind: in the season of summer he seemed, while reaping with his brothers, to be binding sheaves and setting them up, and his own remained at rest, while those of his brothers ran up and did obeisance to his. The other was this: the sun and the moon and the rest of the stars seemed to him to do obeisance to him. When he had related these visions to his father, in the presence of his brothers, he asked to learn their meaning. And he proclaimed good fortune to the child, and that a time would come in which he would be honored and venerated by his parents and his brothers. These things grieved the brothers of Joseph, and they looked askance at the youth. And while the sons of Jacob were grazing the flocks at Shechem, the father sends Joseph to look after them. But they, seeing him, set out to kill him. Reuben, however, counseled them not to become the slayers of their brother with their own hands, but to throw him into a pit nearby, that he might die there, and so the evil would be more moderate. And when the young men assented to the proposal, Reuben, taking the youth, gently let him down into the pit. But Judah, seeing Arab merchants, counseled his brothers to sell Joseph to them. And when this seemed good to them, they sell him to the merchants for twenty minae, being seventeen years old. And Reuben, coming to the pit by night, that he might bring up Joseph and save him without his brothers' knowledge, when he did not find him, in his grief reproached his brothers. But when they told what had been done, he ceases from his grief. And having stained the boy's tunic with the blood of a he-goat, they came to their father and said that they had neither seen Joseph nor known how he had perished, but had found this tunic bloodied and torn. And Jacob sat mourning for the youth, having put on sackcloth. Now Joseph was bought from the merchants by Potiphar, an Egyptian, the chief of the cooks of King Pharaoh, and he held him in honor. But when the wife of his master, on account of his comeliness and his adroitness, was disposed amorously toward him and brought words concerning intercourse, he put aside her demand. And she, sorely besieged by love, brought a second attempt, and despairing of persuasion she wished to use force. And when the young man, leaving his garment behind, leapt out, she sat downcast and confounded. And when her husband came, she accused Joseph and displayed the garment, as though he had left it when he was attempting to use force. And Potiphar casts Joseph into the prison of evildoers, in which the cupbearer of Pharaoh too was shut up in anger, and the chief baker. Having become familiar with these men, he was asked to tell them the meaning of their dreams. For the cupbearer thought he saw a vine, from which three branches grew, on which hung great and ripe clusters, and that he pressed these into a cup and brought it to Pharaoh, and that he received it. Joseph interpreted that the dream signified good things for him; for within the three days following he would be restored to his former office. And he asked that, when he had prospered, he would remember him. But the chief baker said that he seemed to be carrying three baskets upon his head, two full of bread, the other of cooked food and various viands, and that these were snatched away by birds flying down upon them. And Joseph said to this man too that the three baskets signified three days, and that on the third day he was to be hanged and become food for flesh-eating birds. And it came to pass for both of them as Joseph had interpreted.

He began the building of the temple in the fourth year of his reign, four hundred and forty years after the people's departure from Egypt. As to the measures of its height and length and the manner of its construction, the third book of Kings and Josephus, who writes of the temple in the eighth book of the Antiquities, do not agree, but in most points they differ. Whoever wishes to examine carefully the matters concerning the difference, and concerning the two cherubim of gold which he made and set in the inner sanctuary, and concerning the ark and the bronze sea and the lavers, and how great the bronze altar was, and what the golden table was like, and how many vessels of silver and of gold Solomon dedicated to the temple, and concerning the rest—the third book of Kings and Josephus the antiquarian will suffice to set out the exactness of each point. In seven years the king completed the temple and all that concerned it, and summoned the people to Jerusalem. And the priests took up the ark and the tabernacle which Moses had pitched and the vessels used in the sacrifices, and conveyed them to the temple, the king leading the way and all the multitude, and the Levites pouring libations and offering incense. And the ark was set in the inner sanctuary between the two cherubim, holding within it the two stone tablets. When the priests had come out from the inner sanctuary, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord, and a cloud was poured around the whole temple; from which they imagined that God had taken up his abode in the temple, having tabernacled in it. The king, rejoicing at this, gave thanks to God and blessed the people and supplicated that the deity might be attentive to all who prayed in it. Then he offered sacrifices upon the altar. And God, showing how graciously he had received them, caused fire to flash through the air and to be brought to the altar and to consume the whole sacrifice. Seeing this, the people blessed God, and the king gave thanks, and after a lavish festival they dismissed the assembly. A dream came to the king that God had heard his prayer, and that the temple would be preserved and he himself raised to the height of happiness, and that his descendants would rule the land, if he and they and the people did not transgress the divine commandments; but if not, God threatened to cut off his race root and branch, and to subject the people to slavery and countless afflictions, and to deliver the temple to burning and plunder, and the city to overthrow and pillage.

Thus then was the work of the temple completed by Solomon; and after this he built himself a costly and splendid palace, and he further repaired the walls of Jerusalem, and built other cities besides, and having subdued the Canaanites in Mount Lebanon, who had not before been subjected, he made them tributary. Hiram the king of the Tyrians sent him puzzles and riddling sayings, asking him to make them clear; and he solved them all and explained their meaning. Josephus records that these things are mentioned by ancient authors as well, by Dius and besides him Menander. When the wisdom and prudence of Solomon was noised abroad everywhere, a certain queen of Egypt and Ethiopia, who loved and sought wisdom, came to Jerusalem. The king received her with all honour, and the riddles which she set before him he readily solved, so that the queen was astounded and said she saw more than she had heard. She marvelled also at the palace and the lavishness of the banquets and the whole royal service, and the sacrifices in the temple and the good order of those who sacrificed. She presented the king with gold and precious stones and untold spices and balsam-roots, so that from her the balsam grew in Palestine. And Solomon in turn repaid the queen with many good things. And she returned to her own land.

Then, on account of the captivity of his countrymen, again under Darius the ruler of the Medes—who was also named Cyaxares and Ahasuerus, being the son of Astyages—while the prophet was mourning and beseeching God, a certain man named Gabriel touched him. He touched him about the hour of the evening sacrifice, or at the time of the evening service, or for as long a time as the evening service lasted. And he said to Daniel, "Now I have come forth to give you understanding and to announce to you that you are a man of desires. And consider the matter and understand the vision"—that is, give careful heed to what is said, since it is riddling and needs much zeal. For sometimes divine things are made known through riddles, that they may not become plain to all and on this account contemptible. Daniel was called a man of desires either as playing the man against the desires of the flesh and nobly withstanding them, or as desiring to learn what was to come upon the people and his fellow-countrymen, or because he was desirable and beloved on account of the virtue he pursued.

Then the angel adds, "Seventy weeks have been cut short upon your people and upon your holy city, until the transgression is made old and sin is completed, and until the sealing of sin and the propitiation of iniquity and the bringing in of everlasting righteousness, and the sealing of vision and prophet, and the anointing of a Holy of Holies." The prophet, praying, said to God, "your people and your city"; but the angel says to Daniel, "your people and your city," as though the people were not worthy to be called God's. The like is found in the case of Moses too, when the Israelites, having made the calf, offered sacrifice to it; for then too, when the prophet prayed, God spoke likewise. The angel says, then, that Jerusalem will be built and your people will return and will continue for four hundred and ninety years; for the seventy weeks add up to that number, and he reckoned each day for a year. The "have been cut short" stands for "have been decided and determined." "Until the transgression is made old and sin is completed"—that is, until it grow old and increase; for this is what "made old" and "sin become complete" signifies. By these words he sets forth the audacity and frenzy of the Jews against the Lord. For many sins they had committed before this too and paid the penalty, but were recalled again; but when they raged against the Saviour and came to the extreme of wickedness and wrought sin complete, they no longer obtained recall. The "seal sin and propitiate iniquity" signifies the remission of faults bestowed by the Lord on those who believe in him; for this is he who takes away the sin of the world; for the "seal" is significant of "cause to cease." The "bring in everlasting righteousness" means his coming into the world, who is righteousness and redemption and sanctification. The "seal vision and prophet" shows that the prophecies have had their end, either because what was spoken by them concerning Christ has now come to pass, or because the gift of prophecy has failed among the Jews, or both. For Christ, having come, sealed the prophecies—fulfilled them, that is, and confirmed and indeed ended them; for there is no longer among them ruler and prophet and leader. And "bring in everlasting righteousness," which is our Lord and Saviour himself. For the apostle says, "God's wisdom was given to us, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption." And elsewhere, writing of the gospel, he says, "Righteousness is revealed in it." And the Lord teaches, "Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness," which he himself brought, making it manifest to us through his teaching. And the "anoint a Holy of Holies" shows that the Master Christ came to be present. For who else would be called Holy of Holies but our Lord and Saviour? who, being a fountain of holiness, is yet anointed with the Holy Spirit in respect of his humanity, as Isaiah cried out beforehand, saying, "The spirit of the Lord is upon me, for which cause he anointed me," and as David sang, saying, "God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness beyond your fellows," and as the chief and summit of the apostles, Peter, taught, writing of the Saviour that "God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power"; and he seals and confirms the old Scriptures, doing and suffering all that was foretold through them, and propitiates iniquity, reconciling sinners to God the Father and rendering him merciful to those who had transgressed.

Then the divine archangel adds, "And you shall know and understand: from the going forth of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem until Christ the leader, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks." Now the temple began to be built under Cyrus; for Cyrus first granted the return to the nation of the Jews, but it was hindered by Cambyses the son of Cyrus through the envy of the neighbouring nations, and the rebuilding was again entrusted to the Jews when Darius the son of Hystaspes gained the kingdom of the Persians. But the time, reckoned from none of these, is found not to preserve the count according to the archangel's word, but to exceed it; whereas if the time be reckoned from the years of the reign of Artaxerxes, it would be found neither in excess nor deficient. And it must be reckoned from this, because then both a wall was thrown about the city and what was lacking was added to the temple and the city was filled with inhabitants, when Nehemiah, cupbearer to Artaxerxes, begged him that the return to his homeland be granted, and going off walled the city about and settled it and finished the temple that was unfinished. If, then, one reckon the time back from the manifestation of the Saviour—through whom alone remission of sins was given and righteousness brought in and the predictions of the prophets fulfilled—he will find it completed up to the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, when, that is, Nehemiah, having received leave, returned to Jerusalem; which the history, going on in order, will relate more fully. And the one whom he above called the Holy of Holies, he now calls Christ the leader, naming him in respect of his humanity. For as he is called firstborn of the new creation and firstborn from the dead, so he is also called leader. And the divine apostle Peter named the Saviour the Prince of life, in discourse with the Jews, as the divine Luke records in the Acts. As, then, he was called our firstborn and chief according to the great Paul in respect of his humanity, so too he was named leader by the archangel Gabriel.

Then God sends upon Pharaoh two visions of dreams, and the meanings of both. But he remembered the visions and forgot the interpretations. So he summons together the wise men of the Egyptians and reports to them the dreams and demands the meaning; and when they were at a loss, he was angry. And the cupbearer, if not before, yet then came to remember Joseph, and tells Pharaoh about him. So he is led in at once. And Pharaoh says, "Tell me, young man, the interpretation of the dreams that I have seen. I thought that seven well-fed oxen, coming up out of the river, went toward the marsh; and that seven others, lean and wasted with hunger, coming out of the marsh, met these, and that the first and fat ones were devoured by the second, and that they remained still lean as before. And again I see seven ears of grain growing from a single root, flourishing and bowed by the weight of the fruit. And near them I seemed to see an equal number of ears, feeble from lack of dew and unpleasant to the sight, which consumed those that were fruitful and fair." And Joseph says, "Although the dreams are twofold, O king, they have one meaning of things to come. For the oxen, an animal that labors at the plow, devoured by the worse; and the flourishing ears wasted away by the feeble—these announce a famine for so many years upon your country, in an equal number of years previously flourishing in fruits, so that the abundance of these will be consumed by what comes after. But if you store up the goods of the former prosperity for the years of barrenness, you will make the misfortune imperceptible to the Egyptians." And Pharaoh, struck with amazement at Joseph's wisdom on account of the interpretation and the counsel, said, "You yourself shall be the judge and counselor and steward of the things resolved upon." And he gave him his authority, so that he used Pharaoh's seal and clothed himself in purple and rode upon a chariot. Joseph was then thirty years old. And Pharaoh named him Psothomphanech; the name means "discoverer of hidden things." And he joined to him also a wife, called Asenath, the daughter of the chief of the priests in Heliopolis. From her children are born to him before the famine, of whom the elder was Manasseh—the name means "forgetting," because he found forgetfulness of his misfortunes—and the younger was Ephraim, which means "rendering back," because the freedom of his forefathers was rendered back to him. From there came the time of want. And the famine prevailed not only over Egypt, but also over the country in which Jacob dwelt. So he sends his sons into Egypt to buy grain, keeping only Benjamin with himself as the youngest. They, then, came to Joseph. And he, not recognized, recognized his brothers, and said that they had come as spies. But they told from where they came, and that they were of one father, still living, and that there was another younger brother with the father. And Joseph said that they would give him assurance of the truth, if they would bring the younger brother to him. So he gives them grain, and secretly placing the silver in the sack of each; but he kept Simeon to be a hostage for their return. The sons came back to Jacob bringing the grain, and reported what had happened, and the holding back of Simeon caused him grief, and he would not consent to let Benjamin be taken to Egypt. But when the grain had already been spent, since it was not otherwise possible for them to go to Egypt unless they brought Benjamin too, the father, yielding to necessity, gives him, and double the price of the grain, and gifts for Joseph. And when they came to Egypt, they brought him the gifts. But he, seeing Benjamin and being deeply moved, withdrew, that he might not become visible in his tears. Then he takes the brothers to a meal, and honored Benjamin with double portions, and bids the steward of the grain to give them grain and to put the price into the sacks, and into Benjamin's load to throw also a silver cup. When these things had been done, the brothers departed, taking Simeon. But horsemen surround them as they were leaving, charging them with the theft of the cup, and searching they found the cup by Benjamin's load. So the horsemen led Benjamin to Joseph, and his brothers, rending their robes, wept and followed along. And Joseph, having reproached them as ungrateful, set the rest free, but was content with the holding of Benjamin alone. And helplessness gripped them. But Judah, speaking and pleading much that was moving toward compassion, brought Joseph to a breaking of his feeling. And he, no longer able to feign anger, makes himself known to his brothers, and acknowledged his thanks to them as fellow-causes of what had been resolved by God concerning him. "Go, then," he says, "and declare these things to my father, and taking him and all the kindred, remove here; for there will be famine for five years more." Saying this, he embraces his brothers and honors them with gifts.

But the king, who had become the most glorious of all before him and excelled in prudence and wealth, did not abide by the divine ordinances; falling sick with incontinence in matters of the flesh and maddened over women, he was not content with those of his own race, but married very many foreign women also, and to gratify them, through his love, he worshipped their gods as well. For he married seven hundred daughters of distinguished rulers and three hundred concubines, and the daughter of the king of the Egyptians. The Lord therefore said to Solomon, "Because you have not kept what I commanded you, I will tear apart your kingdom and give it to your servant. Yet I will not take the rule from you while you live, for your father's sake, but I will do this to your son when you are dead. And I will not take all the kingdom from him, but leaving him two tribes and Jerusalem for the sake of his grandfather David, I will give the ten to his servant."

Not much time had passed when Hadad too rose to war against Israel. This Hadad was an Idumaean of royal stock, who, when Joab subdued Idumaea in the days of David, being a small child, fled to Egypt, and being kindly received by Pharaoh was beloved and married the sister of Pharaoh's wife. Now this man, when he had grown to manhood and learned that David and Joab were dead, sought to return to his ancestral rule; but he was not permitted by Pharaoh. When, however, Solomon's affairs were now going badly, leave was granted to Hadad too, and he returned to Idumaea. But since that land was securely guarded, he went off to Syria, and getting a band of brigands about him he held it and plundered the land of the Hebrews.

Jeroboam, son of Nebat, while a small youth served the king. Solomon, seeing him noble in spirit, when he set a wall about Jerusalem appointed him overseer of the building. As Jeroboam was going somewhere, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him, and turning him aside from the road tore his own garment into twelve pieces and gave him ten, saying, "So shall the Lord tear apart the kingdom of Solomon, and to his son he will leave two tribes for the sake of his grandfather, but to you he will give the ten and will make you king over them. But do you hold fast to the laws of the Lord and be righteous." Greatly emboldened by this, Jeroboam attempted to make a revolt. And when the king learned of the matter he sought to kill him. But he fled to Egypt and lived there until Solomon died. King Solomon died, as the book of Kings records, having lived fifty-two years—for he is recorded to have come to the kingdom at twelve—and having reigned forty years; but as Josephus wrote, he lived ninety-four years and reigned eighty, living happily and gloriously, but transgressing in his old age, persuaded by foreign women through unholy loves and following their forms of worship.

One might be perplexed why the weeks were reckoned separately, and not all together, but were divided into seven and sixty-two and into one other. Not idly did the archangel do this, but teaching by it certain new things that would come about in the divisions of the times. For if from the building of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, as has been said, the times be reckoned down to the high priest Hyrcanus, under whom the line of the Hasmonaeans ceased to hold the priesthood, the count of the sixty-two weeks is completed. For from the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, who gave Nehemiah the return to Jerusalem to wall it, down to Darius son of Arsames, whom Alexander overthrew, are a hundred and fourteen years; and from the overthrow of the Persian kingdom, which came about in the sixth year of Alexander's expedition against Asia, down to Julius Caesar Gaius, who first attempted the monarchy of the Romans, two hundred and eighty-two years passed; and from the sole rule of Caesar to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ was baptized by John and began his signs, seventy-three years—so that these come together to four hundred and sixty-nine years. And so many years make up four hundred and eighty-three years according to the Hebrew reckoning of the years. For the Hebrews do not reckon the year as we do, but counting it by the course of the moon they reckon it at three hundred and fifty-four days, so that there are eleven days over from each year. And when these surplus days are summed into years, the four hundred and eighty-three Hebrew years result. The angel, speaking with the Hebrew Daniel, surely meant the years known to him. Up to the slaying of the high priest Hyrcanus, then, whom king Herod killed—and the matter concerning this will be told more fully—the sixty-two weeks were measured out. From then on, the high priesthood no longer being fixed for life upon those deemed worthy of it according to the law, but given unlawfully for a year or limited to a shorter time, and those who wished buying it with money—which Josephus too records—the seven weeks passed. Showing this, the divine archangel said, "And after the sixty-two weeks the anointing shall be destroyed, and there is no judgement in it"—that is, the anointing of the high priesthood shall be corrupted. For those advanced to it being unlawfully anointed, neither did the anointing keep its proper power, but, being corrupted, was without the divine grace. Therefore he added, "and there is no judgement in it"—that is, they will be made not by judgement and scrutiny, but without judgement, either by favour or by money. As these things came to pass thus, the seven weeks too slipped by, lasting down to the manifestation of the Lord.

The division of the sixty-two weeks and the seven, then, came about for these reasons. And since to the seventy weeks named at the outset one still remains, the archangel said of this one too, "And he shall confirm the covenant to many for one week, and in the midst of the week sacrifice and libation shall be taken away, and upon these the abomination of desolation upon the temple, and until the consummation of the time a consummation shall be given upon the desolation." The remaining week, he says—the one after the sixty-nine—will bring in the new covenant so strong that through it sacrifices and libations are taken away—that is, set aside—in the midst of the week. For after the baptism Christ, having taught for three years and more and shown signs, so came to the Passion, and when he was sacrificed for the whole world, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, the sacrifice and libation according to the law ceased. And from then the Jews sacrificed—since they still sacrifice—unlawfully, but their sacrifice and libation were unacceptable to God. And otherwise the "he shall confirm a covenant to many" will be taken to mean that that week will make the holy apostles strong for the preaching. For the archangel appears to divide the week into two, into the time before the Passion and the time after the Passion. For the Lord, having preached for about three years and a half, according to the gospel of the son of thunder, and having confirmed his divine apostles in the faith in him by the truth of his words and the display of his wondrous works, so went to the Passion and accepted the cross and endured death. Then, in the remaining time of the week, after the resurrection from the dead and the ascent to the Father's bosom, from which he had never been separated, and the coming of the Paraclete and the divine inspiration, his holy disciples, in Jerusalem confirming the gospel and the preaching by wonders and drawing multitudes of men to the knowledge of the true God, were scattered among the nations and enlightened them. This, then, the archangel foretelling to the prophet Daniel said, "He shall confirm a covenant to many for one week"—that is, he shall gird many with power, the disciples, that is. Having joined together the time before the Passion of the Lord and the time after the Passion—in which at first the apostles remained in Jerusalem and preached, and then went about to the ends of the inhabited world and taught—he again divides this week, saying, "And in the midst of the week sacrifice and libation shall be taken away," by this foreshowing the cessation of the shadow of the law. Then he adds, "And upon the temple the abomination of desolation." For when these things come to pass, he says, the formerly holy and venerable temple shall be reckoned an abomination; or because, after this last week, some abomination shall be brought into the temple, a sign of its desolation and that of the city. This came to pass under Pilate, who by night brought in standards bearing royal images, which were reckoned an abomination by the Jews; for it was forbidden them to possess or to revere a human image or that of any animal. And the Lord said, "When you see the abomination of desolation standing in a holy place, know that its desolation has drawn near"—of Jerusalem, that is. And elsewhere the Lord said, "Behold, your house is left to you desolate." Teaching these things beforehand to Daniel, the archangel adds, after foretelling that the legal service would be set aside, the "And upon the temple the abomination of desolation." And that the desolation might not be thought by the Jews to be temporary, as though the city would again be rebuilt for them and the temple raised up—as had also happened many times before to the temple and the city—he added, "And until the consummation of the time a consummation shall be given upon the desolation"—that is, until the age be consummated the desolation too will remain, and then there will be an end to it as well, when there is no longer time either for the city to rise again or for the temple.

These things Daniel beheld and was instructed in concerning his countrymen. But he also saw other visions and dreams, by which the future change of worldly affairs was made known to him from God. And he was instructed not only in the foreknowledge of the change, but also taught the times in which each of them would be accomplished; which whoever wishes will fully learn by going through more completely the book of the prophet's visions, and would gain thence a sure conviction that nothing is unforeseen or borne along at random and as chance has it, but that all things are both governed and brought to pass by divine providence.
These things, then, are so, and are glorified among the pious.

And they departed; and Jacob, learning about Joseph, set out at once to him, taking along all who were with him; and they were seventy-five. And when he was already near Egypt, Joseph meets him. And from joy he all but fainted. And when Pharaoh heard that Jacob and those with him had come to Egypt, he was glad, and when Jacob came to him he greeted him. And learning that those with him were shepherds, he granted them dwelling in Heliopolis. And as the famine grew worse, Joseph gave out the grain to the Egyptians for money. And when this failed, they bought it with their cattle, then they yielded up even their land, that they might be fed. And so, when Pharaoh had become master of all property except that of the priests—for to these their land remained—when the famine had now abated, Joseph, gathering the Egyptians each to his own city, gave them back the land and exhorted them to industry, paying the fifth of the fruits to Pharaoh. And Jacob, having passed seventeen years in Egypt, fell sick and departed, foretelling how those of his line were to dwell in Canaan. And to the rest of his sons he prayed for the gaining of good things; but of Joseph he recounted a eulogy, that he had not borne a grudge against his brothers, and he commanded his sons that they should reckon the children of Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, as their own, dividing Canaan together with these. And when Joseph had presented his sons to Jacob to be blessed, he set the elder by the right hand, and the younger by the left. But he, placing his hands crosswise upon the heads of the children, assigned the right hand to the younger, and to the elder the left. And when Joseph said to his father that the laying on of hands ought not to be done thus, he was not persuaded to alter the arrangement of his hands. For it was not, as Joseph supposed, that he did not know what he was doing, harmed in his understanding by the depth of his old age; rather, as a prophet he was hinting at things to come, and prefigured the saving cross, and showed that the new people, that is, the people from the nations, would be reckoned at the right hand by God and preferred to the elder—I mean, that is, the Jewish people. And Jacob dies, having lived a hundred and forty-seven years. And Joseph, with Pharaoh's consent, goes to Hebron and buries his father lavishly. And when his brothers feared to return with him, lest, remembering the wrong, he should requite them, he persuaded them to suspect nothing. And he too dies, having lived a hundred and ten years, having commanded that, when those of his line should migrate from Egypt, they should carry up his bones also and bring them into Canaan.

He had as successor to the kingdom his son Rehoboam. And all the people gathered to him, and begged him to lighten for them the yoke of servitude which had been laid upon them by Solomon, and to show himself kinder than his father. He said that he would consider, and would speak after three days. Calling therefore the older of his father's servants, he inquired what answer he should give to the people; and they counselled him to speak to them more gently and not haughtily and with arrogance. But after the council of elders he shared his deliberation with the young men who had been brought up with him, telling them the counsel of the elders. They counselled him to speak more harshly to the people and to make his words proportionate to the dignity of his rule and to his royal worth. And he adhered to these; and when the multitude had again assembled he said, "If my father made your yoke hard, I myself will lay it on heavier; and if he used whips against you, I myself will chastise you with scorpions; and you will find my little finger thicker than my father's loins." When the multitude heard this they cried out, "What portion have we in David?" and in disgust they departed. When Rehoboam sent one of his men to speak to them and pacify them, they killed the man in their anger, stoning him to death.

Rehoboam, in fear, fled to Jerusalem, the tribe of Judah remaining with him and with it the tribe of Benjamin. But the rest, when Jeroboam had now returned from Egypt after Solomon's death, called him and chose him as king. Rehoboam prepared to fight for the kingdom against the Israelites and Jeroboam, but he was prevented by God through the prophet Shemaiah.

And Jeroboam, fearing that the multitude, going off to Jerusalem and mingling with those there, might turn back to their former king and forsake him, made two heifers of gold, and set the one in Bethel and the other in Dan. And assembling the multitude he said, "God is everywhere, O men, and not only in Jerusalem. Behold then, I have made two heifers in the name of God, and there is no longer any need for you to go to Jerusalem. Go to these and worship and sacrifice; for I will appoint priests too from among yourselves." Deceived by this, the people transgressed their ancestral customs and provoked God, so that Israel was even given over into captivity to foreigners. Having made priests and an altar, Jeroboam held a festival, and went up himself to the altar and the priests around it. And when he was now about to sacrifice, a prophet sent from God stood by and said, "Thus says the Lord: O altar, there shall be one from David called Josiah, who will sacrifice your priests upon you and burn their bones. And that it may be clear that my words are true, behold, the altar shall be rent, and the fatness upon it shall be poured out upon the ground." And at once the altar was rent and the fatness of the offerings was poured out. Jeroboam stretched out his hand, commanding the prophet to be seized. But it withered and remained motionless. When Jeroboam begged the prophet, he had his hand again moving and active. And he asked him to dine with him. But he would not consent, saying he had been forbidden by God to eat bread in that city or to drink water or to return by the way by which he had come into the city; and he went off, turning another way. Now there was a false prophet in that city who deceived Jeroboam and conversed with him to please him. This man, learning all that the prophet of God had said and done and that he was departing, pursued after him, and overtaking him asked him to turn back and be his guest. When the prophet refused, since God had forbidden it, "But I too am a prophet," said that wicked man, "and I have come by the command of God to bring you back to share my table." The prophet believed the words of the false prophet and returned. But when the prophet had been entertained there, a word of the Lord came that, because he had not kept what was commanded him, he would be killed on the way by a lion. And as he was returning a lion killed him and sat by, guarding the corpse and the beast of burden. Learning what had happened, the false prophet gathered the body of the dead man and buried it, and charged his own sons to bury him together with the prophet when he himself should die. Why did he contrive this? So that when, according to that prophecy, the altar should be overthrown, and the bones of the priests and false prophets given to the fire, he himself might escape the outrage, if he were laid together with the man of God.

But we must not pass over the affairs of that manly-minded woman Judith, who destroyed Holofernes and saved her city and the whole nation. Her affairs stand thus. In the twelfth year of his reign the chief of the Assyrians, Nabuchodonosor, raised war against Arphaxad the king of the Medes, and summoned the surrounding nations to his alliance. When many others, and the Jews too, did not accept the summons and refused to ally themselves with him, Nabuchodonosor was enraged, and swore that, when he had finished the war against the Medes, he would come against Cilicia and Damascus of Syria and Judaea and Egypt and ravage them and sack them and bring them to desolation. Drawing up, then, against Arphaxad the Mede and overcoming him by force, and mastering his other cities and Ecbatana itself, where Arphaxad had his palace, and taking and killing him, he called Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of his own force, and charged him to fulfill the oath he had sworn, and to march against those who had refused to ally with him, when he came against the Medes, with a heavy force, and to preserve those who submitted themselves to him and to leave their cities unsacked, but not to spare the disobedient, but to put the men to the sword and give their cities over to plunder and ruin.

Nabuchodonosor, then, gave such charge to his chief satrap, and Holofernes, marching out and coming against the nations against which he had been sent, dealt with the others according to his orders; but when he was about to march against the Israelites and raise arms against them—for they did not come to him or submit—he asked who these were and in what trusting they resisted. And Achior the chief of the sons of Ammon told him their genealogy, and how they had settled in those cities from the beginning, and the strength of their God. Then he added, "Now it must be considered; and if they are sinning against their God, we shall go up and make war on them; but if not, let my lord pass by, lest their God shield them and we be defeated." When Achior had said this, Holofernes, seized with rage, ordered those standing by him to bind Achior and lead him away and hand him over to the sons of Israel, that being taken with them he might be punished. And they, seizing the man, led him off to Bethulia, and the men of the city pelted those who approached with slings and arrows. And they threw Achior down bound at the foot of the hill, and turned back. The men of the city, coming down, loosed Achior and led him into their city, and asked what had happened; and he related to them everything. And they called upon God for vengeance. On the next day Holofernes led his army against Bethulia—a hundred and seventy thousand foot and twelve thousand horse, besides the baggage-train—and encamped beside it. Then he resolved not to fight, but to seize beforehand the waters from which they drew, that failing them they might perish of thirst or surrender their city. And he set a part of the army as guards over the waters. For thirty-four days the enemy beset them, and their water failed them, and the people gathered to the rulers and asked them to give over the city and themselves to the enemy, that either, becoming slaves to them, they might live, or, being slaughtered, be rid of their sufferings. But Ozias the chief man of the city said, "Brothers, let us wait five days, and if help comes to us from God, well; but if not, I will do according to your counsel."

But the Egyptians, seeing the Israelites flourishing and having forgotten Joseph, devised various afflictions against them. For they ordered them to cut the river into very many channels, and to build walls for the cities and to raise up embankments, that by these the river might be kept from forming a lake, and to set up pyramids; and with these labors they wore down the Hebrews. For a long time, then, they passed in these very hardships. Then one of the sacred scribes announces to Pharaoh that there would be born at that time among the Israelites one who, when grown, would humble the Egyptians but exalt his own kindred. So Pharaoh, taking fright, commands that every male born to the Hebrews be destroyed by being cast into the river, and that the parents of children who did not do this be killed with their whole household, and that the Egyptian midwives watch over the childbirths of the Hebrew women. And while they were in these straits, a certain man of noble birth was grievously distressed at these things, for his wife was with child, and he prayed to God. And God commanded him in his sleep not to despair. "For the child," He said, "whom the Egyptians suspect will be yours, and will be saved and reared, escaping the notice of those who plot, and will release his kinsmen from the slavery among the Egyptians, and will obtain everlasting remembrance. And his brother will serve me as priest, with his descendants, forever." So his wife bears him a male child, escaping the notice of the guards, and the babe is reared by its parents for three months. But fearing, they entrusted his safety to God, and contriving a kind of basket and smearing it round with bitumen, they put the babe in it and let it go down the river. And the child's sister, Mariamme, watched what would happen. Now while she was playing by the banks of the river, Thermouthis, the daughter of Pharaoh, sees the basket, and sending, she fetches it. And seeing the child, she loved it, both for its beauty and for its size. And Egyptian women are brought to suckle it; but it would not take their breast. And Mariamme, as if happening to be present, said, "O queen, if a Hebrew woman should be called, perhaps the babe will accept the breast of one of its own kind." And she said, "Call her." And she brought the mother, and Thermouthis entrusted the child's nursing to her for wages, and from what had happened she names it. For the Egyptians call water "mo," and those saved from water "yses"; so, putting together both words, she used them as the name of the babe. Now Moses was the seventh from Abraham; for he himself was the son of Amram, and Kohath was the father of Amram, and he was the son of Levi, and Levi was the son of Jacob, and Jacob was born to Isaac, and Isaac sprang from Abraham. When the child was three years old, both the height of his stature and the grace of his form became distinguished by a more divine charm, and his understanding grew far greater than his age. So Thermouthis, being without offspring of her own, adopts him and brings him to her father; and he, embracing the child to his breast, places upon him in affection the diadem. And the child, as if in childish play, throws it to the ground and trampled it with his feet. When the sacred scribe—who had foretold that one of the Hebrews would arise to humble the rule of the Egyptians—saw this, he cried out and said, "This is that child, by whose destruction you may take away the fear of the Egyptians." But Thermouthis forestalled him by snatching the child away, and God made Pharaoh sluggish toward the murder. And when Moses, after such a beginning, came to manhood, he became manifest to the Egyptians for his virtue. The Ethiopians, neighbors of Egypt, were ravaging their country, and the Egyptians make war upon them; and they were defeated, and the Ethiopians, despising them, wore down the whole of Egypt. And by a divine oracle Pharaoh asks his daughter for Moses, now come to manhood, that he might be their general against the Ethiopians. And she gives him, having put her father under oath to do him no harm. And Moses, entrusted with the war, leads the army against the enemy not by the customary road, but by an untrodden one, full of venomous reptiles; and there too he displayed his understanding. For having made baskets and filled them with ibises—which Egypt rears many and tame—he carried these along that road; and the ibises are enemies to these venomous creatures; and using them as champions, going before the army, against the venomous creatures, he came upon the Ethiopians, who had no forewarning, and conquers them and takes not a few of their cities. And they, driven together into Saba, a city that was the royal seat of Ethiopia—which Cambyses later named Meroe after his sister of the same name—were besieged; but the city was hard to besiege. And Tharbis, the daughter of the ruler of the Ethiopians, slipped into love of Moses and sends to him concerning marriage; and he consented, if she should hand over the city to him. The deed forestalled the words, and Moses celebrated the marriage, and led the Egyptians back to their own land. But they hated him even while they were being saved by him, and incited Pharaoh against him. And he, both persuaded by the sacred scribes and on account of the killing of the Egyptian who was scourging the Hebrew—as is contained in the book of Genesis, even if Josephus passed this over—set himself to the slaying of Moses. But Moses, though the roads were guarded, slipped away unnoticed through the wilderness, and goes to the city of Midian, and is received as a guest by the priest of the city, who, bearing two names, was called both Reuel and Jethro. And he gives his daughter Zipporah to Moses in marriage, and makes him a shepherd of his flocks.

So these things came about thus. But Jeroboam clung to the same impiety, which increased daily as he transgressed, and he sold the false priesthood of the high places to those who wished it for money. And this act was reckoned to him as sin, and it became the cause of the destruction and ruin of his house. But if the selling of that unholy priesthood for money was reckoned a sin, what would one say of those who sell and buy the truly divine priesthood, the priesthood that performs the awesome and bloodless sacrifice?

Abijah the son of Jeroboam fell sick; and the king sent his wife to Ahijah the prophet to ask whether he would live. She, having changed into the garb of a commoner, went off. But the prophet, knowing the deception, said, "Do not hide yourself, woman of Jeroboam; go and say to your husband that, since you have forsaken God and made for yourself molten gods, expect both that the kingdom will be taken away and that you yourself will be utterly destroyed with all your kin. And because, when you were impious, the multitude followed you, neither shall that go unpunished. But you, woman, go, and you will find your child dead, who will be buried with mourning; for this one alone of Jeroboam's house was good."
