The woman went off and found the child dead, and reported to her husband what came from the prophet. But he was in no way bettered by these things, being without understanding.

While Rehoboam the son of Solomon reigned in Jerusalem, the priests and Levites among the Israelites, and all of the multitude who understood the good, departing from their own cities, came to Jerusalem; and from this the kingdom of Rehoboam grew. But he too became impious toward God, and all the house of Judah neglected the worship of God. Therefore Shishak the king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem with a heavy force in the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign. When Rehoboam was shut up with the people in the city, he begged God to grant them deliverance, and they confessed how they had sinned against God. God, entreated, said he would not destroy them, but would give them as subjects to the Egyptian. When therefore Rehoboam received the Egyptian into the city upon terms, he broke the treaty and plundered the treasures of God and emptied the royal treasures, and took away the golden shields which Solomon had made and the golden spears which David had dedicated, all of them. Rehoboam died, having lived fifty-seven years, of which he reigned seventeen, leaving as successor his son Abijah, against whom Jeroboam was ever at war, as he was with Rehoboam too. Abijah did not cower before the assault, but drawing up his own men against him won a famous victory, so that Jeroboam no longer dared to draw up against him. Abijah died, having reigned in Jerusalem three years, doing what was wicked before the Lord. And his son Asa reigned, keeping the divine ordinances after the manner of David his own forefather.

Jeroboam too died, having completed twenty-two years in his rule. And his son Nadab succeeded him, who likewise became impious after his father. While besieging Gabathon, a city of the foreigners, he was plotted against by Baasha the son of Ahijah, and died after ruling two years. Baasha, having gained control of the kingdom of the ten tribes, utterly destroyed the whole race of Jeroboam. But he too, like Jeroboam, transgressed the law and likewise made the people sin. And God threatened him through Jehu the prophet that he would destroy his house as the house of Jeroboam. He too died, having reigned over Israel twenty-four years. And his son Elah became successor to his father's kingdom. Him Zimri, the commander of his cavalry, killed while he was drunk, after he had reigned two years, and took away both his kingdom and utterly destroyed the whole race of Baasha. But the army of the Israelites, which was besieging Gabathon, learning that Zimri had killed Elah and become king, proclaimed in the camp its own commander Omri, and, seizing beforehand with him the city Tirzah, took control of it. Zimri, the former king, slipping into the innermost part of the palace and setting it on fire, destroyed himself together with it, having held the rule seven days. Then the people were divided, and one part chose Zimri, and the other Tibni. But Omri's party prevailed, and having killed Tibni, secured for Omri an undisputed rule. He at first lived as king in Tirzah, and then on the mountain Mareon, on which he built a city which is called Samaria, he himself naming the mountain Samareus after the name of Shemer, from whom he had bought it. He became worse than those before him. And he ended his life in Samaria, having reigned twelve years. The kingdom passed to Ahab his son.

So the kings of the Israelites, one after another, were destroyed in a short time because of their transgression; but Asa the king of Jerusalem was beloved of God. In the tenth year of his reign the king of the Ethiopians marched against him with a heavy force. He called upon God as his ally; and engaging the Ethiopians he killed many, and pursued the rest who fled, and plundered their camp, and he and the people carried off much spoil. As the king and the army were returning, the prophet Azariah met them and said that God was the giver of the victory to him and to the people, since they cared for righteousness. And he promised happiness for the future to those who pursued virtue, but said that many sorrows would befall those who neglected God's commandments. Asa therefore, having lived his life in piety and come to a deep old age, died, having reigned forty-one years, leaving the rule to his own son Jehoshaphat.

Now there was in that city a woman named Judith, and she a widow, and chaste and prudent and beautiful in appearance. Hearing, then, what had been decided by the people and the rulers, she sent for Ozias and the other rulers of the city, and reproached them for tempting God in that they had said they would give over the city to the enemy after five days, if within them no help came to them from God. They acknowledged that she spoke well, but set against this the thirst of the people and the violence from it. And she charged them to stand by night at the gate of the city, while she said she would go out with her maid, but not to tell them what she was planning, until it was brought to a successful issue. And they said to her, "Go." And they departed, and she turned to prayer to God. Then, laying aside the mourning garb of her widowhood and washing her body with water and anointing herself with perfume, she changed into a festive robe and put on adornment. And having made herself beautiful to the more alluring effect, she gave her maid to carry in vessels wine and oil and a wallet full of barley-meal and dried fig-cake and bread, and she went out of the city, she and her maid, going to the camp of the enemy. And meeting the outpost of the Assyrians she was taken and brought to Holofernes. He marveled at her beauty and said to her, "Do not fear; for you have come to safety." And the woman said to him, "Receive my words, lord, and let the word that Achior spoke be in your heart; for it is true that, unless the sons of Israel sin, the sword shall not prevail against them. But now, since their food and water have failed them, they have resolved to touch even the things forbidden by the law, and the firstfruits of the grain and the tithes of the wine reserved for the priests, which it is not lawful for another even to handle, they have determined to consume. And these things, being also resolved by those who dwell in Jerusalem, they have sent to the council of elders there, asking release for these things. And if they so transgress, there will be no defence for them from God, and they will be given over to destruction; which I, having learned, am fleeing from the city, that I may escape the destruction. And now I will remain with you, master, and will go out by night into the ravine, and will pray to God, and he will tell me when they have sinned, and I will announce it to you, and will lead you through Judaea as far as Jerusalem, and will set your throne in the midst of it." And her words pleased Holofernes, and he ordered her to be brought into the tent of his treasury and food to be given her. But she said, "I will not eat of your foods, lest it become a cause of stumbling to me, but I will be fed from what I bring." And Holofernes said to her, "If these should fail, from where shall such things be supplied to you?" And she answered, "As your soul lives, my lord, my food will not fail me before God works by my hand what he has resolved." In the middle of the night she asked to go out to the ravine for prayer, and Holofernes allowed it; and for three days she did so. And on the fourth day Holofernes prepared a banquet, and said to the eunuch Bagoas, who was set over all his affairs, "Persuade the Hebrew woman to come to us; for it is shameful for us if we let such a woman pass without having had converse with her." And Bagoas said to Judith, "Come to my lord to be honoured before his face, and you shall drink wine with us, and shall become as one of the women who stand in the house of Nabuchodonosor." And Judith, having adorned herself, went, and entering to Holofernes reclined, and ate and drank what her maid had prepared for her. And the heart of Holofernes was beside itself and inflamed with love of the woman. And as the banquet was prolonged he drank a very great deal of wine and became drunk. And he lay on his bed, heavy-headed from the drink, and all departed, and Bagoas shut the tent, leaving Judith alone within. And she charged her maid to watch for her going out; for she said she would go out for prayer. Holofernes, then, sunk in his drunkenness, lay sleeping the sleep that is brother to death, while she, calling upon God and drawing his scimitar, cut off his head, and going out gave it to her maid, and went off as if to pray according to her custom. And drawing near her city she called to those at the gates to open to her. And entering she told all that God had done wondrously through her, and brought forth the head of Holofernes, and counselled them to hang it from the battlements, and themselves, putting on their full armour, to go out at dawn; "for when the Assyrians see you," she said, "they will run to the tent of their commander, and finding him slain they will be amazed, and fear will fall upon them, and they will turn to flight, and you will follow after them and cut them down, and the plains will be filled with corpses." Having counselled her fellow-citizens these things, "Call me Achior," she said; and when he came she showed him the head of Holofernes. And the man was beside himself, and said, "Tell me all that you did." And she related before all what God had done through her, and how he had preserved her chastity and widowhood undefiled. And Achior believed in God and was circumcised. The rulers of the city and the multitude of it hung the head of Holofernes on the wall and did the rest according to Judith's counsel. And they cut down the Assyrians like grass, and plundering their camp were filled with much spoil. To Judith the tent of Holofernes and all that was in it were given, which, going off to Jerusalem, she dedicated as an offering to God. And she sang a song to him, crowned with a sprig of olive, and all Israel with her; and she returned to her house, and grew old in chastity, and died, having lived a hundred and five years.

Now while Moses was pasturing his flock toward Mount Sinai, he is deemed worthy of the vision of the bush, which fire burned but did not consume. Then he hears a voice from there, which commanded him not to come forward, since the place was holy, and foretold things to come, and ordered him to go to Egypt to free his kinsmen from their affliction there and to lead them out of Egypt, and commanded him to offer sacrifices in that place. These things Moses heard from God out of the fire. But he was at a loss how he should either persuade his own people or constrain Pharaoh to permit the departure. And God promised that He would accomplish these things most easily for him, and, as proof, Moses is commanded to throw his staff to the ground, and when he had thrown it, it became a serpent, then when he took hold of it again, it was a staff. And being commanded to put his right hand into his bosom, he drew it out white as chalk in color, then it was restored to its former appearance. And being bidden to take some of the water nearby and pour it on the ground, he sees what was poured out turned to blood. He was therefore exhorted to take courage at these signs and no longer to delay. Taking, then, his wife and the sons from her—Gershom, which means "into a foreign land," and Eleazar, which signifies that he had used the ancestral God as ally—he set out for Egypt. And as he drew near, his brother Aaron met him. So both come to Pharaoh, and stating the commands from God, they asked him not to act against the divine will. And when he scoffed, they showed the signs in deed, and the rod, when thrown, became a serpent. And when the Egyptian sorcerers had done the same and changed their own staffs into serpents, Moses throws his staff again to the ground, and being changed into a serpent, it devoured the staffs of the Egyptians, which appeared as serpents; then he takes it up again when it had fallen back into its own shape. And as Pharaoh hardened himself, the waters were changed into blood. Then frogs covered the whole land of Egypt. After these, gnats sprang up from the ground. Now the other portents the sorcerers of Pharaoh seemed to produce, but they were not able to conjure up gnats. So they said to Pharaoh, "This is the finger of God"; but he was still unyielding. And there came the dog-fly, and after it the destruction of the cattle. Then, when Moses scattered furnace-soot into the air, sores and blisters broke out both on the cattle and on the men; and again hail rained down, and after it came the locust, and after these darkness covered the Egyptians for three days, and last of all there was brought upon them the destruction of the firstborn. For as Pharaoh hardened himself, God commanded Moses to prepare a sacrifice for the fourteenth of the month—which among the Hebrews is called Nisan, among the Egyptians Pharmuthi, among the Macedonians Xanthikos, and among the Greeks April. And when the fourteenth came, all sacrificed and anointed the doorposts of their houses with the blood of the victim, and having dined, they burned what was left of the flesh. Whence from that time the Hebrews keep a festival at this season and sacrifice, calling the festival Pascha. And some say that "Pascha" means "passage," but Josephus says it means "passing over," because on that night God, passing over the Hebrews, sent upon the Egyptians the destruction of the firstborn. Whence the Egyptians, coming together, begged Pharaoh to release the Hebrews; and he ordered them to depart. And they went out. And the number of those migrating, of military age alone, was six hundred thousand. They went out on the fifteenth of the month Xanthikos by the moon, four hundred and thirty years after Abraham's coming into Canaan, and two hundred and fifteen years after Jacob's sojourn into Egypt. Moses was then in the eightieth year of his life, and Aaron exceeded him by three. And they carried along also the bones of Joseph, fulfilling the command of the man.

Ahab had his palace in Samaria, having outrun those before him in impiety, and he was driven still further into wickedness by his wife Jezebel, who was the daughter of the king of Tyre and Sidon, a bold and reckless woman. She built a temple to her own god Baal, and planted a grove, and appointed priests and false prophets for him. But Elijah the prophet, from the city of Tishbe, in his zeal against the impieties of the king and the people, said to Ahab, "As the Lord lives, there shall be no rain except by my word." And having said this he went off to the brook Cherith at God's command; where he was fed by ravens, which brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening, and the brook supplied him with drink. When the brook dried up, he went, obeying God, to Zarephath, a city between Sidon and Tyre. And before the city, meeting a certain woman, he begged her to bring him water. As the woman went, he asked her also to bring him bread. But she swore that she had only a single handful of flour and a very little oil, and that she was gathering sticks in order to go and make a little food for herself and her children, after which, when it was gone, they too would perish of hunger. But the prophet urged her to take courage; for neither would the flour fail from the vessel that held it, nor the oil from the cruse, until rain should come. She went, and fed the prophet, who was her guest, and herself and her children from that little flour, until the famine had passed. When the son of this woman fell sick and died, she blasphemed against the prophet. But he asked that the dead child be given to him. And taking it up to the upper chamber where he lived, he set it upon his bed; and supplicating God, he breathed three times upon the corpse, and it came to life. And he gave the child living to its mother; and she gave thanks.

After this God charged Elijah to go and foretell to Ahab that there would be rain. The famine had grown strong upon Samaria and the whole land. Ahab, taking with him his steward Obadiah, a good man, went out to see whether he might find fodder for the horses. He himself went one way, and Obadiah another, searching where they might find grass at springs or brooks. Elijah met Obadiah and asked him to announce him to the king. But he said that he was being sought eagerly by Ahab to kill him, if he should be found, and counselled him to hide himself; and he said that he himself was hiding and feeding and so saving a hundred prophets, since Jezebel had killed all the rest. But Elijah swore that he would appear to Ahab on that very day. Obadiah went off and told the king about Elijah. And when the king saw the prophet he asked whether he was the one who was troubling Israel. But Elijah said, "You rather, and your father's house, are troubling the people, having forsaken the Lord and honoured false gods. But gather to Carmel the people and your prophets and your wife's." When all had come together, Elijah said, "I alone am left a prophet of God, but the false prophets are very many. Give me therefore one bull for myself alone, and another for all of them, and having sacrificed the bulls let us lay the offerings upon wood, but let us bring no fire; and let each call upon his own god, and the one by whom fire of itself flashes out and consumes the wood and the offerings, let him be reckoned the true God." The multitude approved his words, and the priests of shame did so, and having sacrificed the calf and laid it upon wood without fire, they called upon Baal from morning until midday. Mocking them, the prophet counselled them to cry aloud, lest their god be asleep or busy about something. When nothing was accomplished though they begged much, the prophet took twelve stones according to each tribe and built an altar, dug a basin, piled the wood-splinters upon the altar, and laying the offerings upon them ordered water to be poured upon the altar, so that the basin too was filled. And upon this he called upon God, and fire was brought down from heaven upon the altar in the sight of all, and consumed the sacrifice and the wood and the stones, the water and the dust. The people, astounded, fell upon the ground, confessing him the true and great God. And seizing the false prophets they killed them at the prophet's command. He said to the king that God would soon send rain, and according to his prediction a violent downpour came. But when Jezebel threatened to kill Elijah, he was afraid and fled, and being in the wilderness he begged God in despair that he might die. Having fallen asleep, he was wakened by one who bade him rise and eat. And he saw there bread of barley-meal and water. Having eaten, he slept again, and again the angel bade him eat, since a long road lay before him. And again having eaten, and being strengthened by that food, he journeyed forty days. And coming to Mount Horeb he entered a cave, and heard a voice: "Why have you come here?" He said, "Because in my zeal I killed the prophets of Jezebel, and she seeks to kill me." And the divine voice said to him again, "Go out tomorrow and stand before the Lord." And he did so, and perceived a wind and an earthquake, and saw a burning fire. Then, a gentle breeze arising, he heard a voice from it commanding him to turn back and to anoint Hazael king of Syria, and Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha as prophet in his own stead, who would destroy the impious. Elijah, turning back as he was commanded, found Elisha ploughing, and cast his mantle upon him. And he, leaving all, followed him, having been deemed worthy to prophesy.

The affairs of Judith, then, stand thus; and next must be related, in summary, the affairs of Tobit. Tobit, then, was descended from the tribe of Naphtali, and had been taken captive in the days of Enemessar, king of the Assyrians. He was pious toward God and just toward men, and when his fellow-countrymen sacrificed to Baal, he himself sacrificed to God, going to Jerusalem, and ordered his life according to the ordinances of the law, and though taken captive he was not defiled by gentile foods. He became honoured in the sight of Enemessar, and acquired much wealth, and shared it with those of his kindred who were in need. Going to Media, he deposited ten talents of silver with one of his countrymen dwelling there, Gabael. And taking a wife of his own people, Anna, he begot of her a son, Tobias. When Enemessar had died, and his son Sennacherib had succeeded to the rule of the Assyrians, and had marched against Judaea and fled thence in disgrace and returned to his own land, and in his rage at the defeat was killing very many of the Israelites, Tobit buried them by night. Being recognized as doing this and being sought, he fled, and all the goods of his house were plundered. But before fifty days had passed, Sennacherib was killed by his sons, and the parricides in fear fled, and another son of his, Nahordan, succeeded to his father's kingdom. He appointed a kinsman of Tobit, called Achiacharus, as steward of his affairs. And he begged the king on Tobit's behalf, and he returned to Nineveh. When Pentecost came on, which the Jews kept every seven weeks, a lavish meal was prepared for Tobit. He says, then, to his son Tobias, "Go, child, and bring whomever you find of our brethren in need, mindful of the Lord, to share our table." And he, going, returned saying, "One of our race lies strangled, cast out in the marketplace." And Tobit at once went off, and taking up the corpse brought it to the house, and when the sun had set buried him. And returning he did not enter the house, since by the law he was unclean as having touched a corpse, but slept by the wall in the courtyard. And sparrows passing the night in the wall dropped dung into his eyes, from which white films came upon them, and from these Tobit was blinded. Being in want, he was fed by his wife who spun for hire. And once, having received her wages, and getting in addition a kid, she came to Tobit. And hearing the bleating of the kid, he asked whether it might be stolen. And she said, "It was given me as a gift over and above my wages." And he insisted, saying, "If it is stolen, let it be given back to its owners." And the woman, in great distress, and as it were mocking the man for his strictness about justice, said, "Where are your charities and your righteous deeds?" And Tobit wept, confounded, and begged God to be released from life.

And on that very day it happened in Ecbatana of Media that Sarra the daughter of Raguel was reproached by her father's maidservants as having strangled her husbands, having been wedded to seven and having been with none of them. For a certain demon named Asmodaeus killed them as they came in to her. And she, not bearing the reproach, resolved to hang herself. But, that she might not give grief and reproach to her father, she did not do this, but standing in prayer she called upon God, asking either to die and be rid of the reproaches, or to be pitied, and so to escape the reproach.

The prayer, then, of both was heard, and Raphael the archangel was sent by God to heal the blindness of Tobit, and to betroth Sarra to Tobias, and to bind Asmodaeus the wicked demon, so that he might work no harm to Tobias if he should take Sarra. Now Tobit, calling his son Tobias and exhorting him much, at last said to him, "I deposited ten talents of silver with Gabael the son of Gabrias at Rages of Media; go, then, and get these." And he gave him the bond concerning them, and charged him to seek a man who for hire would travel with him. And seeking a fellow-traveler he met the archangel Raphael, who appeared to him in the form of a man and professed to know the way and the house of Gabael and to journey with him. And taking him as a man, called Azarias, he set out. And in the evening they came to the river Tigris, and lodged there. And Tobias went down into the river to wash, and a fish leaped up from there to swallow the lad. But the angel bade him take hold of the fish, and when it had been drawn to land told him to cut it open, and suggested to Tobias to take its heart and its liver and its gall, and to keep them safely.

So they departed; but the Egyptians repented, and taking up arms they pursued. They had six hundred chariots and fifty thousand horsemen and two hundred thousand foot soldiers. The Hebrews were brought to despair, since their situation had become straitened, and they were about to stone Moses. But he exhorted them to follow him, and led them to the sea, and standing beside it and calling upon God, he strikes the sea with his staff; and it was driven back and left the ground bare for the Hebrews, and they crossed in haste. Seeing this, the Egyptians too, putting their cavalry in front, pursued. But when the Hebrews had already been brought safely to the land on the opposite side, the sea was poured over the Egyptians, when Moses with his rod struck the water again in the contrary direction and united its divided parts. So all the Egyptians in the waters perished. And the Hebrews were singing hymns and rejoicing, and Moses composed a song to God, set in a hexameter measure, as Josephus says. And the arms of the Egyptians, together with their bodies cast up out of the sea by the wind, the Hebrews took and armed themselves with them. And Moses led them to Mount Sinai, to sacrifice there the thank-offerings for their deliverance, as had been commanded him. But as they were being led there, the scarcity of provisions and the lack of water grieved them. And in this state they come to a place in which there was a well, whose water was undrinkable on account of its bitterness. And the name of the place the book of Exodus calls Marah, but Josephus records that it was called Mar by the Hebrews, saying that the Hebrews call the bitter "mar." And they murmured against their leader; but he, having first prayed to God, took a piece of wood and threw it into the well and sweetened the water. Josephus, however, seems not to believe that the sweetening of the water was a miracle, but, supposing it to have been sweetened naturally, says that Moses, having thrown the wood into the water, ordered them to draw the well dry, and they labored, and the water, exercised and cleansed by the continual drawings, was now drinkable. And he healed the lack of provisions, having prayed to God, by means of quails. For a multitude of quails flew down upon the camp of the Hebrews, which they caught and ate. And after these things God rained the manna upon them, in sweetness like honey, but in size like coriander seed, and called "manna" by them, as they were at a loss what this might be; for "man" also means a question in their language. So Josephus relates these things too. And he had commanded each to gather an assaron of it each day—the assaron is a measure—but if anyone gathered more, it was uneatable on the morrow, corrupted by worms and bitterness. And this was arranged so that, the strong gathering much, there might not be a shortage for the weak. And of this food they made use for forty years, as long as they were in the wilderness. Again, then, they came to a waterless place called Rephidim, and being thirsty they were stirred against Moses. But he, having prayed to God, is commanded to strike the rock with his rod, and he strikes it, from which at once gushed forth water, abundant and very clear. But the Amalekites advanced against the Hebrews, having summoned the neighboring peoples as allies. And Moses, having separated the warlike portion of the people from the rest, and set over them Joshua the son of Nun, and left a part of the army for the guarding of the water, himself withdrew to the mountain, and commanded Joshua to trust in God and to lead the army out against the enemy. So now the battle was joined; and as long as Moses held his hands aloft, the Hebrews handled the Amalekites badly, but whenever Moses let down his hands, wearied by their lifting up, then it came to pass that the Hebrews were worsted. So setting on either side his brother Aaron and Hur, the husband of his sister Miriam, he commanded them to hold up his hands. And thus the Hebrews, conquering the Amalekites, would have destroyed them all, had not night stopped them. And of the Hebrews not one died.

Naboth, who possessed a vineyard near the fields of king Ahab, was asked to sell it to the king or exchange it; but he would not consent. And the king was grieved at this. When Jezebel learned the cause of his grief, she made a writing as if from Ahab to the leading men of the country in which Naboth dwelt, commanding them to accuse the man of having blasphemed against God and the king, and to suborn certain witnesses against him, and to stone him. This writing, sealing it with the king's seal, she sent to the men. And when they had done as commanded, Naboth was stoned and died, and Jezebel charged Ahab to inherit the vineyard of Naboth now that he was dead. He was grieved at the murder, but made the vineyard his own. And Elijah, at God's command, went off to Ahab saying, "Because you have murdered Naboth in order to take his vineyard, therefore thus says the Lord: where the dogs licked his blood, there shall the dogs lick your blood too and that of your wife, and the harlots shall wash themselves in your blood, and your whole race shall be utterly destroyed." Ahab, stricken in conscience at this, wept and put on sackcloth and fasted, repenting of his deeds. And God, on account of his repentance, declared to the prophet that he would not bring upon him the things threatened, but would accomplish them in the days of his son.

The son of Hadad, king of Syria, marched against Samaria with a heavy force and many allies. And besieging it he sent to Ahab, saying, "Your wealth and your wives and your children are mine; for I will take them by war. But if you yield to me to take whatever I wish, I will raise the siege and depart." Ahab said, "I myself and all that is mine are yours." And gathering the elders of the land, he showed them all that the enemy had sent to him. But the multitude counselled him not to yield. So he said to the ambassadors of the enemy that he could not do what was demanded. When this was reported to the king of Syria it moved him to anger, and he ordered a rampart to be thrown up about the city and mounds to be raised. When a certain prophet told Ahab that God was delivering the enemy to him by means of the servant-lads of the commanders if he attacked them, he numbered the lads and found two hundred and thirty-two. While the enemy were feasting and drunk at midday, Ahab went out, taking the lads with him. The king of Syria, seeing them, ordered some of his men to bring those approaching to him bound. But the lads, falling upon those who came, killed many. And the whole force of Israel, following behind the lads, rushed suddenly upon the Syrians and turned them to flight, so that their own king barely escaped and was saved. Returning from the pursuit, Ahab plundered the enemy's camp and went back to Samaria. The prophet again foretold to him an attack of the Syrian. And when spring came on, the Syrian again marched against Israel and encamped in a plain; for those about him had said that the god of the Hebrews had his power in the mountains, but not also in the valleys. When the prophet promised Ahab victory, "so that," he said, "God may show his strength in the valleys also," the armies rested the other days, but on the seventh, when battle was joined, the Syrians fled; and Ahab pursued and killed them. Many who were saved, fleeing to Apheka the city, perished there when the wall fell upon them. The son of Hadad, fleeing with a few, hid himself. Those about him, putting on sackcloth and binding ropes about their heads, came to Ahab and begged him to spare their lord; and he consented. And they brought their leader to Ahab, who rode upon a chariot. He took him up onto the chariot and greeted him and bade him take courage. Then upon terms he let him go, having given him many gifts. But the prophet Micaiah asked one of his own nation to strike him on the head. When the man would not, he foretold that he would be struck by a lion; and the prediction came to pass. Then he made the same request of another; and when that man struck him, he bound up his head and came to Ahab, saying that he had received a prisoner from a captain to guard, and that when the prisoner had fled, the captain had ordered him to die. When Ahab said that this was just, that man, undoing his head, was recognized as the prophet Micaiah. And he said to Ahab, "Because you let go unpunished the king of Syria, a destructive man, you yourself shall die in his stead, and your people in the stead of his people." Ahab was grieved at hearing this. After keeping peace for three years, and then wishing to take from the Syrians the city Ramoth, as belonging to him, he asked the king of Jerusalem, Jehoshaphat, to march out with him. And he consented, and counselled him to ask God through a prophet whether he approved. Ahab, gathering his own prophets, asked whether he should go to war. When they promised victory, king Jehoshaphat sought a prophet of the Lord. Ahab said there was one, but that he was vexed with him for prophesying ill. And Jehoshaphat asked that he be summoned. When Micaiah had been summoned, Ahab asked whether he should fight or not. He said, "I have seen Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock without a shepherd. And the Lord told me that they would be saved and would return, but that you alone would fall at Ramoth." When Micaiah had said this, Ahab said to Jehoshaphat, "Did I not tell you that he ever prophesies evil to me?" And one Zedekiah, of the false prophets, struck Micaiah on the jaw. But he said to him, "After a little you will pass from chamber to chamber, hiding yourself." And king Ahab ordered him to be imprisoned until he himself should return. And Micaiah said, "If you return in peace, the Lord has not spoken in me." When the kings had set out, the king of the Syrians drew up against them, charging his soldiers to fight with none of the others but with Ahab alone. But Ahab, exchanging his royal robe, put on a common one. When the Syrian commanders saw Jehoshaphat arrayed in royal fashion, they thought he was Ahab and surrounded him. But when they perceived that he was not the king of Israel, they withdrew. And one man, drawing his bow, struck Ahab. Knowing himself mortally wounded, he ordered the charioteer to drive the chariot out of the battle, and about sunset he expired. The Syrians, knowing that Ahab was dead, went off to their homes; and the king's corpse, conveyed to Samaria, was buried. The chariot, bloodied with the king's slaughter, they threw down at the spring of Samaria, and the dogs licked the blood, and the harlots bathed at the spring, as Elijah had foretold. Ahab died where Micaiah had predicted, not escaping the destruction that had been foretold him, having reigned twenty-two years. And his son Ahaziah took over the kingdom after him.

As they journeyed and drew near Ecbatana, Tobias said, "Brother Azarias, of what use will the heart of the fish and the liver and the gall be to us?" And he answered, "The heart and the liver, when burned as incense, drive away demons, if they trouble anyone, and the gall, smeared on eyes that have white films, cleanses them and gives sight." And now they drew near Ecbatana, and the angel says to Tobias, "Today we shall lodge with Raguel, who is your kinsman, who has a daughter Sarra, prudent and fair, and I will speak about her, that she be given you to wife." And he said, "I have heard that the girl has been given to seven men, and that all died in the bridal chamber, because a demon loves her and destroys those who wed her; and I fear that I too may be killed by it." And the angel said, "Hear me, and let the demon be no concern to you. For if you go into the bridal chamber, set on coals from the heart and liver of the fish, and the demon, smelling their odour, will flee, and will return no more." And they entered the house of Raguel. And learning concerning Tobias that he was the son of Tobit, he kissed him, and hearing that Tobit was blind, he wept and gladly received them. And the angel told Raguel to join Sarra to him; and he consented, and calling his daughter and taking her by the hand he gave her to Tobias, and taking a book wrote out a contract. And after supper they led Tobias in to her into the chamber. And he, going in, took coals, and setting on them from the heart and liver of the fish made smoke, and the odour of these put the demon to flight. And Raguel by day sent one of the maidservants to see whether Tobias was alive. And when she returned and said he was alive, Raguel blessed God. And he said to Tobias, "Let us keep the wedding for fourteen days, and you shall not go out from here before they have passed. And then, taking the half part of my possessions, go; the rest you shall receive when I and the partner of my life are dead." Tobias therefore says to Raphael, "Brother Azarias, take for me the bond and go to Gabael at Rages, and bring the silver; for if we delay, my father will be greatly grieved." And the angel went and handed Gabael the bond and took the silver and returned. When the days of the wedding had passed, Tobias says to Raguel, "Send me off"; and taking his wife and the half of Raguel's possessions he set out. And when they were near Nineveh, the angel says to him, "Let us run on ahead and prepare the house. Take in your hands the gall of the fish, and your father will open his eyes, and do you anoint them with the gall, and stung, he will rub them and will cast off the white films." His mother sat watching the road, and when she knew her son was coming, hastening she says to Tobit, "Your son is coming," and running to him she kissed him and said, "I have seen you, child, and now, if I die, it is no concern to me." And Tobit went out to the door, stumbling. And Tobias took hold of him and smeared the gall upon his eyes, and they were stung, and he rubbed them, and the white films were peeled from them. And seeing his son he blessed God. And when it was reported to Tobit what had happened to Tobias in Media, Tobit went out to meet his daughter-in-law, and seeing her he blessed her. And those in Nineveh, seeing him see, and having heard how great things God had done, marveled. And Tobit said to his son, "Give now, child, the wage to the man who came with you—rather, indeed, more should be added to him." And he said, "Father, it is just that he take the half of what I have brought." And he said to Raphael, "Take for yourself, brother Azarias, the half of all that we have brought, and go in health." Then the angel, calling the two apart, declared to them all the great work that God had done with them, and said that he was Raphael, and had not come of himself but had been sent by God. And he exhorted them to bless God and to confess all that he had done with them. "For it is good to hide the secret of a king," he said, "but to proclaim gloriously the works of God." And they, hearing this, fell at his feet, and rising saw him no more, and gave thanks to God for the wonders he had done with them.

Tobit was fifty-eight years old when he lost his sight, and after eight years was restored again to sight; and from then on he was the more fearing God and doing good. Having grown very old, he says to his son, "Child, behold, I have grown old and am near to dying; do you take your sons and go off to Media; for I am persuaded that all that Jonah foretold concerning Nineveh, that it will be overthrown, will come to pass, and that Jerusalem will be desolate and the temple burned, and that God will again pity the city, and the people will return and rebuild it. But do you keep the law and be merciful and just." And having charged his son with such things he died, being a hundred and fifty-eight years old. And Tobias buried him honourably and his mother, and went off with his wife to Ecbatana to Raguel his father-in-law; and he buried him too when he had grown old, and inherited him. And Tobias died, a hundred and twenty-seven years old, in Ecbatana of Media, and he heard before his death of the destruction of Nineveh, taken captive by Nabuchodonosor and Ahasuerus.

From there they went forward, and in the third month after the departure from Egypt they came to Mount Sinai, and Moses sacrificed there to God. There too Reuel his father-in-law met him; and seeing his son-in-law beset by a press of business, with all coming to him, he counseled him to entrust the examination of lawsuits to others, but himself to take thought for the greater affairs and for the safety of the people, and to appoint rulers over thousands by ten-thousands, then over thousands, and to set others over five hundreds, and besides these to make commanders of hundreds and of fifties, and to set those who should keep order over thirties and twenties and tens. When Reuel had given this counsel, Moses does according to his suggestion. Then, having commanded the people to encamp near Mount Sinai, he himself went up the mountain; and the people encamped, keeping themselves pure both in other purity and from intercourse with women for three days. And on the third day at dawn a cloud encircled the camp of the Hebrews, and there were fearful lightnings and a violence of winds, which struck the Hebrews with terror as they waited at their tents. But Moses appears, full of courage, and being seen he frees them from their fear and declares to them what God had commanded and what laws they should keep, and he brings the people, together with their wives and children, that they might hear God. And they heard a voice coming from on high. Then again he goes up to the mountain; and when he tarried there, the people gathered to Aaron, saying, "Make us gods; for as for this Moses, we do not know what has become of him." And Aaron, being pressed, ordered each to bring the golden earrings and the ornaments that their wives and daughters wore. And they brought them, and from these they made a molten calf and sacrificed to it. But Moses, coming down from the mountain and carrying in his hands the two tablets of the testimony, of stone, inscribed on both sides, when he drew near the camp, sees the calf, and in anger he shattered the tablets, and taking the calf he burned it and ground it fine and, throwing it into water, made the people drink. And he commanded the sons of Levi, and they went through the camp and killed many, so that those who fell were numbered up to three thousand. And Moses returned to the mountain, saying, "Lord, your people has sinned, and now, if you forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me too out of your book." And the Lord said to him, "Go down, lead this people to the place of which I told you." And the Lord revealed to Moses, who had asked to see Him, His back parts. And he came down to the people again, carrying two tablets that had the ten words written on them, and the appearance of his face was glorified, and the people could not look steadily at him, and he put a veil about his face, and so he spoke with them. And he reported to them what God had commanded concerning sacrifices and purifications, and concerning unclean and clean animals, so that they should abstain from the one and be nourished by the other, and concerning unlawful unions, and whom the priests should take in marriage, and what kind the high priests, and concerning the Sabbath and the seventh year and the fiftieth, which they call the Jubilee; and that God had commanded a tabernacle to be made, into which He would come, brought along with them as they moved; and He showed him the measures of the tabernacle and the form according to which it should be constructed. And the people, rejoicing at these things, brought gold and silver and precious stones and bronze and wood and goat's hair and rams' skins and linen and wool. And he set as master-builders of the tabernacle the son of his sister Miriam, Bezalel, and Eliphaz.

When Jehoshaphat the king of Jerusalem returned from his alliance with Ahab, Jehu the prophet reproached him for having allied himself with an impious man; but he said that he would be saved by God, although God was vexed at his deed. The king gave thanks. Then going about the land under his rule he charged that the laws be kept, and appointing judges everywhere he ordered them to judge justly. When the Moabites and Ammonites, taking the Arabs as allies, came against him, he called upon God for help. A certain prophet said that God would fight for him, and bade him lead out the army, but not to engage the enemy, but to stand and watch the help from heaven. At dawn the king went out with the army, and charged them to stand still, but ordered the priests to go before the army with the trumpets, and the Levites and singers to sing a thanksgiving to God. The enemy, stirred up against one another, killed one another, so that none was saved. Jehoshaphat gave the enemy's camp to his army to plunder. From then on, the foreigners, fearing him as having the deity for an ally, kept quiet.

Ahaziah the king of the Israelites was like his parents in wickedness. About the second year of his reign the Moabites withheld the tribute which they had paid to his father. Falling sick, he sent to the god of Ekron, called Fly, to ask whether he would recover. But Elijah, meeting those sent, ordered them to turn back and to say to the one who had sent them to the god of the foreigners—as though there were no God in Israel—that he would not rise from his bed. The men, returning, said what they had heard. Ahaziah asked who it was that had said these things. When they said they did not know, he demanded that they describe the appearance of that man. When they said that he was hairy and girt with a leather belt, he understood that it was Elijah. And sending a captain of fifty with those under him, he ordered the prophet to be brought. The one sent, finding him on the top of the mountain, bade him come to the king. But when Elijah prayed, fire flowing down from heaven destroyed the captain of fifty and those with him. And the king sent another captain of fifty with his fifty; and them too heavenly fire consumed. And again a third captain was sent with those under him. He, coming to the prophet, fell down and worshipped, and begged off the punishment from him, saying that he came unwillingly, persuaded by the royal command, and entreated him to go to the king. Elijah, when an angel told him to go and not to be afraid, came down from the mountain, and going to the king said, "Because you sent to a foreign god to ask whether you would live, know that you will not rise from your sickness, but will die." Ahaziah therefore died according to the prophet's prediction, leaving the kingdom to his brother Jehoram, who broke in pieces the pillars of Baal which Ahab his father had set up, but in other things was impious and wicked and like his parents.

When Elijah was about to be taken up, he went with Elisha. And coming to the Jordan he struck the water with his mantle, and the water was divided, and both passed over on dry land. Then he said to Elisha, "Ask what I shall do for you." And he asked that a double share of the grace of the spirit that was in him might come upon him. Elijah said that the request was a hard one, "but if you see me taken up, it will be granted you." While they were still speaking, a fiery chariot with horses like it stood by and snatched up Elijah. As he was borne aloft he cast his mantle to Elisha. And he, taking it, no longer seeing Elijah, returned. And coming to the Jordan he made trial whether he had received the grace as he had asked, and struck the water with the mantle; but it was not divided. And he said, "Where is the God of Elijah?" And he struck again; and the water parted, and he passed over. Seeing him, fifty sons of the prophets said, "The spirit of Elijah rests upon Elisha," and they followed him. And they sought leave to go and search, lest perhaps the spirit of the Lord had taken Elijah and cast him upon one of the mountains or hills. Elisha would not permit it; but when they pressed him, he consented. And fifty men went and searched three days and did not find him. Elisha was in Jericho. And the men of the city came to him, asking that the waters of that place, which were bad and caused barrenness, might be changed by him. He asked that salt be brought to him in a new vessel, and when it was brought he cast the salt into the spring of the waters, calling upon God, and the waters were changed from bitterness to sweetness, and nothing harmful remained in them. As the prophet Elisha was going somewhere, some small children mocked him, crying, "Go up, baldhead." Grieved at this, he cursed them. And bears came out from the mountain and killed forty-two of the children.

When Jehoram the son of Ahab was about to march against the Moabites, he asked Jehoshaphat the king of Judah to be his ally. And he promised to take as ally also the king of Idumaea, who was subject to him. The three kings, united, went through the wilderness for seven days. And the water failed the armies. So the three kings came to Elisha and begged him to save them and the army. But he said to Jehoram, "Go to the prophets of your father and your mother," and swore that he would not have answered him save for Jehoshaphat. Then he ordered someone who could play music to be summoned. As the man played, the spirit of the Lord breathed upon the prophet, and he ordered many trenches to be dug along the brook; "for you will see," he said, "the brook full, though no wind has blown nor rain has come, and you will drink your fill, and will master your enemies." So he foretold; and at dawn on the morrow the brook was filled with waters, and when a flood arose the water covered the whole face of that land. When the sun rose fiery and struck upon the waters, they appeared red in the light of the sun. The Moabites, then, who were encamped in the mountains and were watching from above, supposing the water to be blood, and thinking that the kings had fought one another and that their soldiers had killed one another, rushed in disorder to plunder the spoils. And when the enemy surrounded them, some were killed and some fled. The Israelites, pursuing, burst into Moab, and tore down its cities and laid waste the land. The king of Moab, returning to the city, brought his firstborn son up onto the wall and in desperation sacrificed him as a whole burnt-offering to his god. When the kings saw this and pitied him for his despair, they raised the siege. Jehoshaphat, returning to Jerusalem, died, having lived sixty years, of which he reigned twenty-five, a man godly and just. Leaving many sons, he made the eldest his successor in the kingdom, called Jehoram, of the same name as the king of the Israelites, who was his maternal uncle.

The whole nation of the Hebrews, then, as has already been related, having become spear-won by the Assyrians, was removed, and Jerusalem was left desolate, nor was it released from captivity before the rule of the Assyrians was destroyed, according to the prophetic foretelling, by the Medes and Persians, and the seventy years passed which the prophet Jeremiah foretold. It would not be out of place to go briefly through the overthrow of the kingdom of the Assyrians too, and to show the prophetic prediction true, which foretold that it would be destroyed by the Medes and Persians. It is thus.

The kingdom of the Medes and that of the Persians were separate. And of the one Astyages ruled, and Cambyses of the Persians. He was married to the daughter of Astyages, called Mandane, who bore Cambyses a son, Cyrus; who, reared in the laws of the Persians, became most manly and most temperate and sensible and most just. The customs of the Persians were of this kind, as Xenophon wrote. They had a marketplace called Free, in which their palace and the other public buildings were made, from which the wares and the dealers and their crowd and clamour were driven, that they might not be mingled with the good order of those being educated. The Free marketplace was divided into four buildings; of these one was set apart for boys, another for youths, another for grown men, and the remaining one was assigned to those past the years of military service, who were each present in their own quarters. The youths were accustomed to sleep around the buildings with their light arms, except those who had married; these were neither sought after, unless previously bidden, nor permitted to be absent frequently. There were for each twelve rulers; for the Persians were divided into twelve tribes. The boys, going to the schools, learned justice, their rulers judging for them most of the day. For there arose among boys too, as among men, charges of theft and violence and robbery and deceit and insolence and other things. Those whom they found doing these things they punished; and those whom they found accusing unjustly they chastised. They taught the boys temperance, by their giving heed to the elders who lived temperately; and they taught also self-control in food and drink. And when the boys were to be fed, they were fed at the teacher's place, bringing bread from home and cress for relish; and for drink they took a cup of river water. And they learned to shoot and throw the javelin before eating. Until sixteen or seventeen years the boys did these things; and from then they were enrolled among the youths, and for ten years slept around the public buildings, and offered themselves by day for the rulers to use them wherever they had need of them for the common good. And when the king went out to hunt, he led out half their division. They hunted in common, since this exercise seemed kindred to the training for war, and accustomed them to rise earlier and to endure cold and heat, and trained them in marches and runs, and taught them to shoot a wild beast and to throw the javelin, and prepared them to contend against some valiant beast. They carried, when hunting, a more abundant meal than the boys', but otherwise the same. And they did not eat while hunting, unless it was necessary to wait for the sake of a beast, or they wished otherwise to spend time about the hunt. Having eaten this meal, they hunted the next day until supper, and they reckoned these days as one. They did this so that, if it were needful in war, they might be able to do this. They had for relish whatever they hunted, and if not, the cress. The tribes that remained spent their time, besides other things, in practicing to shoot and throw the javelin and to contend in these against one another. The rulers used the youths who remained for public works requiring strength or speed. When the youths had passed ten years in these things, they were enrolled among the grown men, and from then they passed twenty-five years thus. And if they had to go on campaign, they no longer carried bows or javelins, but the close-fighting arms, as they are called—a breastplate about the chest and a wicker shield in the left hand, and in the right a sword or cleaver. And all the magistracies were filled from these. When they had completed the twenty-five years, they were more than fifty years old from birth, and then they passed into the elders. The elders no longer went on campaign outside their own land, but remaining at home judged all public and private matters, and they decided capital cases, and chose all the magistrates. And if anyone, whether among the youths or the men, transgressed any of the laws, the elders expelled him; and he who was expelled remained dishonoured for the rest of his life. It was reckoned shameful among the Persians both to spit and to blow the nose and to be seen full of wind and that anyone should be seen plainly urinating or relieving his bowels. And they could not do these things unless they used a moderate diet and worked off the moisture by exertion.
Such, then, were the manners of the Persians and their customs.

When the tabernacle had now been made, Moses set it up. And the ark had been made of incorruptible wood, which gold covered on every side, in which they placed the two tablets that had the ten words inscribed on them. Of these the first says that there is one God and that He alone must be worshiped; the second, that one should make no image of any living thing nor worship it; the third, not to swear by God for any vain thing; the fourth, to observe the seventh days, resting from every work; the fifth, to honor parents; the sixth, to abstain from murder; the seventh, not to commit adultery; the eighth, not to steal; the ninth, not to bear false witness; the tenth, not to covet anything belonging to another. This ark, then, they bring into the innermost sanctuary. And in the holy place they set a table, and upon it twelve unleavened loaves, and a golden lampstand, and a censer of wood within, but covered with gold without. And before the tabernacle he set up an altar of wood, plated round with bronze scales, opposite which were placed bowls and mixing-vessels with incense-pans, and other utensils that had been prepared for the sacred service, all of gold. And robes are made for the priests, and indeed for the high priest as well. And God appointed Aaron as high priest. And Moses, gathering the multitude together, said, "Men, the work is finished, but God deems Aaron worthy of the honor of the priesthood." And Moses commanded each to bring in half a shekel, that there might be a fund for the needs concerning the tabernacle. The shekel is a Hebrew coin equal to four Attic drachmas. And the number of those contributing was six hundred and five thousand five hundred and fifty. And the contribution was made by those of the free men who had passed their twentieth year and were under the fiftieth. And the tabernacle was made in seven months. And God showed that the work had been done according to His purpose, being present in the tabernacle. And He revealed His presence thus. A mist came over the tabernacle alone, neither deep and dense and like the clouds, nor very thin and rare, so that sight could pass through it; and a pleasant dew flowed from it. And Moses sacrificed in the open court of the tabernacle for seven days, and on the eighth he proclaimed a festival to the people and commanded them to sacrifice. And they vied with one another. And when the sacred offerings were laid upon the altar, a fire was kindled of its own accord and consumed all that was upon the altar. But the elder of the four sons of Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, having sacrificed contrary to what was ordained, were burned in the chest and the face, a fire being kindled of its own accord and consuming them; whose bodies, carried outside the camp, were buried. And he separated the tribe of Levi from the rest and consecrated it, and handed over to them the tabernacle and the sacred utensils, that, as the priests directed, they themselves might minister. After these things he resolved to number the people, and there were found, of those able to bear arms, six hundred and three thousand six hundred and fifty. These were those who had passed their twentieth year and reached the fiftieth. And in place of the tribe of Levi they reckoned among the chiefs of tribes the sons of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, according to the ordinance of their forefather Jacob. But the Levites, when numbered, were found to be twenty-three thousand eight hundred and eighty.

While Elisha was in Samaria, a certain widow woman came to him, weeping that, being in debt and having nothing to repay it, the creditor was taking away her sons, who were to become his slaves. The prophet asked her what she had in the house; she said nothing except a very little oil. And he charged her to take many vessels and to pour out from the oil into all of them. The woman did as commanded, and all were filled with oil; and she reported to the prophet what had happened. And he counselled her to sell the oil and pay the debt and use the surplus for her keep. Being a guest of the Shunammite woman and resting in her house, when she had no child, he foretold to her that she would conceive and bear a son. And according to the prophet's prediction she bore. But when the child had grown it died; and the woman went off to Elisha at Carmel, and falling at his feet she bewailed her misfortune. He charged his disciple Gehazi to go, giving him his own staff, that he might lay it upon the dead child. But the woman swore that she would not return unless he himself would go with her. So the prophet was persuaded, and going off found the child laid upon his bed; and having prayed he went up onto the bed and lay down beside the child and breathed into it. And when the prophet had done this seven times, the dead child came to life, and he gave him living to his mother. From there he went off to Gilgal. And there was a famine, and the sons of the prophets came to him. He ordered his servant to prepare them a pottage. And the man gathered from the field herbs, among which a wild gourd was mixed; and the plant is poisonous; and having boiled it he set it before the men. As they ate they recognized the gourd, and cried out to the prophet that they would die. But he, ordering meal to be cast into the pot, gave them leave to eat, and nothing harmful came to anyone from the food. When someone brought him twenty loaves and dried figs, he charged his servant to set them before the people. When the servant said, "What will these be among a hundred men?" he said, "Give these, and they will be filled and will leave leftovers." And the word came to pass.

Naaman, who was great in the sight of the king of Syria, was a leper. When a young Israelite girl was taken captive, the wife of Naaman had her as a servant. She said to her mistress that if her master went to the prophet Elisha he would be rid of his disease. And the wife reported to her husband the words of the girl, and Naaman conveyed what had been said to the king of Syria. And the king sent a letter about the healing of Naaman to the king of Israel. Naaman, taking ten talents of silver and six thousand pieces of gold and ten changes of garments, went off to Samaria and handed the letter to the king. He, reading it, tore his garments, saying, "The king of Syria seeks a pretext against us." When Elisha learned this, he sent word to the king of Israel, "Let Naaman come to me." And when he came, Elisha sent and told him to go to the Jordan and to wash seven times, and so he would be rid of the leprosy. But Naaman was angry that the prophet did not come out to him and pray and lay his hand upon him, and went off in indignation, saying, "Are there not rivers with us beyond the Jordan? I will go and wash in them and be cleansed." As he withdrew, his servants said to him, "Do the prophet's word, since it is easy." And Naaman went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, and was cleansed; and returning he gave thanks to the prophet, and confessed that there was no other God than the one in Israel, and asked him to take something of what he had brought; but he refused. And Naaman departed. But Gehazi pursued after him and said, "The prophet has sent me to receive from you a talent of silver and two garments, to be given to certain needy men who have just now come to him." And Naaman gave them to him; and Gehazi returned to Elisha. But the prophet knew what Gehazi had done, and said to him, "Because you took the silver and the garments from Naaman, his leprosy will cleave to you and to your seed." And he went out a leper.

The sons of the prophets who were with Elisha went to the Jordan to cut wood, that they might make themselves dwellings; and Elisha went with them. As they were cutting the wood, the iron of one man's axe fell into the river. And the owner of the axe called upon the prophet, and showed him the place where the iron had sunk. He, taking a stick, threw it in there. And the iron rose up, and floating on the surface, the man who had lost it took it.

The king of Syria set an ambush to capture the king Jehoram. But the prophet sent to Jehoram, charging him to be on his guard and not to go out hunting. And so he did not go out; but Hadad, having failed in his plot, suspected that his own men were turning traitor to his designs. When they declared that not they but the prophet Elisha was revealing his secrets to the king, he sent an army to Dothan, that they might seize him. When the prophet's servant saw the host around the city, he came in great fear to him, reporting the matter. But he said, "Do not be afraid," and supplicated God to show his servant how he was guarded by him. And God gave to the prophet's servant the grace to see him surrounded with chariots and horses of fire. The prophet, praying, blinded the eyes of the enemy too, and going out to them said, "Follow me, and I will give you Elisha." And they followed, impaired both in sight and in mind. Leading them to Samaria, he charged the king to set his force about them. And he asked God to take away the mist from their eyes. When it was taken away, the Syrians saw themselves surrounded in the midst of the enemy. But Elisha allowed no one to attack them, and rather counselled the king to entertain them and let them go unharmed. So Jehoram, feasting them lavishly according to the prophet's word, let them go. And they departed and related to their king what had happened; and he was astounded.

Cyrus, reared and educated in these, and having passed the age of youth and been enrolled among the men, was well approved in all things. And when his maternal grandfather Astyages, who reigned over the Medes, had departed life, his son Cyaxares, who was also named Darius, succeeded to his father's rule, being Cyrus's maternal uncle.

The ruler of the Assyrians, his kingdom having grown great, and ruling over the nation of the Assyrians, which was numerous, and having brought the Arabs under him, and having made subjects of the Hyrcanians and tributaries of the Syrians, and besieging the Bactrians and having already subdued the nation of the Hebrews, and having made very many other nations subject to him, supposed that if he weakened the Medes he would the more easily master all those around. Having thought this, he prepared his own subjects, and sent also to Croesus the king of the Lydians and to both the Phrygians, to the Paphlagonians and Indians and to the Carians and Cilicians, asking them to ally with him in his march against the Medes, as the war was profitable to them too, saying that the nation was powerful, having made a marriage-alliance with the Persians and gained their support, and that the one was strengthened by the other, so that, unless one anticipated them and weakened them, they would, coming against each of the nations, master them. He sent such words, then, to each of the nations; and these, some moved by these words, some won over by money and gifts, and some constrained by fear of the Assyrian, agreed to ally with him.

Cyaxares, learning this, both made his own preparations and sent to the Persians, both to the commonwealth and to their king Cambyses, asking for an alliance and that Cyrus his nephew should come as commander of the allies; for he was now reckoned among the grown men. The Persians, then, having agreed to ally, the elders chose Cyrus as commander of the army for the Medes, and gave him thirty thousand peltasts and archers and slingers. When he was chosen, taking leave of his father he went off to the Medes with the army. And when he arrived, the Assyrian not yet being at hand, he ordered his men to practice the arts of war. Meanwhile a messenger came from Cyaxares, saying, "An Indian embassy is here, and you too must be present. And I bring you the fairest robe; for he wishes to bring you forward most splendidly arrayed, that you may so appear to the Indians." When he came to the doors of Cyaxares with his army, and entered to him arrayed in Persian fashion, Cyaxares was vexed at the plainness of the robe. And the Indians, being summoned, said they had been sent by their own king to ask from what the war had arisen between the Medes and the Assyrian, and to learn the same from him too, and to tell both that the king of the Indians, having considered the right, would be on the side of the one wronged. To this Cyaxares said, "We do the Assyrian no wrong, but inquire from him what he says." And Cyrus said, "If the Assyrian says he is wronged by us, O Indians, we choose your king as judge."

They, having heard this, departed; and Cyrus, not wishing his own army to sit idle, says to Cyaxares, "Just now I remember hearing you say that the Armenian neither sends you an army nor pays the tribute, having broken the agreements. If, then, you wish, send me, adding to me a moderate number of horse; and I think, with the gods, that he will both send the army and pay the tribute." When Cyaxares gave leave, promising to send him the horsemen when he should approach the borders of Armenia, Cyrus set out as though going to hunt; for he was wont to hunt on the borders of both, of the Medes, I mean, and of the Armenians. And going off he hunted and went up the mountains of Armenia, advancing forward gently. When Cyaxares perceived this, he sent him the horsemen. When they came, he summoned the captains and disclosed the secret, and said he had come because of the Armenian's faithlessness toward Cyaxares. And he charged Chrysantas to take half of the Persians and go into the mountains of the Armenians, and to take care not to be recognized that an army was there, but to send ahead some men resembling brigands both in number and in dress, so that if any chanced to meet them, they might think them thieves. And Chrysantas went with the Persians into the mountains, while Cyrus, sending to the Armenian, ordered him with all speed to bring both the tribute and the army, and himself came on in order. When the Armenian heard this, he was alarmed, and sent to gather his own army, and sent the women and the younger son and the goods into the mountains; for no wall was built about their dwelling. And when those sent to the mountains fell in with the men lying in wait there, and the women and the son and the daughters of the Armenian were taken, he, at a loss, surrendered himself too to Cyrus.

Then the multitude rose in revolt, blaming Moses because, having taken them away from a good land, he had made them wander in the wilderness. Leading them from there to the place called the Ravine, near the land of the Canaanites, he took one from each tribe and sent them to spy out both the strength of the Canaanites and the quality of the land. They, having traversed the land in forty days, returned, bringing fruits from that land, and praised the country as good, but frightened the multitude, saying that the taking of it was beyond their power, on account of the size of the rivers and the difficulty of the mountains and the strength of the cities. And the multitude again were angry with Moses, and thought to stone both him and Aaron and to return to Egypt. Only of the spies, Joshua the son of Nun and Caleb encouraged the people, asserting that nothing difficult would meet them. But Moses and Aaron supplicated God that He would stop the multitude from its folly. And the cloud was present in the tabernacle and signified the appearing of God. And Moses, taking courage, spoke to the multitude, and said that God was angry, but that He would not destroy them all nor blot out the race, yet would not give them Canaan, but would leave them in the wilderness for forty years, while to their children He would give the land. When Moses had said these things, the multitude was grieved. Then they wished to engage the Canaanites, though God forbade it; and attacking, they were defeated, and some fell, while others fled together into the camp. Then a sedition seized the multitude from such a cause as this. Korah, being of the tribe of Levi, and most conspicuous in lineage and wealth and most persuasive in speech, had envy toward Moses and cried out against the man as exercising a tyranny. "For on what ground," he said, "did he assign the priesthood to Aaron and his sons? If because he is of the tribe of Levi, I have a juster claim to obtain it, being of like lineage but superior in wealth and age. But if it ought to be assigned to another tribe, that of Reuben will be preferred by reason of seniority, and Dathan and Abiram will receive it." These things he said with malice, and there were arrayed with him two hundred and fifty of the leading men, and the multitude too had been stirred up. But Moses, standing in the midst, said, "To me, O Korah, both you and each of those arrayed with you seem worthy of honor; but God assigned the priesthood to Aaron, and now He Himself will again judge whom He wishes to be priest. At dawn, then, all of you who lay claim to the priesthood, come forward, each bringing a censer from his house, and fire and incense; and with you likewise let Aaron come forward. And when you offer incense before the people, whosesoever sacrifice God judges the more pleasing, he shall be your priest." The multitude approved this, and on the next day they came together to the assembly. And Moses, sending to Dathan and Abiram, commanded them to come; but they, not persuaded, threatened against Moses. And Moses, bidding the chief men follow him, went to their tents, and coming near, he raised his hands to heaven and cried with a loud voice, "Since I am suspected of acting wickedly, Master, come yourself as judge, and show that nothing happens of its own accord, but all is governed by your providence. And if it was at your command that I gave the priesthood to Aaron, may the earth gape open about Dathan and Abiram and their families, on the ground on which they stand; but if they speak the truth against me, may I fall into the very things I have called down upon them." This he said weeping. And the earth is shaken all at once, and, a harsh sound being broken forth, it sank in about their tents and carried them and their belongings down into the chasm, and so what had been divided came together again. At these things the people shuddered, and Moses calls those who were contending for the priesthood. And when two hundred and fifty men of the notable ones, and Aaron and Korah, had come together before the tabernacle and consecrated upon the censers what they brought, a great fire blazed forth, such as would be kindled at God's command, by which the two hundred and fifty and Korah were destroyed, so that not even their bodies were found; only Aaron was found unharmed. And Moses ordered the censers of those men to be set about the bronze altar, that they might be a reminder of what had happened to those who came after. And convening the assembly again, he told the chiefs of the tribes to come, bringing the names of the tribes inscribed upon staffs, the priesthood being for him on whose staff a sign should come from God. So the others bring them, and Aaron, having inscribed "Levite" upon his staff. And Moses set them down in the tabernacle of God. On the next day he brought them out. And the others remained just as they were, but the staff of Aaron had sprouted branches and fruit. And the fruit the book of Leviticus calls nuts, but Josephus almonds. So all were amazed, since God had three times appointed Aaron. And since the tribe of Levi was released from wars and military service, that they might not, through lack of necessities, neglect the service of the sanctuary, Moses commanded that when the Hebrews had acquired Canaan they should apportion to the Levites forty-eight cities and land about them, and pay them the tithe of the yearly fruits, both to them and to the priests; and he ordained that the people should furnish them with very many other things, the particulars of which he who inquires will find by opening the book of Leviticus.

After this the king of Syria, coming to Samaria with all his army, besieged it. And there was a most severe famine in it, so that an ass's head was sold for fifty pieces of silver, and a pint of dove's dung for five such pieces. As the king Jehoram was going about the wall, a woman cried out, "Save me, O king." Supposing that the woman was asking for food, he said, blaspheming her, "From where shall I save you, when I have neither threshing-floor nor wine-press?" When she said she was asking for judgement, he gave her leave to speak. And the woman said, "I made a compact with another woman, my neighbour, to sacrifice our children and to feed on each in turn on a single day. And I sacrificed mine, but she transgresses what was agreed." Hearing this the king was in deep anguish and tore his garment, and was enraged against the prophet, because he did not beg God to loose the affliction, and sent the man who should kill him. But Elisha, conversing with his disciples, foretold to them, "The son of the murderer has sent to kill me, but do you shut the door and prevent the slayer's entrance; for the king will follow, having repented." And they did according to the prophet's word, and Jehoram, having changed his mind, came hastening to the prophet and reproached him for not begging God to loose their sorrows. But he said, "Tomorrow two measures of barley will be sold for a shekel, and a measure of fine flour for a shekel." And one of those attending the king said, "You speak incredible things, prophet." And he said, "You will see the things promised, but will not enjoy them, because of your unbelief." During that night God brought into the ears of the Syrians a din of chariots, of horses and of weapons, and the shouting of a multitude. And they, thinking that Jehoram had gathered a great force of allies and was coming upon them, left the camp and fled in great fear. Now there were four lepers outside the city, since the law commanded that lepers be cast out of the cities. These lepers, perishing now from the famine, resolved to go to the Syrian camp, saying, "Either they will spare us and, being fed, we shall live, or, being killed, we shall be rid of our miseries." So they came at dawn to the Syrian camp, and no one was to be seen by them. They entered one tent and found it empty of men; from that they passed to another, and found it deserted; and passing into more, when they met no one, they first ate and drank, and then taking gold and silver and garments from there hid them, and so coming into the city they proclaimed what had happened. But the king, hearing it, said this was an ambush of the enemy, and gave orders not to go forth, but sent men to spy it out. They, going off, met no one along the road, but found it full of garments and gear. Learning this, the king allowed the multitude to plunder the camp. From which there came so great an abundance of necessities that two measures of barley were sold for a shekel, and a measure also—and the measure is the Italic half-medimnus. Only the king's officer of rank did not enjoy that abundance, according to the prophet's word, because he had disbelieved his prediction; for when the multitude streamed to the gate of the city, he was trampled and died.

After this the king of Damascus fell sick. And Elisha at that time went to Damascus; and the sick man heard about the prophet, and sent Hazael, the most honoured of his servants, to him, to ask whether he would live.
