He sent him also many gifts. When the prophet was asked, he foretold that the sick king would die, but charged Hazael to tell him nothing of this; and he himself wept. And being asked by Hazael the cause of his weeping, he said that he wept, foreseeing how many dreadful things would befall the Israelites because of him; "for you will be king of Syria." Returning to his lord, Hazael reported that the prophet had said he would live. But on the next day, casting a wet net over him, he smothered him, and himself seized the kingdom.

Meanwhile the elder son of the Armenian, Tigranes, who had been abroad, drew near, who had once been a fellow-hunter with Cyrus; and learning what had happened he went off at once just as he was to Cyrus; and seeing his father and mother and sisters and his own wife captives, he wept. And Cyrus said, "You have come at a good time." And conversing much with the Armenian and convicting him of wrong, at last he said, "Tell me how great is your force, and how much your money." When he said there were eight thousand horse and forty thousand foot, and money reckoned in silver more than three thousand talents, Cyrus said, "Send me with me half of the army, and of the money, instead of the fifty talents of the yearly tribute, give Cyaxares double; and to me," he said, "lend another hundred." And saying this he gave the wife and children to the Armenian as a gift, and to Tigranes his own bride, being newly wedded, and let all go free.

The Armenians and the Chaldaeans, being neighbours, had always disputes and battles; these Cyrus reconciled to one another, and so departed. And the army which he had taken from the Armenian he sent to Cyaxares, and when he arrived among the Medes he shared the money with his own captains. Then with Cyaxares he invaded the enemy's land, and they encamped and gathered much booty from it. When they learned that the Assyrians too were approaching, they advanced in order, and encamped a parasang apart from one another. On the next day Cyrus, leading out his army, drew it up, and on the other wing Cyaxares with the Medes, while on the other side were the Assyrians and their allies. And the Persians, having heartened one another, charged at a run, and Cyrus himself. The enemy did not stand, but fled to their entrenchment. And the Persians, following them, as they were thrust together, laid many low, and those who fell into the trenches they killed by leaping in upon them. And the horsemen of the Medes drove against the horsemen of the enemy, who gave way; and there was a pursuit of horses and men and slaughter on both sides. When the women of the Assyrians and their allies saw this, they cried out and ran in dismay, and rending their robes and tearing themselves they implored all to defend both them and their children and themselves. There too the kings themselves, with their most faithful, standing at the entrances, fought and exhorted the rest. But Cyrus, fearing that, being few, if they forced their way into the entrenchment, they might be overcome by the many, ordered them to draw back step by step out of range of the missiles; and they quickly did as ordered. Then he led his men back as far as seemed well, and encamped. The Assyrians, their ruler being dead and well-nigh the best with him, were despondent. Seeing this, Croesus and all their other allies grieved. From there they abandoned the camp and departed by night. When by day the enemy's entrenchment appeared deserted, Cyrus brought the Persians across first, and then those about Cyaxares crossed over. To Cyrus, then, it seemed good to pursue the enemy, but to Cyaxares the entire opposite was preferable. And Cyrus said, "Give me, then, some of the Medes to go with me, those, that is, who will be willing to follow me as volunteers." And Cyaxares gave leave, and sent with Cyrus the man to announce this to the Medes.

Meanwhile messengers came from the Hyrcanians. The Hyrcanians are neighbours of the Assyrians, a nation not large, and for this reason they were subjects of the Assyrians; and these used them sparing them neither in toils nor in dangers. And then they had been posted as rearguard, being about a thousand horse, so that if any danger were behind, it might fall on these before the rest. And they, considering what they suffered, sent messengers to Cyrus to say that the Assyrians were justly hated by them, and that if he wished to go against them, they would be his allies and would lead the way. He asked whether they could overtake them; and the Hyrcanians said that if even at dawn the next day they should go light-armed, they would overtake them. And Cyrus asked pledges that they spoke truly; and they undertook to give hostages, if he too would give his right hand and make pledges by the gods. And Cyrus gave them pledges, that indeed, if they made good what they said, he would treat them as friends and faithful, and that they should have no less from him than the Persians or Medes.

Upon this Cyrus, while it was still light, led out his army, and Tigranes with the Armenians was with him, and he ordered the Hyrcanians to wait, that they might go together. Of the Medes well-nigh all went out with Cyrus. He ordered the Hyrcanians to lead the way; and having traversed a long road he came near the army of the Hyrcanians. And the messengers told this to Cyrus, and he ordered, if they were friends, to come to meet him with all speed, holding up their right hands. And the Hyrcanians, hearing this, were at once present, holding up their right hands as had been said. Greeting them, he said, "Tell me, how far is it from here to where the rulers of the enemy are and their main body?" And they said, a little more than a parasang. He ordered the Hyrcanians to lead the way. And they led, while he himself with the Persians went, holding the centre, and he posted the horsemen on each side. When light came and the enemy knew what was being done, none fought, but some fled, and some perished even without a battle.

Having ordained these things, Moses came to Idumaea with the army and asked to pass through it. But the king of the country came out to meet Moses with an armed force. And he proceeded through the wilderness, since God counseled him not to begin a battle. At that time too Mariamme, the sister of Moses, died, in the fortieth year after the departure from Egypt. And he led the people through the wilderness and through Arabia; there too Aaron died, having gone up to a high mountain and handed over the high-priestly robe to his son Eleazar, in the sight of the multitude, having lived a hundred and twenty-three years. And Moses, coming to the country of the Moabites and Amorites, asked passage for the army. But Sihon, the king of the country, prevented the Hebrews from crossing, and when God signified victory to Moses, who inquired, the Hebrews, taking up their full armor, advanced to battle. The Amorites are at once routed and all destroyed, and Sihon their king fell. And they took the cities and seized their land. And Og, the king of Galadene and Gaulanitis, attacks the Israelites, having come as ally to Sihon, who had already perished. So he himself dies in the battle and his army is destroyed, and the cities were taken and the inhabitants perished. From there Moses leads the force along the great plain and encamps opposite Jericho. This is a prosperous city, bearing palms and rich in balsam. And Balak, the king of the Moabites, summons the seer Balaam, that he might come and lay curses to the destruction of the Israelites. And he set out, but on the road, a divine angel having set upon him, the donkey on which Balaam rode, perceiving the divine spirit, would not go forward nor yield to the blows, but speaking in human voice by the divine will, called his master unjust for laying blows upon it and not understanding that it was hindered by God from serving the purpose to which he was hastening. And while he was troubled at the human voice, the angel appeared and said that it was he himself who was hindering the road for the beast; and though Balaam wished to turn back, he urged him to go further forward, and to say whatever should be inspired in him by God. And he comes to Balak, and being brought to a mountain, having offered seven bulls and as many rams as whole burnt offerings, when he saw a turning of events signified, not only did he not curse the Hebrews, but, divinely inspired, he blessed them and their whole race and praised them in song. And when Balak was vexed at this, Balaam said, "It does not rest with us, O king, to be silent or to speak about such things, but whenever the spirit of God takes hold of us, it sends forth through us such utterances as it wishes. But since I wish to gratify you, an altar must again be prepared, and victims." So he sacrifices again, and falling upon his face he foretold what sufferings would come upon kings and what upon cities. But Balak sends Balaam away dishonored. Then he sends the maidens against the Israelites, according to the counsel of Balaam, by whom the young men of the Hebrews were captivated and consorted with them, so that now the transgression spread through the whole army, the young men, out of love of the Midianite women, sacrificing to their gods and tasting unaccustomed foods. But Moses, leading the people to an assembly, said that the young men were doing things unworthy of themselves and of their fathers, and tried to set them right. But Zimri, who was the chief of the tribe of Simeon, and dwelt with a Midianite woman and loved her madly, behaved insolently toward Moses, and swore that he would never leave the woman. And Phinehas, the son of the high priest Eleazar, in great anguish did not cease striking the Midianite woman and Zimri with the sword until he had killed both of them. And other young men too, who cared for virtue, imitating him, slew those of the young men who had transgressed with foreign women. So there perished men not fewer than fourteen thousand. From this Moses, provoked against the Midianites, sent out an army, appointing as its commander Phinehas. And when the battle was joined, their kings fall, being five, and a very great multitude. And the Hebrews plundered their country, and destroying the inhabitants together with the women, they left alive only the maidens, numbered at thirty-two thousand, whom Moses distributed among the priests and the Levites and the people. And being now an old man, he appointed as his successor Joshua the son of Nun, at God's command.

The king of Judah, Jehoram—for both kings bore the same name—was rolled into impiety by his wife Athaliah, who was a daughter of Ahab; and he killed his brothers and his father's servants, and forced the people to share his impiety. As he so lived, the prophet sent to him, declaring to him the destruction that was to come, and the ruin of his wives and children, because of his impiety and the affliction of the people; which things came to pass when the Arabs marched against Judah, one of his sons being saved, Ahaziah. After this Jehoram fell sick, as the prophet had foretold, and died a violent death, having lived forty years and reigned eight. The rule passed to his son Ahaziah.

It happened that Jehoram the other, the king of the Israelites, when he had marched against the Syrians, was struck by an arrow in the battle. And he withdrew to be healed of his wound, leaving as commander of the army Jehu the son of Amasai. Elisha sent one of his disciples to anoint Jehu king, since God had chosen him. He, going and taking Jehu aside privately from the others, as if to tell him something more secret, slipping into an inner chamber poured the oil on his head, saying that God had chosen him as king, that he might destroy the race of Ahab. And he, having spoken, ran hastily out of the chamber; and when those with him asked what the man who had called him wanted, and likened him to a madman, Jehu said, "You judged rightly, since he reported to me words full of madness; for he said that God appoints me king." And the people, hearing this, with trumpets proclaimed Jehu king. He at once, taking the choice horsemen, set out, that he might fall suddenly upon those about Jehoram. When the watchman told Jehoram that horsemen were coming, he sent someone to ask what they wanted. But Jehu, answering nothing, urged him to follow him. Then he sent a second; and when that man too did not return, Jehoram himself, mounting his chariot, with Ahaziah, who had come to visit him, being his sister's son, met Jehu in the field of Naboth, and asked how matters stood with the army; but Jehu poured out blasphemies against him. Jehoram, turning, fled in fear. And Jehu, drawing his bow, struck him. And falling from the chariot he died, and was cast into the field of Naboth, according to the prediction of Elijah which he had made to Ahab. Jehu shot Ahaziah too as he fled, and a little later he died of the wound, having reigned one year. Jezebel, leaning out from the tower, adorned to make herself more enticing, said, "A good servant, who has killed his master." But Jehu ordered the eunuchs to throw her down from above. And as she was hurled down the wall was sprinkled with her blood; and she died. When Jehu ordered her to be buried because of her royal lineage, those commanded found nothing of her body but only bones; for she had been torn apart by dogs, as Elijah had prophesied.

There were in Samaria seventy sons of Ahab. Jehu therefore sent to the rulers of Samaria and to the guardians of Ahab's sons, declaring that they should make whichever of these was the best king over them. Testing the men, he wrote this. But they wrote back that they had him as lord. And again Jehu sent word that, if they acknowledged servitude to him, they should bring him the heads of all the sons of Ahab. And they did what was commanded. He ordered the heads to be set before the gate of the city in two heaps. And when this had been done he came forward and said, "I have killed the king, but these have perished according to the prophet's prediction." And Jehu, searching out all the kinsmen of Ahab, killed them. As he went off to Samaria, Jehonadab met him, and addressing him he blessed him for having utterly destroyed the race of Ahab.

Then, so that none of the false prophets and priests of Baal might escape notice, he proclaimed that he intended to offer a lavish sacrifice, and ordered all the priests and prophets of Baal to be present; and if any were absent, he said the penalty would be death. When they were gathered, he gave them garments, and going with them into the house of Baal, he ordered that no other be mingled among them. When they said that no other was present, he set soldiers about outside, ordering them to kill those within. They killed them all and burned the house of Baal and his pillar; but the golden heifers he did not take away. And God promised him, since he had destroyed the house of Ahab, that the kingdom would endure to the fourth generation of his sons.

Croesus the king of the Lydians sent the women on with the wagons by night, that they might travel more easily in the cool—for it was summer—and himself with the horsemen followed. And the ruler of the Phrygia by the Hellespont, they say, did the same. When those who fled overtook them, and they learned what was happening, they too fled. The king of the Cappadocians, being still near, the Hyrcanians cut down. The rest pursued, but Cyrus ordered those with him to surround the camp, and to kill those who came out armed, and proclaimed to those who remained to bring out their arms bound together, and to leave the horses by the tents; and whoever did not do so should lose his head. So those who had arms threw them down, carrying them to one place, and those appointed burned them. And Cyrus, considering that they had come with neither food nor drink, proclaimed that the stewards of the tents should all be present, and when they were present he said, "Come, men, prepare in each tent twice as much food as you made daily for your masters and their servants." And they did as bidden. And of the Medes, some, having seized wagons that had set off ahead and turned them back, full of what an army needs, drove them on, and some brought up carriages of the noblest women, and showing Cyrus what they brought, drove off again. And Cyrus was stung at this and blamed himself, and gathering the captains he counselled them to gain cavalry and to make the Persians horsemen, that with this they might pursue the horsemen and overtake the fleeing; and the others agreed. When it was already past midday the horsemen of the Medes and Hyrcanians drove up, bringing captive horses and men. To the captive men he said, "Go, work your land and dwell in your houses and live with your wives and enjoy your children, and announce these things to the rest; for there will be one new thing for you, that the same man will not rule you as before, but in all else things will be the same for you." So they, doing obeisance, departed; and Cyrus said, "It is now time, Medes and Armenians, to dine; suppers are prepared for you as we, my good men, were able. And do you too, Hyrcanians," he said, "lead them to the tents, the rulers to the greatest, the rest as seems best, and dine yourselves too; for the tents are whole and untouched for you." And they did as ordered. And Cyrus sent many of the Persians around to watch the camp, that if anyone approached from outside, he might not escape notice, and if any of those within tried to slip away, he might be caught. So the Persians passed the time. On the next day he ordered the spoils to be distributed to the soldiers, and the horses to be given to the Persians, that they too might be horsemen. "And for Cyaxares," he said, "choose such things as you know to be pleasing to him; and for the Persians," he said, "those with me, whatever is left over will suffice; for we have not been reared in luxury, so that perhaps you would laugh at us if you put something stately about us; as I know we shall give you much to laugh at, both seated on the horses and, I think, falling to the ground." And calling the captains, he ordered them to take the horses, and to take them by lot, each an equal number.

The tribes of Gad and Reuben and the half of Manasseh asked Moses to allot to them the land of the Amorites. But he called them cowards, men unwilling to share with their kinsmen in the battle against the Canaanites. They, however, replied that this was not so, but that, abounding in a multitude of cattle, they wished to leave these in that country, which was good for the feeding of four-footed beasts, so that they themselves might set out unencumbered with their kinsmen to the struggles. Moses approved this and allotted them the Amorite land on such terms. And when a certain man of the tribe of Manasseh had died, leaving only daughters, Moses, being asked whose his inheritance should be, answered, "If the maidens marry men of their own tribe, let them go with the inheritance to those men; but if they be betrothed to men of another tribe, let them leave the inheritance in their ancestral tribe." And so he ordained that each one's inheritance should remain within the tribes. And when forty years had now passed, less thirty days, since the Israelites had gone out of Egypt, Moses, having gathered the people, being a hundred and twenty years old, announced to them his own end. And having exhorted them much, and given laws in books and the ordering of their commonwealth, and commanded them to make war against the Amalekites, and required of them an oath concerning the keeping of the laws, and spurred on the leader Joshua to make war against the Canaanites, he said, "Behold, I go to our forefathers; for God has shown me this day of my coming to them." And the multitude wept, and their lamentation was inconsolable and so great that even Moses himself was overcome by the emotion and shed tears. And as he went to where he was to vanish from sight, all followed, beating their breasts. But he, signaling with his hand to those at a distance, bade them remain, and only the council of elders escorted him, and the high priest Eleazar and the general Joshua, until he came to the mountain Nebo, to the peak of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho; from there the Lord showed him the land that the sons of Israel were to inherit, saying to him, "See this with your eyes, but into it you shall not enter." And coming to this mountain, which was high, he sent away the council of elders, but while speaking with Eleazar and Joshua, a cloud suddenly enfolded him and he became invisible. And they have written in the sacred books that he died, lest, on account of the surpassing greatness of his virtue, some should dare to say that he had been made a god. He lived in all a hundred and twenty years, of which he ruled the third part, less one month. And they mourned him for thirty days. These things Josephus says; but the book of Deuteronomy contains, near its end, thus, word for word: "And Moses, the servant of the Lord, died, and no one knows his end to this day." Now when the mourning had abated, Joshua sends spies to Jericho, and having summoned the chiefs of the tribes of Reuben and Gad and Manasseh, he reminded them of their agreements with Moses. And with fifty thousand foot soldiers following him, he advanced to the Jordan. And the spies sent to Jericho, coming there, observed the whole city, but being made known to the king of the country, they are reported; and he at once commanded that they be seized. But when the woman with whom they had taken refuge, called Rahab, learned of the approach of those seeking the men, she hid the spies, having placed bundles of flax over them, and to those seeking she said that those unknown men had dined with her before sunset and had departed. And so, the woman having deceived them, they set out, each in a different direction, pursuing the men. But Rahab bade the men go to their own people and remember her and pay her a recompense when they had become masters of the land of the Canaanites. And they acknowledged that they were grateful, and commanded that, when the city should be taken, she should shut up her possessions and her household in her lodging, and hang a scarlet cord before the doors, that the house might be recognized and preserved. And they were brought safely to their own people and made known what they had done. And though the Jordan was flowing in flood, Joshua thus brought the Hebrews across it. The priests went before, carrying the ark, then the Levites bearing the tabernacle, and the people followed these. And when the stream of the river was cut off as the priests first stepped in, all crossed over in confidence. And the priests stood in the midst until the multitude had crossed; then they too came out, letting the stream flow free. And ten stadia before Jericho

So then the race of Ahab was utterly destroyed. But his daughter Athaliah, who had been wife to Ahaziah the king of Jerusalem, when he was dead and she had control of the kingdom of Judah, made it her own endeavour also to destroy the race of David. And she killed all save one. For the sister of Ahaziah, called Jehosheba, when her brother's sons were being killed, was able to hide one, an infant named Joash, and reared him secretly for six years. In the seventh year Jehoiada the high priest, with whom Jehosheba dwelt, summoning certain of the centurions, showed them Joash, and conferring with the men persuaded them to rise against Athaliah and to recover the ancestral kingdom for the child. And they, confirming their agreement with oaths, went off and gathered the priests and Levites and tribal leaders to Jehoiada. He showed them Joash, saying, "This is your king, of the seed of David." And he surrounded the temple with the people, and setting Joash in the midst he put a diadem upon him and pouring the oil of anointing on him appointed him king; and the people acclaimed him. When Athaliah heard the shouting, in alarm she rushed out from the palace, the army following her. As she came to the temple, the priests received her within, but the multitude barred the entrance to those with her. When she saw the child crowned, she threatened to kill those who had assailed her rule. But Jehoiada charged the centurions to drag Athaliah outside and kill her. And so they did, and Jehoiada made the king and the people swear to honour God and keep the laws. And going at once to the temple of Baal they razed it and broke to pieces the images of Baal and killed his priest. They established the king in the palace, then being seven years old. And the high priest Jehoiada took great care that faith toward the deity be maintained and the laws kept.

When the king had grown up he took two wives. Since the temple had been thrown down in some parts by Athaliah, Joash was eager to renew it. Calling the priest Jehoiada, he ordered that men be sent to ask from the whole country, for the repair of the temple, half a shekel of silver for each head. But Jehoiada, understanding that this would be reckoned burdensome by the people, went about the collection of the money another way. For he made a certain chest, closed on all sides, with a hole made in the top of it, and set it beside the temple, and asked that each cast in through the hole as much as he was minded for the renewal of the temple. Since therefore what was given was left to each one's free choice, they made their gift without resentment and vied with one another in laying down money, so that much gold was gathered and very much silver, from which the temple was repaired and many vessels for the sacrifices were made, the offerings which, as long as Jehoiada lived, were brought to God. But when he, having lived justly and according to the law a hundred and thirty years, had so departed from life, the king Joash became careless about the honour due to the deity, and the tribal leaders and others who led the multitude were corrupted with him; and though prophets testified to them about their impiety toward God, they did not cease. When Zechariah the son of the high priest Jehoiada prophesied and exhorted the king and the people to live according to the laws, Joash, in anger, ordered him to be stoned. As he was being killed, the prophet prayed that God would judge for what cause he was being deprived of life by the one whom his father had benefited. And indeed God judged swiftly; for Hazael the king of the Syrians came up and besieged Jerusalem. And Joash, taking away all the treasures, both the sacred and the royal, and whatever was in the votive offerings, gave them to Hazael; who, pleased with the multitude of the riches, refrained from the siege.
This Syrian, attacking the Israelites, afflicted them grievously. And Jehu the king of the Israelites, having become a transgressor of the divine commandments,

Meanwhile there came Gobryas, an aged Assyrian man, with a mounted retinue, and asked to see Cyrus. He was brought to him and said, "Master, I am by race an Assyrian, having also a strong fortress, and I rule much land; I have also horse to a thousand, which I used to provide to the king of the Assyrians, and I was his friend as much as possible. But since he is dead at your hands, and his son holds the rule, who is most hostile to me because he envied and killed my only and beloved son, I have come to you and give myself to you as servant and ally, and ask you to become my avenger." And Cyrus answered, "If, Gobryas, all that you say is also what you mean, I receive you as suppliant and promise, with the gods, to avenge for you the murder of your son." And he said, "On these terms, speaking truly, I give you my right hand and take yours."

When this was done, he bade Gobryas depart, keeping his arms too. And he departed. And the Medes were present, having chosen for Cyrus the fairest tent and the Susian woman, who is said to have been the fairest woman in Asia, and two of the best music-girls, and for Cyaxares the second choice; and the remaining tents they handed over to Cyrus for the Persians. But Cyrus ordered Cyaxares' goods to be kept by his nearest people, and said, "What is given to me I gladly receive." And calling Araspes the Mede, who had been his companion from boyhood, he ordered him to guard for him the woman and the tent. She was the wife of Abradates the king of Susa, who, when the camp was taken, was not present, having been sent about an alliance by the Assyrian to the king of the Bactrians, being his guest-friend.

Rising at dawn they went off to Gobryas, Cyrus on horseback and the horsemen of the Persians now amounting to two thousand. On the second day, about evening, they came to Gobryas's place, they and the allies. Learning there that the Assyrians at Babylon had prepared a force many times the former one, he said, "Lead us straight on toward Babylon." As they journeyed, on the fourth day they came to the borders of Gobryas's land, and were now in the enemy's country, and he kept with him the foot and some of the horse, and let the other horsemen ride about, ordering them to kill those they met who had arms, and to bring to him the rest and whatever booty they took. He bade the Persians too ride about with them. And many of them came back tumbled from their horses, and many bringing as much booty as possible. Then he went toward Babylon as if drawn up for battle. When the Assyrians did not come out against him, Cyrus ordered Gobryas to ride up and say, if the king wished to come out and fight for his land, that he too would fight with him; but if he would not defend the land, that it was necessary to obey the victors. So Gobryas rode up and said this; and the Assyrian sent and said, "Your master, Gobryas, answers: If you wish to fight, come on the thirtieth day; for now we are not yet at leisure; we are still preparing."

And he reported this to Cyrus, who led the army back, and asked Gobryas about Gadatas. Now Gadatas was the son of a certain king, a companion of the Assyrian, whom, while drinking with him, he seized and gelded and made a eunuch; who, when his father died, then held the kingdom, being a eunuch. To this man, then, Cyrus wished Gobryas to go and bring him to himself. And he went. And meeting him and saying all that Cyrus charged, he returned, and Gadatas, pretending to ally with the Assyrian and by guile seizing a certain fortress of the Assyrian, an outwork of the war, and handing it over to Cyrus, came himself too to Cyrus. And being received he heard, "Gadatas, the Assyrian, it seems, deprived you of getting children, but did not deprive you of acquiring friends." So he spoke. The fortress having come under Cyrus, both Cadusians and Sacae and Hyrcanians in greater numbers joined his army; and upon this Gadatas comes to Cyrus saying that the Assyrian, learning about the fortress and being enraged, was making ready to invade my land. "If, then, you let me go, I would try to save the walls; for the rest I have less concern." Cyrus asked, "If you go, when will you be home?" And he said, "On the third day I will dine in our land." "And I," said Cyrus, "on what day might I arrive there with the army?" And Gadatas answered, "You could not, master, unless you came in six or seven days." And Cyrus said, "Do you, then, go off most quickly, and I will go as I am able." And Gadatas departed, and Cyrus said to the commanders of the allies that they must help Gadatas, who was being warred on by the Assyrian, a benefactor. And all agreed. And he said, "Since it seems good to you too, come, let us go, taking the strongest of horse and men and three days' provisions, that we may go light." And having so equipped themselves, at midnight they took to the road, Gobryas leading them.

they encamp. And Joshua, having set up an altar from the stones that each of the chiefs of the tribes had taken up from the depth of the Jordan at his command, sacrificed upon it and kept the festival of the Passover. At that time too the manna had failed them, after they had used it for forty years; for now they had abundance from the country of all that they needed. And on the first day of the festival Joshua undertook the siege of Jericho, conducting it thus. The priests, carrying the ark, went round the wall, sounding seven horns, and the council of elders followed; then they returned to the camp. And this they did for six days. But on the seventh, when they had done the same and gone round seven times, the wall fell down, and the people, entering, killed all and burned the city. Only Rahab, with her household, the spies saved, since she had hung a scarlet cord before the house. And Joshua gave her fields as a gift and held her in honor. And against those who should wish to raise up the city again he laid curses, that he who laid the foundations should be deprived of his firstborn child, and he who completed it should be bereaved of his youngest. And a great quantity of silver and gold is gathered from the city, and all was dedicated to God as being the firstfruits of their successes; for it had been forbidden to all to appropriate anything from this. But a certain Achar, of the tribe of Judah, finding a garment woven with gold and a lump of gold weighing two hundred shekels, made these his own, having buried them in his tent. After this, when a battle was joined, the Hebrews are routed and thirty-six of their men fall. This grieved the multitude greatly. And Joshua, falling upon his face, prayed to God. And being informed by an oracle that a theft of the consecrated goods had occurred, he committed the judgment to the lot. And when the lot fell upon Achar, he confesses the theft and brings forth the stolen things. And he is killed with stones, together with his household; and Joshua besieges Ai and takes it. But the Gibeonites and their neighbors, who belonged to the Canaanites, fearing that they would suffer the same as the people of Jericho and Ai, send an embassy to Joshua, saying that they dwelt very far off and had no kinship with the Canaanites, and seeking that the Israelites make a treaty and a covenant of friendship with them. So Joshua made friendship with them. But learning afterward that they were of the race of the Canaanites, he charged them with the deceit. They, however, said that they had done this of necessity, fearing destruction. And Joshua, that he might not transgress the oath, appoints them public servants. So says Josephus; but the book of Joshua records that they appointed them hewers of wood and drawers of water for the whole congregation and for the altar of God. And when the king of Jerusalem attacked the Gibeonites on account of their treaty with the Hebrews, Joshua allies himself with them and routs the enemy, and pursued them as they fled. At that time too hail greater than usual and thunderbolts fell from heaven upon the enemy, and the day was lengthened, God having stopped the course of the sun at the entreaty of Joshua, that the enemy might not escape with the coming on of night. And the kings too are caught, hidden in a certain cave, and all are killed. And Joshua returned again to the hill country of Canaan, and having wrought a great slaughter of those in it and taken spoil, he came to the camp at Gilgal. And the place of the camp was called Gilgal, since the Israelites now recognized themselves to be free of the Egyptians and of the hardship in the wilderness; for the Hebrews call freedom "galgala." And the Canaanites about Lebanon and those in the plains make war upon them, allied with the Palestinians. And their army was three hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand horsemen and thirty thousand chariots. And when God had promised victory, a strong battle takes place, so that the whole army of the enemy, except a few, was destroyed, and the kings too fell.

and having reigned twenty-seven years, died; and Jehoahaz his son took over the kingdom. While he reigned, the chief of the Syrians ravaged the country, and seizing many of its cities made his army the work of the sword. In this distress Jehoahaz, having begged God, found deliverance and a respite from his troubles. Having reigned seventeen years he died, with Joash his son as successor to the kingdom, of the same name as the one reigning over the tribe of Judah. But this Joash was not like his father, but good. He wept when Elisha fell sick and was dying, calling him his father and his weapon, since through him he prevailed over his enemies. The prophet comforted him; and bade him take a bow and shoot arrows. When the king had shot three times and stopped, Elisha said, "If you had shot more arrows, you would have cut up by the roots the rule of the Syrians; but now you will conquer them with victories equal in number to the arrows, and will recover for your rule the country which they took away." Then the prophet died and obtained a magnificent burial. Some robbers, having killed a man, threw him into the prophet's tomb; and the man thrown in came to life and rose up. Hazael too, the king of Syria, died, with his son Hadad as successor; with whom Joash the king of the Israelites engaged, and defeating him three times recovered for Israel the country and the cities which Hazael, the father of Hadad, had taken away.

Joash the king of Judah, being seven years old when he was proclaimed, and having reigned forty years, died, killed by his servants. And his son Amaziah girded on the kingdom of Jerusalem, having become pious, being twenty-five years old when he came to the rule, and having held the kingdom for twenty-nine years. Having punished those who had killed his father, he let their children go free as guiltless, according to the law which says, "Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons for fathers." Marching against the Idumaeans and Amalekites, he hired allies from the Israelites. But a certain prophet counselled him to dismiss the allies and to conduct the war with only his own men. Persuaded by him, he released the Israelites, granting them their pay. Engaging the foreigners, then, he conquered. But the dismissed allies, in anger, overran the country of the Jews and killed many. Amaziah, made arrogant by his success and impious toward God, sent to Joash the king of Israel, demanding that he come to him, as being bound to be subject to him, since he was a descendant of David and Solomon. But Joash sent back word to him, saying, "The thistle asked the cedar to make a marriage-alliance for its children with the cedar's. Meanwhile the wild beasts of the field, passing by, trampled down the thistle, and it perished. Let this be a sufficient example to you; and because you have prospered in striking the foreigners, do not be high-minded, nor push your people and yourself into dangers." Angered at this, Amaziah marched against Joash. But fear fell upon his army, and it turned to flight; and Amaziah, left alone, was taken by the enemy and led off to Joash. He, leading him as a prisoner, came to Jerusalem, and tearing down a part of the wall drove through the breach into the city upon a chariot, and took away both the sacred treasures and whatever was stored in the palace. And releasing Amaziah, he returned to Samaria. And having reigned in all sixteen years he died. And Jeroboam his son reigned. Amaziah after this was plotted against and killed, having lived fifty-four years and reigned twenty-nine. And his son Uzziah was anointed king, being sixteen years old.

So Cyrus departed; but as Gadatas was going off, one of his own powerful men plotted against him, and sending to the Assyrian disclosed the force of Gadatas and that he was coming, and charged him to lie in ambush for him, that he might so take both Gadatas himself and those with him. When the Assyrian heard this, he laid an ambush. And as Gadatas came near the ambush and now seemed to be at the point of being taken, the ambush rose up. And the one plotting against Gadatas at this moment struck him, and hit him on the shoulder, not mortally however; and having done this he at once withdrew to the Assyrian and pursued with him. So some of Gadatas's men were taken, and some fled, turning their reins; and now they descry Cyrus approaching. When he understood the matter, he led his army against them. And the enemy, seeing this, turned to flight, and Cyrus ordered the pursuit. And men and chariots were taken, and many were slain, including the very man who had struck Gadatas; and the rest and the Assyrian himself fled to a certain great city of his. And Cyrus, having accomplished this, withdrew to Gadatas's land, and went to visit Gadatas. And Gadatas met him with his wound bound up, and acknowledged his gratitude, saying, "As far as concerned me, I am lost, but as far as concerns you, I am saved, since you helped me so readily."

The Cadusians, posted then as rearguard by Cyrus and having had no share in the pursuit, wishing to do some brilliant thing themselves, without communicating with Cyrus, overran Babylonia. The Assyrian, going out of the city to which he had fled, fell in with them; and learning they were alone, he attacked them, and killed both their ruler and many others, and pursuing for some distance turned back. Those of the Cadusians who were saved came toward evening to the camp. Cyrus handed the wounded over to those who would heal them, and to the rest he himself addressed words of encouragement, and counselled them to choose a ruler for themselves from among themselves. And they chose one. And Gadatas came bringing Cyrus gifts of all kinds and many, and very many horses. But Cyrus said he received the horses, that he might fill out the Persian cavalry and that his horsemen might come to ten thousand, but ordered the money to be taken back to him and kept until he should see Cyrus too able to give in return; and he counselled him to put his city under safe guard, and himself to march with him. And Gadatas was pleased with the counsel, and having equipped himself accompanied Cyrus. As he journeyed thus and came to the border between the Syrians and Medes, there being three fortresses of the Syrians there, the one he himself took by assault and force, while the other two Cyrus, by frightening, and Gadatas, by persuading, brought the guards to surrender.

Then he sent to Cyaxares, asking him to come to the camp, that they might deliberate about what they needed. And the messenger went off; and Cyrus ordered the tent which the Medes had chosen for Cyaxares to be furnished as well as possible, both with the other equipment and by bringing the woman into the women's quarters of the tent, and with her the music-girls who had been chosen for Cyaxares. Meanwhile the messenger reported Cyrus's words to Cyaxares, and he set out with the Median horsemen who had stayed with him. When Cyrus knew he was approaching, taking the horsemen of the Persians, now many, and the Medes present and the Armenians and the best-mounted of the other allies, he went to meet him, displaying his force to Cyaxares. But Cyaxares, seeing Cyrus followed by many good men, and himself by a small and worthless retinue, thought it a dishonour to him, and grief took him, and he was reduced to open tears. Cyrus, taking him aside privately and seating him beside him, conversed with him, and asked the cause of his anger and grief. And having said and heard much, at last he said, "By the gods, uncle, cease for now blaming me; and when you have made trial of us, how we stand toward you, then either acknowledge gratitude to me or blame me." And Cyaxares yielded; and Cyrus, coming up, kissed him. And when the Medes and the Persians and the rest saw this, they were overjoyed. Mounting their horses, then, Cyrus and Cyaxares went off to the camp, and led Cyaxares to the tent chosen for him. And the Medes came to him bringing gifts, each one of the fairest thing he had taken. And when it was time for supper, Cyaxares was about his supper, while Cyrus took thought how the allies might stay with him, and gathering enough of his friends to help him do what was needful, he asked them to contrive how they might persuade the allies not to leave them, but to help still. On the next day all gathered to Cyaxares; and before they met him the friends brought to Cyrus, one this, another that, of the allied nations, who begged him to remain and share in the war with him.

Now the fifth year had already passed, and no longer was any one of the Canaanites left. And Joshua sets up the tabernacle at the city of Shiloh, until it should be possible to build them a temple. And gathering the people to Shiloh, he reckoned up the cities that had been taken and how many armies of the enemy had been destroyed, and that thirty-one of their kings had been killed. But the cities still left, he said, required a long siege on account of their strength, and he asked to release to their homes those from across the Jordan who had set out with them. And summoning those of the two tribes and the half, who were fifty thousand, he permitted them to go to their allotments. And they, crossing the Jordan, set up an altar on the bank. This caused a tumult among the multitude of the Israelites. So they send against them ten of the honored men and Phinehas, charging them concerning the altar. But they said that they had not set up the altar for any innovation, but as a token to those who came after of their kinship with you; for they acknowledged one God, common to all the Hebrews. When they had said these things, Phinehas and those with him returned to Joshua. And Joshua, having allotted the lands to the multitude, passed his time at Shechem. And being now very old and about to die, he made an exhortation to the multitude, and ended his life, having lived a hundred and ten years, of which he passed forty with Moses, and after his death, leading the army, twenty-five. And the high priest Eleazar too dies, leaving the high-priesthood to his son Phinehas. After this the Canaanites, hoping to prevail over the race of the Hebrews now that Joshua was dead, made war against them, entrusting the command to King Adonibezek. The name means "Lord of Bezek"; for "Adoni" in Hebrew means "lord." And the two tribes, that of Judah and that of Simeon, engaging the Canaanites, rout them and capture Adonibezek and maim him. And they took many cities, and the lower city of Jerusalem, and killed the inhabitants; but the siege of the upper city was difficult, both by the nature of the ground and by the strength of the walls. And having taken Hebron too, they put all to the sword, and gave it to Caleb for an inheritance, as Moses had commanded. And to the descendants of Jethro, who were kinsmen of Moses, they allotted land, because, leaving their fatherland, they had accompanied the people of the Hebrews in the wilderness. And the tribes of Judah and Simeon, having greatly prospered, laid down their arms. But the tribe of Ephraim, besieging Bethel, accomplished nothing. And having seized one of the men of the city, they gave him pledges that, if he handed over his fatherland, they would save both him and his kindred. And so he, having thus betrayed it, is saved with his household, while they, killing the inhabitants, held the city. And the Benjamites, since the city of Jerusalem had fallen to their lot, laid tribute upon the inhabitants, permitting them to live, contrary to the divine ordinances. And the other tribes did likewise.

Jeroboam the son of Joash became impious and lawless. And though such a man, when God took pity on the humbled Israelite people, he made war on the Syrians and conquered, the prophet Jonah having foretold him the victory.

This prophet God sent to the city Nineveh to proclaim its overthrow and the destruction of the Ninevites. But he would not go, but fled, embarking on a ship. When a storm arose, the ship was in danger. And when those sailing tried by lot to learn the cause, the lot fell on Jonah. When he was examined as to who he was, he related his own circumstances, and urged them to throw him into the sea; "for not otherwise," he said, "will you escape the danger." So he was thrown out, and the storm abated. A sea-monster swallowed the prophet, and after three days and as many nights vomited him out alive and unharmed. He begged God's pardon for his disobedience, and was sent again to proclaim what had been commanded. Going off, he proclaimed that after three days Nineveh would be overthrown. But the king of the city and all the people, believing the prophet, turned to repentance and supplicated God to have mercy on them. And he, bent by the repentance of the multitude, turned the destruction away from them.
Jeroboam, having reigned forty-one years, died. And after him Azariah his son took control of the rule.

The king of Jerusalem, Uzziah, was pious toward God and just toward his subjects; therefore he conquered many of the foreigners and made them tributary. But growing prosperous and puffed up, he fell away from what was fitting. And, having robed himself as a priest, he attempted to offer incense to God upon the golden altar; and when the high priest Azariah and the priests prevented him and exhorted him not to transgress the law, he threatened them with death if they did not be quiet. Thereupon a kind of light flashing in the temple and striking the king's face caused leprosy to break out upon it. The priests showed the king his misfortune and counselled him to leave the city. And so, having lived some time, he died of despondency, having reigned fifty-two years and lived in all sixty-eight, handing over the rule to his son Jotham.

Azariah the son of Jeroboam, having reigned over the Israelites only six months, died, having lived impiously, treacherously slain by Shallum. Shallum, having reigned thirty days, was killed by Menahem, who reigned over Israel in his stead. When Pul the king of the Assyrians raised war against him, he gave him a thousand talents of silver, which he had collected from the people, and broke off the war. Having reigned ten years, Menahem, who was impious and harsh, died, passing the kingdom to his son Pekahiah. He too became impious and cruel, and was treacherously slain by Pekah the son of Remaliah, who reigned in the stead of the slain man, conducting his rule impiously and lawlessly. At that time Tiglath-pileser the king of the Assyrians, coming upon the land of the Israelites, overthrew many cities and led away into his own land a captivity beyond counting. But Jotham the son of Uzziah, king of Jerusalem, being pious and just, took care of the city and the temple and made the Ammonites tributary, having conquered them in battle. Nahum then prophesying foretold the overthrow of [Nineveh]; and his prediction came to pass when a hundred and fifteen years had passed. Jotham's life failed him when he had lived forty-one years and reigned sixteen.

Meanwhile Cyaxares, coming out of the tent, said, "Fellow-allies, it is necessary to consider whether it seems a time still to make war or now to disband the army." Each, then, coming forward, spoke, and all gave the judgement that they must make war. After all, Cyrus said, "Nor does it escape me, men, that if we disband the army, our affairs would become weaker, while those of the enemy would grow. But I see opponents approaching whom we shall not be able to fight. For winter is coming on and a lack of provisions. For some have been used up by us, and some, because of us, have been carried off by the enemy into strongholds. Who, then, fighting with hunger and cold, could make war? I think we ought to take away the enemy's strongholds, and make for ourselves as many strongholds as possible. For if we have fortresses, these will estrange the country from the enemy, and be to our profit." When these and many such things were said, all said they would zealously join in these, and Cyaxares himself, and they resolved to make siege-engines. But Cyrus, knowing there would be a delay about these things, both put the army in safety, and led it out on foraging expeditions, that they might have provisions in abundance and might be the healthier for their toil, and that they might be reminded of good discipline.

Deserters coming from Babylon said that the Assyrian had gone off to Lydia bringing many talents of gold and silver and all manner of adornment. The mass of the soldiers said he was now removing his money in fear; but Cyrus said the Assyrian was going off to seek allies, and made counter-preparations as though a battle would still be needed. It seemed good to him also to send a scout to Lydia, that he might learn what the Assyrian was doing. And for this Araspes seemed suitable to him—the one guarding the fair woman—who, smitten with love of the woman, had made advances to her; but she refused and was faithful to her husband even in his absence, and indeed reported Araspes to Cyrus. When the lover threatened her that, if she would not yield willingly, he would do it unwillingly, she, fearing the violence, sent the eunuch to Cyrus and bade him tell all. And he, hearing it, laughed, and sent Artabazus with the eunuch, ordering him to tell Araspes not to force such a woman, but to persuade her if he could; he said he did not forbid that. And Araspes, hearing this, was plunged into grief, partly from shame, partly from fear. Cyrus, knowing this, called him aside and said, "Cease, Araspes, being afraid and ashamed. For I hear that the gods too are overcome by love, and I know that men, and very prudent ones, have suffered things from love. And I am the cause of this to you, who shut you up with such an irresistible thing." And Araspes answered, "But you, Cyrus, are gentle in this too and forgiving of human faults; but other men plunge me into grief. For my enemies rejoice over me, and my friends counsel me to get out of the way, lest I suffer something from you." And Cyrus said, "Know well, then, that by this opinion you can both do me a favour and benefit the allies." "Would," said Araspes, "that I might be useful to you at a crisis." "If, then," he said, "pretending to flee from me, you should go over to the enemy, you would be trusted by them." "Yes, by Zeus," said Araspes, "and by my friends too." "You would go, then," he said, "reporting to us all the enemy's affairs."

Araspes, then, so going forth and taking his most faithful servants, departed. And Panthea, learning this, sent to Cyrus and said, "Do not grieve, Cyrus, that Araspes has gone over to the enemy; for if you let me send to my husband, there will come to you a friend more faithful than Araspes." And Cyrus bade her send; and she sent. And Abradates, when he knew the tokens from his wife, gladly went over to Cyrus. When he was at the outposts he sent to Cyrus saying who he was. And Cyrus ordered him to be brought to the woman. When the woman and Abradates saw one another, they embraced from a state of despair. Then Panthea told of the holiness and temperance of Cyrus and his compassion toward her. Upon this Abradates comes to Cyrus, and taking hold of his right hand said, "In return for the good you have done us, Cyrus, I give myself to you as friend and servant and ally." And Cyrus said, "And I receive you."

Now when those of Israel were prospering, luxury corrupted them, and they transgressed the divine laws and were disinclined toward labor, and the aristocracy failed, and the council of elders was no longer appointed. Whence a terrible sedition seizes them from such a cause as this. A man, a Levite, taking along his wife, who was from Bethlehem, was going home. And as it was now evening, he is lodged as a guest with a certain old man in Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin. But certain young men of Gibeah, having seen the woman, came demanding her; and when the old man would not give her, they threatened to kill him. And he offered them his own daughter, that those lodged with him might not suffer any violence. But they, seizing the woman, departed, and having sated themselves with her through the whole night, they let her go at the break of day. And she, cast down by the night's hardship and by shame before her husband and by grief, perished. And her husband, dividing the dead woman into twelve parts, sent a part to each tribe, teaching them both the outrage and those responsible for the calamity. So they send to Gibeah, demanding the surrender of those who had transgressed; but they would not give them up. And the tribes made war against them, and twice, when they engaged, the Israelites are defeated. Then through Phinehas the high priest they pray to God, and so, engaging the Benjamites, they prevailed, so that all fell except six hundred, who fled to the neighboring mountains. And the Israelites burned Gibeah and put to the sword the women and children, and on the other cities too they did the like. And the inhabitants of Jabesh of Gilead, because it had not allied with them, they slay, with women and children, except four hundred maidens, whom they gave to the survivors of the Benjamites, that they might have them as wives, taking pity on their calamity. And they considered how the remaining two hundred too might be provided with women; for they had previously sworn, on account of the outrage, that no one would give a daughter in marriage to a Benjamite. And on consideration it seemed good to them not themselves to give, on account of the oath, but that it should be permitted to the Benjamites, by seizing maidens, to take them as wives for themselves, they neither hindering nor encouraging. And so it seemed good to them about these things, and the Benjamites brought to deed what had seemed good. Now, the Israelites having long before ceased from fighting, the Canaanites despised them and took cities from them. And those of the tribe of Dan fled to the mountain, and from there migrated to the interior. But against the Israelites, who had taken on the customs of the Canaanites and despised their own commonwealth, the Divine was angered. So the king of the Assyrians, Cushan-rishathaim, makes war against them and lays heavy tributes upon them, by which they were oppressed for eight years. Then a man of action of the tribe of Judah, called Othniel, having gathered to himself a few men, by a divine oracle destroys the garrison of the Assyrians among them. And when more had afterward been gathered, having conquered the Assyrians in battle, he drove them off, and for this was chosen to rule the multitude and to judge the people. He, having held the rule for fifty years, departed life. And the Israelites, being without a ruler and despising the Divine, were made subject by Aiglom the king of the Moabites and were charged with annual contributions. He, having built a palace in Jericho, ill-treated them in many ways for eighteen years. But a certain young Benjamite, Aoth by name—Josephus says this man was called Judas—daring and strong, becomes familiar with Aiglom, and continually frequented his presence, flattering the man and ingratiating himself. This man, once bringing gifts to Aiglom with two servants, carried a small dagger concealed. And as the day was now at its middle and the guards had withdrawn to themselves, finding him alone, he goes in as a familiar, and taking him by himself, as though to converse with him about something more secret, he strikes him mortally with the dagger and kills him. And going to the people of Jericho, he persuades them to lay claim to liberty. And they armed themselves, while those about Aiglom, finding him dead, turn to flight and are destroyed as they are pursued. And so the Hebrews are freed from the slavery of the Moabites, and the rule of the multitude was entrusted to Aoth. He, having led the people for eighty years, ended his life. And after him Megar, the son of Dinach, ruling, died in the first year of his rule, having struck down many of the foreigners.

The rule of Jerusalem passed to his son, who became impious toward God and transgressed his laws; for he worshipped idols and set up an altar to them in Jerusalem and offered his own child to them as a whole burnt-offering. Against him Rezin who ruled the Syrians, and Pekah the king of the Israelites, conspiring together, besieged him in Jerusalem for a long time. And Rezin, having mastered other cities, killed their inhabitants and settled Syrians in them, and returned to Damascus; but Ahaz, when only Pekah was left, engaging him was defeated, losing a hundred and twenty thousand of the people and many of the notables and his son. Pekah withdrew to Samaria, he and his army, removing a great multitude of captives to their own land. But a certain prophet in Samaria, meeting them before the walls, reproached them for having taken kindred captive, and counselled them to set them free; and they, persuaded, released the captives. Ahaz asked the king of the Assyrians to help him against the Syrians and the Israelites. He came and ravaged the country of the Syrians and took Damascus and killed Rezin, and overrunning the land of the Israelites led away very many captives. And Ahaz, in return for this, gave Tiglath-pileser both the royal treasures and whatever was stored in the temple. And he became so impious that he not only worshipped the gods of the foreigners, but also shut up the temple and plundered its votive offerings. So living, he died, having lived thirty-six years and reigned sixteen, leaving the kingdom to his son Hezekiah. It happened that the king of the Israelites too died at that time by the plot of Hoshea. And he too was wicked; therefore, when the king of the Assyrians, Shalmaneser, marched against him, he was enslaved to him, being ordered to pay tribute yearly.

Hezekiah, being pious and just, gathered the priests and Levites and charged them to open the temple and to sacrifice as was their law, and ordered the people to prefer nothing to the honour of the deity. He sent throughout the whole country, summoning all to keep the feast of unleavened bread, which had long not been celebrated because of the lawlessness of the rulers. And he urged the Israelites to worship their ancestral God according to the old custom. But they were not persuaded; rather they even killed the prophets who urged the same. Some, however, being persuaded, were turned to piety and gathered at Jerusalem for the worship of God. And the king Hezekiah, going with the leaders of the people to the temple, offered through the priests lavish sacrifices, and shared with the people many animals for feasting, and charged the priests to go out into the country and to purify it. Then he raised war against the foreigners and took cities of theirs.

The king of the Israelites, Hoshea, summoned to alliance So the king of Egypt against the Assyrians. Learning this, Shalmaneser was angered; and for three years he besieged Samaria, and took the city and made an end of the kingdom, and taking the people captive removed them to his own land, and the king of the Israelites Hoshea himself. And removing other nations from a certain place called Cuthah, he settled them in Samaria and its territory. So the ten tribes of the Israelites were removed nine hundred and forty-seven years after they had left Egypt and gone out, and two hundred and forty years and seven months after they had forsaken Rehoboam and chosen Jeroboam for themselves as king. Those removed into Samaria, called Cuthaeans from the place where they had formerly dwelt in Persia, being five nations, again worshipped their own gods. As the fourth book of Kings says, God stirred up lions and destroyed many of them; but as Josephus relates, a plague fell upon them. Perceiving that the evils came upon them through the anger of God, they begged their own king to send them priests from among the Israelites, that these might initiate them into the worship of the Hebrews; and when this was done, the destruction ceased. They are called by the Hebrews Cuthaeans, but by the Greeks Samaritans.

Money came to Cyrus from the Indian, and those bringing it reported that the Indian said, "I am glad, Cyrus, that you made known to me concerning your needs, and I wish to be your guest-friend, and I send you money, and if you need more, send for it; and my men are charged to do whatever you bid." And Cyrus said, "I bid, then, that the rest remain where you have encamped and guard the money, but that three of you come to me into the enemy as though from the Indian about an alliance, and learning the things there, whatever they say and do, report to me and to the Indian as quickly as possible." So the Indians, having equipped themselves, set out the next day, and Cyrus prepared his war-affairs magnificently. For the Persian horsemen were now full to ten thousand, and there were scythe-bearing chariots to a hundred, and Abradates fashioned another hundred, and the Median chariots they put together, another hundred, remade in the same fashion from the Trojan and Libyan driving; and on the camels were posted two archers on each. As Cyrus's war-affairs were being so ordered, the Indians came from the enemy and said that Croesus had been chosen leader and general, and that many kings and many nations and Greeks were ready to ally. When Cyrus's army heard this, they fell into anxiety. When Cyrus perceived fear running through the army, he conversed with them and turned them to a more cheerful temper. Then he said, "It seems to me, men, that we should go against them as quickly as possible." And all agreed. Cyaxares, then, with a third part of the Medes remained behind, that the home country too might not be left desolate, but Cyrus went on as quickly as he could. When the advance scouts seemed to make out smoke or dust rising, and to see men taking fodder and wood, they guessed the enemy's army was somewhere near, and reported to Cyrus. He ordered them to remain at the lookouts and report whatever they saw, and sent a squadron of horse forward to take some prisoners. They, dashing down into the plain, seized men and brought them. And the captives said they were from the camp. And Cyrus said, "How far off from here is the army?" And they said, two parasangs. And he asked further, "Was there any talk of us among them?" "Yes, by Zeus," they said, "and much, that you were now near, approaching." "What then?" said Cyrus, "did they rejoice to hear we were coming?" "No, by Zeus," they said, "but were greatly grieved." "And who is it that marshals them?" said Cyrus. And they answered, "Croesus himself, and a certain Greek man, and a certain Mede, who was said to be a fugitive from you." And Cyrus to this, "O Zeus, may it be mine to take him as I wish." He ordered the captives to be led away. There was not much interval, and the scout sent long ago, Araspes, that is, is announced to be riding up. When Cyrus heard, leaping up he went to meet him and greeted him, while the others were astounded at the matter, until Cyrus said, "Friends, there has come to us a most excellent man, who went off not overcome by anything shameful, fearing me, but sent by me, that learning the enemy's affairs clearly he might report to us. All must therefore honour this man. For he both underwent dishonour and ran into danger for our good." From then all greeted Araspes. And Cyrus said, "Relate, Araspes, all that you have seen." And he related the number of the enemy and the place of their array and the plans of the enemy. And Cyrus ordered each to go off and inspect his own arms and horses, and at dawn to make ready for battle.

Then, then, they departed; and on the next day each armed himself, and Abradates, having drawn by lot to be posted opposite the Egyptians. As he was arming, Panthea brought a golden helmet and arm-pieces and bracelets about the wrists of his hands and a purple tunic reaching to the feet and a crest dyed hyacinth-blue, which she herself had made for her husband. And he, seeing them, said, "You surely, wife, having broken up your own adornment, made the arms for me?" "Yes, by Zeus," said Panthea, "for you are to me the greatest adornment." And saying this she put the arms on her husband, and tried to weep unseen, but the tears fell down her cheeks. When Abradates was now ready to mount the chariot, Panthea, bidding those present withdraw, said, "That I honour you, Abradates, even above my own life, I think you know; nevertheless, being so disposed toward you, I swear by my love and yours that I would rather, with you having proved a good man, be buried in common with you than live in shame with one who is shamed. And to Cyrus I think we owe great gratitude, that when I was made captive and chosen for him he treated me neither as a slave nor as a free woman in a dishonourable name, but kept me for you as one taking a brother's wife. Moreover, when Araspes who guarded me deserted from him, I promised him that, if he would let me send to you so that you should come, you would prove far more faithful and better than Araspes." So she spoke, and Abradates, marveling at her words, prayed, "Grant, O Zeus, that I appear a man worthy of Panthea and a friend worthy of Cyrus." Saying this he mounted the chariot.

And when the people of the Hebrews transgressed the divine laws, God was angered. And Sisera, the commander-in-chief of Jabin the king of Canaan, attacking them, ill-treated them greatly and subjected them to tributes; and they were thus for twenty years. But a certain prophetess Deborah—the name means "bee"—supplicated God on behalf of the people. And God consented, and bids them choose as general Barak; and this means "lightning" in the language of the Hebrews. The man was of the tribe of Naphtali. And Deborah urged Barak to go against the enemy with ten thousand men, since God commanded this. But he demanded that she too share the command. The woman is persuaded, and when battle was joined for them with the ten thousand against Sisera, much rain pours down and hail breaks forth, and these were driven by the wind against the face of the enemy and darkened their sight, and from this they bent to flight. And Sisera too, fleeing, took refuge with a certain woman, asking her to hide him; the woman was named Jael. And she receives him and gives him milk to drink, and he, having drunk, fell asleep. And while he slept, Jael set upon him, and driving a nail through his temple, pinned him to the ground, and shows the dead enemy to those about Barak. And Barak, making war also against Jabin the king of Canaan, killed him and razed his city. And having been general for thirty years, he dies, Deborah also dying at the same time. Then the Midianites, with the Amalekites and Arabs, routed the Israelites in battle. And while they attacked them for seven years there was famine and lack of necessities, and they prayed to God. And Gideon, of the tribe of Manasseh, was secretly beating sheaves of grain in the winepress, and he sees one standing by him in the form of a young man, calling him a friend of God and blessed. And he, in irony, said that the proof of his blessedness was his using the winepress instead of a threshing-floor. And the young man exhorted him to take courage and to hasten for the liberty of his fellow tribesmen. And Gideon begged the one who appeared not to depart from there, and going in he brought a sacrifice. And the angel commanded him to set it by the rock; and touching the rock with his rod, he kindled a fire of its own accord and consumed the sacrifice. Then Gideon asked God that dew should come upon the fleece, and it came; and again he asked that dew should come upon all the ground, but dryness upon the fleece, and so it was. So Gideon is persuaded, and with ten thousand armed himself against the enemy. Then by command of God he leads them all at midday to the river, and taking with himself those who lapped while drinking and drank with haste, as though fearful—these were three hundred—he set out for the war, and left the rest behind. And by night, taking one of the soldiers, he went to the camp of the enemy. And he hears one of the enemy relating to his tent-mate that he had seemed to see in his sleep a barley loaf rolling through the camp, which overthrew the tent of the king and those of the army; and the other judged that the dream signified the destruction of the army, likening to a barley loaf Gideon and those with him, on account of their fewness and weakness. Hearing this, Gideon took courage, and returning he commanded his men to be at their arms, and dividing the army into three hundreds, he ordered each to carry an empty jar and a lighted torch and a ram's horn, and at the fourth watch of the night he led them out against the enemy. And being now near them, they sounded the horns and broke the jars, and with the torches they rushed forward shouting. These things struck terror into the enemy, and some were killed by the enemy themselves, while the greater part were destroyed by one another, since it was night, and nearly all perished, and two of their kings, Oreb and Zeeb. And those of the leaders and the army who were left, fleeing, are caught by Gideon and those with him, and all fell. And Gideon held the rule for forty years, and died an old man, leaving from various wives seventy legitimate sons, and one from a concubine, called Abimelech. He, having killed all his brothers except one, Jotham, who fled, set up a tyranny. But the people, rising against Abimelech, drive him out of the city of Shechem. And he, aided by one of the Shechemites, takes the city by treachery and slays the Shechemites of full age, and razes the city. And he marched against Thebes, another city, and took it by assault. But the multitude ran together into one great tower, which was in the middle of the city. And as Abimelech drew near to its gates, a woman threw down a fragment of a millstone from above upon his head and killed him. And the rule of the Hebrews was entrusted to Jair, who was of the tribe of Manasseh; and he, having directed the rule for twenty-two years, died. Then the Ammonites with the Palestinians next plundered the country. And while the Ammonites were ravaging Gilead, the inhabitants chose Jephthah as leader. He, being about to engage the enemy, made a vow that, if he should conquer, he would sacrifice whatever first met him as he returned. And engaging, he conquers; but as he returned, his little daughter met him, who was his only child and still a virgin. And he lamented aloud, but, that he might not break his promise, he sacrificed the girl and offered her as a whole burnt offering. And when those of the tribe of Ephraim were angry with him because he had not taken them along to the war against the Ammonites, since he could not persuade them with apologies, he killed many of them who fought with him. And having held the leadership for six years, he ended his life. And the rule is taken up by Amesa, who was of the tribe of Judah, and having judged Israel for seven years, he died. And after him Labdon, coming forth from the tribe of Ephraim, was appointed leader, and died an old man, having ruled eight years.

In the fourteenth year of the reign of Hezekiah the king of Jerusalem, Sennacherib who reigned over the Assyrians came against Judah and took all the cities of the two tribes. Fearing for Jerusalem, Hezekiah sent to him, promising to give whatever tribute he should impose. Sennacherib demanded three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, and gave sworn pledges that he would indeed withdraw if he received these. Having received them, he himself marched against the Egyptians and Ethiopians, but left his commander-in-chief Rabshakeh with two other generals and a heavy force to sack Jerusalem. They, having thrown up a rampart before the walls, sought a meeting with Hezekiah. But he was too timid to go out, and sent three of his honoured men. And they said, "If Hezekiah trusts in the Egyptians, he is foolish, leaning upon a man as upon a reed staff, and one that is broken, which has defended none who held it, but has itself collapsed, and the reed has pierced the hand of him who held it. Such is Pharaoh the Egyptian." These things Rabshakeh said to those sent in Hebrew. But they asked him to speak with them in the language of the Syrians, so that the multitude might not understand what was said. He, rather raising his voice, said again in Hebrew, within hearing of all, "Let not Hezekiah deceive you, saying, the Lord will deliver us. Did he deliver Samaria?" And they reported this to Hezekiah. He, hearing it, tore his garments and put on sackcloth, and falling down begged God, asking help in things beyond hope; and sending the prophet Isaiah he asked him to beg God to be merciful to the people. He foretold that the enemy would be defeated without a battle, and that Sennacherib would be killed when he returned from Egypt with nothing accomplished. Sennacherib too sent word to Hezekiah, "Let not your God exalt you, in whom you trust that Jerusalem will not be given into my hands; consider where are the kings of the nations whom my fathers destroyed." Reading this letter, Hezekiah set it in the temple and supplicated God, saying, "Behold, O Lord, and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent reproaching you the living God, and save us from his hand." And Isaiah encouraged the king, declaring that God had heard him. And in the night an angel killed in the camp of the Assyrians a hundred and eighty-five thousand, and by day their corpses were found dead. And the remnant of the army departed from Jerusalem. Sennacherib, besieging Pelusium, raised the siege, mice in a single night having eaten the bowstrings of the Assyrians and the rest of their weapons. This is not recorded in the book of Kings, but Josephus relates it, having found it in Herodotus. And he says that Berossus, who wrote the Chaldaean history, states that Sennacherib, returning from the war with the Egyptians, found the army that was with Rabshakeh at Jerusalem; and when God sent a pestilential disease upon the Assyrians, in a single night a hundred and eighty-five thousand perished with their commanders and captains. Fearing therefore for the rest of his army, he departed from there with the surviving force and went off to Nineveh. And a little later, being plotted against by his elder sons, he was killed, those who killed him fleeing, while his son Nahordan succeeded to the rule.

Hezekiah, freed from his fear, gave thanks to God. And a little later, when he fell sick, Isaiah came to him by God's command and said, "Set your house in order; for you will not live." To him the expectation of death, and that, having no children, he was about to leave the kingdom desolate of a legitimate succession, made the misfortune the greater; and in despondency he wept, asking God to bestow life upon him. Isaiah, coming again, brought him good tidings of health on the third day and an addition of fifteen years to his life. He, reckoning the surpassing nature of the wonder, asked the prophet to show him a sign for the confirmation of what was promised. When the prophet supplicated God that a sign be given, the sun, which had already declined ten degrees and cast a shadow, turned back ten steps. Thereupon Hezekiah was freed from his sickness. The king of the Babylonians, Baladan, sending an embassy to Hezekiah and sending gifts, asked to have him as ally and friend. He showed the ambassadors his treasures and his weapons and all the royal magnificence, and sending gifts in return to the Babylonian, dismissed them. But Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Days will come, and the wealth which you displayed will be carried off to Babylon, and your sons will be eunuchs to the king of Babylon." And Hezekiah, since the word of God could not fail, said, "Let there be peace in my days."
