Living out the time added to him in peace, he died, having completed fifty-four years in life and having reigned twenty-nine.

His son Manasseh, succeeding to the rule, displayed every form of wickedness and impiety beyond his predecessor, defiling the temple and not even sparing the prophets. Angered at this, God stirred up the army of the Babylonians against Judah, which both plundered the country and subdued Manasseh. He, perceiving that he was himself the cause of the misfortune, turned to repentance and supplicated God to loose his hardships. And God, hearing him, both freed him from captivity and restored him to the kingdom. Returning, he himself pursued piety and persuaded the people to pursue it. So living, he became enviable for his piety, and died, having reigned fifty-five years and lived in all sixty-seven.

Cyrus, gathering the leaders, harangued them, encouraging them to the battle, and so set out to go. When they drew near the opposing forces, so as to see one another, Cyrus marshaled his men as well as possible, and going along the ranks he sharpened the men for battle with words. And Croesus, setting his own army opposite Cyrus's force, signaled to them to advance against the enemy. And three phalanxes came on, one in front, and of the two, one on the right, the other on the left, so that fear came upon all Cyrus's army; for it was surrounded by the enemy on every side except behind. Nevertheless Cyrus's men too, when he gave the order, all turned to face the enemy. And there was for a while much silence on every side; and when it seemed to Cyrus to be the time, he began a paean, and the whole army shouted it with him. And Cyrus rose up and with the horsemen engaged the enemy, while the foot drawn up with him followed. And Artagerses, commander of those on the camels, attacked on the left, sending the camels forward, as Cyrus had ordered. And the horses from afar would not endure them, but some fled, some leaped aside, some fell on one another. And the chariots, on the right and the left, charged at once, and many fleeing these were caught by them. And Abradates, crying "Friends, follow," drove on, sparing none of his horses; and the other charioteers charged with him. And Abradates broke into the phalanx of the Egyptians, and with him broke in those nearest posted, while the others swerved aside after the fleeing chariots. And those about Abradates, striking with the rush of the horses, overturned some and ran over those who fell; and whatever the scythes caught, all was forcibly cut through, both arms and bodies. In this indescribable confusion, the wheels leaping over the heaps of all sorts, Abradates falls out, and others too of those who had charged with him. And these were cut to pieces, while the Persians, following close, killed the disordered Egyptians, but those who held together advanced against the Persians; and there was a fierce battle. The Egyptians had the advantage both in number and in arms. The Persians could not hold out, but drew back step by step, striking and being struck, until they came under the engines. When they came there, the Egyptians were struck again from the towers. There was much slaughter of men, much din of arms, much shouting. Meanwhile Cyrus, pursuing those opposite him, comes up. And seeing the Persians forced from their ground, he was grieved, and ordering those with him to follow, rode round to the rear; and falling on them they killed many. When the Egyptians perceived it, they turned about. And foot and horse fought in confusion; and a man fallen under Cyrus's horse and being trodden struck his horse in the belly with a sword, and the horse, convulsing from the blow, shakes Cyrus off. And at once all cried out and falling on fought. And one of Cyrus's attendants, leaping down, set him on his own horse. And when he had mounted, he saw the Egyptians now being struck on every side. And going along by the engines he went up onto one of the towers, and looked down upon the plain full of horses, men, chariots, fleeing, pursuing, mastering, being mastered, but nowhere could he see anything still standing except that of the Egyptians. These, surrounded on every side, sat under their shields, doing nothing now, but suffering many and dreadful things. And Cyrus, admiring them and pitying them, that good men were perishing, allowed no one to fight with them any more, but sent heralds to them asking whether they wished all to perish or to be saved. And they said, "By doing what fair thing might we be saved?" And Cyrus said, "If you give up your arms to us, who choose to save you, though we might destroy you." Hearing this, the Egyptians gave pledges and received them.

Having accomplished this, Cyrus, now in the dark, withdrew and encamped. And those about Cyrus, having supped, slept; but Croesus at once fled to Sardis with his army, and the other nations withdrew in the night where they could. At dawn Cyrus led on toward Sardis, and coming to the city set up his engines and prepared ladders. On the following night he sent up Chaldaeans and Persians by what seemed the steepest part of the Sardian fortress. A Persian man, a slave of one of the guards on the citadel, led the way for these. When the heights were taken, the Lydians fled from the walls. Cyrus at daybreak entered the city, charging that no one from the ranks should move. Croesus, shut up in the palace, called for Cyrus. And Cyrus left guards over Croesus, and having encamped his men went off to Croesus. And seeing him Croesus said, "Hail, master." "And you too," said Cyrus, "Croesus. But would you be willing to give me some counsel?" "I would be willing," he said, "Cyrus." "I, then, Croesus," he said, "seeing the soldiers worn out and having run very many risks and now thinking they hold the richest city in Asia after Babylon, I judge it right that the soldiers be benefited, but I do not wish to let them plunder the city." And Croesus said, "But let me speak to those of the Lydians whom I wish, that I have brought it about with you that there be no pillage; and know that there will be for you, from willing Lydians, everything precious in Sardis. But first send to my treasures and take what you wish."

Cyrus agreed to do this, and they passed the day on these matters; on the next, Cyrus, calling some of his friends, ordered some to take the treasures, and others to take whatever money Croesus delivered. Then he asked whether anyone had seen Abradates; and when one of the attendants said that he had died in the battle, he struck his thigh, and leaping on his horse rode to him. And when he saw Panthea sitting on the ground and the corpse lying, he wept and said, "Alas, good and faithful soul." And the woman said, "I know that it was for my sake that he suffered this, and perhaps, Cyrus, for yours too. For I, fool that I was, often urged him to appear a friend worthy of mention to you, and he himself considered how he might do you a favour. And he has died blamelessly, while I, who urged him, sit beside him alive." And Cyrus for some time wept in silence, then spoke many consolations for the grief, and went off. And the woman bade the eunuchs withdraw, but told her nurse to remain and, when she was dead, to cover both her and her husband with one garment. The nurse sat weeping; but she slew herself, and laying her own head upon her husband's breast she died. And the nurse wailed and covered them both. And the eunuchs, learning what had happened, being three, drawing their scimitars, slew themselves. And Cyrus, when he perceived the woman's deed, admired her and mourned her, and heaped over them a vast monument, burying them magnificently.

Then the Palestinians prevailed over the Israelites and held them tributary for forty years. At that time was born Samson—the name signifies "strength"—who set himself against the Palestinians; and the beginning of his life came about thus. Manoah, being of the tribe of Dan, dwelt with a barren wife and asked God that a child be given to them. So once, when the woman was alone, there appeared a young man, great and fair, bringing the good news of the birth of a child, and he commanded her not to drink wine or strong drink, nor to cut the hair of the child; for he said that the child would be a Nazirite to the Lord—that is, holy—and that Israel would be saved through him from the hand of the foreigners. And she announced these things to her husband. And he prayed to God that the one who had appeared to his wife might appear to him also. So again the angel came to the woman; but Manoah was again absent; and the woman begged him to await the coming of her husband. And Manoah, coming, asked the angel what they should do when the child was born. And he said, "He shall not drink wine or strong drink, and shall eat nothing unclean, and his hair shall not be shaved." And Manoah sought to learn the name of the one speaking with him, but he said that it was wonderful, and was silent. And Manoah, bringing a kid, sacrificed it and offered loaves. And the angel commanded him to set the flesh and the loaves upon the rock, and when they were set he touches them with his rod, and a fire, kindled from there, consumed them, and through the flame the angel went up to heaven, while Manoah and his wife looked on. So after these things the child is born to them and is named Samson, and he grew, and the spirit of the Lord went along with him. And seeing in Thamna, a city of the Palestinians, a girl of the foreigners, he falls in love with the maiden. And though his parents deprecated the marriage with a foreign woman, he prevailed to marry her. And while frequenting the parents of the girl, he meets a lion, and having nothing for defense, he crushed the beast with his hands, and turning aside from the road he threw it into the brushwood. And after some days, going again to his betrothed, he found a swarm of bees gathered in the mouth of the lion. And taking from there a honeycomb, he ate it and brought some to his father and mother. And going to the foreigners, he sets a riddle for the thirty young men who were feasting with him at the wedding; and he agreed, if they should find the solution within seven days, to give each of them a linen cloth and a robe, but if they could not solve the riddle, he demanded that a robe and a linen cloth be given to him by each. And when the young men had agreed, he put forward the question, saying, "Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong, sweetness." And they, unable to perceive the riddle, begged the girl to learn it from the man and report it to them. And Samson, when the girl entreated him to tell her the meaning of the riddle, at first resisted, but when she wept, he told her the whole; and she reported it to the young men. And on the seventh day they said to Samson, "What is sweeter than honey, or what is stronger than a lion?" So Samson was angered, and gave the young men what he had promised, but renounced the marriage. And the father gave the woman to another. And Samson, provoked at this, having caught three hundred foxes, tied lighted torches to their tails and let them loose upon the fields of the Palestinians at the onset of summer, and thus burned up their crops and their vines. And the Palestinians in return burned and consumed with fire the woman who had been his wife and her relatives. And Samson, having killed many of the foreigners, settled himself on a rock; but they made war against the Israelites, saying, "If you wish to be guiltless, give us Samson into our hands." And three thousand armed men went to the rock. And Samson, coming down willingly, gave himself up to his fellow tribesmen, and they handed him over bound to the Palestinians. But he, breaking the bonds and snatching up the jawbone of an ass thrown down somewhere there, killed a thousand of the foreigners with it, and routed the rest. Whence from that time the place was called Siagon ("Jawbone"). Then he thirsted so as to faint from thirst, and he wept, praying to God. And God sent up a spring of water from the cleft that Samson had made by throwing the jawbone to the ground. And he went to Gaza. But the men of Gaza set an ambush for him, and that he might not escape their notice as he went out, they shut the gates of the city. But he, rising about midnight, hoisted upon his shoulders the gates and their posts and the doorframes and carried them up to the summit of the mountain and set them down there. And falling in love with a Palestinian courtesan called Delilah, he consorted with her; and the chief men of the foreigners made many promises to the woman, if she should learn from Samson what was the cause of his strength and report it to them. And she went after the man in various ways, seeking to know whence came such great strength to him; but he, feigning now one cause, now another, told the woman. And the woman, testing his words, found them to be deceptions. But as she pressed and entreated him more warmly, he revealed to her the secret, saying that by the command of God he let his hair grow, since God had commanded not to cut it, and that in this lay his strength. The woman cuts his hair while he slept and hands him over weak to the enemy. And they put out the man's eyes, and he who had once been fearful became a plaything for them. But as time went on, his hair grew again and his strength returned. And when the Palestinians were holding a drinking-feast, and the rulers and nobles were feasting together in a house supported by pillars, Samson too was brought to be made sport of, and a young boy led him by the hand. And there was gathered by the house a multitude of men and women, about three thousand, that they might see Samson abused. And he, being mocked and struck, says to the one leading him by the hand, "Bring me to the pillars, that I may lean upon them, since I need to rest." And grasping the two pillars, he pulled the house down upon himself, and he himself and all those in the house perished. And such was the end of this man, who had judged the people of the Hebrews for twenty years.

The kingdom passed to Amon his son, who imitated the deeds of his father's youth. He died, plotted against, having lived twenty-four years and reigned two. The multitude avenged those who had killed him and made his son Josiah king, who was completing his eighth year of age; he became pious and persuaded the people to be pious. Wishing to repair the temple, he exhorted those under him to give for the repair as much as each wished. When money had thus been gathered, the temple was renewed, and with the surplus he had cups and bowls and dishes made, the high priest Hilkiah supervising these things. He, in bringing out the silver from the sacred treasury, came upon the holy books of Moses, which were stored there, and sent them by the scribe to the king. When they had been read to him, he tore his garment and sent the high priest Hilkiah and others to the prophetess Huldah, the wife of Shallum, asking her to appease God. She said that the deity had already passed sentence against the country and the people for their impiety, but that, for the king's sake, since he was just, he would not bring the evils now, but they would come to pass after his passing. Hearing this, he gathered the people to Jerusalem, and caused the holy books to be read in the hearing of all. Then he demanded oaths from all to keep the laws and to worship God. And the people, sacrificing, propitiated the Lord. He burned the votive offerings of the idols, and killed their priests, and burned the bones of the false prophets upon the altar which Jeroboam had set up, according to the prophet's prediction, who came to him as he sacrificed and foretold that a descendant of David, Josiah, would do these things after three hundred and sixty-one years. Going also to the Israelites, as many as had escaped the captivity, Josiah exhorted them to worship the ancestral God and to live according to the laws. And having banished the idols from the whole country, he gathered the multitude to Jerusalem and celebrated the feast of unleavened bread, which they call the Passover. Having led a peaceful life, he ended it at last by being shot with an arrow. For the king of the Egyptians, Necho, was going off to make war on the Medes, but Josiah barred him from passing through his country. Necho made it clear to him that he was not marching against him. But Josiah would not give way. So they were now drawn up to fight, and as Josiah was arranging his own people, an Egyptian shot him with an arrow and broke off the battle. The king, withdrawing to Jerusalem, died, having reigned thirty-one years, and having lived eight years before his reign. In his time Jeremiah was the prophet, who foretold the dreadful things that would befall Jerusalem, and its capture by the Romans. Not only did he write beforehand of these things, but Ezekiel too was the first to leave two books concerning them. And both were of the priestly tribe.

When Josiah had died, Jehoahaz his son ruled, being twenty-three years old, having become impious; whom the king of the Egyptians, returning from the war, bound, and gave the kingdom to his elder brother Eliakim, renaming him Jehoiakim, and imposed upon the country a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and one of gold. He carried Jehoahaz off to Egypt, where he died. The time of his reign was three months and ten days.

Jehoiakim, who was impious and a wrongdoer, had now completed the fourth year of his reign when Nabuchodonosor girded on the rule of the Babylonians. He, having conquered the Egyptian Necho, tore away a large part of his country. In the eighth year of Jehoiakim's reign he marched against Judah with a heavy force. Jehoiakim, in fear, made his country tributary to the Babylonian. And for three years he brought the tribute, then, hearing that the Egyptians were advancing against the Babylonian, he held back the payment of the tribute, although the prophet Jeremiah foretold the capture of the city by the Babylonian and the death of king Jehoiakim, and not only spoke it, but wrote it and read the writing in the hearing of the multitude. The leaders, taking it, brought it to the king; but he, enraged at what was written, reduced the writing to ashes in the fire, and sought to punish the prophet and Baruch his scribe. But they, fleeing, escaped his anger. Not long after, the Babylonian marched against him, and Jehoiakim received him into the city without resistance. But he killed the better of the citizens and the king himself, and led away three thousand of the fairest as captives, among whom was the prophet Ezekiel, then a child; and he appointed king of Judah the son of the slain king, named Jehoiachin, also of the same name.

So ended Jehoiakim, having lived thirty-six years and reigned eleven. The Babylonian, suspecting that his son would bear a grudge for his father's death and would revolt, sent and besieged him. He, not wishing the city to be endangered for his sake, gave himself and his household over to the enemy on terms that they would do no harm to the city or to them; which terms the Babylonian transgressed, ordering all the youth in the city and the craftsmen to be carried off to him, who numbered ten thousand eight hundred and thirty-two. Jehoiachin and his mother and his friends he imprisoned and kept under guard, after Jehoiachin had reigned three months

The Carians, having fallen into faction and warring with one another, both parties surrendered themselves to Cyrus; and those of Phrygia by the Hellespont gave very many gifts to Cyrus, so as not to receive barbarians into their walls, but to pay tribute to him and to march wherever Cyrus bade. But the king of the Phrygians prepared as if not about to make peace; and when his subordinates revolted from him, he came to grips with Hystaspes. And Hystaspes, leaving Persian garrisons in the heights, went off, bringing with his own men many Phrygian horsemen and peltasts. And Cyrus set out from Sardis, leaving a garrison in Sardis, having Croesus with him bringing very many wagons full of much and varied money, and having accurately written down how much was in each wagon. And he gave the writings to Cyrus; and Cyrus said, "You have done well, Croesus; but those who have taken the money will surely bring it all to me, and if they steal anything, they will steal their own." And Croesus brought also many Lydians, splendidly armed.

Going on toward Babylon, Cyrus subdued the Phrygians in Greater Phrygia, and subdued the Cappadocians, and made subjects of the Arabians; and from all these he equipped of the Persians horsemen not fewer than forty thousand, and to all the allies he distributed many of the captured horses. He came, then, to Babylon bringing many horsemen, and many archers and javelin-men, and slingers innumerable. When he was at Babylon, he set the army about it, and himself, going round with the commanders of the allies and his friends, surveyed the walls. Then he brought the army up and encamped about the city. And seeing the river there flowing into the city and passing through the middle of Babylon, he disclosed his plan to no one, but ordered a trench to be dug around the camp, broad and very deep, that they might perhaps need the fewest guards in the camp. Those making the trench dug a moderate distance from the river, and threw the earth toward the camp; and the Babylonians laughed at the siege, as having provisions for more than twenty years. When the trench was dug, Cyrus, watching for a night on which he knew the Babylonians would keep a feast, drinking and reveling the whole night, on this gathered a multitude and opened the trenches to the river—this is the Euphrates, as Herodotus relates; and the water passed into the trenches in the night, and the channel of the river through the city became passable for men, the water being diverted. Then, sending down into the dry bed of the river attendants and foot and horse, he ordered them to see whether it was passable. Meanwhile, conversing with the leaders of the multitude and rousing them to the work, at last he said, "Come, take up your arms; I will lead; and do you, Gobryas and Gadatas, show the ways, knowing them. And when we are within, lead with all speed to the palace." Upon this they went. And going as quickly as they could, those with Gobryas and Gadatas came to the palace, and found the gates shut, and fell upon the guards as they drank. When a cry and tumult arose, those within, the king having ordered them to see what the matter was, opened the gates, into which the enemy fell and came to the king. And they found him already standing and drawing the scimitar he had. And him those with Gadatas and Gobryas overpowered, and those with him died, some defending themselves, some giving way. And Cyrus sent the squadrons of horse through the streets, having proclaimed that whomever they took outside they should kill, but should proclaim to those in the houses, those who knew how to speak Syriac, to remain within, and that if anyone were caught outside, he would die. Meanwhile Gobryas and Gadatas came, and because they had avenged themselves on the unholy king, first they worshipped the gods, then kissed Cyrus's hands and feet.

Xenophon, relating the affairs of Cyrus, does not give the name of the captured king of the Assyrians; but Josephus, in the tenth book of the Antiquities, records that this was that Baltasar to whom also the hand appeared coming forth from the wall and writing the letters already mentioned, whose interpretation Daniel explained.

No longer did judges lead Israel, but the high priest Eli presided over them; in his time there was a famine, and a certain man of Bethlehem called Abimelech migrated with his wife and two sons into Moab on account of the famine. So he takes Moabite wives for his sons. Within ten years, however, both Abimelech and his sons died, and there were left as widows both Naomi, the wife of Abimelech, and the two wives of his sons, Orpah and Ruth. And Naomi returned to her fatherland, and of her daughters-in-law Orpah, being entreated by her mother-in-law, remained among the Moabites, but Ruth departed with Naomi. And when they had now come to Bethlehem, Boaz, who was a kinsman of Abimelech, received them as guests. And when the woman was addressed by name by the citizens, she said, "Call me not Naomi but Mara"—for "Naomi" means "good fortune," but "Mara" means "grief and bitterness"—"for I went out full and returned empty." And as it was harvest time, Ruth went out, by the counsel of her mother-in-law, to glean in the field of Boaz. And he, seeing the girl and learning who she was, permitted her to reap what she could and to keep it, and commanded the farm-overseer to provide her a meal. And she, having received barley meal from him, kept it for her mother-in-law, and went away late, carrying also the barley she had gathered, and related to her the things she had from Boaz. And again she went out with the maidservants of Boaz. And Naomi resolved to lay Ruth beside him, and sends her daughter-in-law, having instructed her to fall asleep at the feet of the man while he slept on the threshing-floor. And so she did, but Boaz, perceiving about midnight, asked who she was. And learning, he then kept quiet, but at dawn, waking Ruth, he commanded her to go to her mother-in-law, and said, "I myself will ask the one who is a nearer kinsman to you, and if he wishes to take you, you shall go to that man, but if he declines, you shall lawfully dwell with me." So the woman went away and reported everything to Naomi. And Boaz called together before the council of elders Ruth and the kinsman, and said to him, "Do you hold the inheritance of Abimelech our kinsman and of his sons?" And when he had agreed to hold it according to the laws by right of kinship, Boaz said, "Then one must not remember the laws by halves, but in all things do according to them. It remains that you must also marry the wife of Mahlon, the son of Abimelech, that you may raise up seed for the kinsman." But he declined, yielding to him both the inheritance and the woman. So, according to the law, before the council of elders Ruth loosed the sandal of that man and spat in his face. And so Boaz took her, and she bore him Obed—which in Greek is interpreted "serving." And from Obed comes Jesse, and from him David, who reigned over those of Israel and left the rule to his children, which endured for twenty-one generations. And while Eli the high priest, as has already been related, was leading the people, his two sons Hophni and Phinehas were pestilent, transgressing in all things, and not turning back when their father exhorted them. And God, angered on account of their transgressions, through Samuel, who was still a child, made known to Eli what he himself and his children and his house would suffer. Now Samuel was the son of Elkanah, a Levite man, with whom dwelt two wives, of whom the one was named Hannah and the other Peninnah. And to one there were children from Elkanah, but Hannah was without offspring. And when the man came with both wives to Shiloh and had sacrificed, since it was a time of feasting and Peninnah rejoiced with her children, Hannah, because she was alone, wept for herself, and running to the tabernacle of God, prayed to the Lord to grant her offspring, vowing to consecrate the firstborn to God. And as she lingered in her prayers, Eli, sitting before the tabernacle, supposed her to be drunk and sent her away. But she said, "I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, lord, but being in anguish on account of my childlessness I have wasted away." And the priest said to her, "Go, and may God grant you your request." And returning home with her husband, she conceives and bears Samuel—one might call him "asked of God." And when the child had grown, she brings him to Eli, according to the vow, to be reared for God, letting his hair grow and dwelling in the sanctuary and using water for drink. And being now twelve years old, he prophesied. And once, while he slept, God called him by name. And he went to the high priest, supposing that he was perhaps called by him. And this happened three times. And Eli, perceiving that the call was from God, said to Samuel, "If you are called again, say, 'Behold I am here, Lord.'" And when the child had done so, the one who called said to him that there would be a heavy calamity for the Israelites, and that the sons of Eli would die together and the priesthood would pass over to the house of Eleazar. And Samuel was unwilling to disclose the words to the priest, but, constrained by oaths, he reported everything just as he had heard.

and ten days. He gave over the kingdom of Jerusalem to Jehoiakim's uncle Zedekiah, who swore not to favour the Egyptians but to keep the country for him. But he, being young—for he was twenty-one years old when he took over the rule—and contemptuous of what was just and fitting, would not be persuaded by Jeremiah, who exhorted him to leave off his impieties and lawless deeds, nor did he believe him when he told of the calamities that were to come upon him and the people; which Ezekiel too foretold in Babylon and wrote and sent to Jerusalem. Zedekiah disbelieved both prophets, as though perhaps they disagreed. For about the other things they agreed, but concerning Zedekiah himself they seemed to contradict one another. For Ezekiel prophesied that he would not see Babylon, while Jeremiah foretold that he would be led off a prisoner to Babylon. But the events concerning him agreed with both prophets; for, being blinded in Judah and led off a prisoner, he did not behold Babylon.

This Zedekiah, having kept his faith to the Babylonian for eight years, inclined toward the Egyptians. Therefore Nabuchodonosor marched and besieged Jerusalem. When the Egyptians came to the alliance of the Jews, the Babylonian, going to meet them and routing them, pursued them. The false prophets said that the enemy would no longer besiege them; but Jeremiah foretold that they would return and take the city and raze it and burn the temple, and would lead away as spear-won captives the people who would for the present be left, to be enslaved for seventy years, until the Persians and Medes should overthrow the rule of the Babylonians; and that then they would be freed from captivity, and the temple and the city would be rebuilt. So Jeremiah said; but the king and those about him mocked his words. As the prophet was going off to Anathoth his native place, one of the rulers, meeting him and seizing him as a deserter, led him to the rulers; who, after maltreating him, kept him for punishment.

In the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign the Babylonian came a second time against Jerusalem, and for a year and a half mightily besieged the city. With the siege there came a famine, and upon this a plague. Jeremiah, imprisoned, exhorted the multitude to receive the Babylonian; for so they would be saved; but if not, remaining they would perish either by famine or by the sword; "but if anyone goes over to the enemy," he said, "he will escape death." Yet the prophet was reckoned trustworthy by no one, and the leaders even further provoked the king against him. He, to humour them for the time, gave them leave to treat the prophet as they wished. And they cast him into a miry pit. But Zedekiah, learning this, ordered him to be drawn up from there, and secretly summoning him asked what he said as to the present dangers. He counselled him to surrender the city to the Babylonian. Zedekiah said he was afraid of being killed. But the prophet maintained that, doing so, he would experience no hardship. The king released him, but the Babylonian besieged the city with a fierce assault, and took it in the eleventh year of Zedekiah's rule. Zedekiah, with his wives and children and kinsmen and friends, fled from the city. The enemy pursued him and took him, left alone; for his leaders and friends had been scattered. So, taking him alive, with his children and his wives, they brought him to the Babylonian. He reproached him for his ingratitude and faithlessness, and ordered his sons and his friends to be killed before his eyes; then, having blinded his eyes, he led him off a prisoner to Babylon. And then he understood that both prophets had spoken the truth. This was the end of those who had reigned of the seed of David. They were twenty-one in all, five hundred and fourteen years, six months, and sixteen days having passed from the time Saul came to the kingdom.

Nebuzaradan, the chief cook of the Babylonian, being sent, burned both the temple and the palace and razed the city and plundered all that was in the temple. The temple had been burned four hundred and seventy years, six months, and ten days from the time it was built; and one thousand and sixty-two years, six months, and ten days from the departure of the Hebrews out of Egypt; and one thousand nine hundred and fifty-seven years, six months, and ten days from the Flood; and from the production of the first man until then three thousand five hundred and thirteen years, six months, and ten days had passed.

When day came, the holders of the citadel, perceiving that the city was taken and their king dead, surrendered the citadel too. And Cyrus sent into them commanders and guards. Then, calling the magi, since the city was spear-won, he ordered firstfruits to be set apart for the gods, and he distributed houses and public buildings to those who had shared in his deeds; and for himself he intended to prepare a manner of living befitting a king. But that he might not become an object of envy to his friends, he wished to do this with their consent, and conversing with them, by what he said he persuaded them to ask for this. From there he enters the palace, and sets guards about himself, and those who tended his person he gelded and made eunuchs, and chose for bodyguards Persians to the number of ten thousand, and in the city he posted sufficient guards. Having done this, he trained the more honoured of the army not to live without toil and in luxury; and over other matters he set other overseers—receivers of revenues, I mean, and dispensers of expenditures, superintendents of works and guardians of possessions, and overseers of provisions for living, and managers of horses and dogs; but those whom he thought should be guardians of his prosperity, the care of these he assigned to himself. And since to benefit men with money was added to him, he knew that no benefit is more pleasing to men than the giving of food and drink; therefore he ordered much to be set before him like what he himself ate, and enough for very many, and what was set out, except what he and his fellow-diners used, he distributed. And he became the most generous of men. But to surpass in the greatness of gifts, being the richest, is no marvel; but to surpass, while a king, in the care and attention to friends, this is more noteworthy. And a saying of his is remembered, that the works of a good herdsman and of a king are alike; for he said the herdsman should use his beasts after making them well-fed, and the king likewise should use cities and men after making them prosperous.

It is said too that Croesus once said to him that by giving much he would become poor, and was asked by Cyrus, "How much money do you think I would now have, if I had been collecting gold as you bid since I have been in the rule?" And Croesus said some large number. And Cyrus said, "Come now, Croesus, send a man with this Hystaspes. And you, Hystaspes, going round to the friends, tell them that I need money for a certain undertaking, and bid them, each as much as he can, provide me money, and writing it and sealing it, give the letters to Croesus's servant." And writing and sealing all that he charged Hystaspes, he gave it to him to carry to the friends. And he wrote to all to receive Hystaspes as his friend. When he had gone round and Croesus's servant had brought the letters, Hystaspes said, "Cyrus, king, use me now too as a rich man; for I am present with very many gifts because of your letters." And Cyrus said, "Here is one treasury for us, then, Croesus; but survey the others, and reckon how much ready money I have, if I need to use any." It is said that Croesus, reckoning, found many times more than he had said would be in the treasuries for Cyrus if he had been collecting; and upon this Cyrus said, "You see, Croesus, that I too have treasures."

It having seemed good to him to make a procession to the precincts set apart for the gods, calling those who held office among the Persians and the rest, he distributed to them Median robes; and then first the Persians put on the Median robe. When he had distributed the finest robes to the best men, he brought out other Median robes too—for he had prepared very many, sparing neither purple nor dark nor scarlet nor crimson garments—and apportioning to each of the leaders a part of them, he ordered them to adorn their subordinates with these. And one of those present asked him, "And you, Cyrus, when will you adorn yourself?" And he said, "Do I not seem to you now to be adorning myself, while adorning you? For if I can do good to my friends, in whatever robe I am, in that I shall appear fair." Having made the procession and sacrificed to the gods, he dined with his friends, seating those whom he most honoured at his left hand, as being more open to plot against than the right, and the rest at his right. After supper he sent home those who had allied with him as volunteers, except those who wished to remain with him; to these he gave land and houses. And to those who departed, both soldiers and officers, he gave many gifts. Then to the soldiers and officers about him he distributed all the money he had taken from Sardis according to each one's worth. And when they had received what was given, they said of Cyrus, "Surely he himself has much, since he has given so much to each of us too." But others said, "It is not Cyrus's way to amass money, but he delights more in giving than in getting." Perceiving this, Cyrus gathered his friends and all the men of standing and said, "It seems to me a mark of the simplest character for the ruler, having made his power manifest, to contend on the basis of it for nobility. And I, then," he said, "wish to show you all that I have that can be seen, and what cannot be seen, to describe." Saying this, he showed much fair money, and described what was so stored as not to be easily seen. And he said, "Men, you must consider these no more mine than yours; for I gather these that I may have something to give to whoever of you does any fair thing, and that, if any of you needs anything, he may take it by coming to me."

From this the Palestinians make war against the Israelites, and were superior in the battle. And the people ask that the ark be brought to their aid. And when the ark was sent there with the sons of Eli, a battle was joined. And the Hebrews were defeated, and about thirty thousand fell, and the sons of the high priest, and the ark was taken by the enemy. And Eli the high priest was sitting upon a high seat, and learning of the battle and the slaughter of his sons and the capture of the ark, in great anguish he fell from his seat and died, being ninety years old, of which he had led Israel forty years. And the foreigners, having carried off the ark to the city of Azotus, dedicated it to Dagon—for so they called their god. And at dawn, entering the house of Dagon, they found the image lying before the ark upon the ground. And raising it up, they set it upon its former base. But when they found this happen often, and many times having set the idol upright, found it as often lying in the posture of one worshiping the ark, they were astounded and at a loss. Then a destruction fell upon the city and country of the Azotians—a disease among the people about the seat, which Josephus calls dysentery, and many died of it; and mice, springing up from the ground, ravaged the whole country. And at last the Azotians understood that the ark was the cause of their sufferings, and they send it to Ascalon; and those too suffered the like. And so the ark passed through five cities of the Palestinians, and to all became a cause of affliction. So the rulers of the five afflicted cities came together—of Gath and Ekron and Ascalon and Gaza and Azotus—and some counseled one thing about the ark, others another. And at last it seemed good to all to make five golden seats and as many golden mice and to place them upon the ark, and to make a new wagon and yoke to the wagon cows that had borne their first calves, but to keep back their calves, and to set the ark upon the wagon, and, having led the cows to a place where three roads met, to leave them, that it might rest with them to go whichever way they should set out: if they went straight toward the Israelites, they would believe that on account of the ark the evils were being brought upon them, and would not hinder their journey to those people; but if they went somewhere else, they would turn the cows and the wagon and what was on it back again. Having, then, accomplished what seemed good, they let the cows go, themselves following at a distance, that they might see the outcome. And they went straight toward the Hebrews and did not stop before they came to a great plain in Bethshemesh. So when the men of that village saw the ark, they hastened to it, and taking it down from the wagon, they sacrificed the cows and offered them as whole burnt offerings with the wood of which the wagon had been made. And seeing this, the Palestinians returned home. But those who touched the ark, not being priests, God in anger put to death. And the rest made known to the community of the Hebrews the things concerning the ark; and they, taking it, carry it away to Kiriath-jearim and deposit it in the house of Aminadab, who was of the tribe of Levi. And it remained there twenty years, but among the foreigners four months. And Samuel the prophet, having now gained a great name and come to much glory, gathering the people, spoke to them about freedom and persuaded them to lay claim to it. Learning this, the Palestinians come unexpectedly upon the Hebrews and terrified them, so that they ran to Samuel, saying that their safety was despaired of unless he himself asked for them the aid from God. And he exhorted them to take courage, and assured them that God would help them, and having sacrificed a lamb, he prayed to God. And before the sacred flame had consumed the sacrifice, the enemy attacked the Hebrews, supposing they would more easily prevail over them as unarmed. But when the earth was shaken by God with an earthquake, and thunders broke forth and lightnings flashed, the enemy fell into cowardice and turned to flight. And Samuel and the multitude pursued after them and destroyed many, and no longer after this blow did they make war against the Israelites, but Samuel even recovered for the Hebrews the country that they had taken. And he judged the people and ruled over them.

When he had set the affairs in Babylon in good order, he made ready to go off to Persia. And as, journeying, he came to Media, Cyrus turned to Cyaxares, and greeting him said that a house had been chosen for him in Babylon, and gave him many fair gifts. And Cyaxares sent to him his daughter, bringing a golden crown and bracelets and a necklace and a most beautiful Median robe. And the girl crowned Cyrus, and Cyaxares said, "I give you, Cyrus, this very woman to wife, being my daughter, and I give with her as dowry all Media; for I have no legitimate male child." And Cyrus said, "The lineage, Cyaxares, I commend, and the girl and the gifts, but I wish to marry her with the consent of my father and mother." And saying this he journeyed to Persia. Coming to the borders of the Persians, he left the army there, and himself with his friends entered the city, bringing victims enough for all the Persians to sacrifice and feast. He brought gifts for his father and mother such as was fitting, and for his friends such as befitted magistrates and elders; and he gave to all Persians, and indeed to Persian women too. And having spent some time with his parents, he departed. And coming to Media, with his father's consent he married the daughter of Cyaxares; and having married, at once taking her with him he set out.

When he came to Babylon, he sent satraps to the subdued nations—to Arabia, that is, and Cappadocia, to Greater Phrygia, to Lycia and Ionia, to Caria, to Phrygia by the Hellespont and Aeolis. To the Cilicians and Cyprians and Paphlagonians he did not send satraps, because they seemed to march with him willingly; yet these too paid tribute. And that, his rule being great, reports might be conveyed to him quickly even from afar, he considered how long a road a horse driven hard could accomplish, and he made horse-stations so far apart from one another, and set horses in them and those who cared for them, and posted at each a suitable man to receive the dispatches conveyed and to deliver them, and to take the worn-out horses and send others fresh.

When a year had now passed he made a campaign, in which he is said to have subdued all the nations that dwell from where one enters Syria as far as the Red Sea. After this he marches against Egypt and subdues it too; so that from there his rule was bounded on the east by the Red Sea, on the north by the Euxine Sea, on the west by Cyprus and Egypt, and Ethiopia on the south. And he himself, making his abode in the midst of these, passed seven months in Babylon, the winter season, for this country is warm, three months about spring in Susa, and in Ecbatana two months he spent, the height of summer.

Having so lived, and being now very old, Cyrus comes to Persia for the seventh time, his parents having long since died. And as he slept in the palace, there seemed to him in a dream one greater than a man to come to him, saying, "Make ready, Cyrus; for now the gods summon you." From this he guessed that the end of his life was at hand, and on the third day he called his sons, for they accompanied him, and his friends and the rulers of the Persians, and said, "To me the end of life is now at hand, and I must make clear concerning the kingdom, to whom it shall belong after me, that it may not, becoming disputed, cause you trouble. You, then, Cambyses, being the elder, hold the kingdom, the gods granting and I; and to you, Tanaoxares, I give to be satrap of the Medes and Armenians and Cadusians." Having charged his sons with these things and exhorted them much, and having addressed those present and given his right hand to all, he covered himself and so departed. And when he was gone, at once his sons fell into faction, and cities and nations revolted, and all turned to the worse.

These things, then, are related by Xenophon concerning Cyrus; but Herodotus of Halicarnassus says other things about Cyrus's upbringing and end and the rest of his life, which it would be long to relate. And for me, who have made an epitome of history, it is not fitting to set down a work of many lines; but I myself have written the more probable things, and whoever wishes to know what Herodotus too wrote about him, taking up his book will find these things in the first book, to which he gave the title of the first of the Muses, Clio.

And being now grown old, he distributed to his sons the leadership of the people and the office of judging. The name of the elder was Joel, and of the younger Abiah. But they did not walk in the ways of their father, but, turning aside, betrayed justice for gifts and gave their judgments for bribes. And the people, on account of this, gathering to Samuel, said, "Since you are not able to preside over us by reason of age, make us a king, who shall both lead the nation and make war against the enemy." And while Samuel grieved at this, God said to him, "It is not you the people have rejected, but me. Hearken, then, to them, and whomever I shall point out to you, anoint him as king." And gathering the Hebrews, Samuel set forth that he would appoint them a king, but foretold that they would repent and would ask of God a deliverance from kings. But they persisted, seeking a king, and asked him not to be concerned about what was to come. And the prophet said, "Go now, and when I learn whom God gives you as king, I will send for you." Now there was a certain Benjamite, Kish by name, who, having lost his donkeys, sent his son, who was tall and fair and called Saul, in search of the donkeys, with one of his servants. And he, having gone about and sought and not found them, came to Armathaim, to Samuel, to inquire about the donkeys. So God reveals to Samuel that this is he whom He wishes to reign over the people of the Hebrews. So when Saul asked about the donkeys, Samuel said that they had been recovered, and having lodged Saul, he sent him forth at dawn, and going outside the city with him and taking the young man aside alone, he pours oil upon his head. And kissing him, he said, "The Lord has anointed you ruler over his people Israel, and let this be the sign of the anointing: that two men shall meet you about the tomb of Rachel, bringing you the good news of the finding of the donkeys." And he told him other signs of the truth, and that he would prophesy when he came to Gabatha among the prophets there, and he commanded him to come to Gilgal when he should be summoned by him. And then he gathered the people and bade the tribes cast lots, that it might be shown from which the one who was to reign would be. So the lot fell upon Benjamin, then upon the family of Mattari. And when the family had been allotted man by man, the lot fell upon Saul. And as, when sought, he was not found, Samuel is informed by God where he was hidden, and having him brought, set him in the midst. And he was a head taller than all and surpassing all in the stature of his body. And the prophet said to the multitude, "This man the Lord has anointed for you as king, to whom there is none like among you all." And the people shouted approval and said, "Long live the king." So, when Saul had thus become king, many attended him as king and honored him as was fitting, but many despised and mocked him. And after a month Nahash the king of the Ammonites makes war against Jabesh-gilead, saying that he would not otherwise spare the men unless they gave him the right eye of each to put out. And they asked for a respite of seven days; and receiving it, they send messengers to Gabaa. And when those there heard the words of the Ammonite, they wept; but Saul was greatly angered, and taking two oxen, he cut them in pieces and sent them into all the territory of Israel, threatening to do likewise to those who would not march out with him against the Ammonites. And when the people had run together, he numbered them and found seven hundred thousand. And the spirit of the Lord leaped upon Saul, and he prophesied, saying that on the morrow there would be deliverance for the men of Jabesh. And rising, he himself and the people marched all night, and about the morning watch he came upon the Ammonites, dividing the army into three parts. And surrounding them, he killed many, and the king Nahash himself, and turned the survivors to flight; and invading their country and taking very much spoil, he returned in splendor. So no longer was he held in low esteem by any, but he was renowned for his courage and honored even by those who had formerly mocked him. And Samuel, gathering the people again, proclaims Saul king a second time, anointing him again with the oil. So the commonwealth of the Hebrews passed from an aristocracy into a kingship; for in the time of Moses and Joshua they were governed as an aristocracy, then for eighteen years they continued without a ruler, and afterward they were ruled by those called judges, entrusting to the best man the judging and management of all affairs.

And when Samuel adjured the people to say if he had done any wrong to them, all cried out that he had presided over the nation justly and well. And he answered them, "Know that you have greatly sinned in asking a king for yourselves, and by this you have provoked God to anger. And this shall be a sign to you, that in the height of summer there shall come a storm." And according to the word of the prophet there were thunders and lightnings, and hail came down, so that fear fell upon the people and they entreated Samuel to come and reconcile God to them, since they had sinned. And while the Palestinians were subduing the Hebrews and taking away their arms and forbidding them to use iron, Saul, going down to Gilgal, urged the people to rise up against the Palestinians for their freedom. But they were cautious on account of the multitude of the enemy. And the king called Samuel to him. And he promised to come after six days, and to sacrifice on the seventh, that so they might engage the foreigners. But Saul, seeing the people slipping away and abandoning him, sacrificed. And hearing that Samuel was now approaching, he went out to meet him. But he said, "What is this you have done, transgressing my command? Know, then, that your kingdom shall not stand, but the Lord shall seek a man after his own heart." And Samuel withdrew, but Saul and Jonathan his son came to Gabaa with six hundred soldiers. And the foreigners, divided into three parts, plundered the country of the Israelites. And Saul and Jonathan and Ahiah the high priest, seeing from a height what was being done, and not strong enough to defend on account of the fewness of their men, were grieved. But Jonathan, saying nothing to his father, went down from the hill with only his armor-bearer and said, "Let us attack the camp of the foreigners, and if they say to us, 'Stand off,' we will not go up to them, but if they say, 'Come up to us,' we must reckon the word a token of victory for us." And they set out for the camp of the enemy. And the foreigners said to them, "Come up to us, and we will make known to you a matter." This put courage into Jonathan; and withdrawing from there, he crept up from another side with his attendant and came upon the enemy while they slept. And they kill about twenty, and into the rest they put cowardice; who, thrown into confusion and fleeing, were destroyed by one another. And Saul, seeing the camp of the enemy thrown into confusion, and perceiving that his son was absent together with his armor-bearer, himself also attacks the disordered enemy; and those who before, out of fear, had hidden, taking courage, joined the king. And pursuing the enemy he kept killing them. So he laid a curse upon his own men, that if any one, ceasing from the slaughter of the enemy, should eat before night stopped them, he should die. And in the pursuit they came to a certain wood, in which there was a beehive, and Jonathan, taking a honeycomb, ate it; for he had not heard the curse of his father. And Saul, wishing to attack the camp of the enemy, asked God through the high priest whether He would grant victory. And when God did not reveal it, he sought the cause, and said, "I swear by God himself that I will kill the one who has sinned, even if it be Jonathan my son." And when they cast lots, the lot fell upon Jonathan. And he, being examined about the sin, said he was conscious of nothing in himself except that "yesterday, not knowing the curse, I tasted a honeycomb in the pursuit." And hearing this, his father swore that he would kill him. But the people swore in turn that they would not allow the author of the victory to die, and snatching him away, they propitiated God with prayers. And Saul, having destroyed about sixty thousand of the Palestinians, returned. And he subdues the Ammonites and Moabites and Palestinians and Idumaeans and Amalekites, and the king of Suba, and delivered Israel from the hand of the foreigners.

Now Saul had three sons, Jonathan and Ishvi and Malchishua, and two daughters, Merob and Michal; and he had as commander-in-chief Abner, the son of Ner, his kinsman. And Samuel said to Saul that God commanded him to strike Amalek, and, when he had prevailed, to spare nothing—not women, not infants, not beasts of burden, not cattle—but to blot out his name from the earth. And Saul, engaging Amalek, conquers mightily and kills all, and takes captive also the king of the country, named Agag, and did not kill him, admiring him for his beauty and stature; and the choicest of the herds and flocks and the rest he kept for himself, forgetting the divine command. And Samuel, being informed by God, who said that He repented of having made Saul king, met the king. And he said that he gave thanks to God for granting him power over the enemy, and that he had done all that was commanded. And the prophet said, "I hear the bleating of beasts of burden and of other cattle. Whence are these?" And Saul said that the people had kept them for sacrifice to God, but that all the Amalekites had been destroyed except their king. To this Samuel said, "Since you have transgressed what was commanded you by God, know that you shall be deprived of the kingdom." And he confessed that he had sinned, and entreated the prophet to offer a propitiatory sacrifice. And as he withdrew, Saul lays hold of his cloak and tears it, forcing him to stay. And the prophet said, "So shall your kingdom be torn and given to a man righteous and good." And when the king still entreated, he is persuaded, and asks that Agag be brought, and when that man had been killed, at his command, he at once withdraws to Armathaim. And God commands him to go to Jesse and to anoint with oil for king one of his sons, whomever He should point out to him. And going to Bethlehem and sacrificing, he called Jesse and his sons. And seeing the firstborn, tall and fair, he supposed that God favored him. But God said, "Look not upon his appearance, nor upon the greatness of his body; for man looks upon the face, but God upon the heart." And when the other sons of Jesse had passed by, God favored none of them. And Samuel said, "The Lord has not chosen among these, and if there is yet one remaining, let him come." And Jesse said, "There is still left the youngest, tending the flock." So the prophet commanded that he be called. And when David came, being called—a ruddy youth with fair eyes and otherwise fair—God reveals to Samuel that this was the one to be anointed. And he, taking the horn of oil, anointed him in the midst of his brothers. And he went away to Armathaim. And a divine spirit leaped upon David, but departed from Saul, and an evil spirit pursued him, choking and tormenting the man. So it seemed good that there should stand by the king one who knew how to play the harp, that when the demon fell upon him and troubled him, he might play upon the harp and lull the disturbance. So he sends for David as such a one; and the young man was greatly loved by the king, and became his armor-bearer. And when the evil spirit came upon the king, David sang over him, and it departed, and Saul came back to himself. And the foreigners made war against the Israelites, and those of Israel set themselves against them. And in the space between the two armies a certain man of the foreigners stood—Goliath was his name—a powerful man towering above all, for his height was six cubits and a span, and his breastplate weighed five thousand shekels, and his spear was like a weaver's beam, and the head of the spear six hundred shekels; this man, standing in the midst, cried out to the sons of Israel, "Let one of you come down and stand against me; and if he strikes me, we will serve you, but if I lay him low, you shall be servants to us." And this he did for forty days. Now when Saul had sent David back to Jesse, his father sent him to the camp to bring provisions to his brothers who were in the army; for three of the elder ones were following Saul. And when David came to his brothers, the foreigner Goliath again, as was his custom, challenged to single combat and reproached the Hebrews because none dared to engage him. And hearing these words, David was indignant and said to those present, "I will fight him in single combat." This was reported to the king, and to David, standing before him, he said, "You will not be able to go in battle against this uncircumcised man, for you are still a boy." And David said he took courage in God, who had strengthened him against the bear and against the lion when they came upon the flock and snatched the young, whom, he said, he pursued and recovered what had been snatched, and struck the beasts and killed them. In Him, he said, he took courage, that He would grant him to strike down the foreigner too and to take away the reproach from the sons of Israel. So he said this, and the king permitted him to go, and put his own arms upon him. But they were a burden to him, and he took them off, and taking up his staff and putting five stones in his pouch and carrying the sling in his hand, he set out against the foreigner. And he laughed at him and asked whether he came against a dog with a staff and stones. And David answered that he reckoned him worse than a dog. And he, angered, and boasting that he would give his flesh to the birds and the beasts, rushed upon him. But David, being quick and putting a stone in the sling, struck the enemy upon the forehead. And the blow was mighty, and the foreigner fell upon his face. And David, running and drawing his sword, cuts off the head of Goliath and strips off his arms. This put cowardice into the foreigners, and they turned to flight. And Saul leads his own army against them as they fled; and a great multitude of the Palestinians is killed, and more are wounded, and their camp is plundered. And David brings the head of Goliath to Saul, but dedicates the sword to God.

And as the army returned, the women met them, and dancing they sang that Saul had slain thousands, while the maidens answered in song that David had destroyed ten thousands. This stirred Saul to envy, and he said, "What is lacking to him but the kingdom?" And he looked askance at David. And when an evil spirit fell upon Saul, and David sang over him as was his custom, Saul threw his spear at him; and he did this twice. But David turned aside, for the Lord was with him. And the king, fearing him, made him a commander of a thousand, that going against the enemy he might be endangered. But he, with God as ally, prospered, and the people loved him, and the king's daughter Michal loved David. So her love was reported to the king, and he used the love as a handle for a plot. For he said that he would give him his daughter if he would bring him a hundred foreskins, supposing that he would fall fighting the foreigners. Learning this, David went with his men, and struck among the foreigners and brought Saul a hundred foreskins. (But Josephus says that David brought not a hundred foreskins, but six hundred heads of foreigners.) And he joins to him his daughter Michal. But seeing David both allied with God and beloved by the multitude, he feared still more, and plotted against him, and tried to kill him. So he commands his son Jonathan and his most trusted servants to do away with him. But Jonathan, loving David, reveals to him the command, and exhorts him to be on his guard, and promises to speak about him to his father and to disclose everything to him. And indeed he spoke and turned him to gentleness; for, changing his mind, Saul swore that he would do David no wrong. And Jonathan, having revealed this to David, brings him to the king, and he remained with him as before. And when the Palestinians stirred again and came against the Hebrews, David is sent by Saul to set himself against them, and returns with victory. But with the man's successes the envy against him grew in Saul. And when the evil spirit came upon him again and choked him, David was present, striking the harp and singing over him. And Saul, holding his spear, hurled it at David; but he, foreseeing it, turned aside and withdrew. And Saul sent guards by night to David's house, that he might kill him by day. But Michal his wife, learning this, let her husband down through a window, and he fled. And at dawn, when Saul sent for David, Michal, having prepared the bed as though someone lay in it, and having placed under the coverings the liver of a freshly slaughtered goat, so that by its movement the covering, being shaken, might give the appearance that someone lay upon the bed, brings in those who had been sent and says that the man is sick. And they reported it to Saul, and he commanded that he be brought to him on the bed. But those sent, going and lifting the covering of the bed, perceived the trick and reported it to the king. So David, having thus escaped death, came to Samuel at Armathaim and passed his time with him at Nabioth in Rama. So Saul sends there too those who should bring David. But they, going and finding an assembly of prophets, themselves also prophesied. Learning this, the king sends others, and when these too were likewise affected, he sent still others, and when the third group too had been seized by the spirit, he himself set out in anger, and drawing near, he himself also began to prophesy. At which time those present uttered the saying, "Is Saul too among the prophets?" And coming to where Samuel was, becoming as it were out of his mind and stripping off his clothing, he lay naked through a whole day and night.

And David fled from there and made known to Jonathan his father's design against him; but he disbelieved it. And David asked him to make trial of his father's intent and to disclose it to him as he waited outside the city. So Jonathan, bringing words to his father about David, and having learned that his father's purpose thirsted for the man's death, reports everything to him secretly in person, and urges him to save himself. And he adjured David to remember him, and, even should he chance to die, to show some kindness to his offspring. Saying this, Jonathan returned, and David, fleeing to Nob, comes to Abimelech the high priest. And he inquired how he came alone. And David said that something secret had been commanded him by the king, "and that no one might know of it, I am alone; and here he ordered me to meet with my servants." Saying this, he asked for loaves. And the high priest said he had none but the holy ones, and, "If you have kept yourselves from a woman, take these and eat." And he asked that a sword too be given him. But the high priest answered that he had no other weapon except the sword of Goliath, which David himself had dedicated to God. And taking these, David went away to Gath, to Achish the king of the foreigners. And being recognized for who he was and taking fright, he feigned madness and behaved and acted as one out of his mind. And so, escaping safe from the foreigners, he comes to the tribe of Judah, and hides in the cave of Adullam. There his brothers and his kindred came to him; then others too flowed together there, so that all became about four hundred. And he goes from there to the Moabites, and begs the king of Moab to let his parents dwell with him until matters concerning him should come to some end. And he is persuaded and receives Jesse and his household. And David went into the land of Judah, since Gad the prophet commanded this. But Saul, learning that a multitude had gathered to David, called together his friends and reproached them as taking his part. And a certain servant of Saul, a Syrian by race, Doeg by name, who had been present when the high priest gave the loaves to David and the sword of Goliath, standing then beside him, reported to the king that he had seen David come to the high priest and inquire of God through him and receive provisions and the sword. And the king, summoning the high priest, charged him with conspiracy with David. And he commanded the armed men standing by him to kill the high priest and all his kindred; but when they shrank from laying hands on those consecrated to God, he orders Doeg to do the killing. And he killed them all, three hundred and five in number, and struck their city, killing all of full age, sparing neither women nor infants nor any other age. But one son of the high priest alone escaped death, called Abiathar, who, fleeing to David, reported what had happened. And when the foreigners had invaded Keilah and were plundering the country, David, at God's command, came upon them with the four hundred, and struck them and brought back all the spoil. But Saul sends a multitude of soldiers to do away with him there. And he went from Keilah into the wilderness. And Saul did not cease seeking to put him to death. And Jonathan came to David and encouraged him and exhorted him to have good hopes. And when David had taken refuge upon the rock in the wilderness of Maon, and Saul came upon him with a great multitude, David was in danger of being taken, had not a messenger come to Saul that the foreigners had attacked the country; for, leaving David, he set out against the enemy. Then it was reported to him that David was encamped in the wilderness of Gaddi, and taking three thousand he set out. And as he went he was troubled by his bowels. And there was a certain cave there, in which David and those with him were hidden farther within; into this Saul entered to relieve himself. And David was urged by those with him to kill Saul. But he was not persuaded; rather, he secretly cut off the skirt of his cloak and took it. And when the king had gone out, David came forward and called out after Saul. And the king turned at the voice. And David did obeisance and said, "Do not believe slanders. Behold, the Lord delivered you into my hands; for when in the cave I cut off the skirt of your cloak, it was easy for me to kill you also." And at the same time he showed him the piece, and cried out, "May the Lord judge between me and you." And Saul, pierced to the heart at this, lifted up his voice and, weeping, said to David, "You are righteous; for I have been the cause of evils to you, but you have repaid me with good. Whence I am persuaded that God is keeping you to be king of Israel. Give me, then, pledges that you will not destroy my house, but will preserve my line." And David swore to Saul, and they departed from one another.

At that time too Samuel the prophet died, a righteous and good man, who had ruled Israel after Eli, alone for twelve years, but together with Saul for eighteen. And David went into the wilderness of Maon. And he sent to Nabal the Carmelite, a rich man who was shearing his flocks, those who should greet him and ask him to give to those with him and to himself, as he might choose, since they had kept his flocks and his shepherds untouched. But Nabal, being harsh and insolent, answered David's men inhumanly and shamelessly, saying, "Who is David, and who is the son of Jesse?" and calling him a runaway. At this David is angered, and swore to destroy all that belonged to Nabal, and set out against him with four hundred armed men. But Nabal's wife, being sensible and fair, having learned both how David had greeted her husband and how he had kept their property unharmed, and what blasphemous things Nabal had answered David, without communicating anything to her own husband, taking on donkeys gifts of every kind and many, set out to David. And meeting him, she did obeisance, and begged him not to bear a grudge against her husband; for his disposition was according to his name—for Nabal means "folly"—but to lay aside his anger and to receive what was offered. And he both praised the woman and, granting pardon, returned. And the woman, returning to Nabal, made known to him David's coming. And he, seized by fear and grief, surviving not more than ten days, broke off his life. And learning this, David sent to Abigail, wooing her for himself. And she said she was not worthy to dwell with such a man; nevertheless she went, and David took her as his wife. But Saul still plotted against him, and with three thousand chosen men encamps by the hill of Hachilah, where David was passing his time with the six hundred men who were with him. And by night David himself and Amesa went into the camp of Saul, and they entered where Saul was sleeping. And when Amesa set out to kill him, David did not allow it, but, taking the king's spear and the vessel of water, they went out without anyone perceiving, and this though Abner, the commander of his army, and many others lay around the king. And going up to the top of the mountain, David called out to Abner, "Why is it that you do not guard the king? For behold, some men came in to kill him, and you have not known it. Look, then, for the spear and the flask of water, and you will know what a danger has passed you by." And Saul, recognizing David's voice, and how he had spared him again when able to kill him, said that he had sinned and acted foolishly, and exhorted him to take courage and to return to his house. And he said, "May the Lord render to each according to his righteousness and his faith." And David went away with the six hundred who were with him to Achish the king of Gath, and passed four months there. And when the Palestinians wished to make war against Israel, Achish said to David, "Will you go out with me to the war, you and those with you?" And he readily promised to be his ally. But when the foreigners had now advanced into the country of the Israelites, Saul was thrown into confusion and inquired of God whether he should fight. And when He did not answer, he sought out a woman with a familiar spirit and went to her in disguise, that it might not be recognized who he was, and asked that the soul of Samuel be brought up for him. And when, by certain incantations, Saul supposed it had been brought up, he said, "I am greatly distressed, because the foreigners have gathered against me and the Lord has departed from me." And the phantom of Samuel answered, "The Lord has done to you what he foretold through me, and he takes away your kingdom and gives it to David, and subjects the people to the enemy; and you and your sons shall fall tomorrow." And Saul, greatly grieved at hearing this, departed. And the foreigners encamped, and David and the six hundred with him were behind. But it did not please the satraps that David should march with them, saying, "Lest he do us some harm by joining his own people in the battle," and they asked that he be sent back. And Achish, persuaded by the satraps, commanded David to depart. And he went away with those who were with him, and found Ziklag, which Achish had given him for a dwelling, burned with fire, and his two wives and all who were there taken captive by the Amalekites. And David and those with him lamented over this, and he asked God through the high priest Abiathar whether he should pursue after them. And when God permitted it, he pursued with the four hundred, leaving the two hundred to guard the baggage. And finding them scattered, eating and drinking, and falling upon them suddenly, he killed them all except four hundred who had fled on swift camels, and recovered all the spoil. But the four hundred with David, returning, were unwilling that the two hundred too should share with them, and demanded to be content with the recovery of their own wives. But David judged this opinion unjust, and declared that the gain should be divided equally among all. And from that time this became a law also, commanding that those who guarded the baggage should share equally in the spoils with those who fought. And when a battle broke out between the Israelites and the Palestinians, very many of the Hebrews are killed, and the three sons of Saul fell, and Saul himself was wounded in the lower abdomen. And knowing that he had been struck mortally and would not live, he told his armor-bearer to run him through, that he might not be taken alive by the enemy. And when he would not do what was commanded, Saul himself fell upon his sword and died. And his armor-bearer, when he saw the king fallen, killed himself also. And on the next day, while the foreigners were stripping the fallen of the Israelites, they came upon the bodies of Saul and his sons on the mountains of Gilboa, and cutting off their heads, they sent them into their own country, making a show of them everywhere and announcing the good news, and they dedicated their armor to their own gods, but crucified the bodies by the wall of Methsam, which was afterward called Scythopolis. But when the inhabitants of the city of Jabesh in Gilead learned what had befallen Saul, the strongest of them went out, and pressing their march through the whole night, they took down the bodies of Saul and Jonathan, and carrying them to Jabesh, they burned them, and gathering the bones, they buried them. And Saul reigned eighteen years while Samuel was still living, and after his death twenty-two.
